parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English arblast, from late Old English arblast, from Old French arbaleste (modern French arbalète), from Late Latin arcuballista, from Latin arcus (“bow”).

parole.significato: A shady sitting place or pergola usually in a park or garden, surrounded by climbing shrubs, vines or other vegetation.
parole.testo: From Middle English arbour, erbour, from Old French erbier (“field, meadow, kitchen garden”), from erbe (“grass, herb”), from Latin herba (“grass, herb”) (English herb). (Compare Late Latin herbārium, although erbier is possibly an independent formation.) The spelling was influenced by Latin arbor (

parole.significato: To move following a curved path.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English ark, from Old French arc, from Latin arcus (“a bow, arc, arch”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erkʷos (“bow, arrow”). Doublet of arch, arco, and arrow.

parole.significato: An inverted U shape.
parole.testo: From Middle English arch, arche, from Old French arche (“an arch”), a feminine form of arc, from Latin arcus (“a bow, arc, arch”). Doublet of arc and arco. Displaced native Old English bīeġels and Old English hwealf.

parole.significato: A powerful angel that leads many other angels, but is still loyal to a deity, and often seen as belonging to a particul…
parole.testo: From Middle English archangel, from Old French archangele, from Latin archangelus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχάγγελος (arkhángelos) from Ancient Greek prefix ἀρχι- (arkhi-) + ἄγγελος (ángelos, “messenger”). By surface analysis, arch- + angel.

parole.significato: One who shoots an arrow from a bow or a bolt from a crossbow.
parole.testo: from Middle English archer, archere, from Old French archier, from Vulgar Latin *arcārius, alteration of arcuārius, from Latin arcus (“bow”). Displaced native Old English sċytta.

parole.significato: The practice or sport of shooting arrows with a bow.
parole.testo: From Middle English archerie, from Old French archerie, from archier (“archer”). Equivalent to archer + -ery.

parole.significato: An original model of which all other similar concepts, objects, or persons are merely copied, derivative, emulated, or…
parole.testo: From Old French architipe (modern French archétype), from Latin archetypum (“original”), from Ancient Greek ἀρχέτυπον (arkhétupon, “model, pattern”), the neuter form of ἀρχέτυπος (arkhétupos, “first-moulded”), from ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “beginning, origin”) (from ἄρχω (árkhō, “to begin; to lead, rule”), from

parole.significato: To impute (something) as a fault to or upon someone.
parole.testo: From Old French àreter, from à + reter, from Latin reputāre (“to count”).

parole.significato: The metal silver.
parole.testo: From Middle English argent, from Old French argent m (“silver”), from Latin argentum n (“white money, silver”).

parole.significato: Of, from, or pertaining to Argentina or its people.
parole.testo: From Old French argentin (“silvery”), from Latin argentum (“silver”).

parole.significato: Containing or resembling silver.
parole.testo: From Middle English argentyne, borrowed from Old French argentin (“silvery”), from Latin argentum (“silver”), equivalent to argent + -ine.

parole.significato: To show grounds for concluding (that); to indicate, imply.
parole.testo: From Middle English arguen, from Old French arguer, from Latin arguere (“to declare, show, prove, make clear, reprove, accuse”), q.v. for more. Displaced native Old English flītan and reċċan.

parole.significato: To put forward as an argument; to argue.
parole.testo: The obsolete senses are derived from Middle English argumenten (“to argue, discuss; to consider, reflect”), from Old French argumenter (“to argue”), from Latin argūmentārī (“to adduce arguments or proof, prove, reason; to adduce (something) as argument or proof; to conclude”), from argūmentum (“argu

parole.significato: The mathematics of numbers (integers, rational numbers, real numbers, or complex numbers) under the operations of addit…
parole.testo: From Middle English arsmetike, from Old French arismetique, from Latin arithmētica, from Ancient Greek ἀριθμητική (τέχνη) (arithmētikḗ (tékhnē), “(art of) counting”), feminine of ἀριθμητικός (arithmētikós, “arithmetical”), from ἀριθμός (arithmós, “number, counting”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ri-d

parole.significato: A weapon.
parole.testo: Back-formation from arms (plural), from Middle English armes, from Old French armes, from Latin arma (“weapons”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂er-mo-, a suffixed form of *h₂er- (“to fit together”), hence ultimately cognate with etymology 1.

parole.significato: A manufacturer of weapons, especially of guns.
parole.testo: From Middle English armurer, from Old French armurier. By surface analysis, armor + -er.

parole.significato: Weaponry, weapons.
parole.testo: From Middle English armes, from Old French armes, from Latin arma (“weapons”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂er-mo-, a suffixed form of *h₂er- (“to fit together”), hence ultimately cognate with etymology 2.

parole.significato: spider
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English arayne, arane, from Old French araigne, aragne, from Latin arānea, related to or derived from Ancient Greek ἀράχνη (arákhnē). Doublet of Arachne.

parole.significato: To set up; to organize; to put into an orderly sequence or arrangement.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English arengen, arrangen (“to draw up a battle line”), borrowed from Old French arengier, arangier (“to put in a line, put in a row”), derived from reng, rang, ranc (“line, row, rank”), from Frankish *hring (“ring”), from Proto-Germanic *hringaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-Eur

parole.significato: Towards the rear, backwards.
parole.testo: From Middle English arere, from Old French arere, from Vulgar Latin *ad retro (literally “to the rear”).

parole.significato: The condition of being in arrears.
parole.testo: From Middle English arrerage, from Old French arierage (“detriment, legal prejudice”).

parole.significato: A check; a stop; an act or instance of arresting something.
parole.testo: From Middle English arest (noun) and aresten (verb), from Old French areste (noun) and arester (“to stay, stop”, verb), from Vulgar Latin *arrestō, from Latin ad- (“to”) + restō (“to stop, remain behind, stay back”), from re- (“back”) + stō (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand”)

parole.significato: A sharp edge or ridge formed by the intersection of two surfaces
parole.testo: From Old French areste, from Latin arista (“beard (of grain), fishbone”). Doublet of arista.

parole.significato: To reach; to get to a certain place.
parole.testo: From Middle English arriven, ariven, from Old French ariver, from Early Medieval Latin adrīpāre (“to land, come ashore”), derived from Latin rīpa (“shore, river-bank”). parole.significato: Having excessive pride in oneself, often with contempt or disrespect for others.
parole.testo: From Middle English arrogaunt, from Old French arrogant, from Latin arrogāns, present active participle of arrogō.

parole.significato: A saddlebow.
parole.testo: From Middle English arsoun, from Old French arçon, from Vulgar Latin *arciō (“saddlebow”), from Latin arcus (“bow”); compare Italian arcione, Portuguese arção, and Spanish arzón.

parole.significato: The conscious production or arrangement of sounds, colours, forms, movements, or other elements in a manner that affect…
parole.testo: From Middle English art, from Old French art, from Latin artem, accusative of ars (“art”). Partly displaced native Old English cræft, whence Modern English craft. See also archaic English list (“art, craft, cunning, skill”).

parole.significato: sinew, ligament, tendon, artery
parole.testo: Late Middle English arterie, borrowing from Old French artaire and Latin artēria (“a windpipe; an artery”), from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ρτηρῐ́ᾱ (ărtērĭ́ā, “windpipe; artery”).

parole.significato: Any of the muscular- and elastic-walled blood vessels forming part of the circulation system by which blood is conveyed…
parole.testo: Late Middle English arterie, borrowing from Old French artaire and Latin artēria (“a windpipe; an artery”), from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ρτηρῐ́ᾱ (ărtērĭ́ā, “windpipe; artery”).

parole.significato: To bind by articles of apprenticeship.
parole.testo: From Middle English article, from Old French article, from Latin articulus (“a joint, limb, member, part, division, the article in grammar, a point of time”), from Latin artus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂értus (“that which is fit together; juncture, ordering”), from the root *h₂er- (“to join, fit (

parole.significato: A joint or the collection of joints at which something is articulated, or hinged, for bending.
parole.testo: From Middle English articulacioun, from Old French articulacion, from Medieval Latin articulatio. Equivalent to articulate + -ion.

parole.significato: Man-made; made by humans; of artifice.
parole.testo: From Middle English artificial (“man-made”) via Old French (modern French artificiel), from Latin artificiālis from artificium (“skill”), from artifex, from ars (“skill”), and -fex, from facere (“to make”). Displaced native Old English cræftlīċ.

parole.significato: Large projectile weapons, in modern usage usually large guns, but also rocket artillery.
parole.testo: From Middle English artillerie, from Old French artillerie (“collection of military engines, crossbows, lances etc.”), from artillier (“to equip, provide with contraptions”), alteration of atiller (“to arrange, adjust, put on clothes or, especially, pieces of armour”) (influenced by art), itself fro

parole.significato: To move upward, to fly, to soar.
parole.testo: From Middle English ascenden, borrowed from Old French ascendre, from Latin ascendō (“to go up, climb up to”), from ad (“to”) + scandō (“to climb”); see scan. Unrelated to accede other than common ad prefix.

parole.significato: Moving upward; ascending, rising.
parole.testo: PIE word  *h₂éd The adjective is derived from Late Middle English ascendent (“ascending, rising; increasing in quantity; (astronomy) rising above the horizon”) [and other forms], borrowed from Old French ascendant, from Latin ascendentem, the accusative singular of ascendēns (“ascending, rising”), t

parole.significato: The act of ascending; an ascent.
parole.testo: From Middle English ascencioun, from Old French ascension, from Latin ascēnsiō, ascēnsiōnem (“ascent”). Displaced native Old English upfæreld.

parole.significato: To find out definitely; to discover or establish.
parole.testo: From Middle English acerteynen, from Old French acertener, from a- (“to, towards”) + certener (“make sure of”), from the adjective certain, from Latin certus (“certain, fixed”). Compare to Spanish acertar.

parole.significato: To regard as arising from a specified cause or source.
parole.testo: From Middle English ascriben, from Old French ascrivre (“inscribe, attribute, impute”), from Latin āscrībere (“to state in writing”), equivalent to a- + scribe.

parole.significato: Masonry employing flat and well-squared stone or brick, creating an appearance similar to wooden flooring.
parole.testo: From Middle English assheler, acheler, etc., from forms of Old French esselier (“wooden support, traverse beam”), from Medieval Latin ascelāris and assellāris (equivalent to a diminutive of early forms of ais (“plank”)), variant of *axillāris (attested only after the Renaissance), from Latin axilla

parole.significato: A water snake.
parole.testo: From Middle English aspe, from Old French aspe, from Latin aspis, aspidis (“asp, viper”), from Ancient Greek ἀσπίς (aspís, “shield; Egyptian cobra Naja haje”); compare Middle English aspide.

parole.significato: Rough or harsh; severe, stern, serious.
parole.testo: From Middle English aspre, from Old French aspre (modern French âpre), from Latin asper (“rough”).

parole.significato: The quality of having a rough or uneven surface; roughness, unevenness; (countable, chiefly in the plural) a protruding…
parole.testo: From Middle English asprete, asperite, from Old French aspreté (modern French âpreté), from Latin asperitātem, the accusative singular of asperitās (“roughness, unevenness; fierceness, severity; harshness, sharpness; acidity, tartness”), from asper (“coarse, rough, uneven; bitter, fierce harsh; rude

parole.significato: To have a strong desire or ambition to achieve something.
parole.testo: From Middle English aspiren, from Old French aspirer, from Latin aspīrō (“breathe on; approach; desire”).

parole.significato: To attack with harsh words or violent force.
parole.testo: From Middle English assailen, from Old French assaillir, assalir, from Late Latin assalīre, from Latin ad (“at, towards”) + salīre (“jump”). See also assault.

parole.significato: Someone who attacks or assails another violently, or criminally.
parole.testo: From Old French assaillant, from the verb assaillir, from Late Latin assalīre, from Latin ad (“to, towards”) + salīre (“to jump”). Equivalent to assail + -ant.

parole.significato: A violent onset or attack with physical means, for example blows, weapons, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English assaut, from Old French noun assaut, derived from the past participle of the verb assalir, from Late Latin assalīre, from Latin ad (“at, towards”) + salīre (“jump”). See also assail. Spelling Latinized around 1530 to add an l.

parole.significato: To put together.
parole.testo: From Middle English assemblen, from Old French assembler (“to assemble”), from Medieval Latin assimulāre (“to bring together”), from ad- + simulō (“copy, imitate”), from similis (“like, similar”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“together, one”). Doublet of assimilate.

parole.significato: To agree to a proposal.
parole.testo: From Middle English assent (noun) and assenten (verb), from Old French assent (noun) and assentir (verb), from Latin assentiō (whence as-).

parole.significato: To determine, estimate or judge the value of; to evaluate; to estimate.
parole.testo: From Middle English assessen, from Old French assesser, from Medieval Latin assessare, originally the frequentative of Latin assessus, past participle of assidēre, from ad (“to, towards, at”) + sedeō (“sit; settle down”). Cognate with Spanish asentar (“to settle”).

parole.significato: One who assesses a property for tax or insurance evaluation.
parole.testo: From Middle English assessour, from Old French assessour, from Latin assessor (“assistant judge; assessor of taxes”). Cognate with French assesseur.

parole.significato: A siege.
parole.testo: From Old French asegier (“besiege”) (Modern French assiéger); equivalent to a- + siege.

parole.significato: To designate or set apart (something) for some purpose.
parole.testo: From Middle English assignen, from Old French assigner, asigner, from Latin assignō, from ad- + signō (“mark, sign”).

parole.significato: An appointment for a meeting, generally of a romantic or sexual nature.
parole.testo: From Middle English assignacioun, from Old French assignacion, from Latin assīgnātiō.

parole.significato: One to whom a thing is assigned.
parole.testo: From Middle English assigne, from Old French assigné, equivalent to assign + -ee.

parole.significato: The act of assigning; the allocation of a job or a set of tasks.
parole.testo: From Middle English assignement, from Old French assignement. By surface analysis, assign + -ment.

parole.significato: To help.
parole.testo: From Middle English assisten, from Old French assister (“to assist, to attend”), from Latin assistō (“stand at, bestand”, verb).

parole.significato: A session or inquiry made before a court or jury.
parole.testo: From Middle English assise, from Old French assises, feminine plural participle of Old French asseoir (“to sit”), from Latin assidere.

parole.significato: To lessen the intensity of, to mitigate or relieve (hunger, emotion, pain, etc.).
parole.testo: From Middle English aswagen, from Old French asuagier (“to appease, to calm”), from Vulgar Latin *assuāviō (“to sweeten, to butter up, to calm”), derived from Latin ad- + suāvis (“sweet”) + -iō.

parole.significato: The act of assuring; a declaration intended to inspire full confidence; something designed to give confidence to someon…
parole.testo: From Middle English assuraunce, from Old French asseürance, from asseürer; as if assure + -ance.

parole.significato: To make sure and secure; ensure.
parole.testo: From Old French asseurer (Modern French assurer), from Latin ad- + securus (“secure”). Cognate with Spanish asegurar. Doublet of assecure.

parole.significato: Compensation or reparation for a criminal offence.
parole.testo: From assyth + -ment, from Old French aset, asez, originally meaning "enough". See assets.

parole.significato: In shock or confusion; bewildered, astonished.
parole.testo: Apparently from astony, astonie, from Old French estonner, from Vulgar Latin *extonare. Compare English astonish, of which this was claimed in olden sources to be the more "correct" (or at least Biblical) version of the word.

parole.significato: To store; to furnish with stores.
parole.testo: From Middle English astoren, from Old French estorer, from Latin instaurare.

parole.significato: Away from the proper path; in a wrong or unknown direction.
parole.testo: From Middle English astraien or by apheresis straien, from Old French estraier (“to stray”), from late Medieval Latin extravagari (“to wander beyond”), from Latin extra (“beyond”) + vagārī (“to wander, stray”).

parole.significato: An astrologer.
parole.testo: From Middle English astrologien, astrologen, from Old French astrologien.

parole.significato: An astrologer.
parole.testo: From Middle English astronomien and Old French astronomien. See astronomy.

parole.significato: The study of the physical universe beyond the Earth's atmosphere, including the process of mapping locations and proper…
parole.testo: From Middle English astronomie, astronemy, from Old French astronomie, equivalent to astro- + -nomy. Displaced native Old English tungolcræft.

parole.significato: Free of anxiety; not stressed or tense.
parole.testo: From Middle English at ese, calque of Old French a eise, from a (“at”) + eise (“ease”).

parole.significato: To fasten, to join to (literally and figuratively).
parole.testo: From Middle English attachen, from Old French atachier, variant of estachier (“bind”), derived from estache (“stick”), from Frankish *stakkā, *stakō (“stick”), from Proto-Germanic *stakô (“pole, bar, stick, stake”). Doublet of attack. More at stake, stack. Displaced native Old English þīedan.

parole.significato: Convicted, attainted.
parole.testo: From Middle English atteinte, from Old French ateint, past participle of ateindre; in some senses influenced by taint.

parole.significato: To temper by adjusting relative quantities, or blending qualities.
parole.testo: From Middle English attempren, from Old French atemprer (French attremper), from Latin attemperare. Doublet of attemperate.

parole.significato: A tempering, or mixing in equal proportion.
parole.testo: From Old French attemprement.

parole.significato: temperance; temperament
parole.testo: From Middle English attemprance, from Old French atemprance.

parole.significato: To try.
parole.testo: Late 14th century, as Middle English attempten, from Old French atempter, from Latin attemptō (“to try, solicit”), from ad- (“to”) + temptō; see tempt. parole.significato: Senses relating to caring for or waiting on someone, or accompanying or being present.
parole.testo: PIE word  *h₂éd From Middle English attenden, atenden (“to devote oneself (to a task, etc.); to pay attention to (something), to look after; to consider (something); to expect or look forward to (something); to intend to do (something); to help or serve (someone), attend upon; to take care of (somet

parole.significato: The act of attending; the state of being present; presence.
parole.testo: From Middle English attendance, from Old French atendance, from atendre (“to attend, listen”).

parole.significato: One who attends; one who works with or watches over someone or something.
parole.testo: From Middle English attendant, attendaunt, from Old French attendant. By surface analysis, attend + -ant.

parole.significato: Paying attention; noticing, watching, listening, or attending closely.
parole.testo: From Middle English attentif, attentijf, from Old French attentif.

parole.significato: One's dress; what one wears; one's clothes.
parole.testo: The verb is from Middle English atyren, atiren, from Old French atirier (“to equip”), from a- + tire (“rank”), akin to German Zier (“ornament”) and Old Norse tírr (“glory, renown”). The noun is from Middle English atir, from the verb.

parole.significato: To transfer one's obligations from one person to another person.
parole.testo: From Middle English attournen, from Old French atorner (“designate”), from a- (“to”) + torner (“turn”).

parole.significato: A lawyer; one who advises or represents others in legal matters as a profession.
parole.testo: From Middle English attourne, from Old French atorné, past participle of atorner, atourner, aturner (“to attorn”), in the sense of "one appointed or constituted".

parole.significato: The consent of a tenant to the transfer of his relationship to his landlord to another person.
parole.testo: From Old French atorner (“to turn”), through Middle English with the suffix -ment.

parole.significato: The tendency to attract.
parole.testo: From Middle English attraccioun, from Old French attraction, from Latin attractio from past participle of attrahō (= ad + trahō), equivalent to attract + -ion.

parole.significato: A dark reddish-brown colour, often used to describe hair colour.
parole.testo: Early Modern English auburn (“brown, reddish brown”) from Middle English aubourne, abron, abroune, abrune (“light brown, yellowish brown, blond”), alteration (due to conflation with Middle English brun (“brown”)) of earlier auborne (“yellowish-white, flaxen”) from Old French auborne, alborne (“blond

parole.significato: The act or process of augmenting.
parole.testo: From Middle English augmentation, augmentacion, augmentacioun, from Old French augmentacion, from Latin augmentātiō, verbal noun from augmentō (“increase”, verb).

parole.significato: To surround with, or as if with, a halo.
parole.testo: From Middle English aureole, from Old French aureole, from Medieval Latin aureola (corona) (“golden (crown)”). Doublet of oriole.

parole.significato: A keeper of goshawks.
parole.testo: From Middle English ostreger, ostringer, borrowed from Old French ostruchier, austruchier.

parole.significato: Of the same origin as claimed; genuine.
parole.testo: From Middle English authentik, from Old French autentique, from Latin authenticus, from Ancient Greek αὐθεντικός (authentikós, “authentic, genuine”), from Ancient Greek αὐθέντης (authéntēs, “perpetrator, murderer, absolute ruler”). Doublet of effendi.

parole.significato: Power or right to make or enforce rules, give orders, or impose obligation; or a position having such power or right.
parole.testo: From Middle English auctorite, autorite (“authority, book or quotation that settles an argument”), from Old French auctorité, from Latin stem of auctōritās (“invention, advice, opinion, influence, command”), from auctor (“master, leader, author”). For the presence of the h, compare the etymology of

parole.significato: To grant (someone) the permission or power necessary to do (something); to permit; to sanction or consent to.
parole.testo: From Middle English auctorisen, from Old French auctorisier, from Medieval Latin auctōrizāre, from Latin auctor. See author about the orthography with ⟨h⟩. Doublet of octroy.

parole.significato: To turn to the advantage of.
parole.testo: From Middle English availen (“to be of use”), from Old French a (“to”) + vail from valoir (“to be worth”), from Latin valere (“to be worthy, strong”).

parole.significato: To cause to descend; to lower; to let fall
parole.testo: From Middle English avalen, from Old French avaler (“to descend”), a univerbation of a val (“to the valley”).

parole.significato: The vanguard of an army or other force.
parole.testo: From Middle English advaunte-garde, avauntgard, from Old French avangarde, avant-garde, avantgarde, from avant (“before; in front”) + garde (“guard”). Doublet of vanguard and vaward

parole.significato: Excessive or inordinate desire of gain; greed for wealth
parole.testo: From Middle English avarice, from Old French, from Latin avāritia, from avārus (“greedy”).

parole.significato: Actuated by avarice; extremely greedy for wealth or material gain; immoderately desirous of accumulating property.
parole.testo: From Middle English avaricious, from Old French avaricieux, from avarice, from Latin avaritia (“greed”), from avarus (“greedy”), of avere (“crave, long for”).

parole.significato: To advance; to profit.
parole.testo: From Old French avancer (“to move forward”).

parole.significato: Begone; depart; used in contempt or abhorrence.
parole.testo: First used 1275–1325; Middle English, from Old French avant (“to the front”).

parole.significato: A quantity of oats paid by a tenant to a landlord in lieu of rent.
parole.testo: From Old French avenage, from avene, from Latin avena (“oats”).

parole.significato: To take vengeance (for); to exact satisfaction for by punishing the injuring party; to vindicate by inflicting pain or…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English avengen, borrowed from Old French avengier, from a- + vengier.

parole.significato: A curtain or flap of mail, fastened to a helmet, or to a coif (hood) of mail, covering the lower face, neck, and should…
parole.testo: From Middle English aventayle, from Old French esventail (“air-hole”), from esventer (Modern French éventer), from Latin ex (“out”) + ventus (“wind”). Related to ventail.

parole.significato: To thrust forward (at a venture), as a spear.
parole.testo: From Old French venter (“to cast to the wind”).

parole.significato: To assert the truth of (something); to affirm (something) with confidence; to declare (something) in a positive manner.
parole.testo: From Middle English averren, from Old French averer, from Early Medieval Latin advērō, a verb derived from Latin vērus (“true”). Compare Modern French avérer.

parole.significato: The act of averring, or that which is averred; positive assertion.
parole.testo: From Middle English averement, from Old French averrement, averement, from averer (Modern French avérer).

parole.significato: To turn aside or away.
parole.testo: From Middle English averten, adverten, from Old French avertir (“turn, direct, avert; turn the attention, make aware”), from Latin āvertere, from ab + vertō (“to turn”).

parole.significato: Greediness; strong appetite.
parole.testo: From Middle English avidite, from Old French avidite (modern French avidité), from Latin aviditās (“avidity, covetousness”), equivalent to avid + -ity.

parole.significato: advice; opinion; deliberation.
parole.testo: From Middle English avys, from Old French avis.

parole.significato: A vision of a prophetic or admonitory nature.
parole.testo: From Middle English avisioun, from Old French avision.

parole.significato: An advocate; a lawyer.
parole.testo: From Middle English avocat, from Old French avocat, from Latin advocātus. Doublet of advocate.

parole.significato: The official system of weights used in the UK between 1856 and 1963. It had been the customary system in London since 1…
parole.testo: From Middle English avoir de pois, aver de peis, haburdy poyse, haburdepays, haburdepeyse, from Old French aveir + de + peis (“asset of weight”), influenced by Middle French avoir + du + pois; compare French poids (“weight”).

parole.significato: To declare freely and openly; to assert.
parole.testo: From Old French avouchier, from Latin advocāre. Doublet of advocate, advoke, and avow.

parole.significato: An adulterer.
parole.testo: From Middle English avounterer, avouterer, avoutrer(e), avowterer, avowtreer, avowtrer(e), awowterer, from Old French avoutrier, from Latin adulterō or adulter, noun use of an adjective.

parole.significato: To declare openly and boldly, as something believed to be right; to own, acknowledge or confess frankly.
parole.testo: From Middle English avowen, from Old French avouer, from Latin advocare (“to call to, call upon, hence to call as a witness, defender, patron, or advocate”), from ad (“to”) + vocare (“to call”). Doublet of advoke, avouch, and advocate. Not related to vow.

parole.significato: The act of avowing and justifying in one's own right the distraining of goods.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English avowry, avowrie, from Old French avoerie, avouerie (“protection, patronage”), equivalent to avoer or avouer (“to avow”) + -ie.

parole.significato: adultery
parole.testo: From Middle English avoutrie, from Old French avouterie, variant (perhaps influenced by vout, vut (“vow”)) of aouterie, aolterie, from Late Latin adulterium. Doublet of adultery, which replaced it in modern English.

parole.significato: A grandfather.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English ayel, aiel, from Old French aiol, aiuel, from Vulgar Latin *aviolus, ultimately from Latin avus. Compare modern French aïeul.

parole.significato: An arc of the horizon intercepted between the meridian of the place and a vertical circle passing through the center of…
parole.testo: From Old French *azimut (modern French azimut), from Arabic اَلسُّمُوت pl (as-sumūt, “the directions”).

parole.significato: The clear blue colour of the sky; also, a pigment or dye of this colour.
parole.testo: From Middle English asure, from Old French azur, derived from Arabic لَازَوَرْد (lāzaward, “lapis lazuli”), dropping the l as if it were equivalent to the French article l'. The Arabic is from Classical Persian لاجورد (lājward, “lapis lazuli”), from the region of Lajward in Badakhshan. Compare with

parole.significato: An Old World monkey of the genus Papio, having dog-like muzzles and large canine teeth, cheek pouches, a short tail, an…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English babewin, baboin, from Old French babouin, from baboue (“grimace; muzzle”) (whence French babouin), from an imitative origin. According to Oxford English Dictionary, it was an imitative base *bab-, which is in turn from the (reduplicated) syllable ba, characteristic of e

parole.significato: Collectively, aspiring knights.
parole.testo: From Middle English bachelrie, from Old French bachelerie.

parole.significato: To make the sound of a wild animal, to bay.
parole.testo: From Old French bay, combined with aphetized form of abay; verbal form Old French baier, abaier.

parole.significato: Portable cases, large bags, and similar equipment for manually carrying, pushing, or pulling personal items while trave…
parole.testo: From Middle English bagage, from Old French bagage, baguage, from bague (“bundle, sack”), of Germanic/North Germanic origin, probably from the same ultimate source as Old Norse baggi (“pack, bundle”). Compare also bag. By surface analysis, bag + -age. The old meaning of "nasty woman" likely derives

parole.significato: Security, usually a sum of money, exchanged for the release of an arrested person as a guarantee of that person's appea…
parole.testo: From Middle English baille, from the Old French verb bailler (“to deliver or hand over”) and noun bail (“lease”), from Latin bāiulāre (“carry or bear”), from baiulus (“porter; steward”) (English: bailiff).

parole.significato: The outer wall of a feudal castle.
parole.testo: From Old French baile (“palisade, enclosure”), from Latin bacula, plural of baculum (“stick, rod”).

parole.significato: A bailiff.
parole.testo: From Old French bailli (“land steward; officer of justice”).

parole.significato: A bath.
parole.testo: From Middle English bayne~baine, from Old French bain, from Latin baneum, variant of balneum. Doublet of bagnio, balaneion, and banya.

parole.significato: A state in which opposing forces harmonise; equilibrium.
parole.testo: From Middle English balaunce, from Old French balance, from Late Latin *bilancia, from (accusative form of) Latin bilanx (“two-scaled”), from bi- + lanx (“plate, scale”). Displaced the word — Old English wǣġ akin to Modern English: wey from Proto-West Germanic *wāgu (“scales; weight”).

parole.significato: A type of rose-coloured spinel once thought to be a form of ruby.
parole.testo: From Old English bales, balais, from Old French balais, from Arabic بَلَخْش (balaḵš), from Persian بلخش (balaxš), a form of بدخش (badaxš, “balas”), related to بدخشان (badaxšân, “Badakhshan”), the region where they are found.

parole.significato: A broad belt, originally of leather and often richly ornamented, worn diagonally from shoulder to hip (across the breas…
parole.testo: From Middle English baudrik, bauderik, baudry (“belt worn over the shoulder or around the waist for carrying a sword, etc., baldric; (by extension) type of leather strap”), from Old French baldré, baldrei, baudré (“crossbelt, sword-belt”) (modern French baudrier); further etymology uncertain, possib

parole.significato: A rounded bundle or package of goods in a cloth cover, and corded for storage or transportation.
parole.testo: From Middle English bale (“bale”), from Old French bale and Medieval Latin bala, of Germanic origin. Doublet of ball.

parole.significato: keratinous material that makes up the plates in the mouth of the baleen whale (Mysticeti), which it uses to trap its fo…
parole.testo: From Middle English baleyne, from Old French baleine (“whale, whalebone”), from Latin balaena (“whale”), from Ancient Greek φάλαινα (phálaina, “whale”).

parole.significato: A crossbow.
parole.testo: From Old French balestre. See ballista.

parole.significato: arrowslit (a narrow opening through which arrows can be fired).
parole.testo: From balister (“crossbow”), from Old French balestre, ultimately from Latin balaustium, Ancient Greek βαλαύστιον (balaústion). See also arbalister (“crossbowman”).

parole.significato: A bench; a high seat, or seat of distinction or judgment.
parole.testo: From Middle English bank, from Old French banc. Doublet of banco, bank, and bench.

parole.significato: To group together for a common purpose; to confederate.
parole.testo: Derived from Middle English band, from Old French bande, from Old Occitan banda (“regiment of troops”), perhaps from Frankish *bend, from Proto-Germanic *bandiz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ- (“to tie; bond, band”). Compare German Bande (“band”).

parole.significato: To send (someone) away and forbid them from returning.
parole.testo: From Middle English banishen, from Old French baniss-, extended stem of banir (“to proclaim, ban, banish”), of Germanic origin and Old English bannan, from Proto-Germanic *bannaną (“curse, forbid”). Compare French bannir. Doublet of ban.

parole.significato: A row or panel of items stored or grouped together.
parole.testo: From Middle English bank, banke, from Old French banc (“bench”), from Frankish *banki, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz (“bench”). Akin to Old English benċ (“bench”).

parole.significato: A flag or standard used by a military commander, monarch or nation.
parole.testo: From Middle English baner, from Old French baniere (Modern bannière), of Germanic origin. More at band.

parole.significato: A Christian sacrament, by which one is received into a church and sometimes given a name, generally involving the candi…
parole.testo: From Middle English bapteme, baptesme, from Old French batesme or bapteme, from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin baptisma, from Ancient Greek βάπτισμα (báptisma, “dipping, baptism”), from βαπτίζω (baptízō, “I dip in liquid”). Displaced native Old English fulwiht.

parole.significato: A person who baptizes.
parole.testo: From Middle English baptist, baptiste, borrowed from Old French baptiste, from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin baptista, from Ancient Greek βαπτιστής (baptistḗs).

parole.significato: To perform the sacrament of baptism by sprinkling or pouring water over someone or immersing them in water.
parole.testo: From Middle English baptisen, baptizen, from Old French baptiser, batisier, from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin baptizāre, from Ancient Greek βαπτίζω (baptízō, “to immerse, plunge, baptize”).

parole.significato: A solid, more or less rigid object of metal or wood with a uniform cross-section smaller than its length.
parole.testo: From Middle English barre, from Old French barre (“beam, bar, gate, barrier”), from Vulgar Latin *barra, of uncertain origin. Doublet of barre.

parole.significato: To obstruct the passage of (someone or something).
parole.testo: From Middle English barren, from Old French barrer, from Medieval Latin barrare (“to bar”), from the noun. Cognate to Occitan barrar, Spanish barrar, Portuguese barrar. Preposition properly imperative of the verb. Compare barring.

parole.significato: of or relating to a barbarian; uncivilized, uncultured or uncouth
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English barbarik, from Old French barbarique (“barbarous”), from Latin barbaricus, from Ancient Greek βαρβαρικός (barbarikós, “barbaric, savage, fierce”), from βάρβαρος (bárbaros, “barbarian”) + -ικός (-ikós, adjective suffix). See βάρβαρος (bárbaros) for more.

parole.significato: barbarian; non-Christian
parole.testo: From Middle English barbarye (“barbarian, non-Christian”), from Old French [Term?] and Medieval Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: A freshwater fish of the genus Barbus or other closely related taxa in the cyprinid family.
parole.testo: PIE word  *bʰardʰéh₂ From Middle English barbel, from Old French barbel, from Vulgar Latin *barbellus, from Late Latin barbulus, diminutive of Latin barbus (“barbel”); barbus itself is from barba (“beard”). By surface analysis, Latin barb(us) (“beard, barbel”) + -el (diminutive suffix), and also, by

parole.significato: A tower at the entrance to a castle or fortified town.
parole.testo: From Old French barbacane, of uncertain origin: compare Arabic بَرْبَخ (barbaḵ, “aqueduct, sewer”), and Persian بابخانه (bâb-xâne, “gatehouse”).

parole.significato: An agreement between parties concerning the sale of property; or a contract by which one party binds themself to transf…
parole.testo: From Middle English bargaynen (“to bargain, make a pledge for sale”), from Old French bargaigner (“to bargain”), from Frankish *borganjan (“to borrow, lend”), from Proto-Germanic *burgijaną (“to borrow, lend”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰergʰ- (“to protect, secure”). Akin to Old High German boragēn

parole.significato: The party to a contract who receives, or agrees to receive, the property being sold.
parole.testo: Old French bargaigné.

parole.significato: A large flat-bottomed towed or self-propelled boat used mainly for river and canal transport of heavy goods or bulk car…
parole.testo: From Middle English barge, borrowed from Old French barge (“boat”), from Vulgar Latin *barga, a variant of Late Latin barca, a regular syncope of Vulgar Latin *barica, from Classical Latin bāris, from Ancient Greek βᾶρις (bâris, “Egyptian boat”), from Coptic ⲃⲁⲁⲣⲉ (baare, “small boat”), from Demotic

parole.significato: The male ruler of a barony.
parole.testo: From Middle English baroun, from Old French baron, from Latin barōnem, from Proto-West Germanic *barō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to bear”). parole.significato: barons or nobles collectively
parole.testo: From Middle English barnage, from Old French (and Anglo-Norman) barnage, from baron + -age, with the loss of a syllable.

parole.significato: The domain of a baron or baroness, usually as part of a larger kingdom or empire.
parole.testo: From Middle English baronie, baronye, from Old French baronie, equivalent to baron + -y.

parole.significato: The lists in a tournament.
parole.testo: From Old French barras, related to bar.

parole.significato: One who is guilty of barratry, vexing others with frequent and often groundless lawsuits; a brangler and pettifogger.
parole.testo: From Middle English baratour, from Old French barateor (“deceiver”), from Old French barater, bareter (“to deceive, cheat, barter”). Compare barter (intransitive verb).

parole.significato: The act of persistently instigating lawsuits, often groundless ones.
parole.testo: Early 15th century, in sense “sale of offices”, from Old French baraterie (“deceit, trickery”), from barat (“fraud, deceit, trickery”), of unknown origin, perhaps Celtic. In marine sense of “unlawful acts causing loss to owner”, 1620s.

parole.significato: A round (cylindrical) vessel, such as a cask, of greater length than breadth, and bulging in the middle, made of staves…
parole.testo: From Middle English barel, from Anglo-Norman baril, Old French baril, bareil (“barrel”), of uncertain origin. An attempt to link baril to Old French barre (“bar, bolt”) (compare Medieval Latin barra (“bar, rod”)) via assumed Vulgar Latin *barrīculum meets the phonological requirement, but fails to c

parole.significato: A variable resistor made up of a short length of very fine wire (usually platinum) having a positive temperature coeffi…
parole.testo: Apparently a variant of barretter (“ballast resistor”), which in turn may be from Old French barateor (“barrator”).

parole.significato: A ballast resistor.
parole.testo: Likely from Old French bareter (“to exchange”), or barateor (“exchanger”). Compare barrator

parole.significato: Traversed (transversely) by barrulets or small bars.
parole.testo: From Middle English berlē, beurlē, from Old French barlé, burlé, barelé, burelé.

parole.significato: An exchange of goods or services without the use of money.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Old French barater.

parole.significato: To give as its foundation or starting point; to lay the foundation of.
parole.testo: From Middle English base, bas, baas, from Old French base, from Latin basis, from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis). Doublet of basis and bass.

parole.significato: A type of heavy dagger popular in the 14th and 15th centuries.
parole.testo: From Old French baselard, basilard (early 14th century), in English from the later 14th century. parole.significato: A type of cannon.
parole.testo: From Old French basile (“basilisk”).

parole.significato: A mythical snake-like dragon, so venomous that even its gaze is deadly.
parole.testo: From Middle English basilicke, borrowed from Old French basilique, from Latin basiliscus, from Ancient Greek βασιλίσκος (basilískos, literally “minor king or chieftain”), from βασιλεύς (basileús, “king”), possibly based on descriptions or rare encounters with different types of cobra which have crow

parole.significato: A wide bowl for washing, sometimes affixed to a wall.
parole.testo: From Middle English basyn, from Old French bacin, from Vulgar Latin *baccinum (“wide bowl”).

parole.significato: A person who was born out of wedlock, and hence often considered an illegitimate descendant.
parole.testo: From Middle English bastard, bastarde, from Old English bastard (used as an epithet), from Anglo-Norman bastard, Old French bastart (“illegitimate child”), perhaps via Medieval Latin bastardus, of obscure origin. Likely from Frankish *bāst (“marriage, relationship”) + Old French -ard, -art (pejorati

parole.significato: To sew with long or loose stitches, as for temporary use, or in preparation for gathering the fabric.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Old French bastir (“build, construct, sew up (a garment)”).

parole.significato: To sprinkle flour and salt and drip butter or fat on, as on meat in roasting.
parole.testo: From Middle English basten, of uncertain etymon, possibly from Old French basser (“moisten, soak”), from bacin (“basin”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; perhaps; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: To hit with a bat or (figuratively) as if with a bat.
parole.testo: From Middle English batten, baten (“to beat”), from Old French batre (“to beat”), from Late Latin battere, from Latin battuere, of uncertain origin; perhaps of Germanic or Celtic origin. In modern English reinterpreted as a verbal derivative of Etymology 2. Compare batter, battery.

parole.significato: To reduce the force of something; to abate.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English baten (“to abate”), an apheretic form of abaten, from Old French abatre (“to knock down”).

parole.significato: Strife; contention.
parole.testo: * Noun: From the verb, or directly from the noun debate. * Verb: From Middle English bate (“contention”), from Old French batre (French battre), from Latin battere.

parole.significato: Warlike, battle-ready.
parole.testo: From Middle English bataylous, from Old French bataillos, from bataille (“battle”); equivalent to battle + -ous.

parole.significato: A plank or strip of wood, or several of such strips arranged side by side, used in construction to hold members of a st…
parole.testo: The noun is from Middle English bataunt, batent (“finished bar or board (as for panelling)”), from Old French batent (“a beating”), a noun use of the present participle form of batre (“to beat, hit, strike”), from Late Latin battere, the present active infinitive of battō (“to beat”), from Latin bat

parole.significato: A beaten mixture of flour and liquid (usually egg and milk), used for baking (e.g. pancakes, cake, or Yorkshire pudding…
parole.testo: From Middle English bature, from Old French bateure (“the action of beating”), from batre (“to beat”). Doublet of batture.

parole.significato: In fortification: an indented parapet, formed by a series of rising members called cops or merlons, separated by openin…
parole.testo: From Middle English batilment, from Old French bataillement, earlier bastillement (“fortification”), from bastillier (“to fortify, to equip with battlements”), from bastille (“fortress”) (see bastion). By surface analysis, battle + -ment.

parole.significato: One who wages battle against an enemy; a soldier; a general.
parole.testo: From Middle English batailloure, from Old French batailleor; equivalent to battle + -er.

parole.significato: A cheap showy ornament or piece of jewellery; a gewgaw.
parole.testo: From Middle English bable, babel, babull, babulle, from Old French babel, baubel (“trinket, child's toy”), most likely a reduplication of bel, ultimately from Latin bellus (“pretty”).

parole.significato: A long red streamer hoisted by ships during the Middle Ages to indicate combat to the death.
parole.testo: From French, perhaps related to Old French baucent (“black and white; the black and white flag (with red cross) of the templars”), Old Occitan bausan (“black and white (horse)”) despite the change in meaning/colour.

parole.significato: A bundle of wood or twigs, which may be used in broom-making.
parole.testo: Perhaps Old French baffe (“a faggot”).

parole.significato: A fine fellow.
parole.testo: From Old French baud (“bold, gay”) + cock.

parole.significato: One who keeps a brothel, or procures women for prostitution; a procurer or madam.
parole.testo: From Middle English bawde, baude, from Old French baud (“bold, lively, jolly, gay”). Doublet of bold. An association with Welsh bawddyn (“dirty fellow, scoundrel”), from baw (“dirt”), was suggested by the Rev. Henry Todd.

parole.significato: A badger.
parole.testo: From Old French bauzan, bauçant, bauchant (“spotted with white, pied”).

parole.significato: Having white streaks or spots on a black or bay background (especially of an animal's or a mountain's face).
parole.testo: From Old French bausant (“black and white spotted”).

parole.significato: A tree or shrub of species Laurus nobilis (family Lauraceae), having dark green leaves and berries.
parole.testo: From Middle English baye, baie, from Old English beġ (“berry”), as in beġbēam (“berry-tree”), conflated with Old French baie, from Latin bāca (“berry”).

parole.significato: An opening in a wall, especially between two columns.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French baee, beee, from the verb beer (“gape open”), from Early Medieval Latin batāre. Compare Modern French baie. More at bevel, badinage.

parole.significato: Of a reddish-brown colour with a black mane and tail.
parole.testo: From Middle English bay, bai, from Old French bai, from Latin badius (“reddish brown, chestnut”).

parole.significato: Any four-footed land mammal.
parole.testo: From Middle English beeste, beste, from Old French beste (French bête), from Latin bēstia (“animal, beast”); many cognates – see bēstia.

parole.significato: A man with a reputation for fine dress and etiquette; a dandy or fop.
parole.testo: From Middle English beau, beu, bew, bewe, from Old French beau, from Latin bellus (“beautiful”). Doublet of bello and boo.

parole.significato: A father.
parole.testo: From Old French beau (“fair”) + pere (“father”).

parole.significato: To make beautiful; to increase the beauty of.
parole.testo: From Middle English beutifien, from Old French beaute (“beauty”), from Latin bellus (“beautiful, fine”), + -ify, from Latin facio (“make”).

parole.significato: A poleaxe with a modified hammerhead and a spike mounted on the top of the pole.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Old French bec de corbin (literally “crow's beak”).

parole.significato: To smear upon; to soil.
parole.testo: From be- (“thoroughly, extensively”) + daub, from Old French dauber (“to plaster, whitewash”), from Latin dealbō (“whiten over, plaster”).

parole.significato: A member of nomadic Arab tribes dwelling in the desert.
parole.testo: From Old French beduin (compare French bédouin), from Arabic بَدَوِيِّين (badawiyyīn), plural of بَدَوِيّ (badawiyy), from collective noun بَدْو (badw, “nomads”).

parole.significato: A person who begs.
parole.testo: From Middle English beggere, beggare, beggar (“beggar”), from Middle English beggen (“to beg”), equivalent to beg + -ar. Alternative etymology derives Middle English beggere, beggare, beggar from Old French begart, originally a member of the Beghards, a lay brotherhood of mendicants in the Low Count

parole.significato: A member of a semimonastic Christian lay religious order active in Northern Europe, particularly in the Low Countries i…
parole.testo: From Old French béguine.

parole.significato: Human conduct relative to social norms.
parole.testo: From Middle English behavoure, behaver, from behaven (modern behave), morphologically equivalent to behave + -ior. parole.significato: A grandmother.
parole.testo: Inherited from late (1400–1450) Middle English beldame, beldam, from Middle English bel (“attractive, fine, good”) (from Old French bel (“beautiful”), from Latin bellus) + dame, dam (“a mother, lady”), itself ultimately from Latin domina (“a mistress, lady”).

parole.significato: A tower or steeple typically containing bells, especially as part of a church.
parole.testo: From Middle English belfry, bellfray, belfray, berfrey, barfray, from Old French belfroi, berfroi, berfrey, from Late Latin berfrēdus, from Frankish *bergafriþu, from Proto-Germanic *bergafriþuz, equivalent to barrow + frith. English forms containing bel- as opposed to ber- were preferred due to fal

parole.significato: A tree, Moringa oleifera or horseradish tree of Arabia and India, which produces oil of ben.
parole.testo: From Middle English been, from Old French and Medieval Latin, probably from a North African pronunciation of Arabic بَان (bān, “ben tree”).

parole.significato: Divided into diagonal bands of colour.
parole.testo: From Middle English bendee, from Old French bendé (past participle).

parole.significato: Land granted to a priest in a church that has a source of income attached to it.
parole.testo: From Old French benefice, from Latin beneficium.

parole.significato: Disposition to do good.
parole.testo: Circa 1400, original sense “good will, disposition to do good”, Old French benivolence from Latin benevolentia (also directly from Latin), literally “good will”, from bene (“well, good”) + volentia, form of volēns, form of volō (“to wish”), components cognate to English benefit and voluntary, more d

parole.significato: Having a disposition to do good.
parole.testo: From Old French benevolent, borrowed from Latin benevolēns ("benevolent"). Displaced native Old English welwillende (literally well-wishing).

parole.significato: Kind; gentle; mild.
parole.testo: From Middle English benigne, benygne, from Old French benigne, from Latin benignus (“kind, good”), from bene (“well”) + genus (“origin, kind”). Compare malign.

parole.significato: A blessing; benediction.
parole.testo: From Middle English benysoun, beneson, borrowed from Old French beneïson, from Latin benedictiō, benedictiōnem. First known use: 14th century. Doublet of benediction.

parole.significato: Wood avens or herb bennet, a common yellow-flowered plant of Europe (Geum urbanum).
parole.testo: From Middle English *benet (found in Middle English herbe-benet (“hemlock”, literally “blessed plant”)), from Old French benëit, benoit and Latin (herba) benedicta. Doublet of benedict.

parole.significato: A pastoral song.
parole.testo: Old French bergerete, French berger (“a shepherd”).

parole.significato: A mineral of pegmatite deposits, often used as a gemstone (molecular formula Be₃Al₂Si₆O₁₈).
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English beryl, from Old French beril, from Latin bērillus, bēryllus, from Ancient Greek βήρυλλος (bḗrullos, “beryl”), in turn borrowed from Middle Indic forms like Pali veḷuriya or Prakrit 𑀯𑁂𑀭𑀼𑀮𑀺𑀅 (verulia), from Dravidian, probably named after Velur (modern day Belur) in south

parole.significato: A small disc of metal which protects the armpit, a piece of armor typically worn together with a spaulder or pauldron;…
parole.testo: From Middle English besagew, besague, besagu, from Old French besague, whence also besague (“double-edged axe or war-hammer”).

parole.significato: A kind of double-bladed axe.
parole.testo: From Middle English besague, besagu, besagew, from Old French besague, whence also English besagew (“rondel, armor protecting the armpit”), related to Latin bisacuta (Italian bisacuto (“double-edged”)) and besogium. Applied, in the Middle Ages, to a variety of medieval weapons or tools with two blad

parole.significato: To secure or steady; cause to come to a fixed position or state; bring to a halt or stop.
parole.testo: From be- + stay, from Middle English *stayen, steyen, from Old French estaier, estayer (“to prop, stay, support”), from estaye (“prop, support”), of Proto-Germanic origin. More at stay.

parole.significato: Beast-like.
parole.testo: From Middle English bestial, from Old French bestial, from Late Latin bēstiālis, from Latin bēstia (“beast”) (whence English beast).

parole.significato: A lunatic asylum.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Bethleem, from Old French Bethleem and Old English Bethleem, from Latin Bēthlehēmum, from Ancient Greek Βηθλεέμ (Bēthleém), from Hebrew בֵּית לֶחֶם (bēṯ lɛ́ḥɛm, literally “house of bread”). Doublet of bedlam and Belém.

parole.significato: A liquid to consume; a drink, such as tea, coffee, liquor, beer, milk, juice, or a soft drink, often excluding water.
parole.testo: From Middle English beverage, from Old French beverage, variant of bevrage, from beivre (“to drink”), variant of boivre (“to drink”), from Latin bibō. Related to imbibe.

parole.significato: A portion of plate armour to protect the lower face and the neck, typically in two parts, called upper bevor and lower…
parole.testo: From Middle English baviere, from Old French baviere (“child's bib”), from baver (“to slaver”).

parole.significato: A small strip of leather by which bells are fastened to a hawk's legs.
parole.testo: From Middle English bewette, diminutive of Old French beue, bue, buie, boie (“bond, chain”), from Latin boia (“neck collar, fetter”). Compare buoy.

parole.significato: A coin made of gold or silver, minted at Byzantium and used in currency throughout mediaeval Europe.
parole.testo: From Middle English besaunt, from Old French bezant, nominative bezanz, from Latin byzantius (“of Byzantium”).

parole.significato: To plunder; to lay waste to, in riot.
