parole.testo: From Middle English burnet, from Old French brunet, brunete (“brunette”). Doublet of brunette.

parole.significato: To make (something, such as a surface) bright, shiny, and smooth by, or (by extension) as if by, rubbing; to polish, to…
parole.testo: The verb is derived from Middle English burnishen, burnysshen (“to polish, burnish; (figuratively) to brighten, give lustre to; to clean (something) until shiny; to decorate (with something shiny), adorn”) [and other forms], from burniss-, a stem of Old French burnir (compare, for example, the first

parole.significato: A dry measure, containing four pecks, eight gallons, or thirty-two quarts; equivalent in volume to approximately 0.0364…
parole.testo: From Middle English busshel, from Old French boissel, from boisse, a grain measure based on Gaulish *bostyā (“handful”), from Proto-Celtic *bostā (“palm, fist”) (compare Breton boz (“hollow of the hand”), Old Irish bas), from Proto-Indo-European *gwost-, *gwosdʰ- (“branch”).

parole.significato: A soft boot reaching to calf or knee height.
parole.testo: Apparently from Old French bousequin, variant of brousequin (compare modern French brodequin), probably from Middle Dutch broseken, of unknown origin.

parole.significato: A person who prepares and sells meat (and sometimes also slaughters the animals).
parole.testo: From Middle English bocher, boucher, from Old French bouchier (“goat slaughterer”), from Old French bouc (“goat”), from Medieval Latin buccus (“he-goat”), from Frankish *bukk, from Proto-Germanic *bukkaz (“male goat, male deer”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuǵ- (“buck, ram”). See also English buck.

parole.significato: The butchering of meat.
parole.testo: From Middle English bocherie, from Old French. See butcher for more.

parole.significato: A manservant having charge of wines and liquors.
parole.testo: From Middle English butler, butlere, boteler, botelere, from Old French buttiler, butiller, boteillier (“officer in charge of wine”), from Medieval Latin botellārius, equivalent to bottle + -er. Piecewise doublet of bottler.

parole.significato: A butler's pantry; a serving pantry.
parole.testo: From Middle English buttillary, buttlarye, botelerye, botelerie, from Old French boteillerie, butelerie and Medieval Latin butellaria.

parole.significato: A room for keeping food or beverages; a storeroom.
parole.testo: From Middle English boterie, from Old French boterie and Medieval Latin buteria, from Late Latin botāria, from a variant form of butta (“cask, bottle”). The form was probably influenced by butter.

parole.significato: A knob or disc that is passed through a loop or (buttonhole), serving as a fastener.
parole.testo: From Middle English boton, botoun, from Old French boton (Modern French bouton), from Old French bouter, boter (“to push; thrust”), ultimately from a Germanic language. Doublet of bouton, Biden, and beat. More at butt.

parole.significato: A brick, concrete or stone structure built against another structure to support it.
parole.testo: From Old French ars bouterez (noun, literally “supporting arcs”), from bouterez (adjective), oblique plural of bouteret (rare in the singular), from Frankish *bôtan, from Proto-Germanic *bautaną (“to push”). Ultimately cognate with beat.

parole.significato: A small dwelling characteristic of the frontier, especially when built from logs with simple tools and not constructed…
parole.testo: From Middle English caban, cabane, from Old French cabane, from Medieval Latin capanna (“a cabin”); see further etymology there. Doublet of cabana and cabane.

parole.significato: The mendole, Spicara maena; a small Mediterranean fish considered poisonous in ancient times.
parole.testo: From Old French caquerel, cagarel, from the root of English cack.

parole.significato: To confine in a cage; to put into and keep in a cage.
parole.testo: From Middle English cage, from Old French cage, from Latin cavea. Doublet of cadge and cavea and related to jail.

parole.significato: To heat (a substance) to remove its impurities and refine it.
parole.testo: The verb is derived from Late Middle English calcinen (“(alchemy, medicine) to heat (something) until it turns to powder; to change the nature of (something) by heating”) [and other forms], from Old French calciner (modern French calciner (“to calcinate; to calcine”)) and from its etymon Medieval La

parole.significato: To calculate, reckon.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English calcule /calculen /calclen, derived from Old French calculer (compare French calculer, Spanish calcular, Portuguese calcular, Italian calculàre), derived from Latin calculāre (“reckon, calculate”). Doublet of calculate.

parole.significato: Any system by which time is divided into days, weeks, months, and years.
parole.testo: From Middle English kalender, from Old French calendier, from Latin calendarium (“account book”), from kalendae (“the first day of the month”), from kalō (“to announce solemnly, to call out (the sighting of the new moon)”), from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁-. Doublet of calendarium. Displaced native O

parole.significato: The holder of a monarchical title based on a claim to be a successor of Muhammad.
parole.testo: From Middle English calife, caliphe, from Old French caliphe, from Medieval Latin calipha, from Arabic خَلِيفَة (ḵalīfa, “caliph”) and خَلِيف (ḵalīf, “successor”).

parole.significato: A clay tobacco pipe used by Native Americans, especially as a symbol of truce or peace.
parole.testo: From a Norman variant of Old French chalumeau (imported to Canada with Norman colonists), from Latin calamellus, diminutive of calamus (“reed”), from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos).

parole.significato: A false accusation or charge brought to tarnish another's reputation or standing.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English calumnīe (“false accusation, slander; (law) objection raised in bad faith”), borrowed from Old French calomnie (“slander, calumny”) (modern French calomnie), or directly from its etymon Latin calumnia (“false statement, misrepresentation; false accusation, malicious charge”)

parole.significato: A slight convexity, arching or curvature of a surface of a road, beam, roof, ship's deck etc., so that liquids will flo…
parole.testo: From Old French cambre (“bent”), from Latin camurum, from camur (“arched”).

parole.significato: A fine fabric made from wool (originally camel, but later goat) and silk.
parole.testo: From Middle English chamelet, chamelot, chamlot via Old French chamelot, suffixed + -ot from Arabic خَمْلَة (ḵamla, “velvet”).

parole.significato: A white transparent waxy crystalline isoprenoid ketone, 1,7,7-trimethylbicyclo[2.2.1]heptan-2-one, with a strong pungen…
parole.testo: From Old French camphore or Medieval Latin camphora, from Arabic كَافُور (kāfūr), in turn from an Austronesian word such as Malay kapur.

parole.significato: A plant with simple stems, like bamboo or sugar cane, or the stem thereof:
parole.testo: From Middle English cane, canne, from Old French cane (“sugar cane”), from Latin canna (“reed”), from Ancient Greek κάννα (kánna), from Akkadian 𒄀 (qanû, “reed”). Doublet of canna and kaneh. Related to channel and canal.

parole.significato: To bombard with cannons.
parole.testo: Attested from around 1400 as Middle English canon, canoun, from Old French canon, from Italian cannone, from Latin canna, from Ancient Greek κάννα (kánna, “reed”), from Akkadian 𒄀 (qanû, “reed”), from Sumerian 𒄀𒈾 (gi.na) (for more, see cane). Doublet of canyon. This spelling was not fixed until abou

parole.significato: To declare (a deceased person) as a saint, and enter them into the canon of saints.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English canonizen (“to declare as a saint; to appoint to an ecclesiastical office”), from Old French canonisier (modern French canoniser (“to canonize”)), or from its etymon Medieval Latin, Late Latin canōnizāre, the present active infinitive of Latin canōnizō (“to recognize as a sa

parole.significato: A high cover providing shelter, such as a cloth supported above an object, particularly over a bed.
parole.testo: From Middle English canapy, canepie, canapee, canape, canope, from Old French conopé, Medieval Latin canapeum, canopeum, from Latin cōnōpēum (“mosquito net, canopy”), from Ancient Greek κωνωπεῖον (kōnōpeîon, “mosquito net”), from Ancient Greek κώνωψ (kṓnōps, “mosquito”), of uncertain origin. More at

parole.significato: From head to toe, especially of armor or other military accoutrements.
parole.testo: From Old French (de) cap a pié (Modern French de pied en cap).

parole.significato: The ability to hold, receive, or absorb.
parole.testo: From Middle English capacite, from Old French capacite, from Latin capācitās (whence -acity), from capāx (“able to hold much”), from capiō (“to hold, to contain, to take, to understand”).

parole.significato: A piece or point of land, extending beyond the adjacent coast into a sea or lake; a promontory; a headland.
parole.testo: From Middle English cape, gappe, cap, from Old French cap (“cape, headland”), from Latin caput (“head”). Compare Old Norse kobbi (“islet, small cape”). Doublet of capo, caput, chef, and chief, and distantly with head and Howth. For sense development, compare English ness (“a promontory point, cape”)

parole.significato: Money and wealth: the means to acquire or produce goods and services, especially in a non-barter system.
parole.testo: From Middle English capital, borrowed partly from Old French capital and partly from Latin capitālis (“of the head”) (in sense “head of cattle”), from caput (“head”) (English cap) + -ālis (suffix forming adjectives). Use in trade and finance originated in Medieval economies when a common but expensi

parole.significato: The uppermost part of a column.
parole.testo: From Middle English capitale, partly from Old French capital and partly from Late Latin capitellum (“capital or chapiter of a column”), a form of Latin capitulum (“head-like object or structure; chapter”) (whence English capitulum, chapter, and the synonym chapiter (“uppermost part of a column”)), f

parole.significato: A chief or leader.
parole.testo: From Middle English capitain, capteyn, from Old French capitaine, from Late Latin capitāneus, from Latin caput (“head”) (English cap). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap-. Doublet of chieftain, also from Old French.

parole.significato: A deep-red or fiery colored garnet or other dark red precious stone, especially when cut cabochon.
parole.testo: From Middle English carbuncle, charbocle, from Old French carbuncle, charbuncle, from Latin carbunculus (“a small coal; a reddish kind of precious stone; a kind of tumor”), diminutive of carbō (“a coal, charcoal”). Doublet of Garfinkel and Garfunkel.

parole.significato: To check IDs, especially against a minimum age requirement.
parole.testo: From Middle English carde (“playing card”), from Old French carte, from Latin charta, from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs, “paper, papyrus”). Doublet of carte and chart.

parole.significato: Material with embedded short wire bristles.
parole.testo: From Middle English carde, Old French carde, from Old Occitan carda, deverbal from cardar, from Late Latin *carito, from Latin carō (“to comb with a card”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”).

parole.significato: To use a carding device to disentangle the fibres of wool prior to spinning.
parole.testo: From Middle English carden, from Old French carder, from carde (“cotton card”); see Etymology 2 for more.

parole.significato: An herb, native to India (Elettaria cardamomum).
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Old French cardamome or Latin cardamōmum, from Ancient Greek καρδάμωμον (kardámōmon).

parole.significato: Any member of the species Cynara cardunculus of prickly perennial plants which has leaf stalks eaten as a vegetable, re…
parole.testo: From Middle English cardoun, from Old French cardon, from Late Latin cardōnem, from Latin cardus, alternative form of carduus (“thistle”). Respelled on analogy of -oon nouns. Doublet of cardon and chard.

parole.significato: Relating to the physical and especially sexual appetites or activities.
parole.testo: From Middle English carnal, from Old French charnel, from Late Latin carnālis (“fleshy”), from oblique stem of Latin carō, carnis (“meat, flesh”) + -ālis (whence -al).

parole.significato: A round dance accompanied by singing.
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Middle English carole (“round dance with singing; group of people dancing and singing in a circle; song by carollers, carol; religious poem or song; circular thing; braid, chain (?); stall for study or writing; writing table”), from Old French carole (“round dance with singi

parole.significato: Any of various freshwater fish of the family Cyprinidae.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English carpe (“the common carp (Cyprinus carpio)”), from Old French carpe, from Late Latin carpa, possibly from Proto-West Germanic *karpo (possibly due to the introduction from the fish from the Danube into England in the 14th century; whence Middle Low German karpe and Old High G

parole.significato: A fabric used as a complete floor covering.
parole.testo: From late Middle English carpette, from Old French carpite, from Medieval Latin carpita or Italian carpita, introduced in the 13th century by the Florentines from the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia, from Middle Armenian կարպետ (karpet, “carpet, rug”), earlier կապերտ (kapert).

parole.significato: Synonym of caravel (“a light, usually lateen-rigged sailing ship”).
parole.testo: From Middle English carvel, carvelle, carvile, kervel (“small ship; caravel”), from Old French caruelle, carvelle, kirvelle, see further at caravel. The English word is cognate with Middle Dutch karveel.

parole.significato: An actual event, situation, or fact.
parole.testo: From Middle English cas, from Old French cas (“an event”), from Latin cāsus (“a falling, a fall; accident, event, occurrence; occasion, opportunity; noun case”), perfect passive participle of cadō (“to fall, to drop”).

parole.significato: To render moot or void; to annul; to reject
parole.testo: From Middle English cassen, from Old French casser, from Late Latin cassō, from Latin cassus (“empty, hollow”), and perhaps influenced by quassō (“to shake, shatter”).

parole.significato: A feudal lord with a fortified manor.
parole.testo: From Middle English castelain, from Old French castelain (compare modern châtelain), from Latin castellanus (“pertaining to a castle, an occupant of a castle, or a governor of a castle”), from castellum castle, citadel, diminutive of castrum fortified place. See castle. By surface analysis, Old Fren

parole.significato: A small castle.
parole.testo: From Middle English castelet, from Old French castelet, northern form of chastelet. Equivalent to castle + -et. Compare French châtelet, Italian castelletto.

parole.significato: A systematic list of books, names, pictures, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English cathaloge, from Old French catalogue, from Late Latin catalogus, itself from Ancient Greek κατάλογος (katálogos, “enrollment, register”), from καταλέγω (katalégō, “to recount, make a list”), from κατα- (kata-, “downwards, towards”) + λέγω (légō, “to say, to speak, to tell”). Equi

parole.significato: A taxman, one who gathers taxes.
parole.testo: From Old French chacepol (“one who chases fowls”) (or a northern variant thereof).

parole.significato: To provide, particularly
parole.testo: From Middle English catour (“acater, provisioner”), aphetic form of acatour (“acater”), from Old French acater (“to buy, to purchase”). Equivalent to cate + -er.

parole.significato: Relating to the office of a bishop or an archbishop.
parole.testo: From Middle English cathedral, chathedral, cathiderall, from Old French [Term?], from Latin cathedrālis, from cathedra + -ālis, from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra, “chair of a teacher, throne”).

parole.significato: A member of a Catholic (western Christian) church.
parole.testo: From Old French catholique, from Latin catholicus, from Ancient Greek καθολικός (katholikós, “universal”), from κατά (katá, “according to”) + ὅλος (hólos, “whole”).

parole.significato: The source of, or reason for, an event or action; that which produces or effects a result.
parole.testo: * From Middle English cause (also with the sense of “a thing”), borrowed from Old French cause (“a cause, a thing”), borrowed from Latin causa (“reason, sake, cause”), from Proto-Italic *kaussā, which is of unknown origin. Doublet of chose (“(law) a thing; personal property”). See accuse, excuse, re

parole.significato: Prudence when faced with, or when expecting to face, danger; care taken in order to avoid risk or harm.
parole.testo: Recorded since 1297 as Middle English caucioun (“bail, guarantee, pledge”), from Old French caution (“security, surety”), itself from Latin cautiō, from cautus, past participle of caveō, cavēre (“be on one's guard”).

parole.significato: A large, naturally-occurring cavity formed underground or in the face of a cliff or a hillside.
parole.testo: From Middle English cave, borrowed from Old French cave, from Latin cava (“cavity”), from cavus (“hollow”). Cognate with Tocharian B kor (“throat”), Albanian cup (“odd, uneven”), Ancient Greek κύαρ (kúar, “eye of needle, earhole”), Old Armenian սոր (sor, “hole”), Sanskrit शून्य (śūnya, “empty, barre

parole.significato: A large cave.
parole.testo: From Middle English caverne, borrowing from Old French caverne, from Latin caverna (“hollow, cavity, cave”), from cavus (“hollow, excavated, concave”).

parole.significato: Resembling a cavern in size, shape, or atmosphere.
parole.testo: Late Middle English cavernous, cavernose, borrowing from Old French caverneux or Latin cavernōsus (“full of hollows or cavities”), from caverna (“a hollow, cavity, cave”) + -ōsus (“-ous, -ose”, adjectival suffix); equivalent to cavern + -ous.

parole.significato: To criticise for petty or frivolous reasons.
parole.testo: From Old French caviller (“mock, jest, rail”), from Latin cavillor (“jeer, mock, satirise, reason captiously”), from cavilla (“jeering, raillery, scoffing”); cognate with Italian cavillare, Portuguese cavillar, and Spanish cavilar; nominal usage developed within English from the original verbal usag

parole.significato: A coniferous tree of the genus Cedrus in the family Pinaceae.
parole.testo: From Middle English cedre, probably from Old French cedre, from Latin cedrus, from Ancient Greek κέδρος (kédros). Some suggest that the Middle English word was partially from Old English ċeder, but the gap in attestation between the two words makes this proposal unlikely. Possible doublet of citrus.

parole.significato: The overhead closure of a room.
parole.testo: From Middle English celing (“paneling; (bed) cover or hanging”), from celen (“to cover or panel walls”) (from Old French celer (“to conceal”)) + -ing (gerund-forming suffix). By surface analysis, ceil + -ing.

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Chelidonium.
parole.testo: From Middle English celidoine, Old French celidoine, French chélidoine, from Latin chelīdonia, from chelīdonius (“relating to the swallow”), from Ancient Greek χελιδόνιος (khelidónios), χελιδών (khelidṓn). It was traditionally supposed to flower when the swallows appeared, and to perish when they de

parole.significato: The formal performance of a solemn rite, such as Christian sacrament.
parole.testo: From Old French celebration, from Latin celebratio. Equivalent to celebrate + -ion.

parole.significato: A rite or ceremony.
parole.testo: From Middle English celebritē, from Old French celebrite (compare French célébrité), from Latin celēbritās.

parole.significato: Speed, swiftness.
parole.testo: From Old French celeritee (compare French célérité), from Latin celeritas, from celer (“fast, swift”).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or located in the sky or outer space, where the Sun, Moon, planets, and stars are visible.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English celestial (“relating to the heavens or sky; (Christianity) relating to heaven, divine, heavenly”), borrowed from Old French celestial (modern French céleste), from Medieval Latin caelestiālis (“celestial”), or directly from its etymon Latin caelestis

parole.significato: Synonym of celestial: of or resembling the heavens.
parole.testo: From Old French celestin, Latin caelestīnus, from caelestis (“heavenly”) + -inus (“-ine”), from caelum (“sky, heavens, Heaven”). Equivalent to celest + -ine.

parole.significato: A powdered substance produced by firing (calcining) calcium carbonate (limestone) and clay that develops strong cohesiv…
parole.testo: From Middle English syment, cyment, from Old French ciment, from Latin caementum (“quarry stone; stone chips for making mortar”), from caedō (“to cut, hew”). Doublet of cementum.

parole.significato: A place where the dead are buried; a graveyard or memorial park.
parole.testo: From Middle English cimiterie, from Old French cimitiere, from Medieval Latin cimitērium, from Late Latin coemētērium, from Ancient Greek κοιμητήριον (koimētḗrion), from κοιμάω (koimáō, “I put to sleep”); compare cœmeterium. Displaced Middle English charnel (“mass grave, cemetery”) and Old English l

parole.significato: A dining room, especially one on an upper floor (traditionally the room in which the Last Supper took place).
parole.testo: From Middle English cenacle, from Old French cenacle (modern French cénacle), from Latin cēnāculum (“dining room”).

parole.significato: A new or recent member of a Greek monastic religious order; a caloyer.
parole.testo: From Old French cenobite or Ecclesiastical Latin coenobīta, from coenobium, from Ancient Greek κοινόβιον (koinóbion, “community life, convent”), from κοινός (koinós, “common”) + βίος (bíos, “life”).

parole.significato: A census.
parole.testo: Old French cense, French cens, Latin census.

parole.significato: The act of blaming, criticizing, or condemning as wrong; reprehension.
parole.testo: From 1350–1400 Middle English censure, from Old French, from Latin censūra (“censor's office or assessment”), from censēre (“to consider, to assess, to value, to judge, to tax, etc.”).

parole.significato: A period of one hundred consecutive years; often specifically a numbered period with conventional start and end dates,…
parole.testo: From Middle English centurie (“a count of one hundred (of anything); a division of the Roman army; century; a division of land”), from Old French centurie, from Latin centuria, from centum (“one hundred”). The most common modern use is an ellipsis of century of years.

parole.significato: A fleshy, waxy area at the base of the upper beak in certain birds.
parole.testo: From Middle English sere, from Old French cire, from Latin cēra (“wax, cere”), or via Latin cērō (“to smear or coat with wax”).

parole.significato: Sure in one's mind, positive; absolutely confident in the truth of something.
parole.testo: From Middle English certeyn, certein, certain, borrowed from Old French certain, from a Vulgar Latin unattested form *certānus, extended form of Latin certus (“fixed, resolved, certain”), of the same origin as cretus, past participle of cernere (“to separate, perceive, decide”). Displaced native Mid

parole.significato: Certainly, indeed.
parole.testo: From Middle English certes, from Old French [Term?], from Latin certus (“certain”).

parole.significato: To attest to (a fact) as the truth.
parole.testo: From Old French certefier (“confirm, assure, make certain”). Compare French certifier.

parole.significato: Heat excited by friction.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English chaufen (“to warm”), borrowed from Old French chaufer (modern French chauffer), from Latin calefacere, calfacere (“to make warm”), from calere (“to be warm”) + facere (“to make”). See caldron.

parole.significato: A series of interconnected rings or links usually made of metal.
parole.testo: From Middle English cheyne, chaine, from Old French chaeine, chaene (“chain”), from Latin catēna (“chain”), from Proto-Indo-European *kat- (“to braid, twist; hut, shed”). Doublet of catena. Displaced native Middle English rakil and rakent (from Old English racente (“chain”)); see rackan.

parole.significato: To act as chairperson at; to preside over.
parole.testo: From Middle English chayere, chayer, chayre, from Old French chaiere, chaere, from Latin cathedra (“seat”), from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra), from κατά (katá, “down”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “seat”). Partially displaced native stool and settle, which now have more specialised senses. Doublet of cathedra

parole.significato: Not nonchalant; careful, attentive, or concerned.
parole.testo: A back-formation from nonchalant, itself from Old French non- + chalant (“concerning, bothering”). By this process, the original Old French participle was coincidentally re-formed.

parole.significato: A confrontation; a dare.
parole.testo: From Middle English chalenge, variant with palatalization of Middle English kalange (“an accusation, claim”), from Old French chalenge, chalonge, palatalized Central French variants of Old Northern French calenge, calonge (see Continental Norman calengier), from Latin calumnia (“a false accusation,

parole.significato: To enclose in a room.
parole.testo: From Middle English chambre, borrowed from Old French chambre, from Latin camera, from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára, “vaulted chamber”). Doublet of camera.

parole.significato: A high-ranking female servant who attends in a royal's or noble's chamber.
parole.testo: From Middle English chamberere, chamberer, from Old French chamberiere, feminine of chamberier; ultimately from Latin cambra (“room”). By surface analysis, chamber + -er.

parole.significato: A small to mid-size reptile, of the family Chamaeleonidae, and one of the best known lizard families able to change col…
parole.testo: From Middle English camelion, from Old French cameleon, from Latin chamaeleon, from Ancient Greek χαμαιλέων (khamailéōn), from χαμαί (khamaí, “on the earth, on the ground”) + λέων (léōn, “lion”); ultimately a calque from Akkadian 𒌨𒈤𒊭𒆠 (nēšu ša qaqqari, “chameleon, reptile”, literally “lion of the gr

parole.significato: Protective armor for a horse's head, especially the face and ears.
parole.testo: From Old French chanfrain, presumably from champ, chanp (“field, battlefield”) + frein (“bit (between a horse's teeth)”).

parole.significato: Open countryside, or an area of open countryside.
parole.testo: From Old French champaigne, from Late Latin campānia.

parole.significato: Having the quality of champerty; being an instance of champerty.
parole.testo: From Old French champart.

parole.significato: An ongoing winner in a game or contest.
parole.testo: From Middle English champioun, from Old French champion, from Medieval Latin campio (“combatant in a duel, champion”), from Frankish *kampijō (“fighter”), from Proto-West Germanic *kampijō (“combat soldier”), a derivative of *kampijan (“to battle, to campaign”), itself a derivative of *kamp (“battle

parole.significato: The killing of another in self-defence upon a sudden and unpremeditated encounter.
parole.testo: From Old French chance medlée, literally "mingled chance", with postpositive adjective (often confused because of the fact that medley is also a noun).

parole.significato: The space around the altar in a church or cathedral, often enclosed, for use by the clergy and the choir. In medieval c…
parole.testo: From Old French chancel. Doublet of cancellus.

parole.significato: The rank or post of a chancellor.
parole.testo: From Middle English chancelrie, from Old French chancelerie (Modern French chancellerie), from Late Latin cancellaria. Doublet of chancery.

parole.significato: A person who makes or sells candles.
parole.testo: From Middle English chaundeler, from Old French chandelier, from Latin candelarius (“a candle-maker; a candlestick”), from the Latin candela (“a candle”); compare the English term candle.

parole.significato: The hollow bed of running waters; (also) the bed of the sea or other body of water.
parole.testo: From Middle English chanel (also as canel, cannel, kanel), a borrowing from Old French chanel, canel, from Latin canālis (“groove; canal; channel”). Doublet of canal.

parole.significato: To sing, especially without instruments, and as applied to monophonic and pre-modern music.
parole.testo: From Middle English chaunten, from Old French chanter, from Latin cantāre (“sing”). Doublet of cant.

parole.significato: One who chants or sings.
parole.testo: From Middle English chauntour, from Old French chanteor, from Latin cantor; equivalent to chant + -er. Compare French chanteur. Doublet of cantor.

parole.significato: A domestic rooster or cock, especially in fables and fairy tales.
parole.testo: ] From Middle English Chauntecleer, from Old French Chantecler (modern French Chanteclair), the proper name of the cock in the literary cycle of Reynard the Fox, that also gave origin to chantecler, the name of a chicken breed; from chanter (“to sing, to crow”) + cler (“clear, clearly”). Attested in

parole.significato: A female singer or chanter.
parole.testo: From Middle English chaunteresse, from Old French chanteresse; equivalent to chanter + -ess.

parole.significato: An endowment for the maintenance of a priest to sing a daily mass for the souls of specified people.
parole.testo: From Middle English chaunterie, from Old French chanterie, from chanter (“to sing”).

parole.significato: A place of worship, smaller than or subordinate to a church.
parole.testo: From Middle English chapele, chapel, from Old French chapele, from Late Latin cappella (“little cloak; chapel”), diminutive of cappa (“cloak, cape”). Doublet of capelle. Displaced native Old English bēdhūs. (printing office): Said to be because printing was first carried on in England in a chapel ne

parole.significato: The district attached to a chapel; a division of a large parish which has its own district chapel.
parole.testo: From Old French chapelerie, corresponding to chapel + -ry.

parole.significato: A member of a religious body (who is often, although not always, of the clergy) officially assigned to provide pastoral…
parole.testo: From Middle English chapeleyn, from Old French chapelain, from Medieval Latin, Late Latin cappellānus, from cappella. Doublet of capelin. Displaced Old English handprēost.

parole.significato: One of the main sections into which a published work is divided, especially a book.
parole.testo: From Middle English chapitre, from Old French chapitre, from Latin capitulum (“a chapter of a book, in Medieval Latin also a synod or council”), diminutive of caput (“a head”); see capital, capitulum, and chapiter, which are doublets of chapter.

parole.significato: A letter or character.
parole.testo: From Old French characte, from Latin *characta, from Ancient Greek χαρακτός (kharaktós).

parole.significato: A being involved in the action of a story; a persona.
parole.testo: From Middle English caracter, from Old French caractere, from Latin character, from Ancient Greek χαρακτήρ (kharaktḗr, “type, nature, character”), from χαράσσω (kharássō, “to engrave”). Displaced native English thew from Old English þēaw (in the plural) and Old English hād (“person, character”). Dou

parole.significato: The amount of money levied for a service.
parole.testo: From Middle English chargen, from Old French chargier, from Late Latin carricō (“to load”), from Latin carrus (“a car, wagon”); see car. Doublet of cargo.

parole.significato: A two-wheeled horse-drawn cart, used in Bronze Age and Early Iron Age warfare.
parole.testo: From Middle English chariot, from Old French chariot, from char (“cart”), from Latin carrus (“wagon”), itself borrowed from Gaulish *karros, from Proto-Celtic *karros (“wagon”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥sós. Displaced native Old English hrædwæġn (literally “fast wagon”).

parole.significato: A person who drives a chariot.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English charioter, from Old French charioteur (“charioteer”) and charretier (“coachman”). By surface analysis, chariot + -eer.

parole.significato: Pertaining to charity.
parole.testo: From Old French charitable.

parole.significato: An organization, the objective of which is to carry out a charitable purpose.
parole.testo: From Middle English charite, from Old French charité, cherte, chariteit, cariteit, from Latin cāritās. * The Tyndale Bible uses native English love instead.

parole.significato: An object, act or words believed to have magic power (usually carries a positive connotation).
parole.testo: From Middle English charme, from Old French charme (“chant, magic spell”), from Latin carmen (“song, incantation”). Displaced native Old English lybb (“drug, poison, charm”).

parole.significato: A female charmer; an enchantress.
parole.testo: From Middle English charmeresses pl, from Old French; equivalent to charmer + -ess.

parole.significato: Part of a helm, now usually identified as the hinge (near the neck) by which the helm was secured to the breastplate.
parole.testo: From Old French charnel, from Latin cardinālis (“relating to a hinge”); related to French charnière.

parole.significato: Straight threads obtained by unraveling old linen cloth, used for surgical dressings.
parole.testo: From the feminine past participle of Old French charpir (“to pluck”), carpir (“to pluck”), from Latin carpō (“to pluck”). Compare carpet.

parole.significato: A document issued by some authority, creating a public or private institution, and defining its purposes and privileges.
parole.testo: From Middle English charter, chartre, borrowed from Old French chartre, from Latin chartula (diminutive of charta). See chart. Doublet of chartula.

parole.significato: A groove cut in an object; a slot: the chase for the quarrel on a crossbow.
parole.testo: Possibly from obsolete French chas (“groove”, “enclosure”), from Old French, from Latin capsa (“box”). Or perhaps a shortening or derivative of enchase. Doublet of case, cash, and chasse.

parole.significato: Something or someone who chases.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English chaser, chacer, chasour, borrowed from Old French chaceür, chaceor, from chacier (“to chase, hunt”); later senses from or influenced by chase (“pursue”) + -er. Doublet of chasseur.

parole.significato: A reliquary casket.
parole.testo: From Middle English chasse, variant of case, from Old French chasse. Doublet of case, cash, and chase.

parole.significato: Synonym of pure and virtuous, particularly
parole.testo: From Middle English chaste, from Old French chaste (“morally pure”), from Latin castus (“pure”).

parole.significato: To make chaste.
parole.testo: From Middle English chastien, from Old French chastier (“punish”), from Latin castīgō. Doublet of chastise and castigate and related to chaste.

parole.significato: To punish, especially by corporal punishment.
parole.testo: From Middle English chastisen, from Old French chastier, from Latin castīgō. See also the doublets chasten and castigate and cf. also chaste.

parole.significato: The act of chastising; rebuke; punishment.
parole.testo: Old French chastiement, from the verb chastier, from Latin castīgō

parole.significato: The quality of being chaste: the state of abstaining from any sexual activity considered immoral; avoidance of sexual s…
parole.testo: From Middle English chastite, from Old French chasteté, a semi-learned adaptation of Latin castitas, equivalent to chaste + -ity.

parole.significato: The outermost liturgical vestment worn by clergy for celebrating Eucharist or Mass, equivalent to the phelonion of the…
parole.testo: From Middle English chesible, from Old French chesible, from Late Latin casubla, an alteration of Latin casula (“little cottage, hooded cloak”), a diminutive of casa (“house”).

parole.significato: A little castle.
parole.testo: From Old French chastelet, diminutive of chastel. Compare castle.

parole.significato: Tangible, movable property.
parole.testo: From Middle English chatel, from Old French chatel, from Medieval Latin capitāle (English capital), from Latin capitālis (“of the head”), from caput (“head”) + -alis (“-al”). Compare the doublet cattle (“cows”), which is from an Anglo-Norman variant. Compare also capital and kith and kine (“all one’

parole.significato: The entrails of an animal, especially when used as a food ingredient; offal.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English chaudon, chaudoun, chaudron (“sauce made from chopped entrails”), from Old French chaudun (“animal entrails; sauce made from such entrails”) (modern French chaudin (“wrapping of sausages made from pigs’ intestines; Louisiana meat dish cooked in a pig’s stomach”)), from Late

parole.significato: To violate rules in order to gain, or attempt to gain, advantage from a situation.
parole.testo: Verb from Middle English achetan, variant of escheten, from Old French escheat, past participle of escheoir, escheoiter, from Late Latin *excadēre (“fall away, fall out”), from (Latin) ex- + cadere (“fall”). Displaced native Old English beswīcan. Noun from verb and/or Middle English chete, aphetic f

parole.significato: An escheater.
parole.testo: From Middle English chetour, a variant of eschetour, from Old French eschetour, escheteur, equivalent to escheat + -er.

parole.significato: An inspection or examination.
parole.testo: From Middle English chek, chekke, borrowed from Old French eschec, eschek, eschac, from Medieval Latin scaccus, borrowed from Arabic شَاه (šāh, “king or check at chess, shah”), borrowed from Classical Persian شَاه (šāh, “king”), from Middle Persian 𐭬𐭫𐭪𐭠 (mlkʾ /⁠šāh⁠/), from Old Persian 𐏋 (XŠ /⁠xšāya

parole.significato: To inspect; to examine.
parole.testo: From Middle English chekken, partly from Old French eschequier and partly from the noun (see above).

parole.significato: A pattern made up of a grid of squares of alternating colors; a checkered pattern.
parole.testo: By shortening from chequer, from Old French eschequier (“chessboard”), from Medieval Latin scaccarium, ultimately from the same Persian root as above.

parole.significato: Word called out by the victor when making a move that wins the game.
parole.testo: From Middle English chekmat, from Old French eschec mat, from Arabic شَاه مَاتَ (šāh māta), from Classical Persian شاه مات (šāh māt, “the king [is] amazed”).

parole.significato: A fetid water snake.
parole.testo: From Middle English chelidre, chelyder, chelydre, from Old French chelidre, chelydre, from Latin chelȳdrus (“fetid water serpent”), from Ancient Greek χέλυδρος (khéludros, “amphibious serpent”), from χέλυς (khélus, “tortoise”) + ὕδρος (húdros, “water serpent”). Cognate of French chélydre.

parole.significato: To treat with affection, care, and tenderness; to nurture or protect with care.
parole.testo: From Middle English charish, cherishen (“to have affection for, hold dear, treat kindly; to esteem, respect; to cherish; to take care of; to greet; to entertain, treat hospitably; to cheer; to encourage, incite”), from Old French cheriss-, chieriss-, extended stem of cherir, chierir (“to cherish”) (

parole.significato: A board game for two players, each beginning with sixteen chess pieces moving according to fixed rules across a chessbo…
parole.testo: From Middle English ches, chesse, from Old French eschés, plural of eschec, from Medieval Latin scaccus, from Arabic شَاه (šāh, “king [in chess]”), from Classical Persian شاه (šāh, “shah, king”), from Middle Persian 𐭬𐭫𐭪𐭠 (mlkʾ /⁠šāh⁠/), from Old Persian 𐏋 (XŠ /⁠xšāyaθiya⁠/). Compare German Schach an

parole.significato: Of a deep reddish-brown colour, like that of a chestnut fruit (noun sense 1).
parole.testo: The noun is a contraction of chest(en) (“(obsolete) chestnut tree; fruit of this tree, chestnut”) + nut. Chesten is a late variant of chesteine (obsolete), from Middle English chesten, chesteine, chasteine, chesteyne (“chestnut tree (Castanea sativa); fruit of this tree; wood of this tree”), from Ol

parole.significato: A capitation tax; an equal tax or tribute per person.
parole.testo: Old French chevage, from chief (“head”) + -age.

parole.significato: A military raid by cavalry through enemy territory, designed to disrupt rural communities and weaken an opponent.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English chyvachie, from Old French chevauchie, chevauchée, from Medieval Latin caballicāta; the modern form is after modern French chevauchée. Doublet of cavalcade.

parole.significato: To come to an issue; to turn out; to succeed.
parole.testo: From Middle English cheven, from Old French chevir. See chievance.

parole.significato: Kid, as used to make leather.
parole.testo: From Old French chevrele, diminutive form of chèvre (“goat”).

parole.significato: A chub (fish).
parole.testo: From Old French chevesne (“chub”), perhaps from chef (“head”). Compare chavender.

parole.significato: Provision(s), supply.
parole.testo: From Old French chevisance, from chevir (“provide”). The 'chivalrous adventure' sense is thought to be first used by Edmund Spenser, who incorrectly linked chevisance to Old French chevalerie (“chivalry”).

parole.significato: A V-shaped pattern; used in architecture, and as an insignia of military or police rank, on the sleeve.
parole.testo: From Middle English cheveroun, from Old French chevron, the mark so called because it looks like rafters of a shallow roof, from Vulgar Latin *capriō, from Latin caper (“goat”), the likely connection between goats and rafters being the animal's horns.

parole.significato: Either of two plants of the Asteraceae family.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English cicoree, cicory, cicorea, sicory, sycory (“common chicory (Cichorium intybus); heliotrope”), from Old French cicoree (modern French chicorée (“common chicory; endive; coffee substitute made from common chicory”)), or directly from its etymon Medieval Latin cicorea, cichorea,

parole.significato: The leader or head of a tribe, organisation, business unit, or other group.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English chef, borrowed from Old French chief, from Vulgar Latin capus, from Latin caput, from Proto-Italic *kaput, from Proto-Indo-European *káput, from *kap-, possibly from *kap-, possibly borrowed from a substrate language. Doublet of cape (“point of land”), capo, caput, and

parole.significato: A tribute by the chief; a kind of poll tax.
parole.testo: From Old French chevage, from chief (“head”). See chief.

parole.significato: A leader of a clan or tribe.
parole.testo: From Middle English cheveteyn, cheftayne, from Old French chevetaine, from Late Latin capitaneus (English captain), from Latin caput (“head”), from Proto-Indo-European *kauput- (English head), itself from Proto-Indo-European *kap-. Doublet of captain; related to chief.

parole.significato: An unlawful bargain; trade in which money is extorted as discount.
parole.testo: From Old French chevance (“property”), equivalent to chevisance, from chevir (“to accomplish”). See chevisance.

parole.significato: A toll paid for passage through a forest.
parole.testo: From Old French cheminage, from chemin (“way, road”).

parole.significato: A vertical tube or hollow column used to emit environmentally polluting gaseous and solid matter (including but not lim…
parole.testo: From Middle English chymeneye, chymneye, chymene, from Old French cheminee, from Late Latin camīnāta, from Latin camīnus, from Ancient Greek κάμῑνος (kámīnos, “furnace”). Doublet of chimenea.

parole.significato: The top of a ridge.
parole.testo: From Middle English chyne, from Old French eschine, from Frankish *skinu, from Proto-Germanic *skinō. Doublet of shin.

parole.significato: A doctor or surgeon.
parole.testo: From Middle English cirurgien, borrowed from Old French cirurgiien, itself borrowed from Vulgar Latin *chīrurgiānus or formed from the root of cirurgie, borrowed from Latin chirurgia, ultimately from Ancient Greek χειρουργός (kheirourgós). Doublet of surgeon.

parole.significato: Synonym of surgery.
parole.testo: From Old French cirurgerie. Compare surgery.

parole.significato: surgery
parole.testo: From Middle English cirurgie, from Old French cirurgie, from Latin chīrurgia. Doublet of surgery.

parole.significato: Honourable, especially to women; gallant.
parole.testo: From Middle English chivalerous, from Old French chevalerous; see chivalry.

parole.significato: Cavalry; horsemen armed for battle.
parole.testo: From Middle English chivalerie, a late 13th century loan from Old French chevalerie (“knighthood, chivalry, nobility, cavalry”) (11th century), the -erie (“-ery”) abstract of chevaler (“knight, horseman”), from Medieval Latin caballarius (“horseman, knight”), from caballus (“horse”). Medieval Latin

parole.significato: A perennial plant, Allium schoenoprasum, related to the onion.
parole.testo: From Middle English chive~cyve, from Old French chive~cive, from Latin cēpa (“onion”).

parole.significato: Containing the maximum amount possible, flush on all sides, jam-packed, crammed.
parole.testo: From Middle English chokkeful (“crammed full”) c. 1400, possibly from choke (“cheek”), equivalent to cheek + full. Or it may be from Old French choquier (“collide, crash, hit”), similar to shock. The later form chock-a-block full is due to association with chock, used in carpentry and shipbuilding.

parole.significato: A group of people who sing together; a company of people who are trained to sing together.
parole.testo: From Middle English quer, quere, from Old French quer, from Latin chorus, from Ancient Greek χορός (khorós, “company of dancers or singers”). Modern spelling influenced by chorus and French chœur. Doublet of quire, chorus, and hora. Displaced native Old English hād.

parole.significato: Yellow bile.
parole.testo: From Middle English coler (“yellow bile”), from Old French colere (“bile, anger”), from Latin cholera (“bilious disease”), from Ancient Greek χολή (kholḗ, “bile”). Doublet of cholera.

parole.significato: A believer in Christianity.
parole.testo: From Middle English Cristien, from Old French chrestien, from Latin Chrīstiānus, from Ancient Greek Χρῑστιᾱνός (Khrīstiānós), from Χρῑστός (Khrīstós, “Christ, anointed [one]”) + Latin suffix -ānus. The older form is Christen. Doublet of cretin. By surface analysis, Christ + -ian.

parole.significato: Being problematic over an extended period of time.
parole.testo: From chronical, from Old French cronike, from Latin chronicus, from Ancient Greek χρονικός (khronikós, “of time”), from χρόνος (khrónos, “time”). By surface analysis, chron- + -ic.

parole.significato: Originally, any of various green-coloured gems; later specifically peridot.
parole.testo: From Middle English crisolite, from Old French crisolite, from Medieval Latin crisolitus, Latin chrȳsolithus, from Ancient Greek χρῡσόλιθος (khrūsólithos), from χρῡσός (khrūsós, “gold”) + λίθος (líthos, “stone”). By surface analysis, chryso- (“pertaining to gold”) + -lite (“pertaining to rocks, mine

parole.significato: To heal a wound through scarring (by causing a scar or cicatrix to form).
parole.testo: From Old French cicatriser (French cicatriser), from Latin cicātrīx (“scar”), equivalent to cicatrix + -ise.

parole.significato: A costly cloth, of uncertain material, used in the Middle Ages.
parole.testo: From Middle English ciclatoun, from Old French siglaton, (chiefly) Anglo-French cyclaton and Anglo-Latin cyclaton, from Arabic سِقِلّاطُون (siqillāṭūn).

parole.significato: An alcoholic, often sparkling (carbonated) beverage made from fermented apples.
parole.testo: From Middle English sider, cidre, sidre, from Old French cisdre, sidre (“beverage made from fermented apples”), from Medieval Latin sīcera, from Ancient Greek σίκερα (síkera, “fermented liquor, strong drink”), from Hebrew שֵׁכָר (šēḵār, “liquor”). Doublet of cyser. Partially displaced earlier Englis

parole.significato: A wax candle used in religious rites.
parole.testo: From earlier cerge, from Middle English serge, cerge, from Old French cierge, cerge from Latin cereus (“waxy”), from cera (“wax”). The current pronunciation is learnedly taken from modern French cierge (with varying degrees of nativisation).

parole.significato: A kind of belt or other girdle.
parole.testo: From Middle English sengle, from Old French sengle, cengle (Modern French sangle), from Late Latin cingula, from Latin cingulum (“girdle”), from cingere (“to gird”). Doublet of cinch. Compare also Middle English kyngle, kyngll (“girdle, brooch”) from Old Norse kinga (“brooch”).

parole.significato: A deep red mineral, mercuric sulfide, HgS; the principal ore of mercury; such ore used as the pigment vermilion.
parole.testo: First attested in the mid-15th century. From Middle English cynabare, from Old French cinabre, from Latin cinnabaris, from Ancient Greek κιννάβαρι (kinnábari), of unknown origin.

parole.significato: A small evergreen tree native to Sri Lanka and southern India, Cinnamomum verum or Cinnamomum zeylanicum, belonging to…
parole.testo: From Middle English synamome, from Old French cinnamone, from Latin cinnamon, cinnamomum, from Ancient Greek κιννάμωμον (kinnámōmon), later κίνναμον (kínnamon), according to Herodotus from Phoenician [Term?], cognate with Hebrew קִנָּמוֹן (qinnāmōn).

parole.significato: A potentilla (flower).
parole.testo: From Old French cinqfoil, from cinq (“five”) + foil (“leaf”).

parole.significato: A numeric character.
parole.testo: 14th century. From Middle English cifre, from Old French cyfre, cyffre (French chiffre), ultimately from Arabic صِفْر (ṣifr, “zero, empty”), from صَفَرَ (ṣafara, “to be empty”). Doublet of chiffre and zero. Sense 8 (a fault in an organ valve) may be a different word.

parole.significato: To travel around along a curved path; to orbit.
parole.testo: From Middle English circle, cercle, from Old French cercle and Latin circulus, diminutive of Latin circus (“circle, circus”), from Ancient Greek κίρκος (kírkos, “circle, ring”), related to Old English hring (“ring”). Compare also Old English ċircul (“circle, zodiac”), which came from the same Latin

parole.significato: To move in a circle; to go round; to circulate.
parole.testo: From Middle English circuit, from Old French circuit, from Latin circuitus (“a going round”), from circuire (“go round”), from circum (“around”) + ire.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a circle.
parole.testo: From Middle English circuler, circuleer, circulere, from Old French circulier (French circulaire), from Late Latin circularis, from Latin circulus, diminutive of circus (“ring”). By surface analysis, circle + -ar.

parole.significato: To surgically remove the foreskin (prepuce) from the penis of.
parole.testo: From Middle English circumcisen, from Old French circumciser (modern French circoncire) and its etymon Latin circumcīsus, the past participle of circumcīdō (“cut around”), from circum (“about, around; through”) + caedō (“cut, hew”).

parole.significato: The surgical excision of the foreskin and usually all or most of the penile frenulum.
parole.testo: From Middle English circumcisioun, from Old French circumcisiun (modern French circoncision) and its etymon Latin circumcīsiō, from circumcīdō (“cut around”), from circum (“about, around; through”) + caedō (“cut, hew”). By surface analysis, circumcis(e) + -ion.

parole.significato: Something which is related to, or in some way affects, a fact or event.
parole.testo: From Middle English circumstaunce, from Old French circonstance, from Latin circumstantia.

parole.significato: A reservoir or tank for holding water, especially for catching and holding rainwater for later use.
parole.testo: From Middle English cisterne, from Old French cisterne (Modern French citerne) from Latin cisterna, from cista (“box”), from Ancient Greek κίστη (kístē, “box”). Doublet of cisterna.

parole.significato: An official summons or notice given to a person to appear.
parole.testo: From Middle English citacioun, from Old French citation, from Latin citātiō. By surface analysis, cite + -ation.

parole.significato: To quote; to repeat, as a passage from a book, or the words of another.
parole.testo: From Old French citer, from Latin citare (“to cause to move, excite, summon”), frequentative of ciēre (“to rouse, excite, call”). Sense 4 is the original one.

parole.significato: A large settlement, bigger than a town; sometimes with a specific legal definition, depending on the place.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English cite, derived from Old French cite, derived from Late Latin cīvitātem (“city”), in Classical Latin "citizenry", derived from cīvis (“fellow-citizen”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱey- (“lie down; settle”). Cognate with Old English hīwan pl (“members of one's ho

parole.significato: A kind of chive sauce served with game or seafood.
parole.testo: From Middle English cyvee, from Old French civé; equivalent to chive + -ey.

parole.significato: Having to do with people and government office as opposed to the military or religion.
parole.testo: From Middle English cyvyl, civil, borrowed from Old French civil, from Latin cīvīlis (“relating to a citizen”), from cīvis (“citizen”) ultimately from proto-Indo-European *ḱey-. Cognate with Old English hīwen (“household”), hīrǣden (“family”). More at hind; hird. (polite): Compare typologically urba

parole.significato: A person following the pursuits of civil life, especially one who is not an active member of the armed forces.
parole.testo: From Middle English cyvylien, from Old French civilien. Equivalent to civil + -ian.

parole.significato: A demand of ownership made for something.
parole.testo: From Middle English claimen, borrowed from Old French clamer (“to call, name, send for”), from Latin clāmō, clāmāre (“to call, cry out”), from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to shout”), which is imitative. See also Lithuanian kalba (“language”), Old English hlōwan (“to low, make a noise like a cow”),

parole.significato: One who claims; one who makes a claim.
parole.testo: From Old French and Anglo-Norman clamant, present participle of the verb clamer and its variants, from Latin clāmō (“to cry out”), equivalent to claim + -ant. Compare clamant.

parole.significato: A great outcry or vociferation; loud and continued shouting or exclamation.
parole.testo: Recorded in English since c. 1385, as Middle English clamour, from Old French clamor (modern clameur), from Latin clāmor (“a shout, cry”), from clāmō (“cry out, complain”). The verb sense "to silence" may have a distinct (unknown) etymology.

parole.significato: Synonym of gonorrhea.
