parole.significato: To make smaller; to press or squeeze together, or to make something occupy a smaller space or volume.
parole.testo: From Middle English compressen, from Old French compresser, from Late Latin compressare (“to press hard/together”), from Latin compressus, the past participle of comprimō (“to compress”), itself from com- (“together”) + premō (“press”).

parole.significato: To be made up of; to consist of (especially a comprehensive list of parts).
parole.testo: From Middle English comprisen, from Old French compris, past participle of comprendre, from Latin comprehendere, contr. comprendere, past participle comprehensus (“to comprehend”); see comprehend. Compare apprise, reprise, surprise.

parole.significato: A pricking of conscience or a feeling of regret, especially one which is slight or fleeting.
parole.testo: From Middle English compunccion, borrowed from Old French compunction, from Late Latin compunctionem (“a pricking”), from Latin compunctus, the past participle of compungere (“to severely prick”), from com- + pungere (“to prick”).

parole.significato: Curved like the inner surface of a sphere or bowl.
parole.testo: From Middle English concave, from Old French concave, from Latin concavus.

parole.significato: The state of being concave
parole.testo: From Old French concavité. Morphologically concave + -ity.

parole.significato: To hide something from view or from public knowledge, to try to keep something secret.
parole.testo: From Middle English concelen, from Old French conceler (“hide, disguise”), from Latin concēlō, concēlāre (“carefully disguise”).

parole.significato: The practice of keeping secrets.
parole.testo: From Old French concelement (“concealment, secrecy”). By surface analysis, conceal + -ment.

parole.significato: To yield or suffer; to surrender; to grant
parole.testo: From Middle English [Term?], from Old French conceder, from Latin concēdō (“give way, yield”), from con- (“wholly”) + cēdō (“to yield, give way, to go, grant”), from Proto-Indo-European *ked- (“to go, yield”).

parole.significato: Something conceived in the mind; an idea, a thought.
parole.testo: From Middle English conceyte, formed from conceyven by analogy with pairs such as (Modern English) deceive~deceit, receive~receipt etc. Doublet of concept and concetto. Akin to Portuguese conceito.

parole.significato: To have a child; to become pregnant (with).
parole.testo: From Middle English conceyven, from Old French concevoir, conceveir, from Latin concipiō, concipere (“to devise, to conceive”).

parole.significato: The act of conceiving.
parole.testo: From Middle English concepcioun, borrowed from Old French conception, from Latin conceptiō (“a comprehending, a collection, composition, an expression, also a becoming pregnant”), from concipiō, past participle conceptus (“conceive”); see conceive. Equivalent to conceive + -tion.

parole.significato: The end, finish, close or last part of something.
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French conclusion, from Latin conclūsiō, from the past participle stem of conclūdere (“to conclude”), from con- + claudō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂u- (“key, hook, nail”). By surface analysis, conclude + -sion.

parole.significato: Agreement; accordance; consonance.
parole.testo: From Old French concordance, from Late Latin concordantia.

parole.significato: Agreement; concurring.
parole.testo: From Old French concurrence.

parole.significato: Happening at the same time; simultaneous.
parole.testo: From Middle English concurrent, from Old French concurrent, from Latin concurrēns, present active participle of concurrō (“happen at the same time”), from con- (“with”) + currō (“run”).

parole.significato: To strongly criticise or denounce; to excoriate.
parole.testo: From Middle English condempnen, from Old French condamner, from Latin condemnāre (“to sentence, condemn, blame”), from com- + damnāre (“to harm, condemn, damn”), from damnum (“damage, injury, loss”). Displaced native Middle English fordemen (from Old English fordeman (“condemn, sentence, doom”) > Mo

parole.significato: To come down or go down; to descend.
parole.testo: From Middle English condescenden, condescendre (“to deign, condescend; to accede graciously; to agree; to agree to, give consent; to make a concession, yield; etc.”), from Old French condescendre (“to descend, go down; to agree or assent to”) (modern French condescendre), from Ecclesiastical Latin c

parole.significato: Fitting, appropriate, deserved, especially denoting punishment.
parole.testo: From Middle English condigne, from Old French condigne, from Latin condignus, from con- + dignus (“worthy”). Compare deign.

parole.significato: Something used to enhance the flavor of food, for example, salt or pepper, especially when added by the eater to taste…
parole.testo: From late Middle English condiment, from Old French condiment, from Latin condimentum, from condīre (“to preserve, pickle, season”). See also condite and compare recondite.

parole.significato: A state or quality.
parole.testo: From Middle English condicioun, from Old French condicion (French condition), from Latin condicio. An unetymological change in spelling due to a confusion with conditio. Displaced native Old English hād (“state, condition”).

parole.significato: A channel or pathway through which something is conducted, carried, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English conduyt, condit, from Old French conduit, from Latin conductus. Doublet of conduct.

parole.significato: A food item prepared very sweet, frequently decorated in fine detail, and often preserved with sugar, such as a candy,…
parole.testo: From Middle English confescioun, borrowed from Old French confeccion (French confection), borrowed from Latin cōnfectiōnem, from cōnfectus, past participle of cōnficiō (“prepare”), from con- (“with”) + faciō (“to make, do”). By surface analysis, confect + -ion. Originally "the making by means of ing

parole.significato: To confederate.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English confederen (“to confederate; to organize a conspiracy”), borrowed from Old French confederer or directly from Late Latin confoederō. Doublet of confederate.

parole.significato: The open admittance of having done something (especially something bad).
parole.testo: From Middle English confessioun, from Old French confession, from Latin cōnfessiō, cōnfessiōnem (“confession, acknowledgment, creed or avowal of one's faith”). Displaced native Old English andetnes. Doublet of confessio. Morphologically confess + -ion. Sense 6 is a calque of 告白 (kokuhaku).

parole.significato: To set up or arrange something in such a way that it is ready for operation for a particular purpose, or to someone's p…
parole.testo: From Old French configurer, from Latin configurare. See configurate.

parole.significato: To strengthen; to make firm or resolute.
parole.testo: From Middle English confirmen, confermen, from Old French confermer, from Latin cōnfirmāre (“to make firm, strengthen, establish”), from con- (“together”) + firmāre (“to make firm”), from firmus (“firm”).

parole.significato: An official indicator that things will happen as planned.
parole.testo: From Middle English confirmacioun, from Old French confirmacion, from Latin cōnfirmātiō, noun of process from cōnfirmātus (“confirmed”), perfect passive participle of cōnfirmāre, from con- (“with”) + firmāre (“to firm or strengthen”). Morphologically confirm + -ation.

parole.significato: A colleague or fellow, especially a professional one.
parole.testo: From Old French confrere, from Latin confrāter. The word which was originally only used for the second sense became obsolete in the 17th century and reappeared in the mid 18th century as a re-borrowing of Modern French confrère whence the first sense is from.

parole.significato: Synonym of confused.
parole.testo: From Middle English confus, from Old French confus, from Latin cōnfūsus, past participle of cōnfundō.

parole.significato: A lack of clarity or order.
parole.testo: From Middle English confusioun, from Old French confusion, from Latin confusio, confusionem. Morphologically confuse + -ion.

parole.significato: Lawful; done with permission from authority.
parole.testo: From Old French congeable; from congeer + -able.

parole.significato: Leave, formal permission for some action, (originally and particularly)
parole.testo: From late Middle English congie, from Old French congié, congiet (modern French congé), from Latin commeātus (“passage, permission to leave”), from commeō (“to go and come”), from con- + meō (“to go, to pass”). Figurative senses generally borrowed from developments in French congé.

parole.significato: Any of several scaleless marine eels, of the genus Conger, found in coastal waters
parole.testo: From Middle English congre, from Old French congre, from Latin conger, from Ancient Greek γόγγρος (góngros), from Proto-Indo-European *geng-, *gong- (“a lump, rounded object”).

parole.significato: The hindrance or blockage of the passage of something, for example a fluid, mixture, traffic, people, etc. (due to an e…
parole.testo: From late Middle English congestioun, from Old French [Term?], from Latin congestĭō (“heap, accumulation”), from congerō (“to bring together, accumulate, heap up”), formed by the root gerō (“to carry”) and the prefix con-.

parole.significato: The act of congregating or collecting together.
parole.testo: From Middle English congregacioun, from Old French congregacion, from Latin congregātiō, itself from congregō (“to herd into a flock”). Adopted (1520s) by the English Bible translator William Tyndale, to render the Ancient Greek ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía, “those called together, (popular) meeting”) (hence

parole.significato: The quality of agreeing; the quality of being suitable and appropriate.
parole.testo: From Old French congruité.

parole.significato: A statement or an idea which is unproven, but is thought to be true; a guess.
parole.testo: From Old French, from Latin coniectūra (“a guess”), from coniectus, perfect passive participle of cōniciō (“throw or cast together; guess”), from con- (“together”) + iaciō (“throw, hurl”); see jet. Compare adjective, eject, inject, project, reject, subject, object, trajectory, deject, abject, surjec

parole.significato: To join together; to unite; to combine.
parole.testo: From Old French conjoindre, from Latin coniungo, from con- (“together”) + iungo (“join”). Equivalent to con- + join.

parole.significato: The act of joining, or condition of being joined.
parole.testo: From Old French conjonction, from Latin coniūnctiō (“joining”), from coniungere (“to join”).

parole.significato: To perform magic tricks.
parole.testo: From Middle English conjuren, from Old French conjurer, from Latin coniūrō (“to swear together; conspire”), from con- (“with, together”) + iūro (“to swear or take an oath”).

parole.significato: To defeat in combat; to subjugate.
parole.testo: From Middle English conqueren, from Old French conquerre, from Late Latin conquaerere (“to knock, strike; to search for, procure”), from Latin con- + quaerere (“to seek, acquire”). Displaced native Old English oferwinnan.

parole.significato: A female conqueror.
parole.testo: From Middle English conqueresse, conquiris, conquires, probably from Old French; equivalent to conquer + -ess.

parole.significato: Someone who conquers.
parole.testo: From Middle English conquerour, from Old French conquereor, from conquerre. By surface analysis, conquer + -or.

parole.significato: An act or instance of achieving victory through combat; the subjugation of an enemy.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English conquest, borrowed from Old French conqueste.

parole.significato: The ethical or moral sense of right and wrong, chiefly as it affects a person’s own behaviour and forms their attitude…
parole.testo: From Middle English conscience, from Old French conscience, from Latin conscientia (“knowledge within oneself”) (a calque of Ancient Greek σῠνείδησῐς (sŭneídēsĭs)), from consciens, present participle of conscire (“to know, to be conscious (of wrong)”), from com- (“together”) + scire (“to know”).

parole.significato: To express willingness, to give permission.
parole.testo: Recorded in Middle English since circa 1225, borrowed from Old French consentir, from Latin cōnsentīre (“to agree; to assent, consent”), itself from com- (“with”) + sentiō (“to feel”) (whence con-).

parole.significato: One who consents.
parole.testo: From Middle English consenter, consentour, from Old French consenteor and partly from Middle English consenten; equivalent to consent + -er.

parole.significato: An effect; something that follows a cause as a result.
parole.testo: From Middle English consequence, from Old French consequence, from Latin consequentia. While analysable as con- + sequence, its adjective form has a different origin.

parole.significato: The act of preserving, guarding, or protecting; the keeping (of a thing) in a safe or entire state; preservation.
parole.testo: From Old French. By surface analysis, conserve + -ation.

parole.significato: Wilderness where human development is prohibited.
parole.testo: From Middle English conserven, from Old French conserver, from Latin conservare (“to keep, preserve”), from com- (intensive prefix) + servo (“keep watch, maintain”). See also observe.

parole.significato: The thought process of considering, of taking multiple or specified factors into account (with of being the main corres…
parole.testo: From Middle English consideracioun, from Old French consideracion, from Latin cōnsīderātiō. By surface analysis, consider + -ation.

parole.significato: The act or example of consoling; the condition of being consoled.
parole.testo: From Old French consolacion (French consolatio), from Latin cōnsōlātiō, from the deponent verb cōnsōlor (“I console, encourage”) with the -tiō suffix, while cōnsōlor comprises the intensifying prefix con- with the deponent verb sōlor (“I comfort, console”). Equivalent to console + -ation. Doublet of

parole.significato: A sound that results from the passage of air through restrictions of the oral cavity; any sound that is not the dominan…
parole.testo: From Middle English consonant or consonaunt, from Old French consonant, from Latin cōnsonāns (“sounding with”), from the prefix con- (“with”) + the present participle sonāns (“sounding”), from sonāre (“to sound”). The Latin is a calque of Ancient Greek σύμφωνον (súmphōnon).

parole.significato: Any of several healing plants of the genera Symphytum, Consolida, Ajuga, Bellis, etc., especially comfrey.
parole.testo: Inherited from the Middle English consoude, consowde, consol, consold, consaud, consaude, from the Old English consolde, borrowed from the Old French consolde, consoulde, consoude, inherited from the Latin cōnsolida (“common confrey”), so called because of its supposed healing power.

parole.significato: To secretly plot or make plans together, often with the intention to bring bad or illegal results; to collude, to conni…
parole.testo: From Middle English conspiren, from Old French conspirer, from Latin conspirare, conspīrō, from con- (combining form of cum (“with”)) + spīrō (“breathe”).

parole.significato: One holding the lowest rank in most Commonwealth police forces. (See also chief constable.)
parole.testo: From Middle English constable, cunstable, constabil, connestable, cunestable, from Old French conestable, from Latin comes stabulī (“officer of the stables”). For the sense-development; compare marshal. Doublet of connétable.

parole.significato: Unchanged through time or space; permanent.
parole.testo: From Middle English constant, from Old French constant, from Latin constantem, accusative of constans, from cōnstāre (“to stand firm”). Displaced native Old English singal.

parole.significato: An arbitrary formation of stars perceived as a figure (especially one from mythology) or pattern, or a division of the…
parole.testo: PIE word  *ḱóm From Middle English constellacioun, constillacioun (“(astrology) position of the moon or a planet in relation to the ascendant sign of the zodiac; horoscope; (astronomy) formation of fixed stars, constellation; (astronomy) elevation or position of the sun”) [and other forms], borrowed

parole.significato: The act, or process of setting something up, or establishing something; the composition or structure of such a thing; i…
parole.testo: PIE word  *ḱóm From Middle English constitucioun, constitucion (“edict, law, ordinance, regulation, rule, statute; body of laws or rules, or customs; body of fundamental principles; principle or rule (of science); creation”) from Old French constitucion (modern French constitution), a learned borrow

parole.significato: Belonging to, or inherent in, the constitution or structure of one's body or mind.
parole.testo: PIE word  *ḱóm From constitution + -al (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). Constitution is derived from Middle English constitucioun, constitucion (“edict, law, ordinance, regulation, rule, statute; body of laws or rules, or customs; body of fundamental principles; principle o

parole.significato: To force physically, by strong persuasion or pressuring; to compel; to oblige.
parole.testo: From Middle English constreinen, from Old French constreindre, from Latin cōnstringō, from cōn- (“with, together”) + stringō (“to draw, bind or tie tight”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *streyg- (“to stroke, to shear, stiff”).

parole.significato: Something that constrains; a restriction.
parole.testo: From Middle English constreynt, constreynte, from Old French constreinte, past participle of constreindre (“to constrain”), from Latin cōnstringō (corresponding to the past participle cōnstrictus).

parole.significato: The process of constructing.
parole.testo: From Middle English construccioun, construction, from Old French construction, from Latin cōnstructiō, from cōnstruere. Morphologically construct + -ion.

parole.significato: To use up.
parole.testo: From Middle English consumen, from Old French consumer, from Latin cōnsūmere, cōnsūmō, from con- (“with, together”) + sūmō (“take; consume”), from sub- + emō (“to buy, take”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁em- (“to take, distribute”), possibly related to the root *nem- (“to take or give one

parole.significato: The act of eating, drinking or using.
parole.testo: From con- + Latin sūmptus + -ion, from Middle English consumpcioun, from Old French consumpcion, from Latin cōnsūmptiō, from cōnsūmō + -tiō, from con- (“with, together”) + sūmō (“take; consume”). Equivalent to consume + -tion.

parole.significato: A disease spread by contact.
parole.testo: From Middle English (late 14th century), from Old French, from Latin contāgiō (“a touching, contact, contagion”) related to contingō (“touch closely”).

parole.significato: Easily transmitted to others.
parole.testo: From Old French contagieus, from Late Latin contagiosus, from contagio.

parole.significato: To hold inside.
parole.testo: From Middle English conteinen, borrowed from Old French contenir, from Latin continēre (“to hold or keep together, comprise, contain”), combined form of con- (“together”) + teneō (“to hold”).

parole.significato: Someone who contains; something that contains.
parole.testo: From Middle English conteiner, equivalent to contain + -er.

parole.significato: To disdain; to value at little or nothing; to treat or regard with contempt.
parole.testo: From Middle English contempnen, from Old French contemner, from Latin contemnō (“to scorn”). See also contempt.

parole.significato: The act of contemplating; being highly concentrated in thought; musing.
parole.testo: From Middle English contemplacioun, from Old French contemplation, from Latin contemplatio. By surface analysis, contemplate + -ion.

parole.significato: Inclined to contemplate; introspective and thoughtful; meditative.
parole.testo: From Middle English contemplatyve, contemplatyf, from Old French contemplatif, from Latin contemplātīvus.

parole.significato: To be in opposition; to contest; to dispute; to vie; to quarrel; to fight.
parole.testo: From Middle English contenden, borrowed from Old French contendre, from Latin contendere (“to stretch out, extend, strive after, contend”), from com- (“together”) + tendere (“to stretch”); see tend, and compare attend, extend, intend, subtend.

parole.significato: Argument, contest, debate, strife, struggle.
parole.testo: From Middle English contencion, borrowed from Old French contencion, from Latin contentio, contentionem, from contendō (past participle contentus); equivalent to contend + -tion (similar formation to attention).

parole.significato: The voluntary control of urination and defecation.
parole.testo: Dated from the 14th century as Middle English contynence, from Old French continence, from Latin continentia (“a repression”). See also countenance.

parole.significato: Exercising self-restraint; controlled, temperate with respect to one’s bodily needs or passions, especially sex.
parole.testo: From Middle English contynent, from Old French continent, from Latin continentem (“continuous; holding together”), present participle of continēre (“to contain”).

parole.significato: An event which may or may not happen; that which is unforeseen, undetermined, or dependent on something in the future.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French contingent (whence con- and -ent), from Medieval Latin contingens (“possible, contingent”), present participle of contingere (“to touch, meet, attain to, happen”), from com- (“together”) + tangere (“to touch”).

parole.significato: Recurring in steady, rapid succession.
parole.testo: From Middle English continuel, from Old French continuel, formed from Latin continuus (“continuous”) with the suffix -el, equivalent to continue + -al.

parole.significato: The action of continuing.
parole.testo: From Middle English continuance, contynuaunce, from Old French continuance, from continuer.

parole.significato: The act or state of continuing or being continued; uninterrupted extension or succession
parole.testo: From Middle English continuacion, from Old French continuation, from Latin continuātiō. Morphologically continue + -ation.

parole.significato: To proceed with (doing an activity); to prolong (an activity).
parole.testo: From Middle English continuen, from Old French continuer, from Latin continuō. Displaced native Middle English thurghwonen, from Old English þurhwunian.

parole.significato: An agreement between two or more parties, to perform a specific job or work order, often temporary or of fixed duration…
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French contract, from Latin contractus (noun), from contrahere (“to bring together, to bring about, to conclude a bargain”) [from con- (“with, together”) + trahere (“to draw, to pull”)] + -tus (suffix forming nouns from verbs).

parole.significato: Senses relating to becoming involved with or entering into, especially entering into a contract.
parole.testo: PIE word  *ḱóm From Late Middle English contraccioun, contraxion (“spasm, contraction; constriction, shrinking; act of pressing together”), from Old French contraction (modern French contraction), from Latin contractiō(n) (“a drawing together, contraction; abridgement, shortening; dejection, despond

parole.significato: The act of contradicting.
parole.testo: From Middle English contradiccioun, contradiction, from Old French contradiction, from Latin contrādictiō, from contrādīcō (“speak against”).

parole.significato: Contrary or antagonistic.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English contrariaunt, from Old French contrariant, from Late Latin contrāriāns, present participle of contrāriō.

parole.significato: Tending to counter, oppose, resist, argue.
parole.testo: From contrary + -ous, from Middle English contrarious, from Old French contrarious, from Late Latin contrāriōsus.

parole.significato: Opposite; in an opposite direction; in opposition; adverse.
parole.testo: From Middle English contrarie, compare French contraire, from Old French contraire, from Latin contrārius (“opposite, opposed, contrary”), from contrā (“against”).

parole.significato: Something given or offered that adds to a larger whole.
parole.testo: From Middle English contribucioun, contribucion, from Old French contribution, from Latin contribūtiōnem, contribūtiō, from Latin contribuēre. By surface analysis, contribute + -ion.

parole.significato: To make sad, to upset.
parole.testo: From Old French (and modern French) contrister, from Latin contrīstō, from con- + tristis (“sad”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of contristate.

parole.significato: Sincerely penitent or feeling regret or sorrow, especially for one’s own actions.
parole.testo: From Middle English contrit, from Old French contrit, from Latin contrītus (literally “ground to pieces”), perfect passive participle of conterō (“grind, bruise”), from con- + terō (“rub, wear away”).

parole.significato: The state of being contrite; sincere penitence or remorse.
parole.testo: From Old French contriciun (French contrition), from Latin contrītiō.

parole.significato: To invent by an exercise of ingeniosity; to devise
parole.testo: From Middle English contreve (“to invent”), from Old French controver (Modern French controuver), from trover (“to find”) (French trouver).

parole.significato: To exercise influence over; to suggest or dictate the behavior of.
parole.testo: From Middle English controllen, from Old French contrerole, from Medieval Latin contrārotulus (“a counter-roll or register used to verify accounts”), from Latin contrā (“against, opposite”) + Medieval Latin rotulus, Latin rotula (“roll, a little wheel”), diminutive of rota (“a wheel”). Partly displa

parole.significato: A debate or discussion of opposing opinions; (generally) strife.
parole.testo: From Middle English controversie, from Old French controversie, from Latin contrōversia (“debate, contention, controversy”), from contrōversus (“turned in an opposite direction”).

parole.significato: Rudely contemptuous; showing contumely; exhibiting an insolent or disdainful attitude.
parole.testo: From Old French contumelieus, from Latin contumēliōsus (“insulting; abusive”), from contumēlia (“affront, abuse, insult”).

parole.significato: Offensive and abusive language or behaviour; scorn, insult.
parole.testo: From Old French contumelie, from Latin contumēlia (“insult”), perhaps from com- + tumeō (“swell”).

parole.significato: A religious community whose members live under strict observation of religious rules and self-imposed vows.
parole.testo: From Middle English convent, variant of covent, from Old French covent, from Latin conventus, perfect participle of the verb convenio (whence ultimately convene), see con- + venio. Doublet of coven.

parole.significato: Closely familiar; current; having frequent interaction.
parole.testo: From Old French conversant, present participle of converser.

parole.significato: Expression and exchange of individual ideas through talking with other people; also, a set instance or occasion of such…
parole.testo: From Middle English conversacioun, from Old French conversacion and its etymon, Latin conversātiōnem, accusative singular of conversātiō (“conversation”), from conversor (“abide, keep company with”). Displaced native Old English wordlaþu. Doublet of conversazione. Morphologically converse + -ation.

parole.significato: To talk; to engage in conversation.
parole.testo: From Old French converser, from Latin conversor (“live, have dealings with”).

parole.significato: To transform or change (something) into another form, substance, state, or product.
parole.testo: From Middle English converten, from Old French convertir, from Latin converto (“turn around”).

parole.significato: Able to be converted
parole.testo: From Old French convertible, from Late Latin convertibilis (“interchangeable”), from Latin convertere (“to turn back, to turn over, to turn around, to turn upside down”), from con- (“with, together”) + vertere (“to turn”), + -ibilis (“-ible: able to”). Equivalent to convert + -ible.

parole.significato: To move (something) from one place to another.
parole.testo: From Middle English conveien, from Old French conveier (French convoyer), from Vulgar Latin *convio, from Classical Latin via (“way”). Compare convoy.

parole.significato: The act of calling or assembling by summons.
parole.testo: From Middle English convocacioun, from Old French convocation, from Latin convocatio, convocationem.

parole.significato: One or more merchant ships sailing in company to the same general destination under the protection of naval vessels.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French convoier, another form of conveier, from Vulgar Latin *convio (compare Medieval Latin convio (“to accompany on the way”)), from Latin con- (“together”) + via (“way”).

parole.significato: Joint inheritance or ownership of property.
parole.testo: From co- + parcenary (from the Old French parçonerie).

parole.significato: Any of several people who share an inheritance; coheir
parole.testo: Old French copartsonnier, see co- + parcener.

parole.significato: To deal effectively with something, especially if difficult.
parole.testo: From Middle English coupen, from Old French coper, couper (“to strike, to cut”). The noun use went mainstream around 2020.

parole.significato: A tailed pepper plant (Piper cubeba), an Indonesian plant cultivated for its berries and essential oil.
parole.testo: From Middle English quibibe, from Old French quibibe, cubebe, from Arabic كُبَابَة (kubāba). The current form is remodelled after modern French cubèbe.

parole.significato: A man married to an adulterous spouse, especially when he is unaware or unaccepting of the fact.
parole.testo: From Middle English cokolde, cokewold, cockewold, kukwald, kukeweld, from Old French cucuault; a compound of cucu (“cuckoo”) and Old French -auld. The word references the behavior of cuckoo birds where they lay their eggs in another bird’s nest. Cucu is either a directly derived onomatopoeic derivat

parole.significato: To make the call of a cuckoo.
parole.testo: From Middle English cokkou, kokkow, cukkuk, gokkouȝ, probably from Old French cocu, coquu, cucu (whence French coucou); ultimately onomatopoeic of the song of the male Common Cuckoo (Cuculus canorus), perhaps via Latin cucūlus (“cuckoo”). Compare dialectal English gowkoo (“cuckoo”). Displaced Middle

parole.significato: A vine in the gourd family, Cucumis sativus.
parole.testo: From Middle English cucumer, cucumber, from Old French cocombre, ultimately from Latin cucumis, cucumerem (possibly through an Old Occitan intermediate). Probably of Pre-Italic substrate origin. First attested in the late 14c. Displaced native English earthapple (see which for more), which has since

parole.significato: A piece of defensive armor, covering the body from the neck to the girdle.
parole.testo: First use appears c. 1464. From Middle English curasse, curesse, from Old French cuirace, spelling influenced by modern French cuirasse.

parole.significato: An item of leather body armor, a forerunner to the cuirass; a cuirass.
parole.testo: From Middle English quyrre, now respelled according to or reborrowed from its source, Old French cuirie (French cuirie).

parole.significato: A small or light cuisse.
parole.testo: From Middle English quischete, Old French cuissete (modern French cuissette).

parole.significato: To pick or take someone or something (from a larger group).
parole.testo: From Middle English cullen, cuilen, coilen, from Old French cuillir (“collect, gather, select”), from Latin colligō (“gather together”). Doublet of coil.

parole.significato: Synonym of testicle.
parole.testo: From Middle English coilon, borrowed from Old French coillon (“testicle, vile fellow, coward, dupe”), from Vulgar Latin *cōleōnem, from Latin cōleus (“sack, scrotum”). Doublet of culeus and cojones.

parole.significato: Meriting condemnation, censure or blame, especially as something wrong, harmful or injurious; blameworthy, guilty.
parole.testo: From Middle English culpable, from Old French culpable, from Latin culpābilis (“blameworthy”), from culpō (“to blame, condemn”), from culpa (“a fault, crime, mistake”). Compare also culprit.

parole.significato: smartweed
parole.testo: From Old English culrage, culrache; probably from Old French cul (“the buttock”) + rage; compare French curage.

parole.significato: The degradation of a vassal to the position of a serf.
parole.testo: From Old French culvert (“serf”).

parole.significato: The flowering plant Cuminum cyminum, in the family Apiaceae.
parole.testo: From Middle English comyn, from Old English cymen (which is cognate with Old High German kumin) and Old French cummin, both from Latin cuminum, from Ancient Greek κύμινον (kúminon), a Semitic borrowing ultimately to be traced to Akkadian 𒂵𒈬𒉡 (Ú.GAMUN /⁠kamūnu⁠/, “cumin”). Possibly related to caraway

parole.significato: The relationship of a godmother to the other godparents (godsibs or gossips), and the legal parents, of a child.
parole.testo: From Middle English commare, from Old French commere (modern French commère), from Late Latin commāter.

parole.significato: Capable of being cured.
parole.testo: From Middle English curable, curabyll, from Old French curable. By surface analysis, cure + -able.

parole.significato: The act of curating, of organizing and maintaining a collection of artworks or artifacts.
parole.testo: From Middle English curacioun, curacion, from Old French curacion, from Latin cūrātiō.

parole.significato: A method, device or medication that restores good health.
parole.testo: From Middle English cure, borrowed from Old French cure (“care, cure, healing, cure of souls”), from Latin cura (“care, medical attendance, cure”). Displaced native Old English hǣlu, but this survived as heal.

parole.significato: To restore to health.
parole.testo: From Middle English curen, from Old French curer, from Latin cūrāre. Partially displaced Old English ġehǣlan, whence Modern English heal.

parole.significato: Any regulation requiring people to be off the streets and in their homes by a certain time.
parole.testo: From Middle English curfu, from Old French cuevre-fu (French couvre-feu), from the imperative of covrir (“to cover”) + fu (“fire”). Compare kerchief.

parole.significato: Any of several migratory wading birds in the genus Numenius, remarkable for their long, slender, downcurved bills.
parole.testo: From Middle English curlew, from Old French courlieu (see French courlis), claimed to be imitative of the bird's cry but apparently assimilated with dialectal *corliu (“runner, messenger”), a variant of coureur (the bird is adept at running).

parole.significato: Existing or occurring at the moment.
parole.testo: From Middle English curraunt, borrowed from Old French curant (French courant), present participle of courre (“to run”), from Latin currere (“to run”) (present participle currens). Doublet of courant.

parole.significato: A specialist in the leather processing industry, who dresses the leather by beating, rubbing, scraping and colouring.
parole.testo: From Old French corier, from Latin coriarius (“tanner, currier”).

parole.significato: To groom (a horse); to dress or rub down a horse with a curry comb.
parole.testo: From Middle English currayen, from Old French correer (“to prepare”), presumably from Vulgar Latin *conredare, from Latin com- (a form of con- (“with; together”)) + a verb derived from Proto-Germanic *raidaz. More at ready.

parole.significato: To cut short the tail of (an animal).
parole.testo: Alteration of curtal, from Old French courtault (“which has been shortened”), itself from court (“short”) (from Latin curtus) + -ault

parole.significato: A piece of cloth covering a window, bed, etc. to offer privacy and keep out light.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English curtine, from Old French cortine, from Late Latin cōrtīna (“curtain”), a calque from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A soft mass of material stuffed into a cloth bag, used for comfort or support.
parole.testo: From Middle English quysshyn, from later Old French coissin (modern coussin), from Vulgar Latin *coxīnus (“seat pad”), derived from Latin coxa (“hip, thigh”) (with the suffix possibly after Latin pulvīnus (“pillow”)), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *koḱs- (“joint, limb”).

parole.significato: A small cushion or pad, of various uses.
parole.testo: From Old French coissinet, French coussinet. See cushion and compare coussinet.

parole.significato: A habitual patron, regular purchaser, returning client; a person or company who has a custom of buying from a particula…
parole.testo: From Middle English custumer, from Old French coustumier, costumier (compare modern French coutumier), from Medieval Latin custumarius (“a toll-gatherer, tax-collector”, noun), from custumarius (“pertaining to custom or customs”, adjective), from custuma (“custom, tax”). More at custom. By surface a

parole.significato: A knight's attendant or man-at-arms; a knave.
parole.testo: From Old French coustillier (“soldier armed with a coustille (“double-edged sword”)”).

parole.significato: A kitchen-worker, a scullion; any worthless person.
parole.testo: From Middle English quistroun et al., from Old French coistron, quistron et al., from Late Latin cocistrōnem, accusative of cocistro.

parole.significato: Sharp cutting utensils.
parole.testo: From Middle English cotellerie, cutleri (“the cutler’s art or craft”), from Old French coutelerie (modern French coutellerie).

parole.significato: A knife.
parole.testo: From Middle English coutel, from Old French coutel, coltel, cultel, from Latin cultellus. Doublet of couteau. See cutlass.

parole.significato: A concave plate of metal, usually brass or bronze, that produces a sharp, ringing sound when struck: played either in p…
parole.testo: From Middle English cymbal, from Old English cimbal, cimbala and Old French cimbale, both from Latin cymbalum (“cymbal”), from Ancient Greek κύμβαλον (kúmbalon), from κύμβη (kúmbē, “bowl”). See also chime.

parole.significato: An evergreen coniferous tree with flattened shoots bearing small scale-like leaves, whose dark foliage is sometimes ass…
parole.testo: From Middle English cipres, from Old French cipres (French cyprès), from Late Latin cypressus; compare Hebrew גֹּפֶר (gōp̄er), the name of the tree whose wood was used to make the ark (Genesis. vi:14), also κύπρος (relating to aromatic pitch).

parole.significato: A shoal-forming fish of species Leuciscus leuciscus, common to swift rivers in England and Wales and in Europe.
parole.testo: Old variant of earlier darse, from Late Middle English darse (also as dace already), from Old French darz, oblique plural form of dart (“spear; javelin”). For a similar loss of r, compare bass, while for the pronunciation with /eɪ/, see scarce.

parole.significato: A skewer.
parole.testo: From Old French dague (from Old Occitan dague, of uncertain origin, perhaps from Vulgar Latin *daca (“Dacian knife”), from the Roman province Dacia (roughly modern Romania); the ending is possibly the faintly pejorative -ard suffix, as in poignard (“dagger”)); cognate with dagger.

parole.significato: Elegant; delicately small and pretty.
parole.testo: From Middle English deynte (as noun), from Old French deintié, from Latin dignitātem. Doublet of dignity.

parole.significato: Playful flirtation; amorous play.
parole.testo: From Middle English daliaunce et al., from dalien (“to exchange pleasantries, to chat; to flirt”), from Old French dalier, dailer. By surface analysis, dally + -ance.

parole.significato: Injury or harm; the condition or measure of something not being intact.
parole.testo: From Middle English damage, from Old French damage, from Vulgar Latin *damnāticum from Classical Latin damnum. Compare modern French dommage. Largely displaced native Middle English scath (whence unscathed). Cognate with Spanish daño, Portuguese dano, Italian danno, French dam, Romanian daună.

parole.significato: The doing of damage; in particular, the doing by animals such as cattle of damage by trespassing.
parole.testo: From an Old French phrase (compare modern French faisant dommage).

parole.significato: To condemn.
parole.testo: From Middle English dampnen, from Old French damner, from Latin damnāre (“to condemn, inflict loss upon”), from damnum (“loss”).

parole.significato: Capable of being damned.
parole.testo: From Middle English dampnable, from Old French dampnable, from Latin damnābilis. By surface analysis, damn + -able.

parole.significato: The state of being damned; condemnation; openly expressed disapprobation.
parole.testo: From Middle English dampnacioun, from Old French dampnacion, from Latin damnatio.

parole.significato: To damage physically; to injure.
parole.testo: From Old French damnifier, from Latin damnifico.

parole.significato: A young woman (of noble birth).
parole.testo: From Middle English dameisele, from Old French damoisele, from Vulgar Latin *domnicella, a diminutive from Classical Latin domina (“mistress, lady”), from dominus, from *demh₂-. Doublet of demoiselle, doncella, and donzella.

parole.significato: Any of the several species of plant in the genus Taraxacum, characterised by yellow flower heads and notched, broad-end…
parole.testo: From Middle English dentdelyon, from Old French dent de lion (“lion's tooth”), also in Latin dēns leōnis, referring to the jagged shape of the plant's leaves. The term is now rare in French (together with liondent, calque from Germanic), but compare Spanish diente de león, Portuguese dente-de-leão,

parole.significato: A pointed missile weapon, intended to be thrown by the hand; for example, a short lance or javelin.
parole.testo: From Middle English dart, from Old French dart, dard (“dart”), from Medieval Latin dardus, from Frankish *darōþu (“dart, spear”), from Proto-Germanic *darōþuz (“dart, spear”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰerh₃- (“to leap, spring”). Compare Old High German tart (“javelin, dart”), Old English daroþ, de

parole.significato: The fruit of the date palm, Phoenix dactylifera, somewhat in the shape of an olive, containing a soft, sweet pulp and e…
parole.testo: From Middle English date, from Old French date, datil, datille, from Latin dactylus (likely via Old Provençal datil), from Ancient Greek δάκτυλος (dáktulos, “finger”) (from the resemblance of the date to a human finger), probably a folk-etymological alteration of a word from a Semitic source such as

parole.significato: The addition to a writing, inscription, coin, etc., which specifies the time (especially the day, month, and year) when…
parole.testo: From Middle English date, from Old French date, from Late Latin data, from Latin datus (“given”), past participle of dare (“to give”); from Proto-Indo-European *deh₃- (“to give”). Doublet of data.

parole.significato: A spar formerly used on board of ships, as a crane to hoist the flukes of the anchor to the top of the bow, without inj…
parole.testo: The word davit is derived from Middle English and Old French daviot, which is a diminutive of David; thus it means "little David", maybe because those small cranes can handle a much bigger lifeboat.

parole.significato: To lower in character, quality, or value; to degrade.
parole.testo: From de- + base, from Old French bas, from Latin bassus. Cognate with Spanish debajo (“under, beneath, below”). Compare abase.

parole.significato: Open to debate; not fully proved or confirmed.
parole.testo: From Old French debatable (French débattable), equivalent to debate + -able.

parole.significato: To participate in a debate; to dispute, argue, especially in a public arena.
parole.testo: From Middle English debaten, from Old French debatre (“to fight, contend, debate, also literally to beat down”), from Romanic desbattere, from Latin dis- (“apart, in different directions”) + battuō (“to beat, to fence”).

parole.significato: An argument, or discussion, usually in an ordered or formal setting, often with more than two people, generally ending…
parole.testo: From Middle English debat, borrowed from Old French debat, deverbal of debatre, see Etymology 1 for more.

parole.significato: A state of physical or mental weakness.
parole.testo: From Middle English debylite, from Old French debilité (French débilité), from Latin dēbilitās (“weakness”), from dēbilis (“weak”), from dē- + habilis (“able”).

parole.significato: Gracious, courteous.
parole.testo: Via Middle English debonaire from Old French de bon aire (“of good stock; noble”).

parole.significato: The quality of being debonair; debonair character, graciousness.
parole.testo: Old French debonaireté.

parole.significato: Surmounted by an ordinary (or something else).
parole.testo: See debruise. Compare Old French debruisier (“to shatter, break”). Compare bruise.

parole.significato: An action, state of mind, or object one has an obligation to perform for another, adopt toward another, or give to anot…
parole.testo: From Middle English dette, dett, borrowed from Old French dete (French dette), from Medieval Latin dēbita, from Latin dēbitum (“what is owed, a debt, a duty”), neuter of dēbitus, perfect passive participle of dēbeō (“to owe”), contraction of *dehibeō (“I have from”), from de (“from”) + habeō (“to ha

parole.significato: A person or firm that owes money; one in debt; one who owes a debt.
parole.testo: From Middle English dettour, from Old French detour, from Latin debitor, equivalent to debt + -or. Doublet of debitor. Displaced native Old English *sċola.

parole.significato: A group, set, or series of ten , particularly
parole.testo: From Middle English decade, from Old French decade, from Late Latin decādem (“(set of) ten”), from Ancient Greek δεκάς (dekás), from δέκα (déka, “ten”). In reference to a span of ten years, originally a clipping of the phrase decade of years. By surface analysis, dec- + -ade. Doublet of decad and de

parole.significato: Death, departure from life.
parole.testo: From Old French deces (Modern French décès), from Latin dēcessus (“departure”).

parole.significato: No longer alive; dead.
parole.testo: From decease + -ed, from Middle English deceas via Old French [Term?], from Latin dēcessus (“departure”), equivalent to dēced-, variation of dēcēdō, dēcēdere (“to go away”).

parole.significato: An act or practice intended to deceive; a trick.
parole.testo: From Middle English deceyte, from Old French deceite, deçoite, from decevoir (“to deceive”), from Latin dēcipere (“to cheat, mislead”).

parole.significato: An instance of actions and/or schemes fabricated to mislead someone into believing a lie or inaccuracy.
parole.testo: From Middle English decepcioun, from Old French decepcion, from Latin dēcipiō (“to deceive”).

parole.significato: To resolve (a contest, problem, dispute, etc.); to choose, determine, or settle.
parole.testo: From Middle English deciden, from Old French decider, from Latin dēcīdere, infinitive of dēcīdō (“cut off, decide”), from dē (“down from”) + caedō (“cut”).

parole.significato: An emphatic or formal act of saying, telling or asserting something, by speech or writing; a decisive assertion or proc…
parole.testo: From Middle English declaration, declaracion, declaracioun, from Old French declaration (French déclaration), from Latin dēclārātiōnem, accusative of Latin dēclārātiō.

parole.significato: To make clear, explain, interpret.
parole.testo: From Middle English declaren, from Old French declarer, from Latin dēclārō (“to make clear”), from dē- + clārus (“clear”).

parole.significato: An extraction or essence of something, obtained by boiling it down.
parole.testo: From Old French decoccion, decoction, from Latin decoctiō, from decoquō (“to boil down”), from de- + coquō (“to cook”).

parole.significato: An edict or law.
parole.testo: From Middle English decre, decree, from Old French decré (French décret), from Latin dēcrētum.

parole.significato: An award made by an arbiter.
parole.testo: From Old French decré arbitral.

parole.significato: The final judgment of the Court of Session, or of an inferior court, by which the question at issue is decided.
parole.testo: From Old French decré, decreet.

parole.significato: The act of dedicating or the state of being dedicated.
parole.testo: Originated 1350–1400 from Middle English dedicacioun, from Old French dedicacion (“consecration of a church or chapel”), from Latin dēdicātiō, equivalent to dēdicātus+-iōn.

parole.significato: To damage or vandalize something, especially a surface, in a visible or conspicuous manner.
parole.testo: From Middle English defacen, from Old French defacier, desfacier (“to mutilate, destroy, disfigure”), from des- (“away from”) (see dis-) + Late Latin facia.

parole.significato: The act of injuring another person's reputation by any slanderous communication, written or oral; the wrong of maliciou…
parole.testo: From Old French diffamacion (French diffamation), from Latin diffāmātiō. By surface analysis, defame + -ation.

parole.significato: The condition of failing to meet an obligation.
parole.testo: From Middle English defaut, defaute, from Old French defaute (“fault, defect, failure, culpability, lack”), ultimately from Latin de- (“away”) + fallo (“deceive, cheat, escape notice of”).

parole.significato: Having one or more defects.
parole.testo: From Middle English defectif, defective, from Old French defectif, from Late Latin dēfectīvus.

parole.significato: The action of defending, of protecting from attack, danger or injury.
parole.testo: From Middle English defens, defense, from Old French defens, defense, from Late Latin dēfēnsa (“protection”). Displaced Old English bewering.

parole.significato: To furnish with defences; to fortify.
parole.testo: From Middle English defencen, defensen, from Old French defenser or its etymon, Latin dēfēnsō.

parole.significato: To ward off attacks against; to fight to protect; to guard.
parole.testo: From Middle English defenden, from Old French defendre, deffendre (Modern French défendre), from Latin dēfendō (“to ward off”), from Proto-Italic *fendō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰen-. Displaced native Old English bewerian.

parole.significato: Capable of being defended.
parole.testo: From Old French deffendable (French défendable), from défendre + -able.

parole.significato: Serving, or suitable, for defense; defensive, defending.
parole.testo: From Middle English defendaunt (“defending; defending in a suit”), borrowed from Old French defendant, present participle of defendre, from Latin dēfendere.

parole.significato: In civil proceedings, the party responding to the complaint; one who is sued and called upon to make satisfaction for a…
parole.testo: From Middle English defendaunt (“defendant in a suit; defender”), borrowed from Old French defendant, nominalisation of defendant; see above.

parole.significato: female defender.
parole.testo: From Middle English defenderesse, from Old French defenderesse; equivalent to defender + -ess.

parole.significato: The action of defending or protecting from attack, danger, or injury.
parole.testo: From Middle English defens, defense, from Old French defens, defense, from Late Latin dēfēnsa (“protection”). Displaced native Old English bewering. The verb is from the noun.

parole.significato: To furnish with defenses; to defend, protect.
parole.testo: From Middle English defencen, defensen, from Old French defenser or its etymon, Latin dēfēnsō.

parole.significato: Capable of being defended against armed attack.
parole.testo: From Old French defensable, from Latin defensibilem. Equivalent to defense + -ible.

parole.significato: To delay or postpone.
parole.testo: Originally a variant of (and hence a doublet of) differ; from Middle English differren (“to postpone”), from Old French differer, from Latin differō. Doublet of differ and dilate. See also infer, collate and confer, delate and defer, relate and refer as well as prelate and prefer among others.

parole.significato: The feeling, or spirit of being defiant.
parole.testo: From Middle English defiaunce, from Old French desfiance, from desfier. By surface analysis, defy + -ance.

parole.significato: To make (someone or something) physically dirty or unclean; to befoul, to soil.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English defilen (“to make dirty, befoul; rape; abuse; destroy; injure; oppress”) [and other forms], a variant of defoulen (“to make dirty, defile, pollute; have sexual intercourse with; rape; etc.”) (compare also defoilen). Defoulen is a blend of Middle English foulen (“to make dirt

parole.significato: To determine with precision; to mark out with distinctness; to ascertain or exhibit clearly.
parole.testo: From Middle English definen, from Old French definer, variant of definir, from Latin dēfīniō (“limit, settle, define”), from dē + fīniō (“set a limit, bound, end”).

parole.significato: the act of deflowering
parole.testo: From Old French desfloracion (French défloration), from Latin defloratio.

parole.significato: To take the virginity of (somebody), especially a woman or girl.
parole.testo: From Middle English deflouren, from Old French desflorer (modern French déflorer), from Late Latin deflōrāre. By surface analysis, de- + flower.

parole.significato: To defile or despoil.
parole.testo: From Middle English defoil (“to defile”), from Old French defouler.

parole.significato: To withhold land unlawfully from its true owner or from any other person who has a right to the possession of it, after…
parole.testo: From Old French.

parole.significato: A keeping out by force or wrong; a wrongful withholding, as of lands or tenements, to which another has a right.
parole.testo: Old French

parole.significato: A deforciant.
parole.testo: Old French

parole.significato: One who keeps out of possession the rightful owner of an estate.
parole.testo: From Old French deforciant, present participle of deforcier. See deforce.

parole.significato: To change the form of (something), usually thus making it disordered or irregular; to give (something) an abnormal or u…
parole.testo: From Middle English deformen (“to disfigure, distort, or mar; (figuratively) to disfigure morally; to defame; to dishonour”) [and other forms], equivalent to de- + form, from Old French deformer [and other forms] (modern French déformer (“to contort, distort, twist out of shape; (figuratively) to pe

parole.significato: The act of deforming, or state of being deformed.
parole.testo: From Old French deformation, see deform. Morphologically deform + -ation.

parole.significato: To trample underfoot.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English defoulen, from Old French defouler.

parole.significato: To obtain money or property from (a person) by fraud; to swindle.
parole.testo: From Middle English defrauden, from Old French defrauder, from de- + frauder.

parole.significato: Privation by fraud; defrauding
parole.testo: From Old French defraudement.

parole.significato: To challenge (someone) or brave (a hazard or opposition).
parole.testo: From Old French desfier, from Vulgar Latin *disfidare (“renounce one's faith”), from Latin dis- (“away”) + fidus (“faithful”). Meaning shifted in the 14th century from "be disloyal" to "challenge". Contrast confide, fidelity, faith.

parole.significato: A completed curriculum of study in tertiary education.
parole.testo: From Middle English degre, borrowed from Old French degré (French: degré), itself from Latin gradus, with the prefix de-.

parole.significato: To consider it appropriate or worthy to do or give (something), often when it is seen as beneath one's dignity; to cond…
parole.testo: From Middle English deinen, deynen (“to consider (something) suitable to one’s dignity or worth, condescend; to appear worthy; to condescend to grant (something), permit, vouchsafe; to regard (someone) as worthy; to consecrate, dedicate (something)”), from Old French daigner, degnier, deigner, deign

parole.significato: Make sad or dispirited.
parole.testo: From Old French dejeter, from Latin dēiectus, past participle of dēicere (“to throw down”), from dē- (“from, down from”) + iacere (“to throw”).

parole.significato: A state of melancholy or depression; low spirits, the blues.
parole.testo: From Old French dejection, from Latin dejectio (“a casting down”). By surface analysis, deject + -ion.

parole.significato: To dilute, temper.
parole.testo: From Middle English delaien, from Old French delaiier, a variant of delaissier.

parole.significato: Great pleasure; delight.
parole.testo: Attested from the mid 14th century, from Old French delectation (“enjoyment”), from Latin dēlectātiōnem, accusative singular of dēlectātiō, from the verb Latin dēlectō (“to delight, charm, please”), frequentative of dēliciō, from de- (“away”) + laciō (“to lure, to deceive”), from Proto-Italic *lakjō

parole.significato: A person authorized to act as representative for another; a deputy.
parole.testo: From Middle English delegat, from Old French delegat, from Latin dēlēgātus substantivized from the nominative masculine singular of dēlēgātus, the perfect passive participle of dēlēgō (“to send, assign, delegate”), see -ate (noun-forming suffix). See also legate.

parole.significato: The act of deliberating, or of weighing and examining the reasons for and against a choice or measure; careful consider…
parole.testo: From Middle English deliberacioun, from Old French deliberation, from Latin deliberātiō. Morphologically deliberate + -ion.

parole.significato: Delight, pleasure, especially sensual pleasure.
parole.testo: From Old French delice, from Latin dēlicium.

parole.significato: Joy; pleasure.
parole.testo: Attested from the 13th century, from Middle English delite, from Old French deleiter, deliter, from Latin dēlectāre (“to delight, please”), frequentative of dēlicere (“to allure, entice”), from dē- (“away”) + laciō (“to lure, to deceive”), from Proto-Italic *lakjō (“to draw, pull”), of unknown ultim

parole.significato: Delightful.
parole.testo: From Middle English delitable, from Old French delitable. By surface analysis, delight + -able. Piecewise doublet of delectable.

parole.significato: delightful
parole.testo: From Middle English delitous, from Old French delitos.

parole.significato: The act of setting free or extricating from danger, imprisonment, bondage, evil, etc.
parole.testo: From Old French deliverance (French délivrance), equivalent to deliver + -ance.

parole.significato: A great flood or rain.
parole.testo: From Middle English deluge, from Old French deluge, alteration of earlier deluvie, from Latin dīluvium, from dīluō (“wash away”). Doublet of diluvium.

parole.significato: The desire to purchase goods and services.
parole.testo: From late Middle English demaunden, from Old French demander, from Latin dēmandō, dēmandāre. Displaced native Old English ġiwian (“to demand”).

parole.significato: The social, non-verbal behaviors (such as body language and facial expressions) that are characteristic of a person.
parole.testo: From Middle English demenure, from the verb Middle English demenen, demeinen (“to handle, manage”), from Old French demener (“to guide, conduct”), from de- + mener (“to conduct, lead”), from Latin *mināre (“to drive”) and minor (“to project or jut forth”).

parole.significato: A quality of being inadequate; a disadvantage, a fault.
parole.testo: From Middle English demerit, demerite, from Old French desmerite (modern French démérite) and its etymon Latin dēmeritum. By surface analysis, de- + merit.

parole.significato: The ball of the foot, the padded front part of the sole behind the tip of the toes; hence, a ballet position executed w…
parole.testo: From demi- (“half”) + pointe (“tip of the toe”), via Old French demi from Latin dīmidius (“halved”), combined with French pointe (“point, tip”) from Late Latin pūnctum; in this sense short for pointe des pieds (“tippy-toe”, literally “tip of the feet”); cf. French sur la pointe des pieds (“on tiptoe

parole.significato: The process of demolishing or destroying buildings or other structures.
parole.testo: From Old French demolition, from Latin dēmōlītiō (“a tearing down”). Equivalent to demolish + -ion.

parole.significato: Possessed or controlled by a demon.
parole.testo: From Middle English demoniak et al., from Old French demoniaque, from Late Latin daemoniacus.

parole.significato: Able to be demonstrated.
parole.testo: From Middle English demonstrable, from Old French.

parole.significato: demonstration; proof
parole.testo: From Middle English demonstraunce, from Old French demonstrance.

parole.significato: The act of demonstrating; showing or explaining something.
parole.testo: From Middle English demonstracioun, from Old French demonstration, from Latin dēmōnstrātiōnem, from dēmōnstrāre (“show or explain”), from dē- (“of or concerning”) + mōnstrāre (“show”). Morphologically demonstrate + -ion.

parole.significato: An act of objecting or taking exception; a scruple; also, an exception taken or objection to something.
parole.testo: From Middle English demure, demore (“a delay, demur; a sojourn, stay”), from Old French demure, demore, demuere (“a delay, demur”) (modern French demeure), from Old French demorer, demourer (verb): see etymology 1.

parole.significato: the detention of a ship or other freight vehicle, during delayed loading or unloading
parole.testo: 1640s, from Old French demorage, from demorer (English demur), from Latin dēmorārī (“to tarry”). By surface analysis, demur (“delay”) + -age, with doubled ‘r’ to clarify pronunciation and avoid ambiguity with demure.

parole.significato: An inhabitant of a place; one who dwells in a certain place.
parole.testo: From Middle English denisein, from Old French denzein, from deinz (“within”) + -ein, from Late Latin dē intus (“from within”), whence French dans.

parole.significato: The act of naming or designating.
parole.testo: From Middle English denominacioun, from Old French denominacion, from Latin dēnōminātiō. By surface analysis, denominate + -ion.

parole.significato: To make known in a formal manner; to proclaim; to announce; to declare.
parole.testo: From Old French denuncier, from Latin dēnūntiō (“to announce, to denounce, to threaten”), from de + nūntiō (“to announce, to report, to denounce”), from nūntius (“messenger, message”). Doublet of denunciate.

parole.significato: To disallow or reject.
parole.testo: From Middle English denyen, from Old French denoier (“to deny, to repudiate”) (French dénier), from Latin denegare (“to deny, to refuse”), from de- (“away”) and negare (“to refuse”), the latter ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *né (“no, not”). Doublet of denegate.

parole.significato: To leave.
parole.testo: From Old French departir, from Late Latin departiō (“to divide”), from dē- (“away from”) + partiō (“part, divide”).

parole.significato: The act of departing or something that has departed.
parole.testo: From Old French deporteure (“departure; figuratively, death”). By surface analysis, depart + -ure.

parole.significato: To be contingent or conditioned; to have something as a necessary condition
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English dependen, from Old French dependre, from Latin dependeō, from dē- + pendeō (“to be suspended, hang”). In this sense, displaced native Old English hangian (“to hang or depend”).

parole.significato: To waste away; to deteriorate.
parole.testo: From Middle English deperishen, from Old French deperiss-, extended stem of deperir, from Latin deperīre (“to die down, to perish gradually”).

parole.significato: To put down; to lay down; to deposit; to lay aside; to put away.
parole.testo: Recorded since c.1300, from Middle English, from Old French deposer, from de- (“down”) + poser (“to put, place”). Deposition (1494 in the legal sense) belongs to deposit, but that related word and depose became thoroughly confused.

parole.significato: The removal of someone from office.
parole.testo: From Middle English deposicion, from Old French deposicion (French déposition), from Latin depositio.

parole.significato: To speak ill of; to depreciate; to malign; to revile
parole.testo: From Middle English depraven, from Old French depraver, from Latin dēprāvāre (“pervert, distort, corrupt”), from de- + pravus (“crooked, distorted, perverse, wicked”).

parole.significato: To press down.
parole.testo: From Middle English depressen, from Old French depresser, from Latin dēpressus, perfect participle of dēprimō (“to press down, to weigh down”), from dē- (“off, away, down, out”) + premō (“to press”).

parole.significato: A state of mind producing serious, long-term lowering of enjoyment of life or inability to visualize a happy future; an…
parole.testo: From Middle English depression, depressioun, from Old French depression, from Latin dēpressiō. Equivalent to depress + -ion.

parole.significato: Used with “of”, to take something away from (someone) and keep it away; to deny someone something.
parole.testo: From Middle English depryven, from Old French depriver, from Medieval Latin dēprīvō, from Latin dē- + prīvō.

parole.significato: To prove or refute, especially through combat.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English dereynen, from Old French deraisnier (“to explain, defend, to maintain in legal action by proof and reasonings”), from Late Latin derationare (“to discourse, contend in law”).

parole.significato: Disorder, disturbance.
parole.testo: From Old French derroi, desroi, desrei, from des- (from Latin dis-) + roi, rei, rai (“order”). See array and disarray.

parole.significato: Act of treating with disdain.
parole.testo: From Old French derision, from Latin dērīsiōnem, accusative of dērīsiō, from dērīdēre ("to mock, to laugh at, to deride").

parole.significato: To obtain or receive (something) from something else.
parole.testo: From Middle English deriven, from Old French deriver, from Latin dērīvō (“to lead, turn, or draw off (a liquid), draw off, derive”), from dē (“away”) + rīvus (“a stream”); see rival. Unrelated to arrive.

parole.significato: An act which belittles; disparagement.
parole.testo: From Old French derogacion (French dérogation), from Latin dērogātiō.

parole.significato: The act of descending; descent.
parole.testo: From Old French descendance, or descend + -ence.

parole.significato: Descent; the act of descending.
parole.testo: From Middle English descencioun, from Old French descension, from Latin dēscēnsiō, dēscēnsiōnem.

parole.significato: To represent in words.
parole.testo: From Middle English descriven, from Old French descrivre, from Latin dēscrībō (“to copy off, transcribe, sketch off, describe in painting or writing”), from dē (“off”) + scrībō (“write”); see scribe and shrive. Displaced native Old English āmearcian.

parole.significato: A person who descries.
parole.testo: From Old French descrier (“to proclaim, announce, cry”).

parole.significato: A sketch or account of anything in words; a portraiture or representation in language; an enumeration of the essential…
parole.testo: From Middle English descripcioun, from Old French description and its etymon, Latin dēscrīptiō, noun of action of dēscrībō (“to describe”). Equivalent to describe + -tion.

parole.significato: To describe.
parole.testo: Old French descrivre. See describe.

parole.significato: A barren area of land or desolate terrain, especially one with little water or vegetation; a wasteland.
parole.testo: From Middle English desert (“wilderness”), from Old French desert, from Latin dēsertum, past participle of dēserō (“to abandon”). Generally displaced native Old English wēsten. False cognate of Egyptian dšrt.

parole.significato: That which is deserved or merited; a just punishment or reward.
parole.testo: From Middle English desert, deseert, from Old French deserte, from deservir (“to deserve”), from Vulgar Latin dēserviō (“to gain or merit by giving service”).

parole.significato: To be entitled to, as a result of past actions; to be worthy to have.
parole.testo: From Middle English deserven, from Old French deservir, from Latin dēserviō, from dē- + serviō.

parole.significato: A specification of an object or process, referring to requirements to be satisfied and thus conditions to be met for th…
parole.testo: From Middle English designen, from Old French designer, from Latin designō (“to mark out, point out, describe, design, contrive”), from de- (or dis-) + signō (“to mark”), from signum (“mark”). Doublet of designate.

parole.significato: Worthy to be desired; pleasing; agreeable.
parole.testo: From Old French desirable. Morphologically desire + -able.

parole.significato: To want; to wish for earnestly.
parole.testo: From Middle English desir, desire (noun) and desiren (verb), from Old French desirer, desirrer, from Latin dēsīderō (“to long for, desire, feel the want of, miss, regret”), apparently from de- + sidus (in the phrase de sidere, "from the stars") in connection with astrological hopes. Compare consider

parole.significato: Feeling desire; eagerly wishing; eager to obtain.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French desirrous, from desirrer + -ous.

parole.significato: To scatter, to disparkle.
parole.testo: From Old French desparpeillier.

parole.significato: Worthy to be despised.
parole.testo: From Middle English despisable, from Old French.

parole.significato: To regard with contempt or scorn.
parole.testo: From Middle English despisen, from Old French despis-, stem of despire, from Latin dēspicere (“to look down upon, despise, scorn”), from dē (“down”) + speciō (“to look at”). Displaced native Old English forsēon.

parole.significato: In spite of, notwithstanding.
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Middle English despit, dispit, from Old French despit, from Latin dēspectum (“looking down on”), from dēspiciō (“to look down, despise”). The preposition is derived from Middle English dispit, itself derived from the phrase in dispit of (in despite of). Compare typologically

parole.significato: To vex; to annoy; to offend contemptuously.
parole.testo: From Middle English despite, dispite, dyspite, dyspyte, from Old French despitier.

parole.significato: To plunder; to pillage; take spoil from.
parole.testo: From Middle English despoylen, dispoylen, from Old French despoillier ( > French dépouiller), from Latin dēspoliō, dēspoliāre.

parole.significato: Plunder; spoliation.
parole.testo: From Middle English despoylle, dispoyll, from Old French despoille, despueille, deverbal from despoillier.

parole.significato: To preordain.
parole.testo: From Middle English destinen, from Old French destiner. Doublet of destinate.

parole.significato: That to which any person or thing is destined; a predetermined or inevitable eventual state; a condition predestined by…
parole.testo: From Middle English destine et al., from Old French destinee, from Latin dēstinō (English destine). Displaced Old English wyrd.

parole.significato: The action of deserting or abandoning.
parole.testo: From Old French destitution, from Latin dēstitūtiō (“abandoning”), from dēstituō.

parole.significato: To damage beyond use or repair; to damage (something) to the point that it effectively ceases to exist.
parole.testo: From Middle English destroyen, from Old French destruire, Vulgar Latin *destrugō, from Classical Latin dēstruō, from dē- (“un-, de-”) + struō (“to build”).

parole.significato: The act of destroying.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English destruccioun, from Old French destrucion, from Latin dēstructiō, dēstructiōnem.

parole.significato: To take apart from; to take off.
parole.testo: From Old French destachier, from the same root as attach; compare French détacher and Portuguese and Spanish destacar.

parole.significato: To keep something from proceeding or coming to completion; to delay.
parole.testo: From Old French detenir. Doublet of détente. Cognate with Italian detenere, Portuguese deter, Romanian deține, and Spanish detener.

parole.significato: The act of determining, or the state of being determined.
parole.testo: From Middle English determinacion, determynacioun, from Old French determinacion, from Latin dēterminātiō. Morphologically determine + -ation.

parole.significato: To set the boundaries or limits of.
parole.testo: From Middle English determinen, from Old French determiner, French déterminer, from Latin determināre (“to bound, limit, prescribe, fix, determine”), from de + termināre (“to limit”), from terminus (“bound, limit, end”).

parole.significato: A person or thing detained; a detainee.
parole.testo: From late Middle English detenue, from Old French detenue, feminine singular past participle of detenir (“to detain”). See detain.

parole.significato: The act of detracting something, or something detracted; taking away; diminution.
parole.testo: From Middle English detraction, detraccion, detraccioun, from Old French detraccion, from Latin dētractiō.

parole.significato: Harm, hurt, damage.
parole.testo: From Old French detriement, from Latin detrimentum (“loss, damage, literally a rubbing off”), from dēterere (“to rub off, wear”), from dē- (“down, away”) + terere (“to rub”). Detriment is related to the word detritus, and built on similar foundations to the word impediment.

parole.significato: Any piece of equipment made for a particular purpose, especially a mechanical or electrical one.
parole.testo: From Middle English devis, devise, devyce, devys, devyse, from Old French devis and devise, from Latin dīvīsus, past participle of dīvidō (“to divide”). Doublet of devise (noun).

parole.significato: To use one’s intellect to plan or design (something).
parole.testo: PIE word  *dwóh₁ From Middle English devisen, devysen, from Old French deviser, from Vulgar Latin devisō, from Latin dīvisō, frequentative of dīvidō.

parole.significato: Completely without; having none of
parole.testo: From obsolete Middle English verb devoiden, from Old French desvuidier (“to empty out”) (compare French dévider).

parole.significato: The act or state of devoting or being devoted; a feeling of being devoted (to something).
parole.testo: From Old French devocion, from Latin dēvōtiō, from dēvōtum + -tio, from the supine of dēvoveō (“vow, devote”); equivalent to devote + -ion.

parole.significato: To eat quickly, greedily, hungrily, or ravenously.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English devouren, from Old French devorer (Modern French dévorer), from Latin dēvorō, from vorō.

parole.significato: A female devourer.
parole.testo: Shortened from devoureress, from the Old French devoureresse, feminine form of devoreor.

parole.significato: Devoted to religion or to religious feelings and duties; pious; extremely religious; godly.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English devout. From Middle English devout, devot, from Old French devot (French dévot), from Latin dēvōtus, perfect passive participle of dēvōveō. Doublet of devote.

parole.significato: An ornamental headband worn as a badge of royalty.
parole.testo: From Middle English diademe, dyademe, from Old French diademe, from Latin diadēma, from Ancient Greek διάδημα (diádēma, “band, especially worn around a tiara”), from διαδέω (diadéō, “bind around”).

parole.significato: Any formal system of reasoning that arrives at a truth by the exchange of logical arguments.
parole.testo: From Old French dialectique, from Late Latin dialectica, from Ancient Greek διαλεκτική (dialektikḗ, “the art of argument through interactive questioning and answering”), from διαλεκτικός (dialektikós, “relating to dialogue”), from διαλέγομαι (dialégomai, “to participate in a dialogue”), from διά (di

parole.significato: To discuss or negotiate so that all parties can reach an understanding.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English dialog, from Old French dialoge (French dialogue), from Late Latin dialogus, from Ancient Greek διάλογος (diálogos, “conversation, discourse”), from διά (diá, “through, inter”) + λόγος (lógos, “speech, oration, discourse”), from διαλέγομαι (dialégomai, “to converse”), f

parole.significato: Any straight line between two points on the circumference of a circle that passes through the center of the circle; a c…
parole.testo: From Old French diametre (French diamètre), from Latin diametros, from Ancient Greek διάμετρος (diámetros) (γραμμή (grammḗ)) (diametros grammē, “line measuring across”), from διά (diá, “across”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”). By surface analysis, dia- + -meter.

parole.significato: A glimmering glass-like mineral that is an allotrope of carbon in which each atom is surrounded by four others in the f…
parole.testo: From Middle English dyamaunt, from Old French diamant, from Late Latin diamās, from Latin adamās, from Ancient Greek ἀδάμᾱς (adámās, “diamond”). Doublet of adamant. The printing sense is a calque of Dutch diamant, used by Dirck Voskens who first cut it around 1700; compare pearl, ruby (“size of type

parole.significato: An absorbent garment worn around the crotch that retains the wearer's urine and feces, often worn by a baby or young ch…
parole.testo: From Middle English dyaper, diapre, dyapre, from Old French diapre, dyapre, a variant of dyaspre, diaspre (“ornamental silk cloth embellished with decorative patterns”), from Medieval Latin diaspra, diasprum (“a type of rich, valuable silken cloth”), probably from Byzantine Greek δίασπρος (díaspros,

parole.significato: pertness; sauciness
parole.testo: From Middle English dicacite, from Old French dicacité, from Latin dicācitās (whence -acity), from dicāx (“talkative”), from dīcō (“to speak, tell”).

parole.significato: Gaming with one or more dice.
parole.testo: From Middle English dys, plural of dy. See the etymology of die (etymology 2) for further information. The voiceless /s/ was most likely retained because the word felt like a collective term rather than a plural form (compare pence), and the spelling dice is a result of the pronunciation.

parole.significato: The cubical part of a pedestal; a plinth.
parole.testo: From Middle English dee, from Old French de (Modern French dé), from Latin datum, from datus (“given”), the past participle of dō (“to give”), from Proto-Indo-European *deh₃- (“to lay out, to spread out”). Doublet of datum. Replaced Old English tasul, tesul (“die”), from Latin tessella (“die, cube”)

parole.significato: The food and beverage a person or animal consumes.
parole.testo: From Middle English diet, dyet, diete, from Old French diete, from Medieval Latin dieta (“regimen, regulation; assembly”), from Latin diaeta, from Ancient Greek δίαιτα (díaita).

parole.significato: To modify one's food and beverage intake so as to decrease or increase body weight or influence health.
parole.testo: From Middle English dieten, dyeten, diȝeten, from Old French dïeter and Medieval Latin diētāre.

parole.significato: A council or assembly of leaders; a formal deliberative assembly.
parole.testo: From Middle English diet, dyet, from Old French diete, from Medieval Latin diēta, diaeta (“a public assembly; set day of trial; a day's journey”), from Ancient Greek δῐ́αιτα (dĭ́aita, “way of living, living space; decision, judgement”), influenced by Latin diēs (“day”).

parole.significato: Not to have the same traits or characteristics; to be unalike or distinct.
parole.testo: From Middle English differren, from Old French differer, from Latin differō (“carry apart, put off, defer; differ”), from dis- (“apart”) + ferō (“carry, bear”). Compare Ancient Greek διαφέρω (diaphérō). Doublet of defer and dilate, see also infer, confer and collate, refer and relate, as well as pre

parole.significato: The quality of being different.
