parole.testo: From Middle English difference, from Old French difference, from Latin differentia (“difference”), from differēns (“different”), present participle of differre. Doublet of differentia. Morphologically differ + -ence.

parole.significato: Not the same; exhibiting a difference.
parole.testo: From Middle English different, from Old French different, from Latin differēns, present active participle of differō (“to differ”). See also differ. Mostly supplanted native Old English ungelic in common usage, which lives on as unalike in Modern English.

parole.significato: The act or process of differentiating (generally, without a specialized sense).
parole.testo: From differentiate + -ion, from different + -iate, from differ + -ent, from Middle English differen, from Old French differer, from Latin differō (“carry apart, put off, defer; differ”), from dis- (“apart”) + ferō (“carry, bear”); cognate with Ancient Greek διαφέρω (diaphérō, “to differ”).

parole.significato: Hard to work with; stubborn.
parole.testo: From late Old French difficile, from Latin difficilis, from dis- + facilis (“easy”).

parole.significato: Hard, not easy, requiring much effort.
parole.testo: From Middle English difficult (ca. 1400), a back-formation from difficulte (whence modern difficulty), from Old French difficulté, from Latin difficultas, from difficul, older form of difficilis (“hard to do, difficult”), from dis- + facilis (“easy”); see difficile. Replaced native Middle English ea

parole.significato: irregular in form; not uniform; anomalous or dissimilar
parole.testo: From Old French difforme, from Latin dif- = dis- + forma (“form”). Compare deform.

parole.significato: digestible
parole.testo: Improper English spelling based on Old French digestible.

parole.significato: Capable of being digested.
parole.testo: From Old French digestible, equivalent to digest + -ible.

parole.significato: The process, in the gastrointestinal tract, by which food is converted into substances that can be used by the body.
parole.testo: From Old French digestion. Partly displaced native Old English melting (“melting, digestion”).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or functioning in digestion.
parole.testo: From Old French digestif, from Late Latin dīgestīvus. Doublet of digestif.

parole.significato: worthy; honourable; deserving; suitable.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English digne, from Old French digne, from Latin dignus.

parole.significato: To invest with dignity or honour.
parole.testo: From Old French dignifier, from Late Latin dignificare, from dignus (“worthy”) + ficare (in comp.), facere (“to make”). See deign and fact.

parole.significato: The state of being dignified or worthy of esteem: elevation of mind or character.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English dignyte, from Old French dignité, from Latin dignitās (“worthiness, merit, dignity, grandeur, authority, rank, office”), from dignus (“worthy, appropriate”), from Proto-Italic *degnos, from Proto-Indo-European *dḱ-nos, from *deḱ- (“to take”). See also decus (“honor, est

parole.significato: An aside, an act of straying from the main subject in speech or writing.
parole.testo: From Old French digressiun or disgressiun, from Latin dīgressiōnem, from dīgressus + -iō (suffix forming abstract nouns from verbs), the past passive participle of dīgredior (“to step away, to digress”), from dis- + gradior (“to step, walk, go”).

parole.significato: Prolixity; diffuse discourse.
parole.testo: From Old French dilatation, from Late Latin dīlātātio, early 15th c.

parole.significato: To enlarge; to make bigger.
parole.testo: First attested in 1393, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English dilaten, from Old French dilater, from Latin dīlātō (“to spread out”), from dī- + lātus (“wide”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of dilatate.

parole.significato: Intentionally delaying (someone or something), intended to cause delay, gain time, or adjourn decision.
parole.testo: From Middle English dilatorie, from Old French dilatoire, from Latin dīlātōrius (“extending or putting off (time)”), from dīlātor, from differō. Not etymologically related to delay.

parole.significato: Performing with industrious concentration; hard-working and focused.
parole.testo: From Middle English diligent, from Old French diligent, from Latin dīligēns (“careful, attentive, diligent”), present participle of dīligō (“to love, esteem much”, literally “to choose, select”), from dī-, dis- (“apart”) + legō (“to choose”); see elect and select.

parole.significato: To make smaller.
parole.testo: Formed under the influence of both diminue (from Old French diminuer, from Latin dīminuo) and minish.

parole.significato: Very small.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English diminutif, derived from Old French diminutif, derived from Latin dīminutīv|us, ~a, ~um (adjective), from dīminūt|us, ~a, ~um (participle), perfect passive participle of dīmin|uō, ~uere, ~uī, ~ūtum (verb). First attested in 1398.

parole.significato: To eat; to eat dinner or supper.
parole.testo: From Middle English dynen, from Old French disner (“to dine, eat the main meal of the day”), from Vulgar Latin *disiūnāre (“to eat breakfast”), from *disieiūnāre (“to break the fast”), from Late Latin, from dis- + iēiūnō (“to fast”), from Latin ieiūnus.

parole.significato: The main meal of the day, often eaten in the evening.
parole.testo: From Middle English dyner, from Old French disner (“lunch”, but originally “breakfast”), (modern French dîner), from Vulgar Latin *disiūnō, *disiūnāre from Latin dis- + iēiūnō (“to break the fast”).

parole.significato: An administrative division of the later Roman Empire, established by the Herodian tetrarchy.
parole.testo: From Middle English diocise, from Old French diocese, from Late Latin diocēsis, from Latin dioecēsis (“district under a governor”), from Ancient Greek διοίκησις (dioíkēsis, “internal administration”).

parole.significato: A theoretical line (physically or mentally) followed from a point of origin or towards a destination. May be relative (…
parole.testo: From Middle English direccioun, from Old French direccion, from Latin dīrēctiō. Equivalent to direct + -ion.

parole.significato: To cause (someone) to break a habit or become unaccustomed to something that they were previously accustomed to
parole.testo: From Middle English disacustome, from Old French desacostumer (“render unfamiliar”) (compare French désaccoutumer). Equivalent to dis- + accustom.

parole.significato: To draw back, pull back.
parole.testo: From Middle English disavauncen, from Old French desavancer.

parole.significato: A weakness or undesirable characteristic; con; drawback.
parole.testo: From Middle English disavauntage, from Old French desavantage.

parole.significato: Synonym of misadventure, bad luck, an instance of bad luck, a mistake.
parole.testo: From Old French desaventure. Equivalent to dis- + adventure.

parole.significato: To strongly and solemnly refuse to own or acknowledge; to deny responsibility for, approbation of, and the like.
parole.testo: From dis- + avow, or from Old French desavouer.

parole.significato: To pay out, expend; usually from a public fund or treasury.
parole.testo: From Old French desbourser (Modern French débourser). By surface analysis, dis- + burse (“purse”).

parole.significato: To detect with the senses, especially with the eyes.
parole.testo: From Middle English discernen, from Old French discerner, from Latin discernere (“to separate, divide, distinguish, discern”), from dis- (“apart”) + cernere (“to distinguish”); see certain.

parole.significato: To accomplish or complete, as an obligation.
parole.testo: From Middle English dischargen, from Old French deschargier (“to unload”), from Late Latin discarricāre (“unload”). By surface analysis, dis- + charge.

parole.significato: To change or lose color.
parole.testo: From Middle English discoloren, discoloren, from Old French descolorer, discolorer, equivalent to dis- + color.

parole.significato: British and Canadian standard spelling of discolor.
parole.testo: From Middle English discolouren, discoloren, from Old French discolorer, descolorer, equivalent to dis- + colour.

parole.significato: To embarrass (someone) greatly; to confuse; to perplex; to disconcert.
parole.testo: From Middle English discomfiten, from Old French desconfit, past participle of desconfire (“to undo, to destroy”), from des- (“completely”), from Latin dis- + Old French confire (“to make”), from Latin cōnficiō (“to finish up, to destroy”), from com- (“with, together”) + faciō (“to do, to make”). La

parole.significato: Defeat in battle.
parole.testo: From Old French desconfiture (“rout, defeat”); compare French déconfiture.

parole.significato: To interrupt the continuance of; to put an end to, especially as regards commercial productions; to stop producing, mak…
parole.testo: From Old French descontinuer, equivalent to dis- + continue.

parole.significato: To advise (someone) against doing something.
parole.testo: From Old French desconseillier.

parole.significato: To find or learn something for the first time.
parole.testo: From Middle English discoveren, from Old French descovrir, from Late Latin discoperīre < discooperiō, discooperīre, from Latin dis- + cooperiō. Displaced native Old English onfindan.

parole.significato: An uncovered place or part.
parole.testo: Old French descovert, past participle of descovrir (“to uncover”).

parole.significato: discovery
parole.testo: From Old French descoverture.

parole.significato: Respectful of privacy or secrecy; exercising caution in order to avoid causing embarrassment; quiet; diplomatic.
parole.testo: From Middle English discrete, from Old French discret, from Latin discrētus, from past participle of discernere. Doublet of discrete.

parole.significato: Separate; distinct; individual; non-continuous.
parole.testo: From Old French discret, from Latin discrētus, past participle of discernō (“divide”), from dis- + cernō (“sift”). Doublet of discreet.

parole.significato: The quality of being discreet.
parole.testo: From Middle English discrecioun, from Old French discretion, from Late Latin discrētiō, from Latin discerno. Equivalent to discreet + -ion.

parole.significato: Conversation or debate concerning a particular topic.
parole.testo: From Old French discussion, from Late Latin discussiō, from Latin discutiō. By surface analysis, discuss + -ion.

parole.significato: A feeling of contempt or scorn.
parole.testo: From Middle English disdeynen, from Old French desdeignier (modern French dédaigner).

parole.significato: disdainful
parole.testo: From Middle English disdeynous, from Old French desdeignos, desdaigneux (French dédaigneux).

parole.significato: Material (such as clothing, makeup, a wig) used to alter one’s visual appearance in order to hide one's identity or ass…
parole.testo: From Middle English disgisen, disguisen, borrowed from Old French desguiser (modern French déguiser), itself derived from des- (“dis-”) (from Latin dis-) + guise (“guise”) (from a Germanic source).

parole.significato: To disinherit.
parole.testo: From Middle English disheriten, desheriten et al., from Old French desheriter, from Vulgar Latin *dishērētō, from Latin dis- + hērēditō.

parole.significato: To throw into disorder; upheave.
parole.testo: From Old French descheveler (modern French écheveler, ultimately from Old French chevel).

parole.significato: Of a person, with the hair uncombed.
parole.testo: From earlier dishevely, from Old French deschevelé (modern French déchevelé and échevelé), from des- (“dis-”), + chevel (“hair”) (modern French cheveu). See there for more details.

parole.significato: Not honest; shoddy.
parole.testo: From Middle English dishoneste (“dishonourable”), from Old French deshoneste, from Latin dehonestus. Equivalent to dis- + honest. Displaced native Old English unsōþfæst.

parole.significato: The characteristic or condition of being dishonest.
parole.testo: From Middle English dishoneste (“disgrace, filth”), from Old French deshoneste, equivalent to dis- + honesty or dishonest + -y.

parole.significato: American standard spelling of dishonour.
parole.testo: From Old French deshonor, equivalent to dis- + honor.

parole.significato: Shame or disgrace.
parole.testo: From Old French deshonor, equivalent to dis- + honour.

parole.significato: To separate; to disunite.
parole.testo: From Middle English disjoynen, from Old French desjoindre, from Latin disiungere (“to separate”), from dis-, di- (“apart”) + iungere (“to join”). Equivalent to dis- + join.

parole.significato: Not smooth or continuous; disjointed.
parole.testo: From Middle English disjoynen, from Old French desjoindre (“disjoin”), from Latin disiungō, from dis- + iungō (“join”).

parole.significato: The act of disjoining; disunion, separation.
parole.testo: From Old French disjunction, from Latin disiunctiō.

parole.significato: The act of displacing, or the state of being displaced.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French, a borrowing from Medieval Latin dislocātiō, delocatio.

parole.significato: To remove or force out from a position or dwelling previously occupied.
parole.testo: From Middle English disloggen, from Old French deslogier. Compare French déloger. Equivalent to dis- + lodge.

parole.significato: An act of being disloyal; a betrayal, faithbreach.
parole.testo: From Old French desloiauté (Modern French déloyauté), from des- + loiauté (“loyalty”).

parole.significato: To remove the chainmail or armour from (someone).
parole.testo: From Old French desmailler.

parole.significato: To remove the limbs of.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French desmembrer, from des- (“de-”) + membre (“limb”) + -er (“verbal suffix”).

parole.significato: To (cause to) get off (something).
parole.testo: From dis- + mount, probably a calque of Old French desmonter.

parole.significato: Refusal to obey.
parole.testo: From Middle English disobedience, dysobediaunce, from Old French desobedience. By surface analysis, dis- + obedience. Displaced native Old English unhīersumnes.

parole.significato: Not obedient.
parole.testo: From Middle English disobedient, dysobedyent, from Old French desobedient; morphologically, from dis- + obedient.

parole.significato: To refuse or (intentionally) fail to adhere to (a rule) or to obey an order from (somebody).
parole.testo: From Old French desobeir.

parole.significato: A professional storyteller or joker.
parole.testo: From Old French diseur.

parole.significato: Inequality in marriage; marriage with an inferior.
parole.testo: From Middle English disparage (noun), disparagen (verb), from Old French desparage (noun), desparagier (verb), from des- (“dis-”) + parage (“equal rank, rank”).

parole.significato: The act of disparaging, of belittling.
parole.testo: From Old French desparagement.

parole.significato: To scatter around.
parole.testo: Old French desparpeillier.

parole.significato: To scatter, disperse.
parole.testo: From Old French disparpelier, disparpillier et al., apparently from a late prefixed form of Latin papilio (“butterfly”).

parole.significato: To spend or expend.
parole.testo: From Old French despendre ( > French dépendre), from Latin dispendere.

parole.significato: A steward or treasurer.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English dispendour, from Old French despendour. By surface analysis, dispend (“distribute, dispense”) + -er. Doublet of dispenser and spencer.

parole.significato: The act of dispensing or dealing out; distribution
parole.testo: From Middle English dispensacioun, from Old French despensacion, from Latin dispensātiō. By surface analysis, dispens(e) + -ation.

parole.significato: To issue, distribute, or give out.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French dispenser, from Latin dispēnsāre (“to weigh out, pay out, distribute, regulate, manage, control, dispense”), frequentative of dispendere (“to weigh out”), from dis- (“apart”) + pendere (“to weigh”).

parole.significato: To be ruined or lost; to perish.
parole.testo: First attested in 1382, from Middle English disperishen, from Old French desperiss-, extended stem of desperir, from Latin disperīre (“to go completely to ruin”).

parole.significato: The state of being dispersed.
parole.testo: From disperse + -ion, from Middle English dispersioun, from Old French dispersion, from Latin dispersiō.

parole.significato: Displeasure, dissatisfaction.
parole.testo: From Old French desplaisance.

parole.significato: Unpleasant, disagreeable.
parole.testo: From Old French desplaisant, present participle of desplaire (“to displease”).

parole.significato: Unattractive, dislikable, objectionable.
parole.testo: Perhaps a calque of Old French desplaisant, from the verb desplere (“to displease”). By surface analysis, dis- + pleasing.

parole.significato: A feeling of being displeased with something or someone; dissatisfaction; disapproval.
parole.testo: From Old French desplaisir, equivalent to dis- + pleasure. See displease.

parole.significato: To notice with disapprobation or some degree of censure; to disparage, to criticize.
parole.testo: From Old French despreisier. Doublet of disprize.

parole.significato: To prove to be false or erroneous; to confute; to refute.
parole.testo: From Middle English disproven, dispreven, from Old French desprover, from des- + prover, equivalent to dis- + prove.

parole.significato: The act of disputing; a dispute or argument.
parole.testo: English dispute + -ation, from Old French disputation, from Latin disputatio.

parole.significato: An argument or disagreement; a failure to agree.
parole.testo: From Middle English disputen, from Old French desputer (French disputer), from Latin disputāre (“to dispute, discuss, examine, compute, estimate”), from dis- (“apart”) + putāre (“to reckon, consider, think, originally make clean, clear up”), related to purus (“pure”). Compare compute, count, impute,

parole.significato: To disguise or conceal something.
parole.testo: First attested in the beginning of the 15th century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English dissemblen, dissimblen, dissemelen, borrowed from Old French dessambler, dissembler, disembler, itself borrowed from Latin dissimulō and modified after sembler, semblance, etc. Doublet of dissimulat

parole.significato: To treat poorly; to do a disservice to
parole.testo: From Old French desservir, from Latin dis- (“indicating negation”) + servīre (“to serve”).

parole.significato: The act of concealing the truth; hypocrisy or deception.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English dissimulacioun, from Old French dissimulation, from Latin dissimulātiō; equivalent to dissimule + -ation.

parole.significato: The termination of an organized body or legislative assembly, especially a formal dismissal.
parole.testo: From Middle English dissolucioun, from Old French dissolucion, from Latin dissolūtiō (“a dissolving, destroying, breaking up, dissolution”).

parole.significato: To stain, discolour or tarnish
parole.testo: From Old French desteindre.

parole.significato: Far off (physically, logically or mentally).
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English distaunt, from Old French distant, from Latin distāns.

parole.significato: A viral disease of animals, such as dogs and cats, characterised by fever, coughing and catarrh.
parole.testo: From Old French destemprer, from Latin distemperare.

parole.significato: To exude (a liquid) in small drops; also, to give off (a vapour) which condenses in small drops.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English distillen (“to fall, flow, or shed in drops, drop, trickle; to shed drops; to fill (the eyes) with tears; (alchemy, medicine) to subject (something) to distillation; to obtain (something) using distillation; to distil; to condense or vaporize; (figuratively) to give (good fo

parole.significato: Capable of being perceived very clearly.
parole.testo: From Middle English distincte, past participle of distincten (“to distinguish, discern”), from Old French destincter, from Latin distinctus, past participle of distinguere (“to distinguish”); see distinguish.

parole.significato: That which distinguishes; a single occurrence of a determining factor or feature, the fact of being divided; separation…
parole.testo: From Middle English distinccioun, from Old French distinction (attested from the 12th century), borrowed from Latin distinctiōnem, action noun of distinguō (“separate, distinguish”). By surface analysis, distinct (“to distinguish”) + -ion. Attested in English from the late 14th century.

parole.significato: To recognize someone or something as different from others based on its characteristics.
parole.testo: From Middle English distingwen, from Old French distinguer, from Latin distinguere (“to separate, divide, distinguish, set off, adorn, literally mark off”), from di-, dis- (“apart”) + stinguere, related to English stink. Compare extinguish.

parole.significato: To squeeze, press, embrace; to constrain, oppress.
parole.testo: From Middle English distreynen, from Old French destraindre, from Latin distringō (“to pull asunder”), from dis- (“apart”) + stringō (“to draw tight, strain”).

parole.significato: Physical or emotional discomfort, suffering, or alarm, particularly of a more acute nature.
parole.testo: The verb is from Middle English distressen, from Old French destrecier (“to restrain, constrain, put in straits, afflict, distress”); compare French détresse. Ultimately from Medieval Latin as if *districtiō, an assumed frequentative form of Latin distringō (“to pull asunder, stretch out”), from dis

parole.significato: An act of distributing or state of being distributed.
parole.testo: From Old French distribution, from Latin distributio, from distribuere 'to distribute', itself from dis- 'apart' + tribuere 'to' (from tribus). By surface analysis, distribute + -ion.

parole.significato: To trouble greatly; to perplex.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English distroublen, from Old French destrobler, metathetic form of destorbler; by surface analysis, dis- + trouble.

parole.significato: The act of disturbing, being disturbed.
parole.testo: From Middle English disturbaunce, from Old French destorbance, destourbance, from destourber (“disturb”), from Latin disturbō. By surface analysis, disturb + -ance.

parole.significato: To turn aside.
parole.testo: From Old French destourner, French détourner. See detour.

parole.significato: The state of not being used; neglect.
parole.testo: From Old French desuser, equivalent to dis- + use.

parole.significato: A labiate plant of species Origanum dictamnus, formerly renowned for its medicinal properties; dittany of Crete.
parole.testo: From Old French ditan (French dictame), from Latin dictamnum, from Ancient Greek δίκταμνον (díktamnon), reportedly from Δίκτη (Díktē, “Dicte”), a mountain in Crete on whose slopes the plant grew.

parole.significato: An indictment; a charge.
parole.testo: From Old French ditté, from Latin dictatum.

parole.significato: To sing; to warble a little tune.
parole.testo: From Middle English dite, ditee, from Old French ditie or dité, from ditier, from Latin dictāre (participle dictatus).

parole.significato: Increasing the amount or frequency of urination.
parole.testo: From Middle English diuretyk, from Old French diuretique; ultimately from Ancient Greek διουρητικός (diourētikós). By surface analysis, diuresis + -etic.

parole.significato: The quality of being diverse or different; a difference or unlikeness.
parole.testo: From Middle English diversite, from Old French diversité, from Latin dīversitās, equivalent to diverse + -ity. Displaced native Old English mislīcnes.

parole.significato: To turn aside from a course.
parole.testo: From Middle English diverten, Old French divertir (“to turn or go different ways, part, separate, divert”), from Latin di- (“apart”) + vertere (“to turn”); see verse.

parole.significato: The act of divining; a foreseeing or foretelling of future events.
parole.testo: From Old French divination, from Latin divinatio.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a god.
parole.testo: From Old French divin, from Latin dīvīnus (“of a god”), from divus (“god”). Displaced native Old English godcund.

parole.significato: The state, position, or fact of being a god or God.
parole.testo: From Old French divinité, from Latin divinitas. Composed of divine + -ity. Displaced native Old English godcundnes.

parole.significato: Capable of being divided or split.
parole.testo: PIE word  *dwóh₁ From Middle English divisible, from Old French, from Late Latin divisibilis, from the verb Latin divido.

parole.significato: The act or process of dividing anything.
parole.testo: PIE word  *dwóh₁ From Middle English divisioun, from Old French division, from Latin dīvīsiō, dīvīsiōnem, noun of process form from perfect passive participle dīvīsus (“divided”), from dīvidō (“divide”). Doublet of divisio.

parole.significato: The legal dissolution of a marriage.
parole.testo: Derived from Old French divorce, from Latin dīvortium, from dīvertere (“to turn aside”), from dī- (“apart”) + vertere (“to turn”); see verse.

parole.significato: A belief or tenet, especially about philosophical or theological matters.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin doctrina (“teaching, instruction, learning, knowledge”), from doctor (“a teacher”), from docere (“to teach”); see doctor.

parole.significato: A sorrow or grief; dolour.
parole.testo: From Middle English dole (“grief”), from Old French doel (compare French deuil), from Late Latin dolus, from Latin doleo.

parole.significato: Sad, sorrowful.
parole.testo: From Middle English dolent, from Old French dolent, from Latin dolēns, present participle of doleō (“to grieve”).

parole.significato: Solemnly or ponderously sad.
parole.testo: From Middle English dolorous, from Old French dolerous (modern French douloureux), from Late Latin dolōrōsus (“painful”), from Latin dolor. Doublet of dolorose.

parole.significato: Deceitfulness, hidden malice.
parole.testo: From Middle English dolosite, from Old French dolosité, from Latin dolosus.

parole.significato: A geographic area owned or controlled by a single person or organization.
parole.testo: From Middle English demayne, demain (“rule”), from Old French demeine, demaine, demeigne, domaine (“power”), (French domaine), from Latin dominium (“property, right of ownership”), from dominus (“master, proprietor, owner”). Doublet of demesne and dominium, and closely related to dominion and domino

parole.significato: Control by means of superior ability, influence, position, or resources; prevailing force.
parole.testo: From Middle English domynacion, from Old French dominacion, from Latin dominātiō (“rule, dominion”), from dominor (“domineer; rule”); see dominate.

parole.significato: A grammar (book); a primer (of Latin)
parole.testo: From Middle English donet, from Old French, from Latin Donatus, a famous grammarian.

parole.significato: The fortified tower and main residence of a motte or early castle; a keep.
parole.testo: A variant of dungeon remodelled on its etymon, Old French donjon.

parole.significato: A young squire or the attendant to a knight; a page
parole.testo: From Old French danzel and Italian donzello, both ultimately from Medieval Latin domicellus (“young nobleman, squire”), a diminutive of Latin dominus (“master, lord”). Compare donzella.

parole.significato: Inactive, sleeping, asleep, suspended.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin dormiēns, present participle of dormiō (“to sleep”).

parole.significato: A bedroom or dormitory, especially in a monastery.
parole.testo: From Middle English dortour, from Old French dortoir, dortour (modern dortoir), from Latin dormitorium (“dormitory”). Doublet of dormitorium and dormitory.

parole.significato: Any of several different families of large-eyed, silvery, deep-bodied, laterally compressed, and roughly discoid marine…
parole.testo: From Middle English dorry, from Old French doree, past participle of dorer (“to gild”), from Latin deauratus.

parole.significato: A small roll or plug used to stop a sore, wound, etc.; a pledget.
parole.testo: From Middle English dosel, from Old French dosil (“spigot”), from Late Latin ducīculus, diminutive from Latin dux (“guide”). See duct, duke.

parole.significato: Made up of two matching or complementary elements.
parole.testo: PIE word  *dwóh₁ Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *dwi- Proto-Indo-European *-plos Proto-Indo-European *dwiplós Proto-Italic *dwiplos Proto-Italic *duplos Latin duplus Old French dobleder. Middle English double English double From Middle English double, from Old French d

parole.significato: In the metric system, multiplies the attached unit by two.
parole.testo: From Old French double, more at double.

parole.significato: A pair of two similar or equal things; couple.
parole.testo: From Middle English doublet, a borrowing from Old French doublet, from double, duble, doble + -et. Equivalent to double + -et (diminutive suffix)

parole.significato: Capable of being doubted; doubtful; dubious; dubitable. See usage notes below.
parole.testo: From Middle English doutable, from Old French doutable, dotable, equivalent to doubt + -able.

parole.significato: doubt; uncertainty
parole.testo: From Middle English doutaunce, from Old French doutance, from Medieval Latin dubitantia. Equivalent to doubt + -ance. Compare dubitancy.

parole.significato: Sweet; nice; pleasant.
parole.testo: From Middle English douce, from Old French dolz, dous, Middle French doux, douce, from Latin dulcis (“sweet”). Doublet of dolce, doux, and dulce.

parole.significato: A sweetened dish.
parole.testo: From Middle English doucet, from Old French doucet, diminutive of dous (“sweet”). Doublet of dulcet and dolcetto.

parole.significato: To furnish with a dower; to endow.
parole.testo: From Middle English dowen, from Old French douer, from Latin dōtō.

parole.significato: dower; dowry.
parole.testo: From Old French douage, from douer + -age, from Latin dōtō (“to endow”), from dōs (“dowry”). By surface analysis, dow + -age.

parole.significato: The part of or interest in a deceased husband's property provided to his widow, usually in the form of a life estate.
parole.testo: From Middle English dower, dowere, from Old French doeire, from Medieval Latin dōtārium, from Latin dōs. Doublet of dowry.

parole.significato: feathery or woolly down; filament of a feather
parole.testo: Compare Old French douille (“soft”), and English ductile.

parole.significato: A set of twelve.
parole.testo: From Middle English dozen, dozein, doseyne, from Old French dozaine (“a group of twelve”) (Modern French douzaine), from doze (“twelve”) + -aine (“-ish”), from Latin duodecim (“twelve”) (from duo (“two”) + decem (“ten”)) + -ana (“-ish”).

parole.significato: An interpreter, especially for the Arabic and Turkish languages.
parole.testo: From Middle English dragman, from Old French drugeman, from Medieval Latin dragumannus, from Byzantine Greek δραγομάνος (dragomános), from Arabic تُرْجُمَان (turjumān), from Classical Syriac ܬܰܪܓܡܳܢܳܐ (targmānā), from Akkadian 𒅴𒁄 (targumannum, “interpreter”). With the plural form -men, through reint

parole.significato: A mythical reptilian or serpentine creature.
parole.testo: From Middle English dragoun, borrowed from Old French dragon, from Latin dracō(n), from Ancient Greek δράκων (drákōn, “a serpent of huge size, a python, a dragon”), probably from δέρκομαι (dérkomai, “to see clearly”). Displaced Old English wyrm, whence modern worm. Mostly displaced Old English draca

parole.significato: A hook with a lead shank.
parole.testo: From Middle English *drailen (attested as drailed), a variant of Middle English trailen (“to hang loosely, drag along, drag away”), from a merger of Old French trailer, traillier (“to trail”) and Old English trǣġlian, trǣġelian (“to pluck, pull away”). The alteration of trailen to drailen was probab

parole.significato: To drink drams.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English dragme /dramme, from Old French dragme, from Late Latin dragma, from Latin drachma, from Ancient Greek δραχμή (drakhmḗ, “unit of weight; a handful”). Doublet of drachma, diram, dirham, dirhem, and adarme.

parole.significato: A curtain; a drapery.
parole.testo: From Middle English drape (“a drape”, noun), from Old French draper (“to drape; to full cloth”), from drap (“cloth, drabcloth”), from Late Latin drappus, drapus (“drabcloth, kerchief”), a word first recorded in the Capitularies of Charlemagne, probably from Frankish *drapi, *drāpi (“that which is fu

parole.significato: Cloth draped gracefully in folds.
parole.testo: From Middle English draperie, from Old French draperie, from drap (“drape, sheet, large cloth”), ultimately of Germanic origin.

parole.significato: A large shaker for sprinkling spices or seasonings during food preparation.
parole.testo: From Middle English dragge, from Old French dragee, dragie, from Latin tragēmata, from Ancient Greek τραγήματα (tragḗmata, “spices”), plural of τράγημα (trágēma, “dried fruit”).

parole.significato: An item of kitchen furniture, like a cabinet with shelves, for storing crockery or utensils.
parole.testo: From Middle English dressure, dressor, dressour, a borrowing from Old French drecëur, drecëure, from the verb dresser.

parole.significato: The single-humped camel (Camelus dromedarius).
parole.testo: From Middle English dromedari, dromedarie (“dromedary; any camel”) [and other forms], from Old French dromedaire, from Late Latin dromedārius (“kind of camel”), from Latin *dromadārius, from dromas, dromadis (“dromedary”) + -ārius (suffix forming nouns denoting agents of use). Dromas and dromadis ar

parole.significato: Edema, swelling.
parole.testo: From Middle English dropesie, idropesie, from Old French idropsie, ydropisie, from Latin hydrōps, from Ancient Greek ὕδρωψ (húdrōps), from ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”). Doublet of hydropsy and hydrops.

parole.significato: Love, especially sexual love; courtship, sex.
parole.testo: From Old French druerie, droerie (“love, friendship”) et al., from dru (“friend”).

parole.significato: A female tree spirit; a woodnymph or tree nymph.
parole.testo: From Old French driade (“wood nymph”), from Latin Dryas, Dryadis, from Ancient Greek Δρυάς (Druás, “dryad”), from δρῦς (drûs, “oak”), from Proto-Indo-European *derew(o)- (“tree, wood”); cf. Proto-Indo-European *dóru (“tree”).

parole.significato: To confer knighthood; the conclusion of the ceremony was marked by a tap on the shoulder with a sword, the accolade.
parole.testo: From Middle English dubben, from Old English dubbian (“to knight by striking with a sword, dub”) from Old French adober (“to equip with arms; adorn”) (also 11th century, Modern French adouber), both from Proto-West Germanic *dubbōn, from Proto-Germanic *dub- (“to hit, strike”), from Proto-Indo-Europ

parole.significato: The wife or widow of a duke.
parole.testo: From Middle English duchesse, from Old French duchesse. Doublet of duchesse.

parole.significato: Capable of being pulled or stretched into thin wire by mechanical force without breaking.
parole.testo: From Old French, from Latin ductilis (“easily led”).

parole.significato: Owed or owing.
parole.testo: From Middle English dewe, dew, due, from Old French deü (“due”), past participle of devoir (“to owe”), from Latin dēbēre (“to owe”), from dē- (“from”) + habeō (“to have”).

parole.significato: The male ruler of a duchy (female equivalent: duchess).
parole.testo: From Old French duc, through Middle English duk, duke, from Latin dux, ducis. Displaced native Old English heretoga. Was present as duc in late Old English, from the same Latin source. Doublet of doge, duc, duce, and dux. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dewk-, which is also the source of the se

parole.significato: Sweet, especially when describing voice or tones; melodious.
parole.testo: From Middle English doucet, from Old French doucet, from dulz, dulce (“sweet, pleasant”) + diminutive -et, from Latin dulcis (“sweet, pleasant”). Cognate with Spanish dulce, French doux, Italian dolce, Portuguese doce, and Romanian dulce. Doublet of dolcetto and doucet.

parole.significato: A stringed instrument, with strings stretched across a sounding board, usually trapezoidal, played by plucking on the s…
parole.testo: From Old French doulcemelle, probably from Latin dulce melos (“sweet song”), from Ancient Greek μέλος (mélos, “melody, song”).

parole.significato: The ability to last a long time by virtue of the power to resist stress or force.
parole.testo: From Middle English durabilite, from Old French durabilité, from Latin dūrābilitās (“durability”). Corresponding to durable + -ity.

parole.significato: Able to resist wear or decay; lasting; enduring.
parole.testo: From Middle English durable, from Old French durable, from Latin dūrābilis (“lasting, permanent”), from dūrō (“harden, make hard”).

parole.significato: Imprisonment; forced confinement.
parole.testo: From Old French durance, from durer (“to last”).

parole.significato: An amount of time or a particular time interval.
parole.testo: From Middle English duracioun, from late Old French duracion, from Medieval Latin dūrātiō.

parole.significato: To last, continue, endure.
parole.testo: From Middle English duren (“to last”), from Old French durer, from Latin dūrō, dūrāre. Related to Dutch duren (“to last, dure”), German dauern (“to last, dure”). Doublet of endure.

parole.significato: Harsh treatment.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English duresse, from Old French duresse, from Latin dūritia (“hardness”), from dūrus (“hard”).

parole.significato: A bodily disorder; an imbalance of the humours
parole.testo: From Middle English discrasie, from Old French discrasie, from Medieval Latin dyscrāsia, from Ancient Greek δυσκρασία (duskrasía, “bad temperament”), from δυσ- (dus-, “dys-”) + κρᾶσις (krâsis, “mixing, tempering”). By surface analysis, dys- + -crasy.

parole.significato: A disease characterised by inflammation of the intestines, especially the colon (large intestine), accompanied by pus (…
parole.testo: From Middle English dissenterie, from Old French dissenterie, from Latin dysenteria, from Ancient Greek δυσεντερία (dusentería), from δυσ- (dus-, “bad”) + ἔντερα (éntera, “bowels”).

parole.significato: Desirous; keen to do or obtain something.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English egre, eger, from Old French aigre, egre (modern French aigre), from Latin ācrus, variant of ācer (“sharp, keen”); see acid, acerb, etc. Compare vinegar, alegar.

parole.significato: Ebony; an ebony tree.
parole.testo: From Old French eban (modern ébène), from Latin ebenus, from Ancient Greek ἔβενος (ébenos, “ebony tree”).

parole.significato: The act of boiling.
parole.testo: From Old French ebullition, from Latin ēbullītiō, from ēbulliō (“to boil”).

parole.significato: An alignment of astronomical objects whereby one object comes between the observer (or notional observer) and another o…
parole.testo: From Middle English eclipse, from Old French eclipse, from Latin eclīpsis, from Ancient Greek ἔκλειψις (ékleipsis, “eclipse”), from ἐκλείπω (ekleípō, “to abandon, go missing, vanish”), from ἐκ (ek, “out”) and λείπω (leípō, “to leave behind”). Doublet of eclipsis. See also ellipse, ellipsis.

parole.significato: Pertaining to an economy.
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Middle English economike, iconomique (“household management”), and then: * from Middle French iconomique, oeconomique, and Old French iconomike (“(noun) household management; person in charge of household management; (adjective) relating to household management; relating to

parole.significato: Effective management of a community or system, or especially its resources.
parole.testo: From Middle English yconomye, yconomy, borrowed via Old French yconomie or Medieval Latin from Latin oeconomia, from Ancient Greek οἰκονομία (oikonomía, “management of a household, administration”), from οἶκος (oîkos, “house”) + νέμω (némō, “distribute, allocate”). By surface analysis, eco- + -nomy.

parole.significato: Intense pleasure.
parole.testo: From Old French estaise (“ecstasy, rapture”), from Latin ecstasis, from Ancient Greek ἔκστασις (ékstasis), from ἐξίστημι (exístēmi, “to displace”), from ἐκ (ek, “out”) and ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to stand”).

parole.significato: The act of edifying, or the state of being edified or improved; a building process, especially morally, emotionally, or…
parole.testo: From Old French, from Latin aedificationem (“building, construction”), an accusative form of aedificatio, from aedificare.

parole.significato: A building; a structure; an architectural fabric, especially a large and spectacular one.
parole.testo: From Middle English edifice, from Old French edifice, a classical borrowing of Latin aedificium (“building”), derived from aedificāre (“to build, establish”) (whence also English edify).

parole.significato: To build, construct.
parole.testo: From Old French edifier (“to build, to edify”), from Latin aedificare (“build”).

parole.significato: Producing the intended result; entirely adequate.
parole.testo: From Middle English effectual, effectuel, from Old French effectuel, from Late Latin effectualis.

parole.significato: Effective; possessing efficacy.
parole.testo: From Old French efficacieux (whence -acious), from Latin efficāx (“efficacious”) + -ous, from efficere (“to effect, to accomplish”); see effect.

parole.significato: The ability to produce a desired effect under ideal testing conditions.
parole.testo: From Old French efficace, from Late Latin efficācia (“efficacy”) (whence -acy), from efficāx (“efficacious”); see efficacious.

parole.significato: Making good, thorough, or careful use of resources; not consuming extra. Especially, making good use of time or energy.
parole.testo: 1398, “making,” from Old French, from Latin efficientem, nominative efficiēns, participle of efficere (“work out, accomplish”) (see effect). Meaning “productive, skilled” is from 1787. Efficiency apartment is first recorded 1930, American English.

parole.significato: Equal; impartial.
parole.testo: From Middle English egal, from Old French egal, igal, from Latin aequālis. Doublet of equal and aequalis.

parole.significato: The act or result of egesting
parole.testo: From Old French egestion, from Latin ēgestiōnem, accusative of ēgestiō (“emptying, voiding”), action noun from the perfect passive participle of ēgerō (“to carry out”), from ex- + gerō.

parole.significato: eldest; firstborn
parole.testo: Old French aisné, ainsné, from ainz (“before”) + né (“born”). Compare esnecy.

parole.significato: vinegar, verjuice
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English aisel, eisel, from Old French aisil, eisil (“vinegar”), from Vulgar Latin *acētillum, a diminutive of Latin acētum (“vinegar”). Compare Cornish aysel and Welsh aesel.

parole.significato: An exhilarating psychological state of pride and optimism.
parole.testo: From Middle English elacioun, from Old French elacion, from Latin ēlātiōnem, accusative singular of ēlātiō (“exaltation, elevation; pride, elation”), from ēlātus, perfect passive participle of efferō (“bring forth or out; raise; exalt”), from ē (“out of”), short form of ex, + ferō (“carry, bear”).

parole.significato: One of the simplest or essential parts or principles of which anything consists, or upon which the constitution or fund…
parole.testo: From Middle English element, from Old French element, from Latin elementum (“a first principle, element, rudiment”) (see further etymology there). The verb is from Middle English elementen, from the noun.

parole.significato: A large mammal of the family Elephantidae in the order Proboscidea, having a trunk, and native to Africa and Asia.
parole.testo: From Middle English elefant, elefaunt, from Old French elefant, elefan, olifant, re-latinized in Middle French as elephant, from Latin elephantus, from Ancient Greek ἐλέφᾱς (eléphās) (gen. ἐλέφαντος (eléphantos)). Believed to be derived from an Afroasiatic form such as Proto-Berber *eḷu (“elephant”)

parole.significato: The act of raising from a lower place, condition, or quality to a higher; said of material things, persons, the mind, t…
parole.testo: From Old French elevation, from Latin elevatio, equal to elevate + -ion.

parole.significato: Of high birth or social position; aristocratic or patrician.
parole.testo: From Middle English elit, from Old French elit, eslit (“chosen, elected”) past participle of elire, eslire (“to choose, elect”), from Latin eligere (“to choose, elect”), with past participle electus; see elect.

parole.significato: The quality of artistry and persuasiveness in speech or writing.
parole.testo: From Middle English eloquence, from Old French eloquence, from Latin ēloquentia. Doublet of eloquency, directly from Latin.

parole.significato: Fluently persuasive and articulate.
parole.testo: From Old French eloquent, from Latin eloquens (“speaking, having the faculty of speech, eloquent”), present participle of eloquor (“to speak out”), from e (“out”) + loquor (“to speak”).

parole.significato: To arrange in order of battle; to array for battle.
parole.testo: From Middle English enbatelen, embatailen, from Old French embataillier (“to array for battle”), from em- (Latin in) + bataille (“battle”).

parole.significato: To furnish with battlements; to give the form of battlements to.
parole.testo: From Middle English enbatelen, enbatailen, from Old French *embastiller ("to fortify"; > Middle Latin imbataliare, imbattajare), from en- + + bastiller (“to build, fortify, embattle”). More at baste.

parole.significato: Oblique.
parole.testo: From Middle English embelif (“oblique (adj.); obliquely (adv.)”) (compare Middle English embelink), from Old French en belif / beslif, related to Latin ob-līquus.

parole.significato: To make more beautiful and attractive by adding ornamentation; to decorate.
parole.testo: From Middle English embelishen, from Old French embellir, from em- + bel.

parole.significato: To adorn with prominent markings.
parole.testo: From en- + blazon, from Old French blason (“shield”).

parole.significato: A representative symbol, such as a trademark, a badge or logo.
parole.testo: From Old French embleme, from Latin emblēma (“raised ornaments on vessels, tessellated work, mosaic”), from Ancient Greek ἔμβλημα (émblēma, “an insertion”), from ἐμβάλλειν (embállein, “to put in, to lay on”). Doublet of emblema.

parole.significato: An annual crop produced by cultivation, treated as personal property.
parole.testo: 1485, from Old French emblayement, emblaiment (“harvest, crop”), from emblaer, emblaier, emblader (French emblaver, “to sow with grain”), from Medieval Latin imblādāre (“to sow with grain”), from im- + blādum (French blé, “grain”), from Frankish *blād (“produce”), from Proto-Germanic *blēdaz, *blēdō

parole.significato: An obstruction or occlusion of a blood vessel by an embolus, that is by a blood clot, air bubble or other matter that h…
parole.testo: The term was coined in 1848 by Rudolf Virchow. From Old French embolisme (“intercalation of days in a calendar to correct errors”), from Late Latin embolismus, from Ancient Greek ἐμβολισμός (embolismós, “intercalary”), from ἐμβάλλω (embállō, “to insert, throw in”).

parole.significato: To cause (something) to stick out or swell; to extrude; also, to cause (someone or something) to be covered in swelling…
parole.testo: PIE word  *h₁én The verb is derived from Late Middle English embossen, embosen, embocen (“to be bloated; to bulge; to cause to bulge; to ornament in relief, emboss”) [and other forms], from Old French embocer (modern French embosser), from em- (a variant of en- (prefix meaning ‘in, into’)) + boce (“

parole.significato: Of a hunted animal: to take shelter in a forest or wood.
parole.testo: From Middle English embosen, embose, enbose (“of game: to become exhausted from hunting”), possibly from em- (a variant of en- (prefix meaning ‘in, into’)) + Old French bos, bois (“woodland, woods”) (modern French bois) (from Late Latin boscus, Medieval Latin boscus (“woodlands, woods”), ultimately

parole.significato: To clasp (someone or each other) in the arms with affection; to take in the arms; to hug.
parole.testo: The verb is derived from Middle English embracen (“to clasp in one's arms, embrace; to reach out eagerly for, welcome; to enfold, entwine; to ensnare, entangle; to twist, wrap around; to gird, put on; to lace; to be in or put into bonds; to put a shield on the arm; to grasp (a shield or spear); to a

parole.significato: Synonym of embrace, variously
parole.testo: From Middle English embracement, enbracement, from Old French embrassement; equivalent to embrace + -ment.

parole.significato: To set (something) on fire; to burn (something).
parole.testo: From em- (a variant of en- (intensifying prefix)) + broil (“to expose to great heat; (obsolete) to burn”) (from Late Middle English broilen, brulen (“to burn; to scorch, singe; (cooking) to broil, grill”); further etymology uncertain, possibly from Old French bruler, bruillir, brusler (“to burn”) (m

parole.significato: To place or hide in a thicket; to ambush.
parole.testo: From Middle English embushen, enbusshen, enbuschen, from Old French embuissier, enbuschier. Compare ambush, imbosk.

parole.significato: An ambush.
parole.testo: From Middle English embushement, from Old French embuschement.

parole.significato: Any of various green gemstones, especially a green transparent form of beryl, highly valued as a precious stone.
parole.testo: From Middle English emeraude, borrowed from Old French esmeraude, from Vulgar Latin *smaralda, *smaraldus, *smaraudus, variant of Latin smaragdus, from Ancient Greek σμάραγδος (smáragdos), μάραγδος (máragdos), from a Semitic language. Compare Hebrew בָּרֶקֶת (bāréqeṯ, “emerald, flashing gem”), Akkad

parole.significato: Someone of high rank, reputation or social status.
parole.testo: From Old French eminence, from Latin ēminentia (“prominence”, “protuberance”; “eminence”, “excellence”).

parole.significato: Payment for employment or an office; compensation for a job, which is usually monetary.
parole.testo: From Middle English emolument, from Old French emolument, from Latin ēmolumentum.

parole.significato: To stir or arouse emotion in (someone); to cause to feel emotion.
parole.testo: Borrowed into Middle English from Old French esmouvoir, from classical Latin ēmoveō; see emotion.

parole.significato: An empire; the status or dominion of an emperor.
parole.testo: From Middle English emperie, from Old French emperie, from Latin imperium, inperium (“command, control, dominion, sovereignty, a dominion, empire”), from imperare, inperare (“to command, order”), from in (“in, on”) + parare (“to make ready, order”). Doublet of imperium and empire.

parole.significato: A political state, often a monarchy, that has achieved a much greater current size than its initial size by conquering…
parole.testo: From Middle English empire, from Old French empire, empere, from Latin imperium, inperium (“command, control, dominion, sovereignty, a dominion, empire”), from imperare, inperare (“to command, order”), from in (“in, on”) + parare (“to make ready, order”). Doublet of empery and imperium.

parole.significato: A plaster.
parole.testo: From Old French emplastre, from Latin emplastrum, from Ancient Greek ἔμπλαστρον (émplastron).

parole.significato: To poison.
parole.testo: From Middle English empoisounen, impoisounen, from Old French empoisoner, equivalent to em- + poison.

parole.significato: An enterprise or endeavor, especially a quest or adventure.
parole.testo: Noun is from Middle English emprise, from Old French emprise, emprinse, from Late Latin *imprensa, from Latin in- + prehendere (“to take”). The verb is from emprisen, from the same source.

parole.significato: Forms a transitive verb whose meaning is to make the attached adjective
parole.testo: From Middle English en- (“en-, in-”). Originally from Old French en- (also an-), from Latin in- (“in, into”) and Frankish *in-, *int-, *anda-; but also from an alteration of in-, from Middle English in-, from Old English in- (“in, into”), from Proto-Germanic *in (“in”). Both the Latin and the German

parole.significato: To make (a bill) into law.
parole.testo: From Middle English enacten, from en-, from Old French en- (“to cause to be”), from Latin in- (“in”) and Old French acte (“perform, do”), from Latin actum, past participle of ago (“set in motion”).

parole.significato: To cause to be in love.
parole.testo: From Middle English enamouren, a late back-formation from enamoured, itself a partial calque of Old French enamore, past participle of enamorer, enamourer, equivalent to prefix en- + amor + -er. See amour, and compare inamorato.

parole.significato: In love, amorous.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English enamoured, a partial calque of Old French enamore, past participle of enamorer, enamourer; compare amour and enamor, enamour.

parole.significato: Having horns, hoofs, etc. of a different colour from the body.
parole.testo: Old French enarmé (“equipped with a handle”).

parole.significato: To attract and delight, to charm.
parole.testo: From Middle English enchaunten, from Old French enchanter, from Latin incantāre. Doublet of incant.

parole.significato: One who enchants or delights.
parole.testo: From Middle English enchantour, from Old French enchanteor (Modern French enchanteur), from Latin incantātor (“enchanter; spellcaster; conjurer”), from incantāre (“to sing, to consecrate with spells”). Doublet of incantator. Equivalent to enchant + -er.

parole.significato: The act of enchanting or the feeling of being enchanted.
parole.testo: From Middle English enchauntement, from Old French enchantement.

parole.significato: A woman, especially an attractive one, skilled at using magic; an alluring witch.
parole.testo: From Middle English enchaunteresse, from Old French enchanteresse; equivalent to enchanter + -ess.

parole.significato: To give to somebody as a charge; to entrust with a duty or task.
parole.testo: Old French enchargier.

parole.significato: To surround with a wall, fence, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English enclosen, inclosen, from Middle English enclos, from Old French enclose, feminine plural past participle of enclore, from Vulgar Latin *inclaudō, *inclaudere, from Latin inclūdō (doublet of include), from in- (“in”) + claudō (“to shut”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂

parole.significato: Something that is enclosed, i.e. inserted into a letter or similar package.
parole.testo: From Middle English enclosure, from Old French enclosure, from enclore, from Latin inclūdere, inclūdō, from in- (“in”) + claudō (“to shut”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂u- (“key, hook, nail”). Alike to inclusion.

parole.significato: to seize, appropriate
parole.testo: From Middle English encrochen, from Old French encrochier (“to seize”), from Old French en- + croc (“hook”), of Germanic origin. More at crook.

parole.significato: To load down something with a burden.
parole.testo: From Middle English encombren, from Old French encombrer, from en- + combrer (“to hinder”) (See cumber). By surface analysis, en- + cumber.

parole.significato: encumbrance
parole.testo: From Middle English encombrement, from Old French encombrement. By surface analysis, encumber + -ment.

parole.significato: To apply an encumbrance to (property, etc.).
parole.testo: From Middle English encombraunce, from Old French encombrance, from encombrer.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or causing an encumbrance; cumbersome; troublesome.
parole.testo: From Middle English acombrous, encomberous, encombrous, encomerous, encoumberouse, encoumbrous, encumbrous, from Old French encombros. By surface analysis, encumber + ous.

parole.significato: To damage.
parole.testo: From Middle English endamagen, from Old French endamagier.

parole.significato: To write on the back of (a document); to endorse.
parole.testo: From Middle English [Term?], from Old French endosser. Doublet of endorse.

parole.significato: To continue or carry on, despite obstacles or hardships; to persist.
parole.testo: From Middle English enduren, from Old French endurer, from Latin indūrō (“to make hard”). Displaced Old English drēogan, which survives dialectally as dree. Doublet of dure.

parole.significato: Someone who is hostile to, feels hatred towards, opposes the interests of, or intends injury to someone else.
parole.testo: From Middle English enemy, enemye, enmy, borrowed from Old French enemi, anemi (Modern French ennemi), from Latin inimīcus, from in- (“not”) + amīcus (“friend”). Displaced Middle English fend (“enemy”), from Old English fēond (“enemy”), which survived into Modern English as fiend, but with a differe

parole.significato: To drive back to the water; to pursue.
parole.testo: From Old French enewer; see en- and compare modern French eau (“water”).

parole.significato: To make feeble.
parole.testo: From Middle English enfeblen, from Old French enfeblir. Constructed like en- + feeble.

parole.significato: Rendered fierce or frantic.
parole.testo: Calque of Old French enfelonné, past participle of enfelonner (“to irritate; to anger”).

parole.significato: To transfer a fief to, to endow with a fief; to put (a person) in legal possession of a freehold interest.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English enfeffen, enfeoffen (“to grant (property, rights, etc.) under the feudal system”) [and other forms], from Old French enfeffer, enfieffer (compare Anglo-Latin infeoffāre, Anglo-Norman enfeoffer), from en- (prefix meaning ‘in, into’) + fief (“estate held by a person on conditi

parole.significato: To keep up, impose or bring into effect something, not necessarily by force.
parole.testo: From Middle English enforcen, from Old French enforcier, from Late Latin infortiāre, from in- + fortis (“strong”).

parole.significato: The act of enforcing; compulsion.
parole.testo: From Old French enforcement, see enforce + -ment.

parole.significato: Mixed with lightning or fire.
parole.testo: From en- + Old French fouldre (“lightning”), from Latin fulgur (“lightning”), fulgere (“to flash”), + -ed.

parole.significato: To grant the franchise to an entity, specifically:
parole.testo: From Old French enfranchir (“to set free, enfranchise”), from en- (“in”) + franchir (“to set free”), equivalent to en- + franchise.

parole.significato: To interact socially.
parole.testo: From Middle English engagen, from Old French engagier (“to pledge, engage”), from Old French en- (“in, under”) + gage (“pledge”), from Frankish *wadi (“pledge”), from Proto-Germanic *wadją (“pledge, guarantee”), from Proto-Indo-European *wedʰ- (“to pledge, redeem a pledge; guarantee, bail”), equival

parole.significato: To beget (of a man); to bear or conceive (of a woman).
parole.testo: From Middle English engendren, from Old French engendrer, from Latin ingenerāre.

parole.significato: Pertaining to an engine.
parole.testo: From Old French engignos. See ingenious.

parole.significato: To swallow; to swallow up, engulf.
parole.testo: Partly from Old French englotir, partly from en- + glut.

parole.significato: Partly swallowed; disappearing in the jaws of anything.
parole.testo: Via Middle English from Old French engoulé, past participle of engouler.

parole.significato: To encourage, to insist upon.
parole.testo: Early uses are a survival of Middle English enhorten, from Old French enorter, from Latin inhortor. The verb fell out of use during the 19th century and was formed anew in the last few decades of the 20th century as a blend of enjoin + exhort or a similar formation.

parole.significato: To lay upon, as an order or command; to give an injunction to; to direct with authority; to order; to charge.
parole.testo: From Middle English enjoinen, from Old French enjoindre (“to join with”), from Latin iniungo (“to attach”), a compound of in- (“into” “upon”) and iungo.

parole.significato: To receive pleasure or satisfaction from something.
parole.testo: From Middle English enjoyen, from Old French enjoier, anjoier, enjoer (“to give joy, receive with joy, rejoice”), equivalent to en- + joy.

parole.significato: To bind or encircle with lace, or as with lace
parole.testo: From Old French enlacer.

parole.significato: To make (something) larger.
parole.testo: From Middle English enlargen, from Old French enlargier, enlargir. By surface analysis, en- + large.

parole.significato: To illumine; to light up.
parole.testo: From Old French enluminer.

parole.significato: The quality of being an enemy; a hostile or unfriendly disposition.
parole.testo: From Middle English enemyte, from Old French enemisté, ennemistié, from Late Latin, Vulgar Latin *inimīcitās, *inimīcitātem, from Latin inimīcus (“enemy”). Cognate with French inimitié, Portuguese inimizade, Spanish enemistad. By surface analysis, en(e)m(y) + -ity.

parole.significato: To bestow with nobility, honour or grace.
parole.testo: From Middle English ennoblen, from Old French ennoblir. Equivalent to en- + noble.

parole.significato: Deviation from what is normal or standard; irregularity, abnormality.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English ēnorme (“monstrous or unnatural act; enormity”), from Old French énormité (“enormity”), from Latin ēnormitās (“irregularity; enormity”), from ēnōrmis (“irregular, unusual; enormous, immense”) + -itās (suffix forming nouns indicating states of being). Ēnōrmis is derived from

parole.significato: To become angry or wild.
parole.testo: From Old French enrager, enragier, from rage. Equivalent to en- + rage.

parole.significato: An example; a pattern or model for imitation.
parole.testo: From Middle English ensaumple (noun) and ensaumplen (verb), from Old French ensample.

parole.significato: To search; to try to find something.
parole.testo: From Middle English enserchen, from Old French encerchier. See search.

parole.significato: Synonym of besiege.
parole.testo: From Middle English ensegen, from Old French ensegier. Equivalent to en- + siege.

parole.significato: A badge of office, rank, or power.
parole.testo: From Middle English ensigne, from Old French enseigne, from Latin īnsignia, nominative plural of īnsigne, meaning marked, distinguished. Doublet of insignia.

parole.significato: To bewitch or enchant.
parole.testo: From Old French ensorceler (“to cast a spell, enchant; to captivate”), a variant of ensorcerer, from en- (prefix meaning ‘caused’) + sorcier (“sorcerer”) (ultimately from Latin sors (“fate, lot; oracular response”), from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to bind”)).

parole.significato: To follow (a leader, inclination etc.).
parole.testo: From Old French ensu-, stem of some conjugated forms of ensuivre (“follow close upon, come afterward”) (French ensuivre), from Latin īnsequere, from īnsequi (“to pursue, follow, follow after; come next”), from in- (“upon”) (see in-) + sequi (“follow”) (see sequel).

parole.significato: To imply, require, or invoke.
parole.testo: From Middle English entaillen, from Old French entaillier, entailler (“to notch”, literally “to cut in”); from prefix en- + tailler (“to cut”), from Late Latin taliare, from Latin talea. Compare late Latin feudum talliatum (“a fee entailed, i.e., curtailed or limited”).

parole.significato: That which is entailed.
parole.testo: From Middle English entaille (“carving”), from Old French entaille (“incision”), from the verb entailler. See above.

parole.significato: To go or come into an enclosed or partially enclosed space.
parole.testo: From Middle English entren, from Old French entrer, from Latin intrō (“enter”, verb), from intrā (“inside”). Has been spelled as "enter" for several centuries even in the United Kingdom, although British English and the English of many Commonwealth Countries (e.g. Australia, Canada) retain the "re"

parole.significato: A company, business, organization, or other purposeful endeavor.
parole.testo: From Old French via Middle English and Middle French entreprise, feminine past participle of entreprendre (“to undertake”), from entre (“in between”) + prendre (“to take”), from Latin inter + prehendō, see prehensile.

parole.significato: An activity designed to give pleasure, enjoyment, diversion, amusement, or relaxation to an audience, no matter whether…
parole.testo: From Middle English entretenement (“support, maintenance”), from Old French entretenement; see entertain. Morphologically entertain + -ment.

parole.significato: To lure; to attract by arousing desire or hope.
parole.testo: From Middle English enticen, from Old French enticier (“to stir up or excite”), from a Vulgar Latin *intitiāre (“I set on fire”), from in- + titiō (“firebrand (tool)”), from Proto-Italic *tītjō (“heating”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *teih₁- (“to become hot, melt or to end”).

parole.significato: The act or practice of enticing, of alluring or tempting.
parole.testo: From Old French enticement.

parole.significato: The whole; the complete or amount.
parole.testo: From Middle English enterete, from Old French entiereté, from Latin integritās, from integer (“complete, whole”). Doublet of integrity.

parole.significato: To deposit (a corpse) in a tomb.
parole.testo: From Old French entomber (“deposit in a tomb”). Equivalent to en- + tomb.

parole.significato: plural of entrail
parole.testo: From Middle English entraille, entrailles, from Old French entrailles, from Vulgar Latin intrālia, from Latin interānea, from interāneus, from inter. Compare Spanish entraña.

parole.significato: The act of entering.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English entre, from Old French entree (feminine past participle of the verb entrer, Modern French entrée). From Latin intrō. Doublet of entrada and entrée.

parole.significato: To surround, enclose or enfold.
parole.testo: From Middle English envolupen, from Old French anveloper, envoluper (modern French envelopper), from en- + voloper, vloper (“to wrap, wrap up”) (compare Italian -viluppare; Old Italian alternative form goluppare (“to wrap”)) from Vulgar Latin *vuloppare (“to wrap”), from Proto-Germanic *wlappaną, *w

parole.significato: To inject or put venom onto or into (someone or something).
parole.testo: From Middle English envenymen, from Old French envenimer (“to poison, taint”); equivalent to en- + venom.

parole.significato: Resentful desire of something possessed by another or others (but not limited to material possessions).
parole.testo: From Middle English envie, from Old French envie, from Latin invidia (“envy”), from invidere (“to look at with malice”), from in- (“on, upon”) + videre (“to look, see”). Doublet of envie. Cognate to Proto-Slavic *zavistь (“envy”). Displaced native Old English æfest and Old English nīþ.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Epicurus or Epicureanism, his philosophy.
parole.testo: From Old French Epicurien, from Latin Epicureus, from Ancient Greek Ἐπικούρειος (Epikoúreios, “Epicurean”), from Ἐπίκουρος (Epíkouros, “Epicurus”) + -ειος (-eios, “-ey: forming adjectives”).

parole.significato: An inscription on a gravestone in memory of the deceased.
parole.testo: From Old French epitafe, from Late Latin epitaphium (“eulogy”), from Ancient Greek ἐπιτάφιος (epitáphios, “relating to a funeral”), from ἐπί (epí, “over”) + τάφος (táphos, “tomb”). By surface analysis epi- + -taph.

parole.significato: The act or process of equating two or more things, or the state of those things being equal (that is, identical).
parole.testo: From Old French, from Latin aequātiō (“an equalizing”). Morphologically equate + -ion

parole.significato: Of or relating to the spring or autumnal equinox.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English equinoctial, equinoccial, equinoxial, from Old French equinoxial, from Latin (circulus) aequinoctiālis, from aequinoctium + -alis.

parole.significato: Fairness, impartiality, or justice as determined in light of "natural law" or "natural right".
parole.testo: From Middle English equitee, equytee, from Old French equité, from Latin aequitās (“uniformity; impartiality; fairness”).

parole.significato: A logical fallacy resulting from the use of multiple meanings of a single expression.
parole.testo: c. 1380, from Middle English equivocacion, from Old French equivocation, from Medieval Latin aequivocātiō, from aequivocō, from Late Latin aequivocus (“ambiguous, equivocal”), from Latin aequus (“equal”) + vocō (“call”); a calque of Ancient Greek ὁμωνυμία (homōnumía).

parole.significato: A weasel found in northern latitudes (Mustela erminea in Eurasia, Alaska, and the Arctic, Mustela haidarum in Haida Gwa…
parole.testo: From Middle English ermine, ermin, ermyn, from Old French ermin, ermine, hermine. There are two main theories for the origin of Old French ermine. Germanic origin is suggested via Old Dutch *harmino (“stoat skin”), from *harmo (“stoat, weasel”) (compare Dutch hermelijn and dialectal herm), from Prot

parole.significato: In blazon, ermine with a field or instead of argent (gold with black spots).
parole.testo: From Old French.

parole.significato: To make a mistake.
parole.testo: From Middle English erren, from Old French errer (“to wander, err, mistake”), from Latin errō (“wander, stray, err, mistake”, verb), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ers- (“to be angry, lose one's temper”). Cognate with Old English eorre, ierre (“anger, wrath, ire”), Old English iersian (“to be angry wit

parole.significato: the state of being in error; fallibility
parole.testo: from Old French errance.

parole.significato: A Wiccan coven gathering other than one of the Sabbats. While a full moon ritual may be held during an esbat, esbats en…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Old French esbat, from Old French esbatre (“to frolic, to have fun”), cognate to modern ébat (“frolic”).

parole.significato: A carbuncle (gemstone).
parole.testo: Old French escharboncle, see Modern French escaboucle.

parole.significato: A troop or company.
parole.testo: From Middle English eschele, from Old French eschele, eschelle, esciele, eskiele, variants of Old French esquiere, scare ( > modern French échauguette), from Frankish *skaru, from Proto-Germanic *skarō (“a portion, share, division, troop”). Cognate with German Schar. Doublet of share.

parole.significato: The alderman or chief officer of a guild, in the Middle Ages.
parole.testo: Old French eschevin, a sort of magistrate, alderman, French échevin.

parole.significato: A writing.
parole.testo: From Old French escrit, from Latin scrīptum, from scribō (“to write”).

parole.significato: Payment to a lord in lieu of military service.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English scuage, from Old French escuage; in Modern English, remodelled on the Old French etymon.

parole.significato: A defence for the shoulder, composed of flexible overlapping plates of metal, especially as used in the fifteenth centu…
parole.testo: From an Old French word corresponding to French épaulière or espalière. See espalier.

parole.significato: Exceptional in importance or significance; special.
parole.testo: From Middle English especial, via Old French especial, from Latin specialis, from species (“appearance, form, beauty”), from specere (“to look”). Doublet of special. Related to species.

parole.significato: A betrothal.
parole.testo: From Middle English espousal, espousaille, from Old French espousailles, from Latin sponsalia (“a betrothal”), neuter plural of sponsalis, from spōnsus (“one betrothed, a spouse”); see spouse. By surface analysis, espouse + -al.

parole.significato: To marry.
parole.testo: From Middle English espousen, borrowed from Old French espouser, from Latin spōnsāre (frequentative of spondeō), from Proto-Indo-European *spend-.

parole.significato: betrothal; espousal.
parole.testo: Compare Old French espousement.

parole.significato: to inflame with passion or romantic love.
parole.testo: From Old French espris, past participle of esprendre.

parole.significato: To find out or observe (someone or something, especially if not easy to see) by spying or looking; to catch sight of; t…
parole.testo: From Middle English aspien, espien (“to make covert observations of (a person or place) with hostile intent, to spy on; to seek to discover by spying; to act as a spy; to catch sight of, see; to look over, observe; to wait in ambush, to ambush; to plot against; to look for, seek to find; to inquire

parole.significato: A lawyer.
parole.testo: From Middle English esquier, from Old French escuyer, escuier, properly, a shield-bearer (compare modern French écuyer (“shield-bearer, armor-bearer, squire of a knight, esquire, equerry, rider, horseman”)), from Late Latin scūtārius (“shieldmaker, shield-bearer”), from Latin scūtum (“shield”); prob

parole.significato: The lower of the halves into which a square is divided diagonally, a single gyron, but potentially larger (extending ac…
parole.testo: Old French esquiere, esquierre, esquarre (“a square”) (whence modern French équerre), perhaps via a form like based esquire from bas d'esquire ("bottom of a square"), whence attested forms base (e)squire, e(s)quire bast.

parole.significato: To excuse for failure to appear in court.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English essoyne, from Old French essoignier, from Medieval Latin exoniō, essoniō (“excuse oneself; accept an excuse”), from ex- + sonium + -ō, sonium being from Proto-West Germanic *sunnju (“care, need”).

parole.significato: To make stable or firm; to confirm.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English establissen, from Old French establiss-, stem of some of the conjugated forms of establir (modern French établir), from Latin stabiliō, stabilīre, from stabilis (“firm, steady, stable”).

parole.significato: The act or process of establishing; a ratifying or ordaining; settlement; confirmation.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English *establishment, stablishment, stablisshement, from Old French establissement (modern French établissement), from the verb establir. By surface analysis, establish + -ment.

parole.significato: Worthy of esteem; admirable.
parole.testo: From Middle English estimable, estymable, from Old French estimable, from Latin aestimābilis. Equivalent to esteem + -able and estimate + -able.

parole.significato: The process of making an estimate.
parole.testo: From Middle English estimacioun, estimacion, from Old French estimacion, from Latin aestimatio. Morphologically estimate + -ion.

parole.significato: Of or relating to summer.
parole.testo: From Middle English estival, from Old French estival, from Latin aestivalis.

parole.significato: A six-pointed star whose rays are wavy, as opposed to the straight lines of a mullet.
parole.testo: Old French, from Latin stēlla. Doublet of étoile, stella, and stelo; related to aster and star.

parole.significato: A legal principle in the law of equity that prevents a party from asserting otherwise valid legal rights against anothe…
parole.testo: From Middle English *estoppel (found only as stoppel, stoppell, stopple, etc.), probably from Old French estoupail, estopail, estopaille, a bung made of oakum (étoupe), from Latin stuppa ("flax, tow"), from Ancient Greek στύππη (stuppē).

parole.significato: An allowance provided from an estate for a person's support; an allowance of wood for repairs, firewood and fencing.
parole.testo: From Middle English estovers pl, from Old French estover (“obligation”).

parole.significato: To cause to feel less close or friendly; alienate. To cease contact with (particularly of a family member or spouse, es…
parole.testo: From Old French estranger (“to treat as a stranger”), from Latin extraneus (“foreigner, stranger”) (from which also strange, stranger). Also see Spanish extraño.

parole.significato: The act of estranging; the act of alienating; alienation.
parole.testo: Old French estrangement. By surface analysis, estrange + -ment (“act, state”).

parole.significato: To strangle.
parole.testo: From Middle English estranglen, rare and late variant of stranglen, from Old French estrangler.

parole.significato: The indoor layout or plan of a castle.
parole.testo: From Old French estre (“state, plan”). Cognate with some forms of be (including am, is and are).

parole.significato: A true copy, duplicate, or extract of an original writing or record, especially of amercements or penalties set down in…
parole.testo: Old French estrete (“an extract”).

parole.significato: A destructive kind of waste committed by a tenant for life, in lands, woods, or houses.
parole.testo: From Old French estrepement (“damage, waste”).

parole.significato: Lasting forever; unending.
parole.testo: From Middle English eternal, from Old French eternal, from Late Latin aeternālis, from Latin aeternus (“eternal”), from aevum (“age”). Displaced native Old English ēċe.

parole.significato: Eternal.
parole.testo: From Middle English eterne, from Old French eterne, from Latin aeternus.

parole.significato: Existence without end, infinite time.
parole.testo: From Middle English eternyte, from Old French eternité, from Latin aeternitās. Displaced native Old English ēcnes.

parole.significato: A set of principles of right and wrong behaviour guiding, or representative of, a specific culture, society, group, or…
parole.testo: From Middle English etik, ethik, from Old French ethique, from Late Latin ēthica, from Ancient Greek ἠθική (ēthikḗ), from ἠθικός (ēthikós, “of or for morals, moral, expressing character”), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, moral nature”).

parole.significato: The scientific study of the origin and evolution of a word's semantic meaning across time, including its constituent mo…
parole.testo: From Middle English ethymologie, from Old French ethimologie, from Latin etymologia, from Ancient Greek ἐτυμολογία (etumología), from ἔτυμον (étumon, “true sense”) and -λογία (-logía, “study or logic of”), from λόγος (lógos, “word; explanation”). By surface analysis, etymo- + -logy.

parole.significato: A Christian sacrament commemorating the Last Supper of Christ, with the physical forms of bread and usually wine which…
parole.testo: From Middle English eukarist, from Old French, from Ecclesiastical Latin eucharistia, from Ancient Greek εὐχαριστία (eukharistía, “gratitude, giving of thanks”). Displaced native Old English hūsl.

parole.significato: The act of evacuating; leaving a place in an orderly fashion, especially for safety.
parole.testo: From Middle English evacuacioun, from Old French evacuation, from Late Latin ēvacuātiō. Equivalent to evacuate + -ion.

parole.significato: The Christian gospel.
parole.testo: From Middle English evaungel, evangile, from Old French evangile, from Late Latin evangelium, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion, “good news”), from εὐάγγελος (euángelos, “bringing good news”), from εὐ- (eu-, “well”) + ἀγγέλλειν (angéllein, “to announce”) (English angel). The word gospel is f

parole.significato: evangelical
parole.testo: From Old French evangelique (French évangélique).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the doctrines or teachings of the Christian gospel or Christianity in general.
parole.testo: From evangelic + -al, from Old French evangelique, from Latin evangelium, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion, “good news”).

parole.significato: An itinerant or special preacher, especially a revivalist, who conducts services in different cities or locations, now…
parole.testo: From Old French evangeliste, equivalent to evangel + -ist, from ecclesiastical Latin evangelista, from ecclesiastical Ancient Greek εὐαγγελιστής (euangelistḗs, “bringer of good news”), from εὐαγγελίζεσθαι (euangelízesthai, “to evangelize”), from εὐάγγελος (euángelos, “bringing good news”), from εὖ (
