parole.significato: To tell people about (a particular branch of) Christianity, especially in order to convert them; to preach the gospel t…
parole.testo: From Old French évangéliser, equivalent to evangel + -ize, from Late Latin evangelizare, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγελίζω (euangelízō). Displaced native Old English godspellian (literally “to gospel”).

parole.significato: To vanish.
parole.testo: From Middle English [Term?], from Old French esvanir, compare Latin evanescere. See evanesce, vanish.

parole.significato: Facts or observations presented in support of an assertion.
parole.testo: From Middle English evidence, from Old French [Term?], from Latin evidentia (“clearness, in Late Latin a proof”), from evidens (“clear, evident”); see evident.

parole.significato: Obviously true by simple observation.
parole.testo: From Middle English evident, from Old French evident, from Latin ēvidēns (“visible, apparent, clear, plain”) (compare Late Latin ēvideor (“to appear plainly”)), from ē (“out”) + videō (“see”), present participle vidēns, deponent videor (“to appear, seem”). Displaced native Old English sweotol.

parole.significato: To honor; to hold in high esteem; to praise or worship.
parole.testo: From Middle English exalten, from Old French exalter, from Latin exaltō.

parole.significato: The act of exalting or raising high; also, the state of being exalted; elevation.
parole.testo: From Middle English exaltacioun, exaltatioun, from Old French exaltacion and Latin exaltātiō (“exaltation, elevation”), from exaltō (“raise, elevate, exalt”), from ex (“from, out of”) + altus (“high”). By surface analysis, exalt + -ation.

parole.significato: The act of examining.
parole.testo: From Middle English examinacioun, from Old French examinacion, from Latin exāminātiō. Morphologically examine + -ation.

parole.significato: To observe carefully or critically to learn about someone or something.
parole.testo: From Middle English examinen, examenen, from Old French examiner, from Latin exāmināre.

parole.significato: Something that is representative of all such things in a group.
parole.testo: From Middle English example, exaumple, from Old French example, essaumple, from Latin exemplum (“sample, pattern, specimen, copy for imitation, etc.”, literally “what is taken out”); see exempt. Doublet of exemplum and sample. Displaced native Middle English forebisne, from Old English forebȳsn; and

parole.significato: To be larger, greater than (something).
parole.testo: From Middle English exceden, from Old French exceder, from Latin excēdō (“to go beyond”), from ex- (“out, forth”) with cēdō (“to go”); see cede and compare accede etc. Partly displaced native Old English ofersteppan, whence Modern English overstep.

parole.significato: To surpass someone or something; to be better or do better than someone or something.
parole.testo: From Middle English excellen, from Old French exceller, from Latin excellere, excelsum; ex (“out”) + *cellō, an unattested verb root found in culmen (“height, top”); Compare French exceller. See also culminate, column.

parole.significato: The quality of being excellent; brilliance
parole.testo: From Middle English excellence, from Old French excellence, from Latin excellentia.

parole.significato: Having excelled, having surpassed.
parole.testo: From Middle English excellent, from Old French excellent, from Latin excellēns (“elevated, exalted”), present participle of excellō (“elevate, exult”), equivalent to excel + -ent.

parole.significato: The state of surpassing or going beyond a limit; the state of being beyond sufficiency, necessity, or duty; more than w…
parole.testo: From Middle English exces (“excess, ecstasy”), from Old French exces, from Latin excessus (“a going out, loss of self-possession”), from excedere, excessum (“to go out, go beyond”). See exceed.

parole.significato: Exceeding the usual bounds of something; too much (of amount); extravagant; immoderate.
parole.testo: From Middle English excessive, excessif, from Old French excessif, from Medieval Latin excessivus, equivalent to excess + -ive.

parole.significato: The act of exciting or putting in motion; the act of rousing up or awakening.
parole.testo: From Middle English excitacion, excitacioun, from Old French excitation, from Latin excitātiō. Morphologically excite + -ation.

parole.significato: To stir the emotions of; to cause to feel excitement.
parole.testo: From Middle English exciten, from Old French exciter, from Latin excitō (“to call out, call forth, arouse, wake up, stimulate”), frequentative of excieō (“to call out, arouse, excite”), from ex (“out”) + cieō (“to call, summon”). See cite and compare to accite, concite, incite.

parole.significato: The state of being excited (emotionally aroused).
parole.testo: From Middle English excitement, from Old French excitement, equivalent to excite + -ment.

parole.significato: The act of excluding or shutting out; removal from consideration or taking part.
parole.testo: From Middle English exclusion, exclusioun, from Old French [Term?] and Latin exclusiō, from exclūdō. By surface analysis, exclude + -sion.

parole.significato: Possible to excuse; worthy of being excused.
parole.testo: From Old French escusable, from Latin excusabilis.

parole.significato: Of the poorest quality.
parole.testo: From Old French execrable, from Latin execrabilis.

parole.significato: To kill, especially as punishment for a capital crime.
parole.testo: From Old French executer (French exécuter), from Latin exsecutus, past participle of exsequor (“to follow (up/through)”, particularly in the sense “to go through with a deed or punishment”), from ex- (“out”) + sequor (“to follow”).

parole.significato: The act, manner or style of executing (actions, maneuvers, performances).
parole.testo: From Old French execution (c.1360), from Latin exsecutiō, an agent noun from exsequor (“to follow out”), from ex (“out”) + sequor (“follow”). Equivalent to execute + -ion.

parole.significato: A female executor; an executrix.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Old French executeresse (modern French exécutrice), from executeur (“executor”) + -esse (suffix forming female equivalents). By surface analysis, executor + -ess (suffix forming female equivalents).

parole.significato: An act of exempting.
parole.testo: From Old French exemption, from Latin exemptiō, from eximō, equivalent to exempt + -ion.

parole.significato: Funeral rites.
parole.testo: A back-formation from exequies, from Middle English exequies, from Old French exequies, from Latin exsequiās, accusative of exsequiae (“a funeral, seeing-off procession”).

parole.significato: Any activity designed to develop or hone a skill or ability.
parole.testo: From Middle English exercise, from Old French exercise, from Latin exercitium. Displaced native Old English plega (“an exercise”) whence Modern English play.

parole.significato: An instance of exhibiting, or something exhibited.
parole.testo: From Old French exhibicion. Equivalent to exhibit + -ion.

parole.significato: To urge; to advise earnestly.
parole.testo: From Middle English exorten, from Old French exhorter, from Latin exhortārī (“to encourage”), from ex- (“out of, from”) + hortārī (“to incite, spur”).

parole.significato: The act or practice of exhorting.
parole.testo: From Middle English exhortacioun, from Old French exhortacion, from Latin exhortātiōnem, accusative singular of exhortātiō (“encouraging; exhortation”), from exhortor (“to encourage, exhort”), from ex (“out of, from”) + hortor (“encourage”). By surface analysis, exhort + -ation.

parole.significato: The state of being banished from one's home or country.
parole.testo: From Middle English exil, borrowed from Old French essil, exil, from Latin exsilium, exilium (“state of exile”), derived from exsul, exul (“exiled person”).

parole.significato: The state of being, existing, or occurring; beinghood.
parole.testo: From Middle English existence, from Old French existence, from Late Latin existentia (“existence”), from existēns, from existō, exsistō (“I am, I exist”), from ex (“out”) + sistere (“to set, place”) (related to stare (“to stand, to be stood”)), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *stísteh₂ti, from t

parole.significato: Exceeding proper limits; excessive or unduly high; extravagant.
parole.testo: From Middle English exorbitant, through Old French from Late Latin exorbitāns, present active participle of exorbitō (“to go out of the track”), from ex (“out”) + orbita (“wheel-track”); see orbit. Compare French exorbitant.

parole.significato: The ritual act of driving out evil spirits from persons, places or things that are possessed by them.
parole.testo: From Old French exorciser, from Late Latin exorcizō, from Ancient Greek ἐξορκίζω (exorkízō, “to ward off, to charge under oath, adjure”), from ἐξ (ex) + ὅρκος (hórkos).

parole.significato: Marked by expectation.
parole.testo: From Old French expectant, from Latin expectans.

parole.significato: The quality of being fit or suitable to cause some desired end or the purpose intended; propriety or advisability under…
parole.testo: From Middle English expedience, from Old French expedience, from Late Latin expedientia, from Latin expediens.

parole.significato: Suitable to effect some desired end or the purpose intended.
parole.testo: From Middle English expedient, from Old French expedient, from Latin expediens (stem expedient-), present participle of expedire (“to bring forward, to dispatch, to expedite; impers. to be profitable, serviceable, advantageous, expedient”), from ex (“out”) + pēs (“foot, hoof”).

parole.significato: The effect upon the judgment or feelings produced by any event, whether witnessed or participated in; personal and dire…
parole.testo: From Middle English experience, from Old French, from Latin experientia (“a trial, proof, experiment, experimental knowledge, experience”), from experiens, present participle of experiri (“to try, put to the test, undertake, undergo”), from ex (“out”) + peritus (“experienced, expert”), past particip

parole.significato: A test under controlled conditions made to either demonstrate a known truth, examine the validity of a hypothesis, or d…
parole.testo: From Middle English experiment, from Old French esperiment (French expérience), from Latin experimentum (“experience, attempt, experiment”), from experior (“to experience, to attempt”), itself from ex + *perior, in turn from Proto-Indo-European *per-.

parole.significato: Extraordinary capable or knowledgeable.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English expert, derived from Old French expert (“experienced”), espert, from Latin expertus (contracted from *experitus), perfect active participle of experior (“to try”), from ex- + *-perior.

parole.significato: To make plain, manifest, or intelligible; to clear of obscurity; to illustrate the meaning of.
parole.testo: From Middle English explanen, from Old French explaner, from Latin explanō (“to flatten, spread out, make plain or clear, explain”), from ex- (“out”) + planō (“to flatten, make level”), from planus (“level, plain”); see plain and plane. Compare esplanade, splanade. Displaced Old English reċċan.

parole.significato: A heroic or extraordinary deed.
parole.testo: From Old French esploit (noun), esploitier (verb).

parole.significato: Able to be exploited, especially commercially.
parole.testo: From Old French exploitable or exploit + -able.

parole.significato: To reveal; to uncover; to make visible; to bring to light.
parole.testo: From Middle English exposen, from Old French exposer (“to lay open, set forth”), from Latin expōnō (“set forth”), with contamination from poser (“to lay, place”). Doublet of expone and expound (via Old French espondre (“to set forth, explain”)), from the same Latin term.

parole.significato: The action of exposing something to something, such as skin to the sunlight.
parole.testo: From Middle English exposicioun, from Old French esposicion, from Latin expositiō, from expōnere (“to put forth”). The sense meaning "exhibition" is a later semantic loan from French exposition.

parole.significato: To set out the meaning of; to explain or discuss at length.
parole.testo: From Middle English expounden, from Old French espondre, from Latin exponere. Doublet of expone and expose.

parole.significato: To convey or communicate; to make known or explicit.
parole.testo: From Old French espresser, expresser, from frequentative form of Latin exprimere.

parole.significato: To take by storm; capture.
parole.testo: From Middle English expugnen, from Old French expugner, from Latin expugnō (“to take by storm”), from ex- + pugnō (“fight”), from pugnus (“fist”).

parole.significato: The act of expelling or the state of being expelled.
parole.testo: From Middle English expulsioun, from Old French expulsion, from Latin expulsio, expulsionem.

parole.significato: Shocking; astounding.
parole.testo: From Old French estoner.

parole.significato: The act of extracting or the condition of being extracted.
parole.testo: From Old French estraction, from Medieval Latin extractio.

parole.significato: Of a place, the most remote, farthest or outermost.
parole.testo: Borrowed into late Middle English from Old French extreme, from Latin extrēmus, the superlative of exter.

parole.significato: The most extreme or furthest point of something.
parole.testo: From Middle English extremite, from Old French extremité, from Latin extrēmitātem (“extremity; border, perimeter; ending”), from extrēmīs (“furthest, extreme”) + -itās (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ts (suffix forming nouns indicating a state of being); see extreme. Extrēmīs is derived f

parole.significato: The act of exulting; great joy at success or victory, or at any advantage gained; rapturous delight
parole.testo: From Middle English exultacion, from Old French exultacion, from Latin exsultātiō, exsultātiōnem.

parole.significato: An object that consists of a rim and small hole or perforation to receive a cord or fastener, as in garments, sails, et…
parole.testo: From Middle English oylet, from Old French oillet, equivalent to Old French oil (“eye”) + -et (diminutive suffix). Spelling and pronunciation were later on influenced by eye (which is distantly related to oil via Proto-Indo-European) as though suffixed with -let (a double diminutive also from -et).

parole.significato: A journey taken by certain Medieval English itinerant judges (justices in eyre)
parole.testo: From Middle English eire, from Old French erre (“journey, march, way”), from Latin iter, itineris (“a going, way”), from the root of ire (“to go”). Compare errant, itinerant, issue.

parole.significato: The nest of a bird of prey.
parole.testo: From Middle English eire, aire, from Old French aire or Medieval Latin aeria. Old French aire, in the sense of an eagle's nest, may have derived from Latin ager, or may less likely be related to the other senses, ultimately from Latin ārea.

parole.significato: A fictitious narrative intended to enforce some useful truth or precept, usually with animals, etc. as characters; an a…
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French fable, from Latin fābula, from fārī (“to speak, say”) + -bula (“instrumental suffix”). See ban, and compare fabulous, fame. Doublet of fabula.

parole.significato: A short, farcical, often bawdy tale of a genre written in the North of France in the 12th, 13th and 14th centuries.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Old French fabliau, diminutive of fable.

parole.significato: The front part of the head of a human or other animal, featuring the eyes, nose, and mouth, and the surrounding area.
parole.testo: From Middle English face, from Old French face, from Late Latin facia, from Latin faciēs (“form, appearance”). Doublet of facies. Displaced native onlete (“face, countenance, appearance”), anleth (“face”), from Old English anwlite, andwlita, compare German Antlitz; Old English ansīen (“face”), Middl

parole.significato: Something actual as opposed to invented.
parole.testo: From Old French fact, from Latin factum (“an act, deed, feat, etc.”); also Medieval Latin for “state, condition, circumstance”; neuter of factus (“done or made”), perfect passive participle of faciō (“do, make”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to put, place, set”). Old/Middle French l

parole.significato: The academic staff at schools, colleges, universities or not-for-profit research institutes, as opposed to the students…
parole.testo: From Middle English faculte (“power, property”), from Old French faculte, from Latin facultas (“capability, ability, skill, abundance, plenty, stock, goods, property; in Medieval Latin also a body of teachers”), another form of facilitas (“easiness, facility, etc.”), from facul, another form of faci

parole.significato: A gender-neutral third-person singular subject pronoun, equivalent to singular they, and coordinate with gendered prono…
parole.testo: From Old French fae, from Medieval Latin fāda. The use of the pronoun appears c. 2013.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; perhaps; nodo incerto nell'albero; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: A bundle of sticks or brushwood intended to be used for fuel tied together for carrying. (Some sources specify that a f…
parole.testo: From Middle English fagot, from Old French fagot (“bundle of sticks”), of uncertain origin. Unlikely from Old Occitan fagot or Italian fagotto, as these appear later than the Old French term. Compare also Italian fangotto and Spanish fajo (“bundle, wad”). Perhaps from a diminutive of Vulgar Latin *f

parole.significato: To make a fagot of (objects); to bind (objects) together in a fagot or bundle.
parole.testo: Most likely from Italian fagotto, from Latin fascis.

parole.significato: To be unsuccessful.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English failen, borrowed from Old French falir, from Vulgar Latin *fallire, alteration of Latin fallere (“to deceive, disappoint”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰāl- (“to lie, deceive”) or Proto-Indo-European *(s)gʷʰh₂el- (“to stumble”). Compare Alemannic German fääle (“to lack”)

parole.significato: fault; failure; omission
parole.testo: From Old French faillance, from faillir. Doublet of fallency.

parole.significato: A fabric woven from silk, cotton, or rayon with slight ribs.
parole.testo: From Old French.

parole.significato: To achieve or obtain (something) by complicated or deceitful methods; to finagle, to wangle.
parole.testo: Uncertain; perhaps: * related to Old French fornoiier, fornier (“to deny”), from for- (prefix expressing error, exclusion, or inadequacy) + noiier, nier (“to deny”) (compare Late Latin forīsnegāre (“to renege, repudiate”), where the Frankish for- is rendered into Latin as forīs), from Latin negāre (

parole.significato: An irresponsible or lazy person.
parole.testo: From Old French fay neant, alteration of feignant (“idler”), present participle of feindre, modelled on fait (“does”) + neant (“nothing”).

parole.significato: Lacking strength; weak; languid; inclined to lose consciousness
parole.testo: From Middle English faynt, feynt (“weak; feeble”), from Old French faint, feint (“feigned; negligent; sluggish”), past participle of feindre, faindre (“to feign; sham; work negligently”), from Latin fingere (“to touch, handle, form, shape, frame, form in thought, imagine, conceive, contrive, devise,

parole.significato: A community gathering to celebrate and exhibit local achievements.
parole.testo: From Middle English feyre, from Old French foire, from Latin fēriae.

parole.significato: A mythical being of human form with magical powers, known in many sizes and descriptions, although typically depicted a…
parole.testo: From Middle English faierie, fairie, from Old French faerie, from fae (from Latin fāta (“goddess of fate”)) + -erie. Equivalent to fay + -ry. Attested in English from about 1330, in King Alisaunder, first in the sense of "enchantment, illusion, dream" ("that thou herdest is fairye") and shortly ther

parole.significato: A trust or confidence in the intentions or abilities of a person, object, or ideal from prior empirical evidence.
parole.testo: From Middle English faith (also fay), borrowed from Old French fei, feid, from Latin fidem. Doublet of foy. Displaced native Old English ġelēafa, which was also a word for belief. * Old French had [θ] as a final devoiced allophone of /ð/ from lenited Latin /d/; this eventually fell silent in the 12t

parole.significato: A somewhat curved, single-edged medieval sword of European origin, with the cutting edge on its convex side, whose desi…
parole.testo: From Middle English fauchoun, from Old French fauchon (cognate with Italian falcione), from Vulgar Latin *falciōnem, from Latin falx.

parole.significato: Any bird of the genus Falco, all of which are birds of prey.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English faucoun, falcon, faulcon, from Old French falcun, from Late Latin falcō (“falcon”), of Germanic origin, probably via Frankish *falkō (“falcon, hawk”), from Proto-Germanic *falkô (“falcon”), from Proto-Indo-European *pol̑- (“pale”), from *pel- (“fallow”). Cognates Cognat

parole.significato: A person who breeds or trains hawks or other birds of prey.
parole.testo: From Middle English fauconer, from Old French falconer, fauconer, from faucon (“falcon”).

parole.significato: Characterized by fallacy; false or mistaken.
parole.testo: From Old French fallacieux (whence -acious), from Latin fallācia, from fallāx, from fallere.

parole.significato: Deceptive or false appearance; that which misleads the eye or the mind.
parole.testo: From Middle English fallaci, fallace, fallas, from Old French fallace (whence -acy), from Latin fallācia (“deception, deceit”), from fallāx (“deceptive, deceitful”), from fallere (“to deceive”).

parole.significato: Something said or reported; gossip, rumour.
parole.testo: From Middle English fame, from Old French fame (“celebrity, renown”), itself borrowed from Latin fāma (“talk, rumor, report, reputation”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰéh₂-meh₂, from *bʰeh₂- (“to speak, say, tell”). Cognate with Ancient Greek φήμη (phḗmē, “talk”). Related also to Latin for (“speak, s

parole.significato: To starve (to death); to kill or destroy with hunger.
parole.testo: From Middle English famisshe, from famen (“starve”), from Old French afamer, ultimately from Latin famēs (“hunger”). Compare affamish, famine. Cognate with Spanish hambre (“hunger”).

parole.significato: The imagination.
parole.testo: From Middle English fansy, fantsy, a contraction of fantasy, fantasye, fantasie, from Old French fantasie, from Medieval Latin fantasia, from Late Latin phantasia (“an idea, notion, fancy, phantasm”), from Ancient Greek φαντασία (phantasía), from φαντάζω (phantázō, “to render visible”), from φαντός

parole.significato: To appreciate without jealousy or greed.
parole.testo: From Middle English fancien, fantasien, fantesien, from Old French fantasier, from the noun (see above)).

parole.significato: A vestment reserved only for the Pope for use during a pontifical Mass.
parole.testo: From Middle English fanon, fanoun, from Old French fanon, from Medieval Latin fanō, from Frankish *fano, from Proto-Germanic *fanô. Doublet of fane and vane.

parole.significato: That which comes from one's imagination or the act of imagining things.
parole.testo: Noun inherited from Middle English fantasie, from Old French fantasie (“fantasy”), from Latin phantasia (“imagination”), from Ancient Greek φαντασία (phantasía, “apparition”), from φαντάζω (phantázō, “to render visible”), from φαντός (phantós, “visible”), from φαίνω (phaínō, “to make visible”); from

parole.significato: A bundle or burden.
parole.testo: From Middle English fardel, from Old French fardel (“pack, bundle”), from Spanish fardel, diminutive of fardo (“pack, bundle”), from Arabic فَرْد (fard, “one of a pair”), as applied to saddlebags.

parole.significato: Someone or something that farms, as:
parole.testo: From Middle English fermour (“a steward, bailliff, collector of taxes”), from Old French fermier (“a farmer, a lessee, husbandman, bailliff”), from Medieval Latin firmarius (“one to whom land is rented, a collector of taxes, deputy”), from firma; equivalent to farm + -er. Compare Old English feormer

parole.significato: To insert vernacular paraphrases into (a Latin liturgy).
parole.testo: From Old French farsir. Doublet of farce.

parole.significato: The ends of ribbons.
parole.testo: From Old French fatraille (“trumpery”).
