parole.significato: An exposed plumbing fitting; a tap or spigot; a regulator for controlling the flow of a liquid from a reservoir.
parole.testo: From Middle English faucet, fawcett, from Old French fausset, of uncertain origin: * Possibly from Late Latin falsāre (“to falsify”) or from a diminutive of Latin faux, faucēs (“throat”). * Alternatively, from Old Norse foss, fors (“waterfall”), thus, cognate with English force, foss.

parole.significato: flattery; cajolery; deceit
parole.testo: From Old French favele, from Latin fabella (“short fable”), diminutive of fabula. See fable.

parole.significato: yellow or dun in colour
parole.testo: From Old French fauvel, favel, diminutive of Old French fauve; of German origin. See fallow (adjective).

parole.significato: A kind or helpful deed; an instance of voluntarily assisting (someone).
parole.testo: From Middle English favour, favor, faver, from Anglo-Norman favour, from mainland Old French favor, from Latin favor (“good will; kindness; partiality”), from faveō (“to be kind to”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂weh₁yeti (“to be favourable to”), from the root Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂

parole.significato: Apt to win favour; pleasing.
parole.testo: From Middle English favourable, from Old French favorable, from Latin favōrābilis, from favor. By surface analysis, favour + -able.

parole.significato: A young deer.
parole.testo: From Middle English fawne, fowne, foun, from Old French faon, foon, feon, from Vulgar Latin *fētōnem, from Latin fētus (“offspring, young”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suckle, nurse”). Displaced native Old English hindċealf (literally “deer calf”). Doublet of fetus.

parole.significato: faith
parole.testo: From Middle English fei, from Old French fei

parole.significato: A fair, a market.
parole.testo: From Old French foire, from Latin fēriae.

parole.significato: A holiday, festival, especially a religious one
parole.testo: From Middle English feeste, feste, borrowed from Old French feste, from Late Latin festa, from the plural of Latin festum (“holiday, festival, feast”), from Proto-Italic *fēs-tos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰéh₁s (“god, godhead, deity”); see also Ancient Greek θεός (theós, “god, goddess”)

parole.significato: To partake in a feast, or large meal.
parole.testo: From Middle English feesten, festen, from Old French fester, from Medieval Latin festāre, from the noun. See above.

parole.significato: Neat, pretty.
parole.testo: From Middle English fetis, from Old French fetis, faitis, from Latin factīcius. Doublet of factitious. The spelling reflects an assumption that the word was derived from feat (“dexterous, neat”) + -ous.

parole.significato: feebleness; weakness; frailty
parole.testo: From Middle English feblesse, from Old French feblesce.

parole.significato: An amount charged in return for permission to do something
parole.testo: From Middle English fee, fe, feh, feoh, from Old English feoh (“cattle, property, wealth, money, payment, tribute, fee”) with contamination from Old French fieu, fief (from Medieval Latin fevum, a variant of feudum (see feud), from Frankish *fehu (“cattle, livestock”); whence fief), both from Proto-

parole.significato: The private ownership of property (real estate) in which the owner has the right to control, use, and transfer the prop…
parole.testo: From Old French fief simple.

parole.significato: Feebleness; weakness, infirmity.
parole.testo: From Old French feblesce, from feble (“feeble”).

parole.significato: To make a false show or pretence of; to counterfeit or simulate.
parole.testo: From Middle English feynen, feinen, borrowed from Old French feindre (“to pretend”), from Latin fingere (“to form, shape, invent”). Compare French feignant (present participle of feindre, literally “feigning”). Also compare feint, figment and fiction.

parole.significato: The condition of being happy.
parole.testo: From Middle English felicite (“bliss, happiness, joy; delight, pleasure; a source of happiness; good fortune; prosperity; well-being; of a planet: in an influential position”) [and other forms], borrowed from Old French felicité (modern French félicité (“bliss, happiness; felicity”)), from Latin fēl

parole.significato: Of a person or animal, their actions, thoughts, etc.: brutal, cruel, harsh, heartless; also, evil, wicked.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Middle English feloun, felun (“base, wicked; hostile; of an animal: dangerous; of words: angry, harsh, slanderous; of things: dangerous, deadly; false, fraudulent; unlucky”) [and other forms], from Old French felon (“bad, evil, immoral”) (compare fel (“evil; despicable,

parole.significato: A small infected sore; an abscess, a boil.
parole.testo: From Middle English feloun, felone (“type of carbuncle or sore with pus; swelling on a hawk’s body”), possibly from Old French *felon, from Latin fel (“bile, gall; bitterness; poison; venom”): see etymology 1.

parole.significato: Evil, wicked.
parole.testo: From Middle English felenous(e), felenows, fellenouse, felonous(e), felonows(e), felonus, from Old French feloneus. By surface analysis, felon (“an evil or wicked person”) + -ous.

parole.significato: A serious criminal offense, which, under United States federal law, is punishable by a term of imprisonment of not less…
parole.testo: From Middle English felony, felonie, from Old French felonie (“evil, immoral deed”), from felon (“evildoer”). Ultimately of Proto-Germanic origin. More at felon. By surface analysis, felon + -y.

parole.significato: One of the female (feminine) sex or gender.
parole.testo: From Middle English female, an alteration of Middle English femele, from Old French femele, femelle (“female”), from Medieval Latin fēmella (“a female”), from Latin fēmella (“a girl, a young female, a young woman”), diminutive of fēmina (“a woman”). The English spelling and pronunciation were remode

parole.significato: The lantern, louvre, or covering placed in the ridge of a hall roof for the purpose of ventilation or letting out the s…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle English fumerelle, from Old French fumeraille; ultimately derived from Latin fumus (“smoke”). Likely a doublet of fumarole.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the female gender.
parole.testo: From Middle English feminine, femynyne, femynyn, from Old French feminin, feminine, from Latin fēminīnus, from fēmina (“woman”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-m̥h₁n-eh₂ (“(the one) nursing, breastfeeding”). Related to fetus, feminism, filial, fellatio.

parole.significato: A woman; a wife; (now chiefly Canada, US) a young woman or girl.
parole.testo: From Middle English femme, itself borrowed from Old French fame (whence French femme), from Latin femina (“woman”). Doublet of feme, femina, and hembra.

parole.significato: A thin artificial barrier that separates two pieces of land or forms a perimeter enclosing the lands of a house, buildi…
parole.testo: From Middle English fence, fens, short for defence, defens (“the act of defending”), from Old French defens, defense (see defence). The sense "enclosure" arises in the mid 15th century. Also from the 15th century is use as a verb in the sense "to enclose with a fence". The generalized sense "to defe

parole.significato: To take care of oneself; to take responsibility for one's own well-being.
parole.testo: From Middle English fenden (“defend, fight, prevent”), shortening of defenden (“defend”), from Old French deffendre (Modern French défendre), from Latin dēfendō (“to ward off”), from dē- + *fendō (“hit, thrust”), from Proto-Italic *fendō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰen- (“strike, kill”).

parole.significato: A slit or crack.
parole.testo: From Old French fente, from Latin findēre (“to cleave”).

parole.significato: Any of the species leguminous plant, Trigonella foenum-graecum, eaten as a vegetable and with seeds used as a spice.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English fenygreke, borrowed from Old French fenigrec, from Latin foenum-graecum (literally “Greek hay”), from foenum (“hay”, variant of faenum) + graecus (“Greek”).

parole.significato: One who enfeoffs or grants a fee.
parole.testo: Old French

parole.significato: The grant of a feud or fee.
parole.testo: From Old French feoffement, fieffement. Compare Latin feoffamentum.

parole.significato: A holiday.
parole.testo: From Middle English ferie, from Old French ferie, from Latin feriae (“holidays”). See fair.

parole.significato: An often domesticated mammal (Mustela putorius furo) rather like a weasel, descended from the European polecat and ofte…
parole.testo: From Middle English furet, ferret, from Old French furet, from Vulgar Latin *furittum (“weasel, ferret”), diminutive of Latin fūr (“thief”).

parole.significato: The medieval chess piece that developed into the modern queen.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle English fers, from Old French fierce, from Medieval Latin ferzia, from Classical Persian فَرْزِین (farzīn).

parole.significato: Very hot; burning, scorching; also, glowing with heat.
parole.testo: From Middle English fervent, from Old French fervent (modern French fervent), from Latin ferventem, the accusative masculine or feminine singular form of fervēns (“burning, fiery; hot; zealous; etc.”), the present active participle of ferveō (“to burn; to be hot; (figurative) to be agitated, fired u

parole.significato: An intense, heated emotion; passion, ardor.
parole.testo: From Middle English fervour, from Old French, from Latin fervor (“a boiling or raging heat, heat, vehemence, passion”), from fervere (“to boil, be hot”); see fervent. By surface analysis, Latin ferv- + -or (“abstract noun suffix”).

parole.significato: A straw, wire, stick, etc., used chiefly to point out letters to children when learning to read.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English festu, from Old French festu (modern fétu), from Late Latin *festūcum, from Latin festūca (“stalk, stem, straw”).

parole.significato: A horizontal band across the middle of the shield.
parole.testo: From Middle English fesse, from Old French fesse, an alteration of faisse, from Latin fascia. Cognate with fajita, fascia, and fascism.

parole.significato: A fistula.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English festre, festur, borrowed from Old French festre (cognate with Italian fistola, Occitan fistola, Spanish fístula), from Latin fistula. The verb is derived from the noun, while the “condition of something that festers” noun sense is derived from the verb. Doublet of fistu

parole.significato: Pertaining to a feast or feast day; festive. (Now only as the noun used attributively.)
parole.testo: From Middle English festival (adjective), from Old French festival (“festive”), from Late Latin fēstīvālis, from Latin fēstīvus (“festive”). By surface analysis, festive + -al. Displaced native Old English frēols. The noun is shortened from festival day, from Middle English festival dai, festiuall d

parole.significato: A state of long-standing mutual hostility.
parole.testo: Inherited from Northern Middle English fede, feide, from Old French faide, feide, fede, from Proto-West Germanic *faihiþu (“hatred, enmity”) (corresponding to foe + -th), from Proto-Indo-European *peyḱ- (“hostile”). Cognate to Old English fǣhþ, fǣhþu, fǣhþo (“hostility, enmity, violence, revenge, ve

parole.significato: Of, or relating to feudalism.
parole.testo: From Old French feodal, from Medieval Latin feodalis, from feodum, feudum, fevum (“fief, fee”), from Frankish *fehu (“cattle, owndom, property, fee”), from Proto-Germanic *fehu (“cattle”). By surface analysis, feud (“estate”) + -al. More at fee.

parole.significato: A higher than normal body temperature of a person (or, generally, a mammal), usually caused by disease.
parole.testo: From Middle English fever, fevere, from Old English fefer, fefor (“fever”) and Old French fievre (“fever”), from Latin febris (“a fever”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷʰ- (“to burn”). Displaced native Old English hriþ (“fever”). Compare also Saterland Frisian Fiewer, German Fieber, Danish feber, S

parole.significato: Signs left by game that is hunted, such as tracks or scent, the track itself.
parole.testo: From Middle English feute, itself from Old French fuite (“the fleeing, flight”), as of what is left and seen from fleeing game.

parole.significato: A support or holder for a spear, attached to a saddle or breastplate.
parole.testo: From Middle English feuter, fewtre, from Old French feutre, from Medieval Latin filtrum, of Germanic origin. Doublet of filter.

parole.significato: Literary type using invented or imaginative writing, instead of real facts, usually written as prose.
parole.testo: From Middle English ficcioun, from Old French ficcion (“dissimulation, ruse, invention”), from Latin fictiō (“a making, fashioning, a feigning, a rhetorical or legal fiction”), from fingō (“to form, mold, shape, devise, feign”). Displaced native Old English lēasspell (literally “false story”); see f

parole.significato: Often followed by to or towards: faithfulness or loyalty towards a person, a group, one's civic or moral duties, etc.;…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English fidelite (“allegiance, fealty; faithfulness, trust; agreement made in good faith”), from Old French fidélité (“faithfulness, fidelity”) (modern French fidélité), from Latin fidēlitās (“faithfulness, fidelity”), from fidēlis (“dependable, trustworthy; faithful, loyal”) + -tās

parole.significato: Sometimes followed by on or upon: used to express distaste, disgust, or outrage.
parole.testo: From Middle English fy, from Old French fi, from Latin fī. (with a possible additional influence from Old Norse). Compare Swedish fy.

parole.significato: Exceedingly violent, severe, ferocious, cruel or savage.
parole.testo: From Middle English fers, fiers, borrowed from Old French fers (“wild", "ferocious”), nominative of fer, from Latin ferus (“wild", "untamed”).

parole.significato: Representing by means of a figure; emblematic.
parole.testo: From Old French figural, from late Latin figūrālis, from figūra (“figure”).

parole.significato: A drawing or diagram conveying information.
parole.testo: From Middle English figure, borrowed from Old French figure, from Latin figūra (“form, shape, form of a word, a figure of speech, Late Latin a sketch, drawing”), from fingō (“to form, shape, mold, fashion”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeyǵʰ- (“to mold, shape, form, knead”). Cognate with Ancient Gree

parole.significato: To commit (official papers) to some office.
parole.testo: From Old French fil (“thread”), from Latin fīlum (“thread”). Doublet of filum.

parole.significato: A headband; a ribbon or other band used to tie the hair up, or keep a headdress in place, or for decoration.
parole.testo: From Middle English filet, vylette, felet, filette, flette, from Old French filet, diminutive of fil (“thread”), from Latin fīlum (“thread”).

parole.significato: A final examination; a test or examination given at the end of a term or class; the test that concludes a class.
parole.testo: From Middle English final, fynal, fynall, from Old French final, from Latin fīnālis (“of or relating to the end or to boundaries”), from fīnis (“end”); see fine. Replaced native English endly (“final”).

parole.significato: Senses referring to subjective quality.
parole.testo: From Middle English fin, fyn, from Old French fin (“fine, minute, exact”), of obscure origin, but probably derived from Latin fīnīre (“to finish”) or fīnis (“boundary, limit, end”), with an abstract sense of fine or thin also arising in many Romance languages (compare Italian, Portuguese, and Spanis

parole.significato: A fee levied as punishment for breaking the law.
parole.testo: From Middle English fyn, fyne, from Old French fin, from Medieval Latin fīnis (“a payment in settlement or tax”). Doublet of fin and finis.

parole.significato: To finish; to cease.
parole.testo: From Middle English finen, fynen, from Old French finer, finir. See finish (transitive verb).

parole.significato: Especially in Gothic architecture: an ornament, often in the form of a bunch or knot of foliage, on the peak of the gab…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English finial (“(adjective) final; (noun) ornament at the upper extremity of a pinnacle, spire, etc.”) [and other forms], a variant of final (“pertaining to the close or end of something, last, final”), from Old French final (“last, final; definitive”) (modern French final), from L

parole.significato: An end; the end of anything.
parole.testo: From Middle English finishen, finisshen, finischen, from Old French finiss-, stem of some of the conjugated forms of finir, from Latin fīnīre, from fīnis (“end, limit, border, boundary”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ- (“to stick, set up”) or from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- (“to split”)

parole.significato: Steadfast, secure, solid (in position)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English ferme, borrowed from Old French ferme, from Medieval Latin ferma. From Middle English ferme, from Old French ferme, from Latin firmus (“strong, steady”). Doublet of dharma.

parole.significato: To make firm or strong; fix securely.
parole.testo: From Middle English fermen (“to make firm”), partly from (either through Old French fermer or directly) Latin firmō, from firmus (“firm”, adjective), and partly a new formation on the adjective.

parole.significato: A long, narrow crack or opening made by breaking or splitting, especially in rock or earth.
parole.testo: From Middle English fissure, from Old French fissure, from Latin fissūra (“a cleft, chink”), from findō (“to cleave, split, divide”) + -tūra (nominal suffix).

parole.significato: polecat
parole.testo: From Middle English fitchewes (mistaken as a plural), variant of Middle English fichouse, ficheux, from Old French fissiauls (plural) and fichau, fissel (“polecat”), from Middle Dutch vitsche, visse, fisse (“polecat”), ultimately (via a Northern French dialect) from Latin vissiō (“stench”). Compare

parole.significato: To pierce; now generally replaced by transfix.
parole.testo: From Middle English fixen, borrowed from Old French *fixer (attested only as ficher, fichier; > English fitch), from fix (“fastened; fixed”), from Latin fīxus (“immovable; steady; stable; fixed”), from fīgō (“to drive in; stick; fasten”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ- (“to jab; stick; set”). Rel

parole.significato: The act of fixing.
parole.testo: From Old French fixation. By surface analysis, fix + -ation.

parole.significato: A barrel-shaped bottle, or a flagon.
parole.testo: From Old French flasquet (“little flask”), diminutive of flasque (“a flask”).

parole.significato: Guilty of terrible crimes; wicked, criminal.
parole.testo: From Old French flagitieux or Latin flāgitiōsus, both ultimately from flāgitium (“shameful crime”), related to flagrum (“whip”).

parole.significato: A natural or innate talent or aptitude.
parole.testo: From Middle English flayre, from Old French flair (“scent, odour”), from flairier (“to reek, smell”), from Latin flāgrō, dissimilated variation of frāgrō (“emit a sweet smell”, verb). More at fragrant.

parole.significato: To produce flames; to burn with a flame or blaze.
parole.testo: From Middle English flawmen, from Old French flamber, flammer.

parole.significato: A flange (rim or projection).
parole.testo: Old French flanche (“flank”). See flank.

parole.significato: A piece of armor designed to be attached to the sides of a saddle to protect the flanks of the horse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French flanchard.

parole.significato: To attack the flank(s) of.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English flanc, from Late Old English flanc (“flank”), from Old French flanc, of Germanic origin, probably Frankish *hlanca, from Proto-West Germanic *hlanku (“bend, curve, hip, flank”), from Proto-Germanic *hlankaz (“flexible, sleek, bendsome”), from Proto-Indo-European *kleng- (“to

parole.significato: A long, shallow basket with two handles.
parole.testo: From Middle English flasket, from Old French flaschet, diminutive of Old French flasche, from Late Latin flasca. Related to Welsh fflasged (“a vessel of straw or wickerwork”), fflasg (“flask, basket”), and English flask.

parole.significato: To beat or strike; pound
parole.testo: From Middle English flatten, from Old French flatir (“to knock or strike down, dash”), from Frankish *flattjan (“to move the palm of the hand”), from Proto-Germanic *flatjaną (“to make flat, flatten”).

parole.significato: Excessive praise or approval, which is often insincere and sometimes contrived to win favour.
parole.testo: From Middle English flaterye, flaterie, from Old French flaterie, from the verb flater (“to flatter”). By surface analysis, flatter + -y (forming abstract nouns).

parole.significato: The quality produced by the sensation of taste or, especially, of taste and smell in combined effect.
parole.testo: From Middle English flavour meaning “smell, odour”, usually pleasing, borrowed from Old French flaour (“smell, odour”) (cfr. Sicilian ciàguru, its etymology and semantic), from Vulgar Latin *flātor (“odour, that which blows”), from Latin flātor (“blower”), from flō, flāre (“to blow, puff”), ultimate

parole.significato: A flan (custard-based dessert)
parole.testo: From Middle English flaun, flaon, flawn, from Old French flaon, from Late Latin fladonem, accusative of flado, from Frankish *flaþō. Doublet of flan, flathe, and flathon.

parole.significato: A sharp instrument used to open a vein, to lance gums, or the like.
parole.testo: From Middle English fleme, fleom, from Old French flieme, flemie (“open vein”), probably via a Proto-Germanic source (compare Old Saxon flēma, Old High German fliotuma, fliodema, Old English flȳtme (“fleam, lancet”)), borrowed from Vulgar Latin fletoma, *fletomus, from Late Latin flebotomus, phlebot

parole.significato: One who fletches or feathers arrows.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English fleccher, from Old French flechier; equivalent to fletch + -er.

parole.significato: An ornament or knob in the shape of a flower
parole.testo: From Old French floron (“flower”), spelling later changed to match modern French fleuron.

parole.significato: Coarse tufts of wool or cotton used in bedding.
parole.testo: From Middle English flok (“tuft of wool”), from Old French floc (“tuft of wool”), from Late Latin floccus (“tuft of wool”), probably from Frankish *flokko (“down, wool, flock”), from Proto-Germanic *flukkōn-, *flukkan-, *fluksōn- (“down, flock”), from Proto-Indo-European *plewk- (“hair, fibres, tuft

parole.significato: A small flower, especially one of a cluster in a composite flower.
parole.testo: From Old French florete, diminutive of flor (“flower”). Doublet of fleuret and floweret.

parole.significato: Any of several gold coins once produced in Florence, Italy; model for the other currencies.
parole.testo: From Middle English florin, floren, from Old French florin, from Italian fiorino (“little flower”). Doublet of fiorino and forint.

parole.significato: A small stream of water.
parole.testo: From dialectal flosh (“a flush, stream of water, sluice”), from Middle English flosche, flusche, flasche, flaske (“a watery or marshy place, swamp”), perhaps from Old French flache, from Middle Dutch vlacke (“a flat area, plain”), ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *fleutan. Compare also Germ

parole.significato: The state of floating.
parole.testo: From Old French flotage (modern French flottage).

parole.significato: Represented as flying (fluttering) or floating mid-air or in water.
parole.testo: Old French flotant, (French flottant), present participle of floter (“to float”).

parole.significato: To thrive or grow well.
parole.testo: From Middle English floryschen, from Old French florir (via the arrhizotonic stem floriss-), from Late Latin flōrīre, from Latin flōrēre, from Latin flōrem (“flower”, noun). Corresponds to flower + -ish.

parole.significato: A floret, or small or component flower
parole.testo: From Middle English flourette, from Old French florete. By surface analysis, flower + -et; compare flowerlet. Doublet of fleuret and floret.

parole.significato: A ravine or gorge, usually one with water running through.
parole.testo: From Middle English flum, from Old French flum, flun, from Latin flumen, from fluere (“to flow”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; perhaps; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: A woodwind instrument consisting of a tube with a row of holes that produce sound through vibrations caused by air blow…
parole.testo: From Middle English fleute, floute, flote, from Old French flaute, fleüte, from Old Provençal flaüt, of uncertain origin. Perhaps ultimately from three possibilities: * Blend of Provencal flaujol (“flageolet”) + laüt (“lute”) * From Latin flātus (“blowing”), from flāre (“to blow”) * Imitative. Doubl

parole.significato: The act of flowing; a continuous moving on or passing by, as of a flowing stream.
parole.testo: From Old French flux, from Latin fluxus (“flow”).

parole.significato: To prevent (something) from being accomplished.
parole.testo: From Middle English foilen (“spoil a scent trail by crossing it”), from Old French fouler (“tread on, trample”), ultimately from Latin fullō (“to trample, full”).

parole.significato: A thrust.
parole.testo: From Old French foene (“harpoon, fizgig”), from Latin fuscina (“trident”).

parole.significato: An abundance, a rich supply of.
parole.testo: From Middle English foisoun, from Old French foison, from Latin fūsiōnem. Doublet of fusion.

parole.significato: A type of light and fast-sailing ship.
parole.testo: From Old French fuste (“stick, boat”), from Latin fustis (“cudgel”).

parole.significato: A cask for wine.
parole.testo: From Old French fust (whence also French fût), from Latin fustis.

parole.significato: Foolishness that results from a lack of foresight or lack of practicality.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English folie, from Old French folie (“madness”), from the adjective fol (“mad, insane”).

parole.significato: To incite or cause troublesome acts; to encourage; to instigate.
parole.testo: From Middle English fomenten, a borrowing from Old French fomenter, from Late Latin fōmentāre, from Latin fōmentum (“lotion”), from fovēre (“heat, cherish”).

parole.significato: A person with poor judgment or little intelligence.
parole.testo: From Middle English fol (“fool”), from Old French fol (cf. modern French fou (“mad”)) from Latin follis. Doublet of fals and follis. Displaced native Old English dwæs.

parole.significato: Marked by unthinking recklessness with disregard for danger; boldly rash; hotheaded.
parole.testo: From Middle English folehardy, foolhardi, folherdi, from Old French fol hardi (“foolishly bold”), from Old French fol (“foolish, silly; insane, mad”) (from Latin follis (“bellows; purse, sack; inflated ball; belly, paunch”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵʰ- (“to swell”)) + Old French har

parole.significato: Fodder for animals, especially cattle and horses.
parole.testo: From Middle English forage, from Old French fourage, forage, a derivative of fuerre (“fodder, straw”), from Frankish *fōdar (“fodder, sheath”), from Proto-Germanic *fōdrą (“fodder, feed, sheath”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- (“to protect, to feed”). Cognate with Old High German fuotar

parole.significato: A sudden or irregular incursion in border warfare; hence, any irregular incursion for war or spoils; a raid.
parole.testo: From Middle English forrayen (“to pillage”), a back-formation of forrayour, forreour, forrier (“raider, pillager”), from Old French forrier, fourrier, a derivative of fuerre (“provender, fodder, straw”), from Frankish *fōdar (“fodder, sheath”), from Proto-Germanic *fōdrą (“fodder, feed, sheath”), fr

parole.significato: To exile; banish.
parole.testo: From Middle English forbannen, partly from Middle English for- + bannen, equivalent to for- + ban; and partly from Old French forbenir (“to banish”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian ferbonne (“to banish”), West Frisian ferbanne (“to banish”), Dutch verbannen (“to banish”), German Low German verbannen

parole.significato: Ability to influence; strength or energy of body or mind; active power; vigour; might; capacity of exercising an influe…
parole.testo: From Middle English force, fors, forse, from Old French force, from Late Latin fortia, a noun derived from the neuter plural of Latin fortis (“strong”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ- (“to rise, high, hill”).

parole.significato: To make someone or something do something, often regardless of their will.
parole.testo: From Middle English forcen, from Old French forcier, from Late Latin *fortiāre, from Latin fortia.

parole.significato: Done by force, forced.
parole.testo: From Middle English forcible, forsable, from Old French forcible, from forcier (“to conquer by force”), equivalent to force + -ible.

parole.significato: To repossess a mortgaged property whose owner has failed to make the necessary payments; used with on.
parole.testo: Partially from Middle English foreclosen, forclosen, from Old French forclos, past participle of forclore (“to exclude”), from for- (“(prefix used to express error, exclusion, or inadequacy)”) + clore (“to shut”), and partially from Middle English forclusen (“to close up”), from Old English forclȳsa

parole.significato: Located outside a country or place, especially one's own.
parole.testo: From Middle English foreyn, forein, from Old French forain, from Vulgar Latin *forānus (“outsider, outlander”), from Latin forās (“outside, outdoors”) or forīs (“outside, outdoors”). Displaced native Old English elþēodiġ (“foreign”) and now-dialectal English fremd, from Old English fremde (“strange,

parole.significato: A kind of coarse parchment for book covers; a forrill.
parole.testo: From Middle English forel (“case, sheath”), from Old French forrel, fourrel.

parole.significato: A person who practices forestry.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English forester, a borrowing from Old French forestier, from forest + -ier; equivalent to forest + -er. Displaced native Old English wuduweard.

parole.significato: The science of planting and growing trees in forests.
parole.testo: From Middle English *forestrie, *forsterie (suggested by Middle English forster, forester (“forester”)), from Old French foresterie, from forest.

parole.significato: A penalty for or consequence of a misdemeanor.
parole.testo: From Middle English forfait from ca. 1300, from Old French forfait (“crime”), originally the past participle of forfaire (“to transgress”), and Medieval Latin foris factum. During the 15th century, the sense shifted from the crime to the penalty for the crime.

parole.significato: A legal action whereby a person loses all interest in the forfeit property.
parole.testo: From Middle English forfeture, from Old French forfaiture.

parole.significato: A furnace or hearth where metals are heated prior to hammering them into shape.
parole.testo: From Middle English forge, from Old French forge, early Old French faverge, from Latin fabrica (“workshop”), from faber (“workman in hard materials, smith”) (genitive fabri). Cognate with Franco-Provençal favèrge. Doublet of fabric and fabrica. Partially displaced English smithy. * Computing sense p

parole.significato: A person who creates forgeries, falsifies documents with intent to defraud, e.g. to create a false will or illicit copi…
parole.testo: From Middle English forger, forgere, from Old French forgiere; equivalent to forge + -er.

parole.significato: To exclude, oust, or dispossess by a judgment; prohibit (from).
parole.testo: From Middle English forjugen; in sense 1, from Old French fourjugier (“to judge illegally, dispossess”); in sense 2, from Middle English for- + jugen (“to judge”), equivalent to for- + judge. Compare fordeem.

parole.significato: In accordance with established forms.
parole.testo: From Middle English formel, borrowed from Old French formel, from Latin fōrmālis, from fōrma (“form”); equivalent to form + -al.

parole.significato: The act of assembling a group or structure.
parole.testo: From Middle English formacioun, formation, borrowed from Old French formacion, from Latin fōrmātiō, from fōrmō (“form”, verb); see form as verb. Morphologically form + -ation.

parole.significato: Capable of forming something.
parole.testo: From Middle English formatyve, formatif (“having the ability to form”), from Old French formatif, formative (modern French formatif), from Medieval Latin formātīvus, from Latin fōrmātus + -īvus (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘doing’ or ‘related to doing’). Fōrmātus is the perfect passive

parole.significato: A writ of right for a tenant in tail in case of a discontinuance of the estate tail.
parole.testo: From Old French [Term?], from Latin [Term?], so called because the plaintiff claimed “by the form of the gift”: per formam doni.

parole.significato: Causing fear, dread, awe, or discouragement as a result of size, strength, or some other impressive feature; commanding…
parole.testo: From Middle English formidable, from Old French formidable, formible, from Latin formīdābilis (“formidable, terrible”) (whence -able), from formīdō (“fear, dread”).

parole.significato: Beauty.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English formosite, formosyte, from Old French formosité, from Latin fōrmōsitās (“beauty”). Cognate to French formosité, Scots formosite.

parole.significato: Sexual intercourse by people who are not married to each other, or which is considered illicit in another way.
parole.testo: From Middle English fornicacioun, from Old French fornicacion, from Latin fornicātiō, from fornix (“brothel”).

parole.significato: To give power, strength, or vigour to (oneself or someone, or to something); to strengthen.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English fortifien, fortfien (“to strengthen (a castle, etc.) from attack; to strengthen (an army, etc.); to strengthen (a person), aid, support; to reinforce, support; to improve; to increase the efficacy of”), from Old French fortifier (modern French fortifier), from Late Latin for

parole.significato: Mental or emotional strength that enables courage in the face of adversity.
parole.testo: From Middle English fortitude, from Old French, from Latin fortitūdō (“bravery, strength”), from fortis (“brave, strong”).

parole.significato: A fortified place; a large and permanent fortification, sometimes including a town; for example a fort, a castle; a str…
parole.testo: Early 14 c., from Old French forteresce, forteresse, forterece (“strong place, fortification”), variant of fortelesse, from Medieval Latin fortalitia, from Latin fortis (“strong”) (see fort) + -itia, added to adjectives to form nouns of quality or condition. French -ess, from Latin -itia is also in

parole.significato: Destiny, especially favorable.
parole.testo: From Middle English fortune, from Old French fortune, from Latin fortuna (“fate, luck”). The plural form fortunae meant “possessions”, which also gave fortune the meaning of “riches”.

parole.significato: To go out of the way; go astray; err; make a mistake; sin.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English forwayen, forweyen (“to go astay, go out of the way”), partly equivalent to for- + way (compare Old English forweġan (“to overcome, kill”)); and partly continuing, in altered form, Middle English forveien, forsveien, forvoyen (“to err, go astray”), from Old French forsveer,

parole.significato: To flash like lightning; to lighten; to gleam; to thunder.
parole.testo: From Middle English fouldre (“lightning”), from Old French foudre also fouldre (modern French foudre), from Latin fulgur. See fulgor.

parole.significato: To start (an institution or organization).
parole.testo: From Middle English founden, from Old French founder (Modern French: fonder), from Latin fundāre. Compare fund.

parole.significato: To melt, especially of metal or glass in an industrial setting.
parole.testo: From Middle English founden, from Old French fondre, from Latin fundere. Cognate with Spanish fundir and hundir, and French fondre.

parole.significato: The act of founding, fixing, establishing, or beginning to erect.
parole.testo: From Middle English foundacioun, fundacioun, from Old French fondacion, from Latin fundātiō (“founding, foundation”).

parole.significato: One who founds or establishes (a company, project, organisation, state, etc.).
parole.testo: From Old French fondeur, from Latin fundātor, equivalent to found + -er.

parole.significato: A natural source of water; a spring.
parole.testo: From Middle English [Term?]; from Old French fontaine (whence modern fontaine); from Late Latin fontana, from Latin fontanus, fontaneus, adjectives from fons (“source, spring”).

parole.significato: Bioluminescence created by some types of fungus, particularly those growing on rotting wood.
parole.testo: Possibly from fox + fire, though the semantic connection is unclear. Alternatively, the first element may be ultimately from Old French fols (“false”), or the term may derive by folk etymology from phosphor.

parole.significato: A part of a whole, especially a comparatively small part.
parole.testo: From Middle English fraccioun (“a breaking”), from Anglo-Norman, Old French fraccion, from Medieval Latin fractio (“a fragment, portion”), from earlier Latin fractio (“a breaking, a breaking into pieces”), from fractus, past participle of frangere (“to break”) (whence English frangible), from Proto-

parole.significato: An instance of breaking, a place where something has broken.
parole.testo: From Middle English fracture, from Old French fracture, from Latin frāctūra (“a breach, fracture, cleft”), from frangere (“to break”), past participle frāctus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreg-, whence also English break. See fraction. Doublet of fraktur.

parole.significato: Easily broken physically; not firm or durable; liable to fail and perish.
parole.testo: From Middle English frele, fraill, from Old French fraile, from Latin fragilis. Cognate to fraction, fracture, and doublet of fragile.

parole.significato: A basket made of rushes, used chiefly to hold figs and raisins.
parole.testo: From Middle English frayel, from Old French frael, fraiel, of unknown origin; possibly a dissimilatory variant of flael, flaiel (“flail”).

parole.significato: The condition quality of being frail, physically, mentally, or morally; weakness of resolution; liability to be deceive…
parole.testo: From Middle English frelete, frailte, from Old French fraileté, from Latin fragilitās. By surface analysis, frail + -ty. Doublet of fragility.

parole.significato: The right to vote at a public election or referendum; see: suffrage.
parole.testo: From Middle English franchise, fraunchise, from Old French franchise (“freedom”), a derivative of franc (“free”). More at frank.

parole.significato: To confer certain powers on; grant a franchise to; authorize.
parole.testo: From Middle English franchisen, fraunchisen, from Old French franchir (stem franchiss-, “to set free”), from franc (“free”). More at frank.

parole.significato: One of the Franks, a Germanic federation that inhabited parts of what are now France, the Low Countries and Germany.
parole.testo: From Middle English Frank, partially from Old English Franca (“a Frank”); and partially from Old French Franc, and/or Latin Francus (“a Frank”), from Frankish *Franko (“a Frank”); both maybe from Proto-Germanic *frankô (“javelin”). Cognate with Old High German Franko (“a Frank”), Old English franca

parole.significato: Honest, especially in a manner that seems slightly blunt; candid; not reserved or disguised.
parole.testo: From Middle English frank, from Old French franc (“free”), in turn from the name of an early Germanic confederation, the Franks, from Proto-West Germanic *frankō (“javelin, spear”). Doublet of Frank, franc, and farang.

parole.significato: A pigsty.
parole.testo: From Old French franc.

parole.significato: A type of incense obtained from the Boswellia thurifera tree.
parole.testo: From Old French franc encens (“noble incense”).

parole.significato: Insane, mentally unstable.
parole.testo: From Middle English frantike, frentik, variant of frenetik, from Old French frenetique, from Late Latin phreneticus, alteration of phreniticus, from φρενιτικός (phrenitikós, “mad, suffering from inflammation of the brain”), from φρενῖτις (phrenîtis, “inflammation of the brain”), from φρήν (phrḗn, “t

parole.significato: To draw together tightly; to secure by many turns of a lashing.
parole.testo: From Middle English frapen, from Old French fraper.

parole.significato: The quality of being brothers or brotherly; brotherhood.
parole.testo: PIE word  *bʰréh₂tēr From Middle English fraternite, borrowed from Old French fraternité, from Latin frāternitās, ultimately from frāter (“brother”).

parole.significato: The condition of being fraudulent; deceitfulness.
parole.testo: From Old French fraudulence, from Latin fraudulentia (“deceitfulness, disposition to defraud; fraudulence”), from fraudulentus (“deceitful, fraudulent”) + -ia (suffix forming abstract nouns). Fraudulentus is derived from fraus (“deceit, fraud”) (from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrew- (“to mislead”)) + -ul

parole.significato: Dishonest; based on fraud or deception.
parole.testo: From Middle English fraudulent, from Old French fraudulent, from Latin fraudulentus, from fraus (“fraud”).

parole.significato: To rub or wear away (something); to cause (something made of strands twisted or woven together, such as cloth or rope)…
parole.testo: The verb is derived from Late Middle English fraien (“to beat so as to cause bruising, to bruise; to crush; to rub; to wear, wear off”), borrowed from Old French fraier, freier, freiier (modern French frayer (“to clear, open up (a path, etc.); (figuratively) to find one’s way through (something); (o

parole.significato: Unravelled; worn at the end or edge.
parole.testo: From fray + -ed, from Old French froiier (“to rub against, scrape; thrust against”), from Latin fricare (“to rub, rub down”).

parole.significato: Frenzied and frantic, harried; having extreme enthusiasm or energy.
parole.testo: From Middle English frenetik (also frentik, frentyk, frantike > modern English frantic), from Old French frenetike, from Latin phreneticus, from Ancient Greek φρενητικός (phrenētikós, “delirious”), from φρενῖτις (phrenîtis, “delirium”), from φρήν (phrḗn, “mind”). Doublet of frantic and phrenitic. Et

parole.significato: A state of wild activity or panic.
parole.testo: From Middle English frensy, frenesie, from Old French frenesie, from Latin phrenesis, from Ancient Greek *φρένησις (*phrénēsis), a later equivalent of φρενῖτις (phrenîtis, “inflammation of the brain”): see frantic and frenetic. Doublet of phrenesis.

parole.significato: Done or occurring often; common.
parole.testo: From Old French frequent, from Latin frequens (“crowded, crammed, frequent, repeated, etc.”), possibly from a Proto-Indo-European *bʰrekʷ- (“to cram together”).

parole.significato: To visit often.
parole.testo: From Old French frequenter, from Latin frequentare (“to fill, crowd, visit often, do or use often, etc.”), from frequens (“frequent, crowded”).

parole.significato: A flood resulting from heavy rain or a spring thaw.
parole.testo: From Old French freschete, a diminutive of fres (“fresh”) via its feminine form fresche.

parole.significato: An ornamental pattern consisting of repeated vertical and horizontal lines, often in relief.
parole.testo: From Middle English frēten (“to decorate”), from Old French freté, freter, fretter (“to fret (decorate with an interlacing pattern)”), from Old French fret (from fraindre (“to break”), from Latin frangō (“to break, shatter”), + Old French -er (suffix forming verbs) (from Latin -āre, ultimately from

parole.significato: A channel or passage created by the sea.
parole.testo: From Old French frete, fraite, fraicte, possibly partly confused with fret (“channel, strait”).

parole.significato: A member of a mendicant Christian order such as the Augustinians, Carmelites (white friars), Franciscans (grey friars)…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English frere, borrowed from Old French frere, from Latin frāter, from Proto-Italic *frātēr, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr. Doublet of bhai, brother, bru, frater, pal, and vai.

parole.significato: To shake or shiver as with cold (with reference to a hawk).
parole.testo: From Old French friller.

parole.significato: A decorative border.
parole.testo: From Middle English frenge, from Old French frenge, from Vulgar Latin *frimbia, a metathesis of Latin fimbriae (“fibers, threads, fringe”, plural), of uncertain origin. Compare German Franse and Danish frynse. Displaced native Middle English fnæd (“fringe”), Middle English byrd (“fringe”), Middle En

parole.significato: A member of the Germanic ethnic group which is native to the region of Frisia (which is in the Netherlands, northern Ge…
parole.testo: From Middle English Frisoun, taken from Old French frison (“a Frisian”), itself derived from Latin Frīsiī (“Frisians”). Displaced native Old English Frīsa (“a Frisian”) whence modern English Frise; see the plural Frīsan for more.

parole.significato: Of hair, to form into a mass of tight curls.
parole.testo: From Middle English frysen, from Old French friser, frizer (“to frizzle, crisp, curl, ruffle, braid, touch lightly, graze, scratch”), of Proto-Germanic origin, perhaps via Old Frankish *fris (“curl”), from Proto-Germanic *frisaz (“frizzy, curly”). Cognate with Old Frisian frisle, frēsle ("the hair o

parole.significato: A dress, a piece of clothing, which consists of a skirt and a cover for the upper body.
parole.testo: From Middle English frok, frokke, from Old French froc (“frock, a monk's gown or habit”), perhaps via Medieval Latin hrocus, roccus, rocus (“a coat”), from Frankish *hrokk (“skirt, dress, robe”), from Proto-Germanic *hrukkaz (“robe, jacket, skirt, tunic”), from Proto-Indo-European *kreḱ- (“to weave”

parole.significato: The foremost side of something or the end that faces the direction it normally moves.
parole.testo: From Middle English front, frunt, frount, from Old French front, frunt, from Latin frōns, frontem (“forehead”). Doublet of frons.

parole.significato: A decorative drapery covering the front of an altar.
parole.testo: From Middle English frountel, from Old French frontel, from Latin frontāle (“a frontlet, metal band for the forehead”).

parole.significato: The part of a country which borders or faces another country or unsettled region.
parole.testo: From Middle English frounter, from Old French fronter (whence Modern French frontière), from front.

parole.significato: The forehead.
parole.testo: From Old French frontelet, diminutive of frontel. Compare armlet.

parole.significato: To rub one's penis against another person's penis for sexual gratification.
parole.testo: From Middle English frotten, froten, from Old French froter (“to rub, polish”), of obscure origin.

parole.significato: A canker in the mouth of a hawk.
parole.testo: From Middle English frouncen, from Old French froncir "to wrinkle, frown", from Frankish *hrunkiju (“a wrinkle”), from Proto-Germanic *hrunkijō, *hrunkitō (“fold, wrinkle”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn, bend”). Akin to Old High German runza "fold, wrinkle, crease" (German Runzel "wri

parole.significato: To bear fruit; to generate useful products or ideas.
parole.testo: Borrowed into Middle English from Old French fructefier.

parole.significato: A product of fertilization in a plant, specifically
parole.testo: From Middle English fruyt, frut (“fruits and vegetables”), from Old French fruit (“produce, fruits and vegetables”), from Latin fruitus (“enjoyment, proceeds, profits, produce, income”), frūctus and frūx (“crop, produce, fruit”) (compare Latin fruor (“have the benefit of, to use, to enjoy”)). Cognat

parole.significato: A porridge made by boiling hulled wheat, typically with additional ingredients such as milk, egg yolks, and/or almond m…
parole.testo: From Middle English furmente, from Old French fourmenté, from furment (“grain”), from Latin frūmentum. Doublet of furmint.

parole.significato: To break up, smash.
parole.testo: From Old French fruscher, from Vulgar Latin *frustiāre (“break into pieces”), from Latin frustum (“bit, fragment”). Compare French froisser.

parole.significato: A method of cooking food.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English fryen, borrowed from Old French frire, from Latin frīgō. Cognate with Ancient Greek φρύγω (phrúgō, “to roast, bake”), Sanskrit भृज्जति (bhṛjjati, “to roast, grill, fry”). Replaced native Middle English hirsten, from Old English hierstan (“to fry”). Related to bhurji, bh

parole.significato: Substance consumed to provide energy through combustion, or through chemical or nuclear reaction.
parole.testo: From Middle English fuayle, from Old French fouaille, feuaille (“firewood, kindling”), from feu (“fire”), from Late Latin focus (“fire”), from Latin focus (“hearth”), whence English focus. Cognate with Spanish fuego (“fire”), and Portuguese fogo (“fire”).

parole.significato: Hearth tax.
parole.testo: From Old French fumage, fumaige, from Latin fumus (“smoke”).

parole.significato: A gas or vapour/vapor that is strong-smelling or dangerous to inhale.
parole.testo: From Middle English fume, from Old French fum (“smoke, steam, vapour”), from Latin fūmus (“vapour, smoke”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂mós (“smoke”), from *dʰewh₂- (“to smoke, raise dust”). Doublet of thymus and thymos. More at dun, dusk, dust.

parole.significato: The act of fumigating, or applying smoke or vapor, as for disinfection.
parole.testo: From Middle English fumygacioun, from Old French fumigation, from Late Latin fumigatio, fumigationem, from Latin fumigo.

parole.significato: Any plant of the taxonomic genus Fumaria of annual herbaceous flowering plants in the family Papaveraceae, native to te…
parole.testo: From late Middle English fumyter (with remodelling of suffix), from Old French fumeterre, from Latin fūmus terrae.

parole.significato: The quality of being fumous.
parole.testo: From Middle English fumosite, from Old French fumosité.

parole.significato: Foundation.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French fundement, fondement, from Latin fundāmentum (“foundation”), from fundō (“to lay the bottom, to found”). Doublet of fondamento.

parole.significato: A fungus.
parole.testo: From Old French *funge, from Latin fungus.

parole.significato: To use a funnel.
parole.testo: From Middle English funell, fonel, probably through Old French *founel (compare Middle French fonel, Old Occitan fonilh, enfounilh), from Latin fundibulum, infundibulum (“funnel”), from infundere (“to pour in”); in (“in”) + fundere (“to pour”); compare Breton founilh (“funnel”), Welsh ffynel (“air h

parole.significato: To polish or burnish.
parole.testo: From Middle English furbisshen, from Old French forbir (stem furbiss-, “to clean, polish”), from Frankish *furbēn (“to clean, polish”).

parole.significato: Furious; raging; tormenting.
parole.testo: From Middle English furial, from Old French furial, from Latin furiālis (“furious, frenzied”).

parole.significato: Feeling great anger; raging; violent.
parole.testo: From Middle English furious, from Old French furieus, from Latin furiōsus. Displaced native Old English hātheort (literally “hot-hearted”).

parole.significato: To lower, roll up and secure (something, such as a sail or flag)
parole.testo: Perhaps from Old French ferlier, modern French ferler.

parole.significato: An industrial heating device, such as for smelting metal or firing ceramics.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English forneys, borrowed from Old French fornais, from Latin fornāx.

parole.significato: Material used to create an engineered product.
parole.testo: From Middle English furnysshen, from Old French furniss-, stem of certain parts of furnir, fornir (Modern French fournir), from Germanic, from Frankish *frumjan (“to complete, execute”), from Proto-Germanic *frumjaną (“to further, promote”), from Proto-Indo-European *promo- (“front, forward”). Cogna

parole.significato: A person who secures accommodation for an army.
parole.testo: From Middle English forreour, from Old French forrier, forrour, feureur. See foray.

parole.significato: Extreme anger.
parole.testo: From Middle English furie, from Old French furie, from Latin furia (“rage”).

parole.significato: Able to be fused or melted.
parole.testo: From Middle English fusible, from Old French fusible, from Medieval Latin fusibilis.

parole.significato: A bearing of a rhomboidal figure, originally representing a spindle in shape, longer than a heraldic lozenge.
parole.testo: From Middle English fusill, from Old French fusel, fuisel, from a late Latin diminutive of Latin fūsus (“spindle”).

parole.significato: A strong musty smell; mustiness.
parole.testo: From Middle English fust, from Old French fust (“wood; bole, tree trunk”) (modern French fût), from Latin fūstis (“knobbed stick, cudgel, club”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew- (“to hit”) or *gʷʰen- (“to strike; to kill, slay”).

parole.significato: Originally, a kind of coarse fabric made from cotton and flax; now, a kind of coarse twilled cotton, or cotton and line…
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Middle English fustian (“type of fabric, probably made from cotton, flax, or wool; piece of fustian spread over a bed or mattress”) [and other forms], from Old French fustaine, fustaigne (modern French futaine), from Medieval Latin fūstāneum, from (pannus) fūstāneus or (tela

parole.significato: Having to do with or occurring in the future.
parole.testo: From Middle English future, futur, from Old French futur, from Latin futūrus, irregular future active participle of sum (“to be”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to become, be”). Cognate with Old English bēo (“to become, will be; to be”). More at be. Doublet of futur. Displaced native Old English

parole.significato: The triangular area at the peak of an external wall adjacent to, and terminating, two sloped roof surfaces (pitches).
parole.testo: The southern English term gable probably came from Old French gable (compare modern French gâble), from Old Norse gafl. The northern form gavel is perhaps also akin to Old Norse gafl, masculine, of the same meaning (compare Swedish gavel, Danish gavl). See gafl for more etymology information.

parole.significato: A tool consisting of a large metal hook with a handle or pole, especially the one used to pull large fish aboard a boat.
parole.testo: From Middle English gaffe, from Old French gaffe, from Old Occitan gaf (“hook”), derivative of gafar (“to seize”), from 𐌲𐌹𐌱𐌰𐌽 (giban, “to give”). Doublet of gaffe. Etymology 1, noun sense 5 apparently derives from the idea that the garment tricks or deceives others about the wearer's genitalia.

parole.significato: To bind (someone) by pledge or security; to engage.
parole.testo: From Middle English gage, from later Old French or early Middle French gager (verb), (also guagier in Old French) gage (noun), ultimately from Frankish *waddi, from Proto-Germanic *wadją (whence English wed). Doublet of wage, from the same origin through the Old Northern French variant wage. See als

parole.significato: The horses, oxen, ploughs, wains or wagons and implements for carrying on tillage.
parole.testo: From Old French gaignage (“pasturage, crop”), French gaignage (“pasturage”). See gain (verb).

parole.significato: A man considered to be pure, noble, or chivalrous.
parole.testo: From Old French Galahad, of obscure origin and meaning. Suggestions include Old Welsh, or biblical Gilead.

parole.significato: Any of several east Asian plants of genera Alpinia and Kaempferia in the ginger family, used as a spice, but principall…
parole.testo: From Middle English galyngale, from Old French galingal, from Arabic خَلَنْجَان (ḵalanjān), from Persian قولنجان (qulenjân, qulanjân), from Sanskrit कुलञ्जन (kulañjana), perhaps from Chinese 高良薑／高良姜 (gāoliángjiāng), from 高涼 /高凉 (Gāoliáng) (a prefecture or county in China) + 薑 /姜 (jiāng, “ginger”).

parole.significato: A spiced, thickened sauce served with fish or poultry.
parole.testo: From Old French galentine, galantine, variant of galatine, from Latin gelāta (“frozen”) + Old French -ine. Compare gelatin.

parole.significato: The Milky Way; the apparent band of concentrated stars which appears in the night sky over earth.
parole.testo: From Middle English galaxye, galaxie, from Old French galaxie, from Latin galaxias, from Ancient Greek γαλαξίας (galaxías, “Milky Way”), shortening of γαλαξίας κύκλος (galaxías kúklos, “milky circle”), from γάλα (gála, “milk”).

parole.significato: A narthex, particularly in the United Kingdom and the Church of England; a vestibule, a fully-enclosed yet porch-like s…
parole.testo: From late Middle English galilie, from Old French galilee, from Medieval Latin galilaea, from Latin Galilaea (“Galilee”). Possibly the allusion is to Galilee being an outlying region of Biblical Palestine.

parole.significato: A blister or tumor-like growth found on the surface of plants, caused by various pathogens, especially the burrowing of…
parole.testo: From Middle English galle, from Old French galle, from Latin galla (“oak-apple”).

parole.significato: A type of rowable vessel of the 16th and 17th centuries, similar to a galley but larger, and normally equipped with sai…
parole.testo: 1540s, from Old French galleasse, from Italian galeaza ‘large galley’, from Latin galea.

parole.significato: A long, slender ship propelled primarily by oars, whether having masts and sails or not; usually a rowed warship used i…
parole.testo: From Middle English galeie, from Old French galee, from Latin galea, from Byzantine Greek γάλεα (gálea) of unknown origin, probably from Ancient Greek γαλέη (galéē), a kind of a small fish, from γαλεός (galeós, “dog-fish or small shark”).

parole.significato: The fastest gait of a horse, a two-beat stride during which all four legs are off the ground simultaneously.
parole.testo: From Middle English galopen (“to gallop”), from Old French galoper (compare modern French galoper), from Frankish *wala hlaupan (“to run well”), from *wala (“well”) + *hlaupan (“to run”), from Proto-Germanic *hlaupaną (“to run, leap, spring”), from Proto-Indo-European *klaup-, *klaub- (“to spring, s

parole.significato: An overshoe or boot worn in wet weather:
parole.testo: From Middle English galoche, from Old French galoche (“a shoe with a wooden sole”), but its further history is uncertain. further theories * From Vulgar Latin *galopium or Late Latin calopedia (“a wooden shoe; a shoe with a wooden sole”), from Ancient Greek κᾱλοπόδιον (kālopódion), diminutive of κᾱλ

parole.significato: A defensive garment formerly in use for the body, made of cloth stuffed and quilted, often worn as padding under armor.
parole.testo: From Middle English gambison, from Old French gambeson, gambaison, from gambais, wambais (“quilted jerkin”), from Medieval Latin wambāsium (“doublet, waistcoat”), from Frankish *wamba (“abdomen, belly”), from Proto-Germanic *wambō (“belly, womb”): compare Middle High German wambeis, German Wams (“wa

parole.significato: A cut of quick-cured pork leg.
parole.testo: From Middle English *gammon, gambon, from Old French gambon (compare modern French jambon (“ham”)), from gambe (“leg”), from Late Latin gamba, from Ancient Greek καμπή (kampḗ). Doublet of jambon and jamon.

parole.significato: Dated spelling of jail.
parole.testo: From Middle English gayole, gaiol, gaylle, gaille, gayle, gaile, via Old French gaiole, gayolle, gaole, from Medieval Latin gabiola, for Late Latin caveola, a diminutive of Latin cavea (“cavity, coop, cage”). See also cage.

parole.significato: A wheatsheaf.
parole.testo: From Middle English garbe, from Old French garbe, variant of jarbe; akin to German Garbe. Doublet of gerbe.

parole.significato: Disorder; uproar.
parole.testo: From Old French garbouil, connected with Latin bullire (“to boil”).

parole.significato: An inflammation on a cow's or sheep's udder; synonym of mastitis.
parole.testo: From Middle English garget, gargate (“throat”), from Old French gargate. Compare gorge.

parole.significato: A carved grotesque figure on a spout which conveys water away from the gutters.
parole.testo: From Old French gargouille, from Latin. Doublet of gargle. The Académie Française suggests the first attestation as gargoule in 1294.

parole.significato: A circular or linear decoration, especially one of plaited flowers or leaves, worn on the body or draped as a decoratio…
parole.testo: From Middle English garland, garlaunde, gerland, from Old French garlande, garlaunde, gerlande, guerlande (compare French guirlande), from Frankish *wierlōn, *wieralōn, a frequentative form of Frankish *wierōn (“to adorn, bedeck”), from *wiera (“a gold thread”), from or related to Proto-Germanic *wī

parole.significato: To clothe in a garment.
parole.testo: From Middle English garment, garement, garnement, from Old French garnement, guarnement, from Old French garnir, guarnir (“to protect, fortify, clothe, garnish, adorn”), from Frankish *warnijan (“to ward off, refuse, deny”). More at English garnish.

parole.significato: A granary; a store of grain.
parole.testo: From Middle English gerner, from Old French gernier, guernier, variant of grenier, from Latin grānārium (“granary”). Doublet of granary.

parole.significato: A hard transparent mineral that is often used as gemstones and abrasives.
parole.testo: From Middle English gernet, granate, from Old French grenate, from grenat (“pomegranate red”). Doublet of grenade.

parole.significato: To decorate with ornaments; to adorn; to embellish.
parole.testo: From Middle English garnysshen, from Old French garniss-, stem of certain forms of the verb garnir, guarnir, warnir (“to provide, furnish, avert, defend, warn, fortify, garnish”), from a conflation of Old Frankish *warnijan (“to refuse, deny”) and *warnōn (“warn, protect, prepare, beware, guard ones

parole.significato: An attic or semi-finished room just beneath the roof of a house.
parole.testo: From Middle English garett, garite, from Old French garite, guerite (“watchtower”), from garir, guarir (“to defend, protect”) (compare English garrison), ultimately of Germanic origin (see English garage). Doublet of guerite.

parole.significato: A permanent military post.
parole.testo: From Middle English garisoun, garysoun, from Old French garison, guarison, from guarir + -ison, ultimately of Germanic origin; thus a doublet of warison. Compare guard, ward; the modern meaning is influenced by (now obsolete) garnison.

parole.significato: A deep cut.
parole.testo: Alteration of older garsh, from Middle English garsen, from Old French garser, jarsier (Modern French gercer), from Vulgar Latin *charaxāre, from Ancient Greek χαρακτήρ (kharaktḗr, “engraver”).

parole.significato: Protective armor for the hands, formerly thrown down as a challenge to combat.
parole.testo: From Middle English gauntelett, gantlett, a borrowing from Old French gantelet (“gauntlet worn by a knight in armor, a token of one's personality or person, and symbolizing a challenge”), diminutive of gant (“glove”), a borrowing from Frankish *want (“glove; mitten”) and reinforced by Medieval Latin

parole.significato: A small heap of grain, not tied up into a bundle.
parole.testo: From Old French gavelle (cf. Modern French javelle) probably diminutive from Latin capulus (“handle”), from capere (“to lay hold of, seize”); or compare Welsh gafael (“hold, grasp”). Compare heave.

parole.significato: Homosexual:
parole.testo: From Middle English gay, from Old French gai (“joyful, laughing, merry”), usually thought to be a borrowing of Old Occitan gai (“impetuous, lively”), from Gothic *𐌲𐌰𐌷𐌴𐌹𐍃 (*gaheis, “impetuous”), merging with earlier Old French jai ("merry"; see jay), from Frankish *gāhi; both from Proto-Germanic *gan

parole.significato: To congeal.
parole.testo: From Middle English gelen, from Old French geler, from Latin gelāre, from gelu. See gelid. Scots jeel, geal.

parole.significato: A twin (also attributively).
parole.testo: From Middle English gemow, from Old French gemel, from Latin gemellus, diminutive of geminus (“twin”). The modern form is influenced by the Latin etymon.

parole.significato: Class; kind.
parole.testo: From Middle English gendre, borrowed from Old French gendre, borrowed from Latin genere (“type, kind”). Doublet of genre and genus. The verb developed after the noun. Displaced native Old English hād (“sex, gender”).

parole.significato: The descent of a person, family, or group from an ancestor or ancestors; lineage or pedigree.
parole.testo: From Middle English genealogie, genologie, genelogie, from Old French genealogie (Modern French généalogie), from Late Latin genealogia, from Ancient Greek γενεαλογία (genealogía), from γενεά (geneá, “generation, descent”) + -λογία (-logía, “study of”), equivalent to Ancient Greek γενεά (geneá) + -l

parole.significato: a biological parent (either male or female), or the direct cause of an offspring.
parole.testo: From Middle English genitour, from Old French genitor, geneteur, from Latin genitor, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénh₁tōr; the Latin is also equivalent to genō + -tor.

parole.significato: A testicle.
parole.testo: From Old French genitoire.

parole.significato: Birth; begetting.
parole.testo: From Old French géniture (the same word in modern French), or its source Latin genitura, from the base of gignere (“to beget”).

parole.significato: Noble; well-bred, courteous; graceful.
parole.testo: From Middle English gent, from Old French gent, ultimately from Latin genitum (“born”).

parole.significato: Courtesy, refinement; gentleness.
parole.testo: From Middle English gentilesse, from Old French gentilesce.

parole.significato: The state of being elegant, genteel, having good breeding, or being socially superior.
parole.testo: From Old French gentilité.

parole.significato: Tender and amiable; of a considerate or kindly disposition.
parole.testo: From Middle English gentil (“courteous, noble”), from Old French gentil (“high-born, noble”), from Latin gentilis (“of the same family or clan”), from gens (“[Roman] clan”). Doublet of gentile, genteel, and jaunty.

parole.significato: Any well-bred, well-mannered, or charming man.
parole.testo: From Middle English gentilman, morphologically gentle + man, partial calque of Old French gentilhome.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being high-born; gentility.
parole.testo: From Middle English gentryse, from Old French genterise, variant form of gentelise, from gentil.

parole.significato: Birth; condition; rank by birth.
parole.testo: From Old French genterie (“noble people collectively; nobility of character or manners”), from gent (“well-born”) + -erie.

parole.significato: The branch of mathematics dealing with spatial relationships.
parole.testo: From Middle English gemetry, geometrie, from Old French geometrie (modern French géométrie), from Latin geōmetria, from Ancient Greek γεωμετρία (geōmetría, “geometry, land-survey”), from γεωμέτρης (geōmétrēs, “geometer, land measurer”), from γῆ (gê, “earth, land, country”) + -μετρία (-metría, “measu

parole.significato: Having the same mother and father; a full (brother or sister).
parole.testo: From Old French germain, from Latin germānus, from germen (“seed, sprout, bud”). See also germane, a formal variant which has survived in specific senses. Not related to the proper noun German.

parole.significato: A mythical human or humanoid of very great size.
parole.testo: From Middle English geaunt, geant, from Old French geant, gaiant (Modern French géant) from Vulgar Latin *gagās, gagant-, from Latin gigās, gigant-, from Ancient Greek γίγας (gígas, “giant”). Cognate to giga- (“1,000,000,000”). Largely Displaced native Old English ent (“giant”), Old English eoten (“

parole.significato: A female giant.
parole.testo: From Middle English geauntesse, geaunesse, from Old French; equivalent to giant + -ess.

parole.significato: The internal organs of poultry birds, used as food.
parole.testo: From Middle English giblets, from Old French gibelet (“game bird stew”), probably from gibier (“birds hunted for sport”).

parole.significato: Originally (music), a performing engagement by a musician or musical group; (by extension, film, television, theater) a…
parole.testo: The etymology of the noun is unknown, but compare Old French gigue (“a fiddle”). The verb is derived from the noun.

parole.significato: Any of several units of volume, most of which are a quarter of a pint or near to that amount.
parole.testo: From Middle English gille, from Old French gille (“a wine measure”), from Medieval Latin gillo (“earthenware jar”).

parole.significato: A device for suspending something, such as a ship's compass, so that it will remain level when its support is tipped.
parole.testo: Alteration of gemel, from Old French gemel, jumel (“twin”) (French jumeau), from Latin gemellus.

parole.significato: A trick; a device or instrument.
parole.testo: Partly from Middle English gin, ginne (“cleverness, scheme, talent, device, machine”), from Old French gin, an aphetism of Old French engin (“engine”); and partly from Middle English grin, grine (“snare, trick, stratagem, deceit, temptation, noose, halter, instrument”), from Old English grin, gryn,

parole.significato: A type of cake whose main flavoring is ginger.
parole.testo: From Middle English gyngebred, gyngebrede, from Old French gingembras, gingimbrat (“preserved ginger”), from Medieval Latin *gingimbrātus (“gingered”, presumably referring to ginger that perhaps had a pharmaceutical use for some medicinal preparation), with the intrusive m added to gingiber, from La

parole.significato: A type of polearm having a spearhead and a reverse hooked spike on the back.
parole.testo: From Middle English gisarme, from Old French guisarme; compare modern French guisarme.

parole.significato: The main idea or substance, or the most essential part, of a longer or more complicated matter; the crux, the heart, th…
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Old French gist, a noun use of the third person singular indicative of gesir (“to lie down”) (modern French gésir; compare Anglo-Norman (cest) action gist (literally “(law) (this) action lies”)), from Latin iacēre, the present active infinitive of iaceō (“to lie down, lie pr

parole.significato: A stop for lodging or rest in a journey, or the place where this happens; a rest.
parole.testo: From Middle English giste, geste (“resting or stopping place, hostel, lodgings; food, refreshment; (figurative) seat of the soul”), from Old French giste (“resting place”) (modern French gîte (“lodging, shelter; self-catering holiday home”)), a noun use of the past participle form of gesir (“to lie

parole.significato: A small, quill-plucked, gut-strung musical instrument, most commonly with three to four strings in doubles courses; it…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English giterne, from Old French guiterne, ultimately from Latin cithara. Doublet of cittern.

parole.significato: A specialized organ constructed of thick muscular walls found in the digestive tract of some animals, including archosa…
parole.testo: From Middle English gyser, geser, from Old French gesier, giser et al. (French gésier), from Latin gigēria.

parole.significato: Egg white, especially as used in various industrial preparations.
parole.testo: From Middle English glaire, from Old French glaire, from Vulgar Latin *clāria, a substantive use of Latin clārus (“clear”).

parole.significato: A light lance with a long, sharp-pointed head.
parole.testo: From Middle English gleyve (“lance, glaive”), from Old French glaive (“lance; sword”), from Late Latin glavus. parole.significato: To turn (one's eyes or look) at something, often briefly.
parole.testo: The verb is derived from Late Middle English glenchen (“of a blow: to strike obliquely, glance; of a person: to turn quickly aside, dodge”) [and other forms], a blend of: * Old French glacier, glachier, glaichier (“to slide; to slip”) (whence also Middle English glacen (“of a blow: to strike oblique

parole.significato: An infectious disease of horses, mules, and donkeys caused by the bacterium Burkholderia, one species of which may be t…
parole.testo: From Middle English glandres, glaundres, from Old French glandres, plural of Old French glandre, from Latin glandula. Doublet of glandule.

parole.significato: To collect (fruit, grain, or other produce) from a field, an orchard, etc., after the main gathering or harvest.
parole.testo: The verb is derived from Late Middle English glenen (“to gather (heads of grain left by reapers), glean; to gather (things) together, collect”), from Old French glener, glainer (modern French glaner (“to gather, glean”)), from Late Latin glen(n)are, the present active infinitive of glen(n)ō (“to mak

parole.significato: Turf; soil; ground; sod.
parole.testo: From Old French glebe, from Latin glaeba (“lump of earth, clod”). Doublet of gleba.

parole.significato: Stomach mucus, especially of a hawk.
parole.testo: Old French glette.

parole.significato: Great beauty and splendor.
parole.testo: From Middle English glory, glorie, from Old French glorie (“glory”), from Latin glōria (“glory, fame, renown, praise, ambition, boasting”). Doublet of gloria. Displaced native Old English wuldor.

parole.significato: A brief explanatory note or translation of a foreign, archaic, technical, difficult, complex, or uncommon expression, i…
parole.testo: From Middle English glosse, alteration of glose, from Old French glose, from Late Latin glōssa (“obsolete or foreign word requiring explanation”), from Ancient Greek γλῶσσα (glôssa, “language”). Doublet of glossa and gloze.

parole.significato: To add a gloss to (a text).
parole.testo: An alteration of Middle English glosen after Etymology 2, from Old French gloser; compare Medieval Latin glossāre.

parole.significato: A comment in the margin; explanatory note; gloss; commentary.
parole.testo: From Middle English glosen, from Old French gloser, from Medieval Latin glossa. Doublet of gloss and glossa.

parole.significato: A hard gelatin made by boiling bones and hides, used in solution as an adhesive; or any sticky adhesive substance.
parole.testo: From Middle English glew, glue, from Old French glu (“glue, birdlime”), from Late Latin glūs (stem glūt-), from Latin glūten. Related to clay. Partially displaced native Old English līm (“glue”) and ġelīman (“to glue”) (whence modern lime).

parole.significato: An excess, too much.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English glotien /glotten, probably derived from Old French gloter /glotir /glotoiier (“to eat greedily”) [compare French engloutir (“to devour”), French glouton (“glutton”)], derived from Latin gluttiō, gluttīre (“to swallow”). Compare Russian глота́ть (glotátʹ, “to swallow”).

parole.significato: Gluttonous; greedy; gormandizing.
parole.testo: From Middle English glotoun, from Old French gloton, gluton, from Latin gluttō, gluttōnis (“glutton”).
