parole.significato: The vice of eating to excess.
parole.testo: From Old French glutonie, from gloton + -ie, from Latin glutio, equivalent to glutton + -y.

parole.significato: A lump of soft or sticky material.
parole.testo: From Middle English gobbe (also Middle English gobet), from Old French gobet, gobe (“lump, mouthful”), from Transalpine Gaulish *gobbo- (“neb, muzzle”).

parole.significato: A drinking vessel with a foot and stem.
parole.testo: From Middle English goblet (= Middle Low German gobelet, kobelet (“goblet”)), from Old French gobellet, diminutive of gobel, from or related to the verb gober (“to ingest”).

parole.significato: Compony.
parole.testo: From gobbon (“piece, portion, slice”) + -y, from Old French gobon, gobet (“piece”). Cognate with English gubbins (“assorted stuff”).

parole.significato: A wandering student of the 12th or 13th century, whose convivial lifestyle included minstrelsy and a typical satirical…
parole.testo: Uncertain, possibly from Old French goliard (“glutton”); compare Italian goliardo (“university student”).

parole.significato: One who bears the gonfalon.
parole.testo: From Middle English gonfalonier, from Old French gonfalonier.

parole.significato: The front aspect of the neck; the outside of the throat.
parole.testo: From Middle English gorge (“esophagus, gullet; throat; bird's crop; food in a hawk's crop; food or drink that has been eaten”), a borrowing from Old French gorge (“throat”) (modern French gorge (“throat; breast”)), from Vulgar Latin *gorga, *gurga, from Latin gurges (“eddy, whirlpool; gulf; sea”), p

parole.significato: To stuff the gorge or gullet with food; to eat greedily and in large quantities.
parole.testo: The verb is derived from Middle English gorgen (“to eat greedily; to gorge”), a borrowing from Old French gorger, gorgier (modern French gorger (“to eat greedily; to gorge”)), from gorge (“throat”); see further at etymology 1. The noun is derived from the verb.

parole.significato: A piece of armour protecting the throat and/or the upper part of the chest.
parole.testo: From Middle English gorget, from Old French gorgete, from gorge (“throat”).

parole.significato: Senses relating to cutting tools.
parole.testo: From Middle English gouge (“chisel with concave blade; gouge”), from Old French gouge, goi (“gouge”), from Late Latin goia, gubia, gulbia (“chisel; piercer”), borrowed from Gaulish *gulbiā, from Proto-Celtic *gulbā, *gulbi, *gulbīnos (“beak, bill”). The English word is cognate with Italian gorbia, g

parole.significato: A person given to excess in the consumption of food and drink; a greedy or ravenous eater.
parole.testo: From Middle English gourmaunt, gormond, gromonde, from Old French gormant (“a glutton”, noun), from gormant (“gluttonous”, adjective), of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: An extremely painful inflammation of joints, especially of the big toe, caused by a metabolic defect resulting in the a…
parole.testo: From Middle English goute, from Old French gote, gute, from Latin gutta (“drop”). Compare Spanish gota (“drop, droplet”). Doublet of goutte and gutta. The sense shift derived from humorism and "the notion of the 'dropping' of a morbid material from the blood in and around the joints".

parole.significato: A charge in the form of a teardrop shape, originally with wavy sides, but now often with straight sides.
parole.testo: From Middle English goute, from Old French goutte, goute, gote, from Latin gutta (“drop”). Doublet of gout and gutta.

parole.significato: The process, or the power, of governing; government or administration.
parole.testo: From Middle English governaunce, from Old French gouvernance, governance, equivalent to govern + -ance.

parole.significato: Obsolete spelling of governoress.
parole.testo: From Middle English governeresse, from Old French governeresse; equivalent to governer + -ess.

parole.significato: A woman paid to educate children in their own home.
parole.testo: From Middle English governesse, a contracted form of governeresse, from Old French governeresse (“female ruler or administrator”). In later senses, equivalent to govern(or) + -ess.

parole.significato: The chief executive officer of a first-level administrative division of a country.
parole.testo: From Middle English governour, from Old French gouvreneur, from Latin gubernator, from Ancient Greek κυβερνήτης (kubernḗtēs, “steersman, pilot, guide”), from κυβερνάω (kubernáō, “to steer, to drive, to guide, to act as a pilot”), of disputed origin. By surface analysis, govern + -or. Doublet of gube

parole.significato: A woman employed to educate children in private households.
parole.testo: Originally from Middle English governeresse, from Old French governeresse. In this form (with -o-; unlike governeress, governer seems to have never been more common than the -o- form) and later uses, directly from governor + -ess.

parole.significato: A loose, flowing upper garment.
parole.testo: From Middle English gowne, from Anglo-Norman goune, gune (“fur-trimmed coat, pelisse”), from Old French goune, from Late Latin gunna (“leather garment, a fur”). Cognate with Manx gooyn, Irish gúna.

parole.significato: Charming, pleasing qualities.
parole.testo: From Middle English grace, from Old French grace (modern French grâce), from Latin grātia (“kindness, favour, esteem”), from grātus (“pleasing”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerH- (“to praise, welcome”); compare grateful. The word displaced the native Middle English held, hield (“grace”) (from Old En

parole.significato: Of, related to, full of, or exhibiting grace.
parole.testo: From Middle English gracious, from Old French gracieus, from Latin gratiosus, from gratia (“esteem, favor”). See grace. Displaced native Old English hold (“gracious”). Doublet of gracioso and grazioso.

parole.significato: A small shoot or scion of a tree inserted in another tree, the stock of which is to support and nourish it. The two uni…
parole.testo: From Middle English graffe, from Old French greffe (“stylus”), from Latin graphium (“stylus”), from Ancient Greek γραφείον (grapheíon), from γράφειν (gráphein, “to write”); probably akin to English carve. So named from the resemblance of a scion or shoot to a pointed pencil. Doublet of graphium. Com

parole.significato: The Holy Grail.
parole.testo: From Middle English graal, greal, from Old French graal, greal (“cup”), from Medieval Latin gradalis, possibly corrupted over time from Latin crater (“bowl”).

parole.significato: A book of offices in the Roman Catholic Church; a gradual.
parole.testo: From Middle English grayel, from Old French grael, ultimately from Latin graduale. Doublet of gradual.

parole.significato: The harvested seeds of various grass food crops, especially wheat, maize, rye, barley, and rice.
parole.testo: From Middle English greyn, grayn, grein, from Old French grain, grein, from Latin grānum (“seed”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm (“grain”). Doublet of corn, gram, granum, and grao.

parole.significato: Grammar; learning.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English gramarie, from Old French gramarie, a variant of gramaire; thus a doublet of glamour, glamoury, grammar, and grimoire. The word was revived by Scottish historical novelist, playwright and poet Sir Walter Scott (1771–1832).

parole.significato: Used as an expression of gratitude: thanks; many thanks.
parole.testo: From Middle English gramerci, from Old French grant merci (“great thanks”). Still in use in south of France's Provençal language as 'gramerci'.

parole.significato: To discourse according to the rules of grammar; to use grammar.
parole.testo: From Middle English gramere, from Old French gramaire (“classical learning”), from unattested Vulgar Latin *grammāria, an alteration of Latin grammatica, from Ancient Greek γραμματική (grammatikḗ, “skilled in writing”), from γράμμα (grámma, “line of writing”), from γράφω (gráphō, “write”), from Prot

parole.significato: A grandmother.
parole.testo: From Middle English graundame, from Old French grant dame. Doublet of grande dame.

parole.significato: A granary.
parole.testo: From Middle English graunge, borrowed from Old French grange (“granary; barn; small farm”), from Vulgar Latin *grānica, from Latin grānum (“grain”).

parole.significato: The person to whom something is granted.
parole.testo: From Middle English grauntees pl, from Old French granté, participle of granter, equivalent to grant + -ee.

parole.significato: Containing grapes or having a grape flavor.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English grape, borrowed from Old French grappe (“cluster of fruit or flowers, bunch of grapes”), deverbal from graper (“to pick grapes”, literally “to hook”), borrowed from Frankish *krappō (“to hook”), from Proto-Indo-European *greb- (“hook”) or *gremb- (“crooked, uneven”), fr

parole.significato: A tool with claws or hooks which is used to catch or hold something.
parole.testo: From Middle English *grapple, *graple, from Old French grappil (“a ship's grapple”) (compare Old French grappin (“hook”)), from Old French grape, grappe, crape (“hook”), of Germanic origin, from Frankish *krappō (“hook”), from Proto-Indo-European *grep- (“hook”), *gremb- (“crooked, uneven”), from Pr

parole.significato: To shred (things, usually foodstuffs), by rubbing across a grater.
parole.testo: From Middle English graten, from Old French grater (“to scrape”) ( > French gratter), from Frankish *krattōn, from Proto-Germanic *krattōną. Cognate with Old High German krazzon ( > German kratzen (“to scrawl”) > Danish kradse), Icelandic krassa (“to scrawl”) and Danish kratte.

parole.significato: a tool with which one grates, especially foods such as cheese, to facilitate getting small particles or shreds off a so…
parole.testo: From Old French grateor. See grate. By surface analysis, grate (“to scrape, etc.”) + -er.

parole.significato: Small fragments of rock, used for laying on the beds of roads and railways, and as ballast.
parole.testo: From Middle English gravel, grauel, from Old French gravele, diminutive of grave (“gravel, seashore”), from Medieval Latin grava, ultimately from Proto-Celtic *grāwā (“gravel, pebbles”) (compare Breton groa, Cornish grow, Welsh gro), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰroh₁weh₂, from *gʰreh₁w- (“to grind”).

parole.significato: Full of, covered with, or similar to gravel or pebbles.
parole.testo: From Middle English gravelli (“covered with gravel or sand; (pathology) containing sand-like matter”), from gravel (“sand; grain of stand; gravel, pebbles; (pathology) sand-like matter in the urine, calculus”) + -lī (suffix forming adjectives). Gravel is derived from Old French gravel, gravele, grav

parole.significato: Synonym of gravelly.
parole.testo: From Middle English gravelous, from Old French gravelos.

parole.significato: A piece of armour that protects the leg, especially the shin, and occasionally the tops of the feet.
parole.testo: From Middle English greve, grayve, from Old French greve (“shin”), of uncertain origin; possibly from Egyptian Arabic جورب (“stocking, leg cover”). parole.significato: A flight of stairs.
parole.testo: From Middle English grece (“staircase”), from Old French grez, greis et al., plural of gre (“gree”) taken as a collective singular.

parole.significato: One of a flight of steps.
parole.testo: From Middle English gre, from Old French gré, from Latin gradum (“step”). Compare degree. Doublet of grade.

parole.significato: Pleasure, goodwill, satisfaction.
parole.testo: From Middle English gre, from Old French gré (“pleasure, goodwill”), from Latin gratum, a noun use of the neuter of gratus (“pleasing”).

parole.significato: To agree.
parole.testo: From Middle English green (“to agree”), from Old French greer, from gré (hence Etymology 3).

parole.significato: Suffering, hardship.
parole.testo: From Middle English greef, gref, from Old French grief (“grave, heavy, grievous, sad”), from Latin gravis (“heavy, grievous, sad”). Doublet of grave.

parole.significato: Something which causes grief.
parole.testo: From Old French grievance, from the verb grever (“to irritate; to bother; to annoy”) + -ance, equivalent to grieve + -ance.

parole.significato: To cause sorrow or distress to.
parole.testo: From Middle English greven, from Old French grever (“to burden”), from Latin gravō, gravāre, from adjective gravis (“grave”). parole.significato: A mythical creature with the body of a lion and head and wings of an eagle.
parole.testo: From Middle English griffoun, from Old French griffon, from Late Latin grȳphus, from Classical Latin grȳps, from Ancient Greek γρῡ́ψ (grū́ps).

parole.significato: A small, carnivorous South American mammal, of the genus Galictis, somewhat resembling a weasel.
parole.testo: From Old French gris (“gray”) + -on (diminutive suffix). Doublet of Grisons.

parole.significato: A dark grey colour.
parole.testo: From Middle English grisel, gryselle, from Old French grisel, from gris (“grey”), from Frankish *grīs, from Proto-Germanic *grīsaz.

parole.significato: A person who retails groceries (foodstuffs and household items) from a grocery.
parole.testo: From Old French grossier (“wholesaler”). Compare gross.

parole.significato: To grunt; to growl; to snarl; to murmur.
parole.testo: From Middle English groynen, from a mixture of Old French groignier, grougnier (from Latin grunniō) and Old English grunnian (from Proto-Germanic *grunnōną).

parole.significato: remarkably great, big, vast in an often unpleasant way; (of behaviour) Highly or conspicuously offensive.
parole.testo: From Middle English gros (“large, thick, full-bodied; coarse, unrefined, simple”), from Old French gros, from Latin grossus (“big, fat, thick”, in Late Latin also “coarse, rough”), of uncertain further origin but perhaps related to Proto-Celtic *brassos (“great, violent”).

parole.testo: Attested in the 1530s, as grows ("moorhen"), a plural used collectively. parole.significato: An often wooden structure that projects from a coastline to prevent erosion, longshore drift etc.; a breakwater.

parole.significato: Deep-seated and/or long-term animosity or ill will about something or someone, especially due to perceived mistreatment.

parole.significato: Red, e.g. on a coat of arms, typically represented in engraving by vertical parallel lines.

parole.testo: From Middle English golet, borrowed from Old French goulet, from Latin gula.

parole.testo: From Middle English gusset, gysset, from Old French gosset, gousset (“the hollow of the armpit”), diminutive of gose, gosse (“bean pod, hull, husk”).

parole.significato: A guide; a leader or conductor.

parole.significato: To drink or eat quickly, voraciously, or to excess; to gulp down; to swallow greedily, continually, or with gusto.

parole.significato: dwelling; abode; residence

parole.testo: From Middle English historian, historien, from Old French historien, from Latin historia (“story, history”), equivalent to histor(y) + -ian. More at history.

parole.significato: The aggregate of past events, both unrecorded and recorded.
parole.testo: From Middle English historie, from Old French estoire, estorie (“chronicle, history, story”) (French histoire), from Latin historia, from Ancient Greek ἱστορίᾱ (historíā, “learning through research”), from ἱστορέω (historéō, “to research, inquire (and) record”), from ἵστωρ (hístōr, “the knowing, wis

parole.significato: A fairy; a sprite; an elf; a bogey.
parole.testo: From Middle English Hob (a diminutive of Robin, an Old French [Term?] diminutive of Robert), through its connection with Robin Goodfellow and (later) the devil. Compare hobgoblin; see robin.

parole.significato: One who by tenure was to maintain a horse for military service; a kind of light-horseman in the Middle Ages who was mou…
parole.testo: Old English also hobeler, Old French hobelier, Medieval Latin hobellarius (“light horseman”). See hobby (“a horse”).

parole.significato: Any of four species of small falcons in the genus Falco, especially Falco subbuteo.
parole.testo: From Middle English hoby, hobeye, from Old French hobé, hobei, hobet, from Medieval Latin hopētus, diminutive of harpe.

parole.significato: A collection containing a variety of miscellaneous things.
parole.testo: From Middle English hochepoche, a variation of hochepot, from Old French hochepot, from Middle Dutch hutspot (“beef or mutton cut into small pieces and mixed and boiled together in a pot”), from hotsen, hutsen (“to shake; jog; jolt”) + pot (“pot”), equivalent to hotch + pot. Compare German Low Germa

parole.significato: A demonstration of respect, as towards a person after his or her retirement or death.
parole.testo: From Middle English homage, from Old French homage, hommage, from Medieval Latin homināticum (“homage, the service of a vassal or 'man'”), from Latin homō (“a man, in Medieval Latin a vassal”) + -āticum (noun-forming suffix). The American pronunciations in /-ɑːʒ/ and with silent h are due to confusi

parole.significato: The killing of one person by another, whether premeditated or unintentional.
parole.testo: From Old French homicide, from Latin homicīda (“man-slayer”) and homicīdium (“manslaughter”).

parole.significato: A sermon, especially concerning a practical matter.
parole.testo: From Middle English omelī, omelīe, omelye, from Old French omelie and directly from Late Latin homīlia (“homily”), from Ancient Greek ὁμῑλίᾱ (homīlíā, “homily; instruction”), from ὅμῑλος (hómīlos, “crowd, throng”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, suffix forming abstract feminine nouns). ὅμῑλος is derived from ὁμός (ho

parole.significato: Scrupulous with regard to telling the truth; not given to swindling, lying, or fraud; upright.
parole.testo: From Middle English honest, honeste (“honourable, appropriate, excellent”), from Old French honeste, from Latin honestus, from honor. For the verb, see Latin honestāre (“to clothe or adorn with honour”), and compare French honester. Displaced native Old English sōþfæst (literally “truth-firm”).

parole.significato: The act, quality, or condition of being honest.
parole.testo: From Middle English honeste (“honour, integrity”), from Old French honesté (compare modern French honnêteté). By surface analysis, honest + -y. Displaced native Old English sōþfæstnes and non-native Middle English prodonomee, from Old French prodomie. The plant is named so after the visibility of th

parole.significato: Behaving in a manner that shows honor; decent, having integrity.
parole.testo: From Middle English honourable, from Old French honorable, honurable, from Latin honōrābilis, from honōrō (“to honour”); cognate with Italian onorabile, Spanish honorable. By surface analysis, honor + -able. In this sense, largely displaced Old English ārfæst.

parole.significato: honorable, honourable.
parole.testo: From Old French honoros, onoros.

parole.significato: UK standard spelling of honorable.
parole.testo: From Middle English honourable, from Old French honorable, honurable, from Latin honōrābilis, from honōrō (“to honour”); cognate with Italian onorabile, Spanish honorable. By surface analysis, honour + -able. In this sense, largely displaced Old English ārfæst.

parole.significato: The quality of being horrible.
parole.testo: From Middle English horribilite, horrybylyte, from Old French horribleté, from Medieval Latin horribilitas.

parole.significato: A thing that causes horror; a terrifying thing, particularly a prospective bad consequence asserted as likely to result…
parole.testo: First attested in Middle English (alternately as horrible and orrible) in 1303: from Old French horrible, orrible, orible, from Latin horribilis, from horr(ēre) (“tremble”) + -ibilis (“-ible”).

parole.significato: An intense distressing emotion of fear or repugnance.
parole.testo: From Middle English horer, horrour, from Old French horror, from Latin horror (“a bristling, a shaking, trembling as with cold or fear, terror”), from horrere (“to bristle, shake, be terrified”). Displaced native Old English ōga.

parole.significato: A large medical facility, usually in a building with multiple floors, where seriously ill or injured patients are given…
parole.testo: From Middle English hospital, hospitall, from Old French hospital (Modern French hôpital), from Late Latin hospitālis, hospitāle (“hospice, shelter, guesthouse”), from noun use of Latin hospitālis (“hospitable”), from hospes (“host, guest”). Doublet of hotel and hostel. Displaced native Middle Engli

parole.significato: The act or service of welcoming, receiving, hosting, or entertaining guests; an appropriate attitude of openness, respe…
parole.testo: From Middle English hospitalite, from Old French hospitalité (modern French hospitalité), from Latin hospitālitās (“hospitality”), from hospitālis (“hospitable”), from hospes (“guest", "host”). Displaced native Old English cumlīþnes (literally “guest gentleness”).

parole.significato: One which receives or entertains a guest, socially, commercially, or officially.
parole.testo: From Middle English hoste, from Old French oste (French: hôte), from Latin hospitem, accusative of hospes (“a host, also a sojourner, visitor, guest; hence, a foreigner, a stranger”), from *hostipotis, an old compound of hostis and the root of potis, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstipotis (“master of

parole.significato: A multitude of people arrayed as an army; used also in religious senses, as: Heavenly host (of angels)
parole.testo: From Middle English oost, borrowed from Old French ost, oste, hoste, from Latin hostis (“foreign enemy”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstis (as opposed to inimicus (“personal enemy”)). Doublet of guest.

parole.significato: The consecrated bread of the Eucharist.
parole.testo: From Middle English host, oist, ost, from Old French hoiste, from Latin hostia (“sacrificial victim”). Doublet of hostie.

parole.significato: An overnight lodging place for travelers, with dormitory accommodation and shared facilities, especially a youth hostel.
parole.testo: From Middle English hostel, from Old French hostel, ostel, from Late Latin hospitale (“hospice”), from Classical Latin hospitalis (“hospitable”) itself from hospes (“host”) + -alis (“-al”). Doublet of hotel and hospital. Not in use from late 17th c. (in the usual sense from mid 16th c.) to 1808, whe

parole.significato: The state of being hostile.
parole.testo: From Middle English hostilitie, hostilite, from Old French hostilité, from Latin hostīlitās. By surface analysis, hostile + -ity.

parole.significato: A hostelry.
parole.testo: From Old French hosterie, from hoste (“host”). Doublet of osteria.

parole.significato: A robe or long tunic that is worn belted or with a fitted bodice often having full long sleeves and lined with fur.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English hopeland, hopland, houpelond, hoppelande, from Old French houppelande (1281), probably a calque from Old English hōppāda (“upper tunic”).

parole.significato: A unit of time of one twenty-fourth of a day (sixty minutes).
parole.testo: From Middle English houre, hour, oure, from Old French houre, from Latin hōra (“hour”), from Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra, “any time or period, whether of the year, month, or day”), from Proto-Indo-European *yóh₁r̥ (“year, season”). Akin to Old English ġēar (“year”). Doublet of hora and year. Compare hor

parole.significato: A shout or cry.
parole.testo: From Old French hu or Old French heu, a hunting cry.

parole.significato: Very large.
parole.testo: From Middle English huge, from Old French ahuge (“high, lofty, great, large, huge”), of unknown origin. One theory derives it from an underlying Old French a hoge (“at height”), from a (“at, to”) + hoge (“a hill, height”), the latter from Frankish *haug or cognate Old Norse haugr (“hill”); both from

parole.significato: A Hugo Award, a statuette given out by the World Science Fiction Society.
parole.testo: From Old French Hugo, of Germanic origin, from Frankish *hugi (“thought, mind, spirit”).

parole.significato: An outer garment (robe or cloak) worn by men and women in Europe in the Middle Ages, either as civilian clothing or ove…
parole.testo: From Old French huque, from Latin huca. See Dutch huik (“sleeveless cape”).

parole.significato: Humankind; human beings as a group.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English humanyte, humanite, humanitye, from Old French humanité, from Latin hūmānitās. By surface analysis, human or humane + -ity. Partly displaced mankind, from Old English mancynn (literally “human race”).

parole.significato: Not pretentious or magnificent; unpretending; unassuming.
parole.testo: From Middle English humble, from Old French humble, umble, humle, from Latin humilis (“low, slight, hence mean, humble”) (compare Greek χαμηλός (khamēlós, “on the ground, low, trifling”)), from humus (“the earth, ground”), humi (“on the ground”). See homage, and compare chameleon, humiliate. Displac

parole.significato: Humility, humbleness.
parole.testo: From Middle English humblesse, from Old French humblesse, from humble.

parole.significato: Containing perceptible moisture (usually describing air or atmosphere); damp; moist; somewhat wet or watery.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French humide, from Latin humidus (“moist”). Via Proto-Indo-European *wegʷ- (“wet”) related to English weaky.

parole.significato: Dampness, especially that of the air.
parole.testo: From Middle English humidite, borrowed from Old French humidité, from Medieval Latin hūmiditās, from Latin ūmidus (“damp, moist, wet”). By surface analysis, humid + -ity.

parole.significato: The characteristic of being humble; humbleness in character and behavior.
parole.testo: From Middle English humilite, from Old French (h)umilité, from Latin humilitas (“lowness, meanness, baseness, in Late Latin humility”), from humilis (“low, lowly, humble, earth”). Equivalent to humble + -ity, with /mb/ reduced to /m/ (compare plumbing). Displaced native Old English ēaþmōdnes. Double

parole.significato: The quality of being amusing, comical, funny.
parole.testo: From Middle English humour, from Old French humor, humour, from Latin hūmor, correctly ūmor (“liquid”), from hūmeō, correctly ūmeō (“to be moist”). The h in these words, which was silent in late Classical Latin, is folk etymological, due to the erroneous association with the word humus (“soil”). The

parole.significato: Miscellaneous household items; odds and ends.
parole.testo: From Middle English ostelment, borrowed from Old French ostillement, ultimately from Vulgar Latin *usitilium, from neuter plural *usitilia, from Latin utensilia (“utensils”).

parole.significato: Any bulbous plant of the genus Hyacinthus, native to the Mediterranean and South Africa.
parole.testo: From Middle English jacinth, partly from Old French jacincte, from Medieval Latin jacintus, and partly from Old English iacinþ, from Medieval Latin jacinthus, both from Latin hyacinthus, from Ancient Greek ὑάκινθος (huákinthos, “any of several dark blue flowers”), ultimately from a non-Indo-European

parole.significato: Dropsical; pertaining to or suffering from dropsy (edema).
parole.testo: From Middle English ydropik, ydropyk, from Old French ydropique, from Latin hydropicus, from Ancient Greek ὑδρωπικός (hudrōpikós), from ὕδρωψ (húdrōps).

parole.significato: Any of the medium-sized to large feliform carnivores of the family Hyaenidae, native to Africa and Asia and noted for t…
parole.testo: From Middle English hiena, variant of hyene, from Old French hiene, from Medieval Latin hyēna, from Latin hyaena, from Ancient Greek ὕαινα (húaina). Displaced native Old English nihtgenġe (literally “night walker”).

parole.significato: A song of praise or worship, especially a religious one.
parole.testo: From Middle English ymne, from Old English ymen (reinforced by Old French ymne), from Latin hymnus, borrowed from Ancient Greek ὕμνος (húmnos).

parole.significato: The writing, composing, or singing of hymns or psalms.
parole.testo: From Old French hymnodie, from Latin hymnodia, from Ancient Greek ὑμνῳδία (humnōidía), from ὑμνῳδέω (humnōidéō, “to sing a hymn”), from ὕμνος (húmnos, “song of praise”) + ἀείδω (aeídō, “to sing”).

parole.significato: The contrivance of a false appearance of virtue or goodness, while concealing real character or inclinations, especiall…
parole.testo: From hypo- + Ancient Greek κρί(σις) (krí(sis)) + -isy. From Middle English ipocrisie, from Old French ypocrisie, from Late Latin hypocrisis, from Ancient Greek ὑπόκρισις (hupókrisis, “answer, stage acting, pretense”), from ὑποκρίνομαι (hupokrínomai, “I answer (a fellow actor on stage), play a part,

parole.significato: Someone who practices hypocrisy, who pretends to hold beliefs, or whose actions are not consistent with their claimed b…
parole.testo: From Old French ypocrite (Modern French hypocrite), from Latin hypocrita, from Ancient Greek ὑποκριτής (hupokritḗs, “actor, hypocrite”), from ὑποκρίνομαι (hupokrínomai, “to answer, act, feign”). Displaced native Old English līċettere.

parole.significato: The ninth letter of the English alphabet, called i and written in the Latin script.
parole.testo: Old French i, from Latin ī, from Etruscan I (i).

parole.significato: A person of low general intelligence.
parole.testo: From Middle English idiote, ydiote, from Old French idiote (later idiot), from Latin idiota, from Ancient Greek ἰδιώτης (idiṓtēs, “a private citizen, one who has no professional knowledge, layman”), from ἴδιος (ídios, “one's own, pertaining to oneself, private”). Doublet of idiota. By surface analys

parole.significato: A graven image or representation of anything that is revered, or believed to convey spiritual power.
parole.testo: From Middle English ydole, from Old French idole, from Latin idolum, from Ancient Greek εἴδωλον (eídōlon, “image, idol”), from εἶδος (eîdos, “form”), from Proto-Indo-European *wéydos (“seeing, image”), from *weyd- (“to see”). Doublet of aidoru, eidolon, and idolum and related to idea.

parole.significato: The worship of idols.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English ydolatrie, from Old French idolatrie, from Ecclesiastical Latin īdōlatrīa, from Late Latin īdōlolatrīa, from Ancient Greek εἰδωλολατρίᾱ (eidōlolatríā, “worship of idols”), back-formation from εἰδωλολάτρης (eidōlolátrēs), from εἴδωλον (eídōlon, “idol”) & λάτρις (látris,

parole.significato: Fiery; of or pertaining to fire.
parole.testo: From Old French ignel, from Late Latin *ignealis, from Latin igneus (“fiery”), from ignis (“fire”).

parole.significato: The condition of being uninformed or uneducated; lack of knowledge or information.
parole.testo: From Middle English ignoraunce, ignorance, from From Old French ignorance, from Latin ignōrantia. By surface analysis, ignor(e) + -ance.

parole.significato: Unknowledgeable or uneducated; characterized by ignorance.
parole.testo: From Old French ignorant, from Latin ignōrāns (“unaware, unknowing”). By surface analysis, ignore + -ant.

parole.significato: Synonym of illuminate.
parole.testo: From Middle English illuminen (“to light, light up; to shine; (figuratively) to enlighten spiritually; to make illustrious”) [and other forms], from Old French illuminer (“to light up, illuminate; (figuratively) to enlighten”) (modern French illuminer), from Latin illūmināre, the present active infi

parole.significato: A distortion of sensory perception where real stimuli lead to a false or misleading impression of reality.
parole.testo: From Old French illusion, from Latin illūsiō, from illūdere, from in- (“at, upon”) + lūdere (“to play, mock, trick”). Displaced native Old English dwimmer.

parole.significato: A visual or other representation of the external form of something in art.
parole.testo: From Middle English ymage, borrowed from Old French image, from Latin imāgō (“a copy, likeness, image”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eym-; the same PIE root is the source of imitari (“to copy, imitate”); see imitate. Doublet of imago.

parole.significato: One who images or forms likenesses; a sculptor.
parole.testo: From Middle English ymageour, from Old French imageor; equivalent to image + -er.

parole.significato: The image-making power of the mind; the act of mentally creating or reproducing an object not previously perceived; the…
parole.testo: From Middle English ymaginacioun, from Old French imaginacion, ymaginacion, from Latin imāginātiō. Equivalent to imagine + -ation.

parole.significato: To stain [with in or with ‘blood, slaughter, etc.’].
parole.testo: From Middle English embrewen, from Old French *embrever (whence Middle French embreuver), metathetic variant of embevrer (“to imbibe, steep, penetrate, soak”) (with same stem variation found in French abreuver and beuverie), from Vulgar Latin imbiberāre.

parole.significato: Happening right away, instantly, with no delay.
parole.testo: From Old French immediat (French immédiat), borrowed from Late Latin immediātus (“without in-between, moderation”), from Latin in + mediātus, perfect passive participle of mediō (“to halve, to be in the middle”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from medius (“middle”). By surface analysis, im-

parole.significato: Huge, gigantic, very large.
parole.testo: From Middle English immens, inmens, from Old French immense, from Latin immensus, from in- (“not”) + mensus (“measured”). Compare incommensurable.

parole.significato: unmeasurable, immeasurable; not able to be measured, therefore connoting extremely large
parole.testo: From Middle English immensurable, from Old French, from Latin immēnsūrābilis, from im- (“not”) (variant form of in-) + mēnsūra (“measure”) + -bilis (“able”).

parole.significato: Fixed, not movable.
parole.testo: From Old French immobile, from Latin immōbilis, equivalent to im- + mobile.

parole.significato: The condition of being immortal.
parole.testo: From Middle English immortalitee, immortalite, from Old French immortalité, from Latin immortālitās. Morphologically immortal + -ity.

parole.significato: The state of being insusceptible to something; notably:
parole.testo: From Middle English immunite, from Old French immunité, from Latin immūnitās, in the legal sense; for the medical use see immunization. Equivalent to immune + -ity. Displaced native Old English frēols (“privilege, immunity”).

parole.significato: To weaken; to affect negatively; to have a diminishing effect on.
parole.testo: From Middle English impairen, empeiren, from Old French empeirier, from Early Medieval Latin impeiōrāre, from in- + Late Latin peiōrāre (“worsen”), from peiōrem (“worse”), comparative of malus (“bad”).

parole.significato: To hold discourse; to parley.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Old French emparler.

parole.significato: Only used in parson imparsonee.
parole.testo: From Old French empersone. See in- and parson.

parole.significato: The quality of being impatient; lacking patience; restlessness and intolerance of delays; anxiety and eagerness, especi…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English impacience, from Old French impacience (modern French impatience), from Latin impatientia. By surface analysis, im- + patience.

parole.significato: Restless, short of temper, and intolerant of delays.
parole.testo: From Old French impacient (modern French impatient), from Latin impatiēns. By surface analysis, im- + patient.

parole.significato: Not perfect.
parole.testo: From Middle English imperfit, from Old French imparfit (modern French imparfait), from Latin imperfectus. Spelling modified 15c. to conform Latin etymology. See im- + perfect.

parole.significato: Those qualities or features that are imperfect; the characteristic, state, or quality of being imperfect.
parole.testo: From Old French imperfeccion, from Latin imperfectiōnem, accusative of imperfectiō, from in- + perfectiō. By surface analysis, im- + perfection.

parole.significato: Related to an empire, emperor, or empress.
parole.testo: From Middle English imperial, from Old French imperial, from Latin imperiālis (“of the empire or emperor, imperial”), from imperium (“empire, imperial government”) + -ālis, from imperō (“command, order”), from im- (“form of in”) + parō (“prepare, arrange; intend”). Displaced Old English cāserlīċ.

parole.significato: Making arbitrary decisions, especially in an impulsive and forceful manner.
parole.testo: From Middle English impetuous, from Old French impetueux, from Late Latin impetuōsus (“violent”), from Latin impetus (“attack, violence”).

parole.significato: The state of being impious.
parole.testo: From Old French impieté, from Latin impietas, from in- (“not”) + pietas (“piety”), from pius (“pious, devout”) + -tās (“-ty, -dom”). By surface analysis, impious + -ety.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being implacable.
parole.testo: From Old French, from Latin implacabilitas (“unappeasable”).

parole.significato: Not able to be placated or appeased.
parole.testo: From Middle English implācāble (“immitigable, unappeasable”) from Old French implacable (“harsh, unrelenting; implacable”) (modern French implacable), from Latin implācābilis (“unappeasable, implacable; irreconcilable”), from im- (variant of in- (prefix meaning ‘not’)) + plācābilis (“placable; appea

parole.significato: To have as a necessary consequence; to lead to (something) as a consequence.
parole.testo: From Middle English implien, emplien, borrowed from Old French emplier, from Latin implicare (“to infold, involve”), from in (“in”) + plicare (“to fold”). Doublet of employ and implicate.

parole.significato: Something brought in from an exterior source, especially for sale or trade.
parole.testo: From Middle English importen, from Old French emporter, importer, from Latin importō (“bring in from abroad, import”, verb), from in (“in, at, on; into”) + portō (“to carry, bear; convey”).

parole.significato: The act of imposing, laying on, affixing, enjoining, inflicting, obtruding, and the like.
parole.testo: From Middle English imposicioun, from Old French imposicion, from Latin impositio.

parole.significato: An abscess.
parole.testo: From Old French empostume, alteration of apostume (“apostume, large abscess”), from Latin apostema, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστεμα (apóstema, “separation of pus into an abscess”).

parole.significato: Lacking physical strength or vigor; weak
parole.testo: From Old French impotent, from Latin impotēns, from in- (expresses negation) + potēns (“powerful”).

parole.significato: To impregnate; to make fruitful.
parole.testo: First attested in the early 15ᵗʰ century, in Middle English; from Middle English impregnen (“to make a woman pregnant, impregnate”), from Old French enpreignier, enpreigner (French imprégner), ultimately from Medieval Latin impraegnō. Doublet of impregnate.

parole.significato: Of a fortress or other fortified place: able to withstand all attacks; impenetrable, inconquerable, unvanquishable.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English imprenable, impregnable (“impossible to capture, impregnable”), from Old French imprenable (modern French imprenable (“impregnable”)), from im- (a variant of in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + prenable (“(military) of a building, position, etc.: takable”) (from prendre (“to take”)

parole.significato: The act of making pregnant; fertilization.
parole.testo: From Middle English impregnacioun, from Old French impregnacion, in turn from Late Latin impregnatio.

parole.significato: The indentation or depression made by the pressure of one object on or into another.
parole.testo: From Old French impression, from Latin impressio. Equivalent to impress + -ion.

parole.significato: An impression; the mark left behind by printing something or by pressing on something, or the figurative counterpart of…
parole.testo: From Old French empreinte, from the past participle of empreindre, from Latin imprimere.

parole.significato: To leave a print, impression, image, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English emprinten, enprinten, from Old French empreinter, from the past participle of empreindre, from Latin imprimere.

parole.significato: To put in or as if in prison; confine somebody against their will.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English imprisonen, emprisounen, emprisonen, from Old French emprisonner. Equivalent to im- + prison.

parole.significato: The act of impelling or driving onward, or the state of being impelled; the sudden or momentary agency of a body in mot…
parole.testo: From Middle English impulsioun, from Old French impulsion, from Latin impulsio, impulsionem.

parole.significato: Instead of; in place of.
parole.testo: From Middle English in liue of, a partial calque of Old French au leu de (modern French au lieu de).

parole.significato: The act of removing the contents of something; the state of being empty.
parole.testo: From Middle English inanicioun, borrowed from Old French inanition, itself borrowed from Late Latin inānītio, from inānīre (“to make empty”), from inānis (“empty, vain”); see inane.

parole.significato: The act or process of using formulas and/or usually rhyming words, sung or spoken, with occult ceremonies, for the purp…
parole.testo: From Middle English incantacioun, from Old French incantation, from Latin incantatio. More at enchant.

parole.significato: An incarnate being or form.
parole.testo: From Middle English incarnacion, borrowed from Old French incarnacion, from Medieval Latin, Ecclesiastical Latin incarnatio, from Late Latin incarnari (“to be made flesh”).

parole.significato: Capable of, or used for, or actually causing fire.
parole.testo: From Middle English incendiarie, from Old French incendiaire, from Latin incendiārius (“setting alight”), from incendium (“destructive fire”), from incendō (“to set on fire, kindle”), from in- (“into, in, on, upon”) + candeō (“to be hot”).

parole.significato: Biotic material that releases fragrant smoke when burnt, often used in religious rites or for aesthetic reasons.
parole.testo: From Middle English encens, from Old French encens (“sweet-smelling substance”) from Late Latin incensum (“burnt incense”, literally “something burnt”), neuter past participle of incendō (“to set on fire”). Compare incendiary. Doublet of incienso. Displaced native Old English rēcels.

parole.significato: Uncertainty.
parole.testo: From Old French incertaineté.

parole.significato: A physical tilt or bend.
parole.testo: From Middle English inclinacioun, inclinacyon, from Old French inclination and Latin inclīnātiō. Morphologically incline + -ation.

parole.significato: To bend or move (something) out of a given plane or direction, often the horizontal or vertical.

parole.significato: Lack of self-restraint, an inability to control oneself; unchastity.
parole.testo: From Middle English incontinence, from Old French incontinence or its etymon Latin incontinentia. Doublet of incontinency.

parole.significato: Unable to contain or retain.
parole.testo: From Middle English incontinent, from Old French incontinent, from Latin incontinens, from in + continens.

parole.significato: The quality of being inconvenient.

parole.significato: The act of incorporating, or the state of being incorporated.
parole.testo: From Middle English incorporacioun, from Old French incorporacion, from Late Latin incorporatio. By surface analysis, incorporate + -ion.

parole.significato: Unwillingness or inability to believe; doubt about the truth or verisimilitude of something; disbelief.
parole.testo: Attested since 1430. From Middle English incredulite, from Old French incredulité, from Late Latin incredulitas, from Latin incredulus (“unbelieving”) + -itas (“-ity”), equivalent to incredulous + -ity.

parole.significato: Of an illness, condition, etc, that is unable to be cured; healless.
parole.testo: From Old French incurable, from Late Latin incurabilis.

parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French, from Latin incursiō.

parole.significato: To bring into debt; to place under obligation.
parole.testo: From Middle English endetten, Old French endetter, from en- + detter, from dette (“debt”), by surface analysis, in- + debt. See debt.

parole.significato: A cut or notch in the margin of anything, or a recess like a notch.
parole.testo: Partly from Middle English indenten (“to dent in”), equivalent to in- + dent (see dent); partly from Middle English indenten, endenten, from Old French endenter (“to cut notches into”), from en- (“in-, en-”) + dent (“tooth”), from Latin dēns.

parole.significato: An act of pointing out or indicating.
parole.testo: From Old French indication, from Latin indicātiō (“a showing, indicating the value of something; valuation”), from indicō (“point out, indicate, show; value”); see indicate; compare French indication, Spanish indicación, Italian indicazione. By surface analysis, indicate + -ion.

parole.significato: index
parole.testo: From Old French indice, from Latin indicium, from index.

parole.testo: From Old French indiction or its source, Latin indictiōnem, accusative singular of indictiō, from indicere.

parole.significato: Ambivalent; unconcerned; uninterested, apathetic.
parole.testo: From Old French indifferent, from Latin indifferens. By surface analysis, in- + different.

parole.significato: Extreme poverty or destitution.
parole.testo: From Middle English indigence, late 14th century, from Old French indigence (13th century), from Latin indigentia, from indigentem, form of indigēre (“to need”), from indu (“in, within”) + egēre (“be in need, want”). Only relation to antonym affluence is common Latinate suffix + -ence.

parole.significato: Poor; destitute; in need.
parole.testo: From Middle English indigent, from Old French indigent, from Latin indigēns, present participle of indigeō (“to need”), from indu (“in, within”) + egeō (“to be in need, want”).

parole.significato: A condition of heartburn, nausea, or other stomach-related pain, sometimes caused by eating too quickly.
parole.testo: From Middle English indigestioun, from Old French indigestion, from Late Latin indigestio, by surface analysis, in- + digestion.

parole.significato: An anger aroused by something perceived as an indignity, notably an offense or injustice.
parole.testo: From Middle English indignacioun, borrowed from Old French indignation, from Latin indignātiō, from indignor (“to scorn, resent”), from indignus (“unworthy, not fitting”), from in- (“not”) + dignus (“worthy, appropriate”). Attested since ca. 1374. Doublet of indignatio.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being indiscreet; lack of discretion
parole.testo: From Old French, from Late Latin indiscrētiō.

parole.significato: To physically make (letters and words) on a writing surface; to inscribe.
parole.testo: Originally a variant of indict; from Middle English enditen, endyten, from Old French enditer, from Late Latin indictāre, from in- + dictare (“to declare”). Doublet of indict.

parole.significato: An act of inducting.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English induction, from Old French induction, from Latin inductiō, from indūcō (“to lead”). By surface analysis, induct + -ion or induce + -tion.

parole.significato: Hardness.
parole.testo: From Middle English induracioun, from Old French induracion (“hardness, obstinacy”) or directly from Medieval Latin induratiō.

parole.significato: The tendency to work persistently.
parole.testo: From Middle English industry, industrie, from Old French industrie, from Latin industria (“diligence, activity, industry”), from industrius (“diligent, active, zealous”), from Old Latin indostruus (“diligent, active”); origin unknown. parole.significato: Absence of equality.
parole.testo: From Middle English inequalite, from Old French inequalité, from Medieval Latin inaequālitās, from Latin inaequālis (“unequal”), from in- (“not”) + aequālis (“equal”). Morphologically inequal + -ity and in- + equality.

parole.significato: The state of being infamous.
parole.testo: From late Middle English infamie, from Old French infamie, from Latin īnfāmia (“infamy”), from īnfāmis (“infamous”), from in- (“not”) + fāma (“fame, renown”). Displaced native Old English unhlīsa (literally “bad fame”).

parole.significato: The act or process of infecting.
parole.testo: From Old French infection, from Late Latin īnfectiō. Equivalent to infect + -ion.

parole.significato: To inhabit a place in unpleasantly large numbers; to plague, harass.
parole.testo: From Middle English infesten, from Old French infester (“to infest”), from Latin īnfestō (“assail, molest”, verb), from īnfestus (“hostile”), of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: Indefinably large, countlessly great; immense.
parole.testo: From Middle English infinite, from Old French infinit and its etymon Latin īnfīnītus, from in- (“not”) + fīnis (“end”) + the perfect passive participle ending -ītus. By surface analysis, in- + finite. Doublet of infinito. Displaced native Old English unġeendodlīċ.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being infinite or having no limit.
parole.testo: From Old French infinité, from Latin infinitas (“unlimitedness”), from negative prefix in- (“not”), + finis (“end”), + noun of state suffix -tas.

parole.significato: Endlessness, unlimitedness, absence of a beginning, end or limits to size.
parole.testo: From Middle English infinite, from Old French infinité, from Latin īnfīnitās (“unlimitedness”), from negative prefix in- (“not”), + fīnis (“end”), + noun of state suffix -tās. By surface analysis, infinite + -ity.

parole.significato: An act, instance of, or state of expansion or increase in size, especially by injection of a gas or liquid.
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French inflation (“swelling”), from Latin īnflātiō (“expansion", "blowing up”), from īnflātus, the perfect passive participle of īnflō (“blow into, expand”), from in (“into”) + flō (“blow”). By surface analysis, inflate + -ion.

parole.significato: The power to affect, control or manipulate something or someone; the ability to change the development of fluctuating t…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English influence, from Old French influence, borrowed from Medieval Latin īnfluentia, from Latin īnfluēns + -ia. Doublet of influenza.

parole.significato: To instruct, train (usually in matters of knowledge).
parole.testo: From Middle English informen, enformen, borrowed from Old French enformer, informer (“to train, instruct, inform”), from Latin īnfōrmō (“to shape, form, train, instruct, educate”), from in- (“into”) + fōrma (“form, shape”), equivalent to in- + form.

parole.significato: A product consisting of a liquid which has had other ingredients steeped in it to extract useful qualities.
parole.testo: From Middle English infusioun, from Old French infusion, from Latin infusio, infusionem (“a pouring into, a wetting, a dyeing, a flow”), from infundo.

parole.significato: A lack or absence of gratitude; thanklessness.
parole.testo: From in- + gratitude, from Old French ingratitude, from Late Latin ingrātitūdō. By surface analysis, in- + Latin grat(us) + -itude.

parole.significato: To live or reside in.
parole.testo: From Old French enhabiter, from Latin inhabitāre (in + habitāre).

parole.significato: Someone or thing who lives in a place.

parole.significato: To receive (property, a title, etc.), by legal succession or bequest, usually after the previous owner's death.
parole.testo: From Middle English enheriten, from Old French enheriter, from Late Latin inhereditare (“make heir”). Displaced native Old English ierfan.

parole.significato: The act of inhibiting.
parole.testo: From Middle English inhibicioun, inhibicione from Old French inibicion, from Latin inhibitio. Morphologically inhibit + -ion.

parole.significato: Deviation from what is right; gross injustice, sin, wickedness.
parole.testo: From Middle English iniquite, jniquite (“evil, wickedness, iniquity; evil act; hostility, malevolence; hostile act; a calamity, misfortune”), from Old French iniquité (modern French iniquité (“iniquity”)), from Latin inīquitās (“iniquity; inequality, unfairness; inequity, injustice”), from inīquus (

parole.significato: The act of enjoining; the act of directing, commanding, or prohibiting.
parole.testo: From Middle English iniunccyon, iniunccion, from Old French injonctïon, from Latin iniūnctiō (“command, injunction”).

parole.significato: Unjust, unfair.
parole.testo: From Middle English injuste, from Old French injuste; equivalent to in- + just.

parole.significato: Absence of justice; unjustice.
parole.testo: From Middle English injustice, from Old French injustice, from Latin iniustitia. Equivalent to in- + justice. Displaced native Old English unrihtwīsnes.

parole.significato: A pigment (or dye)-based fluid used for writing, printing etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English ynke, from Old French enque, from Latin encaustum (“purple ink used by Roman emperors to sign documents”), from Ancient Greek ἔγκαυστον (énkauston, “burned-in”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + καίω (kaíō, “burn”). In this sense, displaced native Old English blæc (“ink”, literally “black”).

parole.significato: Absence of responsibility for a crime, tort, etc.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English innocence, from Old French innocence, inocence, from Latin innocentia. Doublet of innocency. Displaced native Old English unsċyld.

parole.significato: Free from guilt, sin, or immorality.
parole.testo: From Middle English innocent, from Old French innocent, inocent, borrowed from Latin innocēns (“harmless, inoffensive”), from in- (“not”) + nocēns, present participle of noceō (“to hurt”). By surface analysis, in- (“not”) + nocent (“harmful; guilty”). Displaced native Old English unsċyldiġ.

parole.significato: Not obedient; disobedient.
parole.testo: From Middle English inobedient, from Old French inobedient, from Latin inoboediens (“not obedient”), present participle of inoboedire (“to disobey”). Compare French inobedient. See obedient.

parole.significato: The act of inquiring; a seeking of information by asking questions; interrogation; a question or questioning.

parole.significato: An inquiry or investigation into the truth of some matter.

parole.significato: Eager to acquire knowledge; acquisitive.
parole.testo: Late 14th century, from Old French inquisitif, from Late Latin inquisitivus, from Latin inquisitus, past participle of inquirere. See also inquire.

parole.significato: A person who inquires, especially searchingly or ruthlessly.
parole.testo: From Old French inquisiteur, from Latin inquīsītor.

parole.significato: To make to understand; to instruct.

parole.significato: The property of being insensible.

parole.significato: Unable to be perceived by the senses.

parole.significato: foolish; lacking wisdom; stupid

parole.significato: The state of being insistent.

parole.significato: The act of instigating, or the state of being instigated; incitement; especially to evil or wickedness.
parole.testo: From Middle English instigacioun, from Old French instigacïon and Latin instīgātio.

parole.significato: The act of instructing, teaching, or providing with information or knowledge.
parole.testo: From Middle English instruccioun, from Old French instruccion, from Latin instructio; equivalent to instruct + -ion.

parole.significato: To apply measuring devices.
parole.testo: From Middle English instrument, from Old French instrument, from Latin īnstrūmentum (“an implement, tool”), From īnstruō (“build, construct; arrange”) + -mentum.

parole.significato: Pertaining to, or performed by, the intellect; mental or cognitive.
parole.testo: From Old French intellectuel, from Latin intellectualis.

parole.testo: From Middle English intelligence, from Old French intelligence, from Latin intelligentia, which is most likely from inter- (“between”) + legere (“to choose, pick out, read”). Doublet of intelligentsia.

parole.significato: intemperateness; severity, excess or inclemency

parole.significato: To fix the mind upon (something, or something to be accomplished); be intent upon

parole.significato: Something that is intended.
parole.testo: Existing since Middle English entente, from Old French entent or entente, ultimately from Latin intentus. Modified later in spelling to align more closely with the Latin word. Compare intention.

parole.significato: Paying attention; attentive, heedful.

parole.significato: Communication, conversation.
parole.testo: From Old French entrecours, from Late Latin intercursus.

parole.testo: From Middle English interest, from Old French interesse and interest (French intérêt), from Medieval Latin interesse, from Latin interesse.

parole.significato: To get involved or involve oneself, causing disturbance.
parole.testo: From Old French entreferir, from entre- + ferir (“to hit, to strike”), itself from the Latin verb ferio.

parole.significato: To mix together, intermeddle, intermix.
parole.testo: From Old French entremeller.

parole.significato: The act of burying a dead body; burial.
parole.testo: From Middle English enterement, interment, from Old French enterrement. By surface analysis, inter + -ment.

parole.significato: The act of interposing, or the state of being interposed; a being, placing, or coming between; mediation.
parole.testo: From Middle English interposicion, from Old French interposicion, from Latin interpositio.

parole.significato: The act of interrogating or questioning; an examination by questions; an inquiry.
parole.testo: From Middle English interrogacion, from Old French interrogacion, from Latin interrogātiō, from interrogō, from inter- (“between; among”) + rogō (“to ask; to request”). Equivalent to inter- + rogation or interrogate + -ion.

parole.significato: The act of interrupting, or the state of being interrupted.
parole.testo: From Middle English interrupcioun, from Old French interrupcion, from Latin interruptio.

parole.significato: A small opening or space between objects, especially adjacent objects or objects set closely together, such as between…

parole.significato: A distance in space.

parole.significato: An official face-to-face meeting of monarchs or other important figures.
parole.testo: From Old French entreveue (French entrevue), feminine singular past participle of entrevëoir, from entre- + vëoir (“to see”). Equivalent to inter- + view.

parole.significato: To give tone or variety of tone to; to vocalize.

parole.significato: To cause (someone) to be acquainted (with someone else).

parole.significato: The act or process of introducing.

parole.significato: The forcible inclusion or entry of an external group or individual; the act of intruding.
parole.testo: From Middle English intrusioun, from Old French intrusion, from Medieval Latin intrūsiō, from intrūdō, from Latin in- + trūdō.

parole.significato: The act of inundating; an overflow; a flood; a rising and spreading of water over grounds.

parole.significato: To design a new process or mechanism.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to invention; pertaining to the act of devising new mechanisms or processes.
parole.testo: From Middle English inventif, inventyfe, borrowed from Old French inventif, borrowed from Medieval Latin inventivus. By surface analysis, invent + -ive.

parole.significato: The act of investigating; the process of inquiring into or following up; research, especially patient or thorough inqui…
parole.testo: From Middle English investigacioun, from Old French investigacion, from Latin investigatio. Morphologically investigate + -ion.

parole.significato: Unable to be seen; out of sight; not visible.
parole.testo: From Middle English invisible, from Old French invisible, from Late Latin invīsibilis. Displaced native Old English unġesewenlīċ. Morphologically in- + visible. Piecewise doublet of unvisible.

parole.significato: The act or form of calling for the assistance or presence of some superior being, especially prayer offered to a divine…
parole.testo: From Middle English invocacioun, from Old French invocacion, from Latin invocatio, invocationem. Equivalent to invoke + -ation.

parole.significato: To call upon (a person, a god) for help, assistance or guidance.
parole.testo: From Middle English *invoken, envoken, borrowed from Old French envoquer, from Latin invocāre (“to call upon”), itself from in- + vocare (“to call”). Doublet of invocate.

parole.significato: Easily provoked to outbursts of anger; irritable.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French irascible, from Late Latin īrāscibilis, from Latin īrāscī (“to be angry, enraged”) + -bilis. See also -ible.

parole.significato: Great anger; wrath; keen resentment.
parole.testo: From Middle English ire, from Old French ire (“ire”), from Latin īra (“wrath, rage”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eysh₂- (“to fall upon, act sharply”) (compare Old English ofost (“haste, zeal”), Old Norse eisa (“to race forward”), Ancient Greek ἱερός (hierós, “supernatural, holy”), οἶστρος (oîstros,

parole.significato: Incapable of being recuperated
parole.testo: From Middle English irrecuperable, from Old French.

parole.significato: Nonstandard; not conforming to rules or expectations.
parole.testo: From Middle English irreguler, from Old French irreguler, from Medieval Latin or Late Latin irrēgulāris, from in- + regularis, equivalent to ir- + regular.

parole.significato: Not remissible.
parole.testo: From Middle English irremyssible, from Old French irremissible, from Late Latin irremissibilis, from in- + remissus + -ibilis.

parole.significato: An island, usually very small. Compare with islet.
parole.testo: From Middle English ile, yle (with s added, similar to English island), borrowed from Old French ille, idle, isle, from Latin insula. Not related to island. Doublet of insula.

parole.significato: The action or an instance of flowing or coming out, an outflow
parole.testo: From Middle English issue, from Old French issue (“an exit, a way out”), feminine past participle of issir (“to exit”), from Latin exeō (“go out, exit”), from prefix ex- (“out”) + eō (“go”). parole.significato: Made of ivory.
parole.testo: From Old French ivorin, ivoirin, from ivoire (“ivory”); later also from ivory + -ine.

parole.significato: A translucent, reddish type of zircon used as a gemstone; a hyacinth.
parole.testo: From Middle English jacynct, partly from Old French jacincte, and partly from Old English iacinþ, both from Medieval Latin jacintus, jacinthus, from Latin hyacinthus, from Ancient Greek ὑάκινθος (huákinthos). Doublet of hyacinth.

parole.significato: A glossy leather calf-covering military boot, commonly associated with German soldiers of the WWII era.
parole.testo: From Old French jaque (“coat of mail”).

parole.significato: Of or related to the Jacobin Club in France.
parole.testo: From Middle English Jacobin, from Old French jacobin, from Latin Jācōbīnus, from Latin Jācōbus (“James, Jacob, etc.”) + -īnus (“-ine: forming adjectives”), from Ancient Greek Ἰάκωβος (Iákōbos), from Biblical Hebrew יַעֲקֹב (Ya'akóv), q.v. In reference to the Dominican Order, from the proximity of th

parole.significato: One who enforces confinement in a jail or prison.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English gayoler, gayler, jayler, from Old French jaiolier, gaiolier, from jaiole. By surface analysis, jail + -er.

parole.significato: Either of the vertical components that form the side of an opening in a wall, such as that of a door frame, window fram…
parole.testo: From Middle English jambe, jaumbe, from Old French jambe (“leg”), from Late Latin gamba (“hock, shank, leg, thigh”), from Ancient Greek καμπή (kampḗ, “turning post, bend or flexure”). Doublet of gam, gamb, gamba, and jambe.

parole.significato: A silver Genovese coin, first used in England in the 14th century.
parole.testo: From Old French Jannes (“Genoa”).

parole.significato: To cause (something) to make a rattling metallic sound.
parole.testo: From Middle English janglen (“to talk excessively, chatter; to talk idly, gossip; to nag; to complain, grumble; to argue, debate; to discuss, talk; to talk indistinctly, jabber; to make a noise or outcry; of a bird: to chatter, twitter”) [and other forms], from Old French jangler (“to chatter, gossi

parole.significato: A joke or quip.
parole.testo: From Middle English japen (“to deceive, play tricks on; act foolishly, joke; have sex with”), of uncertain origin, but perhaps combining Old French japer (“to bark, howl, scream; chatter, gossip”) with gaber (“to mock, deride”). See also gab, Old Occitan japar, jaupar (“to bark, yelp, yap”), related

parole.significato: A technical terminology unique to a particular subject.
parole.testo: From Middle English jargoun, jargon, from Old French jargon, a variant of gargon, gargun (“chatter; talk; language”).

parole.significato: Any bright-coloured kind of chalcedony apart from cornelian.
parole.testo: From Middle English jasper, jaspre, from Old French jaspre, a variant of jaspe (modern French jaspe), from Latin iaspis, from Ancient Greek ἴασπις (íaspis).

parole.significato: To prance; to frolic.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English jouncen, perhaps from Old French jancer (“to jolt, jog”), from North Germanic, related to Swedish ganta (“to sport, romp, jest, play the fool”), from Old Norse ganta(sk), of uncertain origin, possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₂- (“to gape, yawn”). More a

parole.significato: A light spear thrown with the hand and used as a weapon.
parole.testo: From Middle English chafeveleyn, gavelong, from Old French javelline, diminutive of javelot, diminutive of *javel, from Vulgar Latin *gabalus, from Gaulish gabulum (compare Old Irish gabul (“fork”), Welsh gafl), from Proto-Celtic *gablā (“fork, forked branch”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeh₁bʰ-. Th

parole.significato: A coat of defense of Arab origin, made of small plates of metal sewn upon linen or similar, like a brigandine.
parole.testo: From Middle English jessera(u)nt, gessera(u)nt(e), from Old French jazerant, from Old Occitan jazerenc, from Arabic جَزَائِرِيّ (jazāʔiriyy, “Algerian, of Algiers”), derived from الجَزَائِر (al-jazāʔir, “Algiers; Algeria”).

parole.significato: Suspecting rivalry in love; troubled by worries that one might have been replaced in someone's affections; suspicious o…
parole.testo: First attested in 1382. From Middle English jelous, gelous, gelus, from Old French jalous, from Late Latin zelosus, from Ancient Greek ζῆλος (zêlos, “zeal, jealousy”). Doublet of zealous.

parole.significato: A state of being jealous; a jealous attitude.
parole.testo: From Middle English jalousie, from Old French jalousie, equivalent to jealous + -y. Doublet of jalousie. Related also to zeal, zealous. Displaced native Old English æfest and Old English nīþ.

parole.significato: Denim.
parole.testo: From the Middle English Gene (“Genoa”), from the Old French Jannes. Bleu de Gênes (“Genovese blue”) was a blue dye made in Genoa used to tint the denim cloth produced in Nîmes (de Nîmes). Doublet of Genoa and Geneva and distantly related to knee.

parole.significato: To make into jelly.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English gele. Doublet of gelee.

parole.significato: A female ass or donkey; a jenny.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English genet, from Old French genet, from Old Catalan genet or Old Spanish ginete (“small fast horse; light horseman”), from Andalusian Arabic زَنَاتِي (zanātī), the Zenati or Zenata Berbers, known as excellent horse breeders. Doublet of Zenati.

parole.significato: An oversight in pleading, or the acknowledgment of a mistake or oversight.
parole.testo: From Old French j'ai failli (“I have failed”).

parole.significato: To put in jeopardy; to expose to loss or injury
parole.testo: From Middle English juparte, from jupartie (“jeopardy”) and Old French jeu partir.

parole.significato: Describing a charge which appears over, or covers, another charge as well as the field.
parole.testo: From Old French gesant. Doublet of jacent.

parole.significato: An act performed for amusement; a joke.
parole.testo: From Middle English geste (“idle tale”), from Old French geste (“acts, exploits”), from Latin gesta (“acts, deeds”). Doublet of gest.

parole.significato: A hard, black form of coal, sometimes used in jewellery.
parole.testo: From Middle English get, geet, gete, from a northern form of Old French jayet, jaiet, gaiet, from Latin gagātēs, from Ancient Greek Γαγάτης (Gagátēs), from Γάγας (Gágas, “a town and river in Lycia”). Doublet of gagate.

parole.significato: An adherent of Judaism.
parole.testo: From Middle English Jew, Giu, Giw, Ju, from Old French juiu, Giu, gyu, from Latin iūdaeus (“Judean (i.e. Jew)”), from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαῖος (Ioudaîos), from Ἰουδά (Ioudá), Ἰούδας (Ioúdas, “Judah, Judas, Jude”) + -ιος (-ios, suffix forming adjectives), from Biblical Hebrew יְהוּדָה (y'hudá, “male gi

parole.significato: Collectively, personal ornamentation such as rings, necklaces, brooches and bracelets, made of precious metals and some…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English juelrye, from Old French juelerye, equivalent to jewel + -ery.

parole.significato: A female Jew.
parole.testo: From Middle English Jewesse, from Old French juiesse, juise; equivalent to Jew + -ess.

parole.significato: Jewish people considered collectively.
parole.testo: From Middle English Jewery, from Old French juerie. By surface analysis, Jew + -ry.

parole.significato: The mouth, sometimes particularly the tongue, underlip, or tooth.
parole.testo: From Middle English gibbe (“a swelling or protrusion in the body”), from Old French gibbe and/or Medieval Latin gibba (“hump”).

parole.significato: A facetious or insulting remark; a jeer, a taunt.
parole.testo: Uncertain; possibly from Old French giber (“to engage in horseplay; to play roughly in sport”). Compare English jib (“usually of a horse: to stop and refuse to go forward”), Old Norse geipa (“to talk nonsense”). The noun is derived from the verb.

parole.significato: A light, brisk musical movement; a gigue.
parole.testo: Unknown. Derivation from Middle English gyge (“fiddle”), from Old French gigue (“a fiddle”) has been proposed, but the connection and sense development are obscure. The sense “a type of dance” of modern French gigue is borrowed from English.

parole.significato: A hinge.
parole.testo: From Middle English gemow, from Old French gemel, from Latin gemellus (“twin”).

parole.significato: Jovial; exuberant; lighthearted; merry and in high spirits; exhibiting happiness.
parole.testo: From Old French jocond, from Latin iūcundus (“pleasant, agreeable”). Doublet of jucund.

parole.significato: To connect or combine into one; to put together.
parole.testo: From Middle English joinen, joynen, joignen, from Old French joindre, juindre, jungre, from Latin iungō (“join, yoke”, verb), from Proto-Indo-European *yewg- (“to join, unite”). Cognate with Old English iucian, iugian, ġeocian, ġyċċan (“to join; yoke”). More at yoke.

parole.significato: The joining of a litigant to a suit.
parole.testo: Substantivisation of the Old French verb joindre (“to join”), from Latin iungō (“join”).

parole.significato: A maker of wooden furniture or fittings.
parole.testo: From Middle English joynour (“maker of furniture, small boxes, etc.”), from Old French joigneor (“joiner, carpenter”), agent noun from joindre (“to join”), equivalent to join + -er.

parole.significato: United, combined
parole.testo: The noun is from Middle English joynt (attested since the late 13th century), from Old French joint (“joint of the body”) (attested since the 12th century). parole.significato: A joining; a joint.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English joynture, from Old French jointure, from Latin iūnctūra. Doublet of juncture.

parole.significato: A piece of timber or steel laid horizontally, or nearly so, to which the planks of the floor, or the laths or furring s…
parole.testo: From Old French giste, feminine of gist, the past participle of gesir (“to lie down”).

parole.significato: The state of being jolly; jolliness, cheerfulness.
parole.testo: From Middle English jolyfte, from Old French joliveté (“gaiety, cheerfulness; amorous passion; life of pleasure”), from jolif. Equivalent to jolly + -ty.

parole.significato: To bump into or brush against while in motion; to push aside.
parole.testo: Originally justle (“to have sex with”), formed from Middle English jousten, from the Old French joster (“to joust”), from Latin iuxtā (“next to”), from iungō (“join, connect”), equivalent to joust + -le.

parole.significato: A set amount of travelling, seen as a single unit; a discrete trip, a voyage.
parole.testo: From Middle English journe, from Old French jornee, from Vulgar Latin *diurnāta, from Late Latin diurnum, from Latin diurnus, from diēs (“day”). Displaced native Old English fær and Old English faru.

parole.significato: A tradesman who has completed an apprenticeship or equivalent educational path in a trade.
parole.testo: From Middle English jorneman; from journe (from Old French jornee (“a day's work, a journey”)) and mon; equivalent to journey + -man.

parole.significato: A tilting match: a mock combat between two mounted knights or men-at-arms using lances in the lists or enclosed field.
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French jouster (modern French jouter), from Vulgar Latin *juxtō, *iuxtō, *iuxtāre, from Latin iūxta (“close to”). English since the early 14th century.

parole.significato: A feeling of extreme happiness or cheerfulness, especially related to the acquisition or expectation of something good.
parole.testo: The noun is from Middle English joye, borrowed from Old French joie, from Late Latin gaudia, neuter plural (mistaken as feminine singular) of Latin gaudium (“joy”), from gaudēre (“to be glad, rejoice”). parole.significato: Full of joy; happy.
parole.testo: From Middle English joyous, joious, from Old French joieus, from joie + -eus.

parole.significato: A triumphant shouting of great happiness; rejoicing, especially as celebratory outbursts; a feeling of joyous exultatio…
parole.testo: From Old French jubilacion, from Latin iūbilātiō (“a shouting for joy”). Cognate with Spanish jubilación (“retirement”).

parole.significato: A public official whose duty it is to administer the law, especially by presiding over trials and rendering judgments;…
parole.testo: From Middle English juge, jugge, from Old French juge, from Latin iūdex. Displaced native Middle English deme (from Old English dēma (“judge”)) and demere (from Old English dēmere (“judge”)), see also deemer, deemster.

parole.significato: The act of judging.
parole.testo: From Middle English juggement, borrowed from Old French jugement, from Late Latin iūdicāmentum, from Latin iūdicō. Partially displaced doom. By surface analysis, judge + -ment.

parole.significato: To manipulate objects, such as balls, clubs, beanbags, rings, etc. in an artful or artistic manner.
parole.testo: From Middle English jogelen, partly a back-formation of Middle English jogeler (“juggler”), and partly a borrowing from Old French jogler, jongler (“to have fun with someone”), a conflation of Latin joculāri (“to jest; joke”) and Old French jangler (“to regale; entertain; have fun; trifle with; teas

parole.significato: Witchcraft, sorcery; magical trickery, legerdemain.
parole.testo: From Old French juglerie, jouglerie, from jouglere (“juggler”).

parole.significato: A liquid made from plant, especially fruit.
parole.testo: From Middle English jus, juis, from Old French jus, jous, from Latin jūs (“broth, soup, sauce”), from Proto-Indo-European *yéwHs, from *yewH- (“to mix (of meal preparation)”). parole.significato: A refreshing drink flavored with aromatic herbs, especially mint, and sometimes alcohol.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French julep, from Medieval Latin julapium, via Arabic جُلَاب (julāb) from Persian گلاب (golâb, “rosewater”), from گل (“rose”) + آب (“water”).

parole.significato: Factually right, correct; factual.
parole.testo: From Middle English juste, from Old French juste, from Latin iūstus (“just, lawful, rightful, true, due, proper, moderate”), from Proto-Italic *jowestos, related to Latin iūs (“law, right”); ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yew-. parole.significato: The state or characteristic of being just or fair.
parole.testo: From Middle English justice, from Old French justise, justice (Modern French justice), from Latin iūstitia (“righteousness, equity”), from iūstus (“just”), from iūs (“right”), from Proto-Italic *jowos, perhaps literally "sacred formula", a word peculiar to Latin (not general Italic) that originated

parole.significato: To provide an acceptable explanation for.
parole.testo: From Middle English justifien, from Old French justifier, from Late Latin justificare (“make just”), from Latin justus, iustus (“just”) + ficare (“make”), from facere, equivalent to just + -ify.

parole.significato: The gutter at the edge of a street; a surface drain.
parole.testo: From Middle English canel, from Old French canel, from Latin canālis (“channel; canal”), from Latin canna (“reed, cane”), from Ancient Greek κάννα (kánna, “reed”), from Akkadian 𒄀 (qanû, “reed”), from Sumerian 𒄀𒈾 (gi.na). Cognate with English channel, canal.

parole.significato: Weights (often scrap or pig iron) used as permanent ballast on ships.
parole.testo: From Old French quintelage (“ballast”).

parole.significato: A bandana.
parole.testo: From Middle English kevercher, kercher, from Old French cuevrechier.

parole.significato: A piece of cloth used to cover the head; a bandana.
parole.testo: From Middle English keverchef, coverchef et al., from Old French couvrechief, from couvrir (“to cover”) + chief (“head”). Compare curfew.

parole.significato: A ruler over various Turkic and Mongol peoples in the Middle Ages.
parole.testo: Via late Middle English can, chan from Old French chan, from Medieval Latin chanis, from Turkic *qan, contraction of *qaɣan.
