parole.significato: A small ticket or sign giving information about something to which it is attached or intended to be attached.
parole.testo: From Middle English label (“narrow band, strip of cloth”), from Old French label, lambel (Modern French lambeau), from Frankish *lappā (“torn piece of cloth”), from Proto-Germanic *lappǭ, *lappô (“cloth stuff, rag, scraps, flap, dewlap, lobe, rabbit ear”), from Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“blade”). C

parole.significato: Requiring much physical effort; toilsome.
parole.testo: From Old French laborios, from Latin laboriosus. By surface analysis, labor + -ious

parole.significato: An effort expended on a particular task; toil, work.
parole.testo: From Middle English labor, labour, labur, from Old French labor (modern labeur) and its etymon, Latin labor.

parole.significato: To toil, to work.
parole.testo: From Middle English labouren, from Old French laborer, from Latin laborare (“(intransitive) to labor, strive, exert oneself, suffer, be in distress, (transitive) to work out, elaborate”), from labor (“labor, toil, work, exertion”); perhaps remotely akin to robur (“strength”). Displaced native Englis

parole.significato: A light fabric containing patterns of holes, usually built up from a single thread.
parole.testo: From Middle English lace, laace, las, from Old French las, from Vulgar Latin *laceum, based on Latin laqueus. Doublet of lasso.

parole.significato: To fasten (something) with laces.
parole.testo: From Middle English lacen, lasen, from Old French lacer, lacier, lasser, lachier, from the noun (see above).

parole.significato: Goods or materials found or left on the sea floor, attached to a floating marker that indicates ownership.
parole.testo: Per Littré, from Old French lagan, from Medieval Latin laga maris (“law of the sea”), from Old Norse lǫg (“law”) and Latin maris (“of the sea”)

parole.significato: A mostly North European medieval form of lyrical, narrative poem written in octosyllabic couplets that often deals with…
parole.testo: From Middle English lai, lay, from Old French lai (“song, lyric, poem”), from Old Frankish *laik, *laih (“play, melody, song”), from Proto-Germanic *laikaz, *laikiz (“jump, play, dance, hymn”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyg- (“to jump, spring, play”). Akin to Old High German leih (“a play, skit, me

parole.significato: A device that generates light, heat, or other electromagnetic radiation. Especially an electric light bulb.
parole.testo: From Middle English laumpe, lampe, from Old French lampe (“lamp, light”), from Latin lampas (“torch, lamp, light”), from Ancient Greek λαμπάς (lampás, “torch, lamp, beacon, light, meteor”), from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂p- (“to shine”). Cognate with Lithuanian lópė (“light”), Welsh llachar (“bright”

parole.significato: European river lamprey (Lampetra fluviatilis).
parole.testo: From Middle English laumproun, adopted from Old French lampreon, diminutive of lampreie (“lamprey”).

parole.testo: From Middle English laumprei, from Old French lampreie (modern French lamproie), from Medieval Latin lampreda, possibly alteration of Late Latin lampetra (“lamprey”), whose further origin is unknown, though it is traditionally thought to be a combination of lambō (“to lick, lap”) + petra (“stone, ro

parole.significato: A weapon of war, consisting of a long shaft or handle and a steel blade or head; a spear carried by horsemen.
parole.testo: From Middle English launce, from Old French lance, from Latin lancea.

parole.significato: A type of spear, javelin or lance.
parole.testo: From Middle English launcegay, from Old French lancegaye, from lance (“lance”) + zagaye (“assagai”).

parole.significato: A sharp, pointed, two-edged surgical instrument used in venesection and for opening abscesses etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English launcet, from Old French lancete, a diminutive of lance. By surface analysis, lance + -et.

parole.significato: A body of words, and set of methods of combining them (called a grammar), understood by a community and used as a form…
parole.testo: From Middle English langage, language, from Old French language, from Vulgar Latin *linguāticum, from Latin lingua (“tongue, speech, language”), from Old Latin dingua (“tongue”), from Proto-Indo-European *dn̥ǵʰwéh₂s (“tongue, speech, language”). parole.significato: A tongue-shaped implement, specifically:
parole.testo: From Old French languete (modern French languette), diminutive of langue (“tongue”), from Latin lingua.

parole.significato: Alternative form of languet.
parole.testo: From Old French languete (modern French languette), diminutive of langue (“tongue”), from Latin lingua. By surface analysis, Old French langue + -ette.

parole.significato: A leather thong.
parole.testo: From late Middle English lainer, lainere, lanyer, from Old French laniere, lasniere (“thong, lash”) (see modern French lanière (“lanyard, strap”)).

parole.significato: A case of translucent or transparent material made to protect a flame, or light, used to illuminate its surroundings.
parole.testo: From Middle English lanterne (13th century), via Old French lanterne from Latin lanterna (“lantern”), itself a corruption of Ancient Greek λαμπτήρ (lamptḗr, “torch”) (see lamp, λάμπω (lámpō)) by influence of Latin lucerna (“lamp”). The spelling lanthorn was current during the 16th to 19th centuries

parole.significato: A short rope used for fastening rigging, as a handle, etc.
parole.testo: From late Middle English lainer, lainere, lanyer (“strap or thong used to fasten armour”) (with the ending modified in the 17th century under the influence of yard), from Old French laniere, lasniere (“thong, lash”) (see modern French lanière (“lanyard, strap”)). The French word is ultimately from G

parole.significato: Fat from the abdomen of a pig, especially as prepared for use in cooking or pharmacy.
parole.testo: From Middle English lard, from Old French lard (“bacon”), from Latin lārdum, lāridum (“bacon fat”).

parole.significato: To stuff (meat) with bacon or pork before cooking.
parole.testo: From Middle English larden, from Old French larder and Medieval Latin lārdō.

parole.significato: Meat strips used for larding, especially salted pork.
parole.testo: From Middle English lardon, lardun, from Old French lardon.

parole.significato: Of considerable or relatively great size or extent.
parole.testo: From Middle English large, from Old French large, from Latin larga, feminine of largus (“abundant, plentiful, copious, large, much”), of uncertain ultimate origin; see there for more. parole.significato: Remiss, lax.
parole.testo: From Old French lasche (French lâche).

parole.significato: A small lever action crossbow with the cocking lever built into the top of the stock and a top mounted trigger.
parole.testo: From Middle English lachet, from Old French lachet, variant of lacet, diminutive of laz (“lace”).

parole.significato: Existing or present, but concealed or inactive.
parole.testo: From Middle English latent, latente, from Old French latent, from Latin latēns, present participle of lateō (“lie hidden”).

parole.significato: Synonym of interpreter.
parole.testo: From Old French latimier, latinier (“interpreter”), etc. and directly from Vulgar Latin latimarus, from Latin latinarius (“interpreter, speaker of Latin”), from lingua Latina + -arius (“-ary”). Equivalent to Latin + -er and compare Latiner.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Latin: the language spoken in ancient Rome and other cities of Latium.
parole.testo: From Middle English Latyn, Latyne, Latin, from Old French latin, latyn, from Latin latīnus, from Latium (“the region around Rome”) + -īnus (adjective suffix). Displaced or merged with Old English Lǣden. Doublet of Ladin and Ladino.

parole.significato: The angular distance north or south from a planet's equator, measured along the meridian of that particular point.
parole.testo: Borrowed into Middle English from Old French latitude, from Latin lātitūdō (“breadth, width, latitude”), from lātus (“broad, wide”), from older stlātus. Possibly related with lateral, though this is uncertain.

parole.significato: An alloy of copper and tin, similar to bronze, with a sufficient portion of tin to make it a pewter-like color with yel…
parole.testo: From Middle English laten, latun, latoun, from Old French laton, laiton, from Arabic لَاطُون (lāṭūn, “copper, copper alloy”), itself from Proto-Common Turkic *altun (“gold”). See Turkish altın, Old Turkic 𐰞𐱃𐰆𐰣 (altun, “gold”), Karakhanid اَلْتُونْ (altūn, “gold”).

parole.significato: Glorification or praise.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English lauden, from Old French lauder, from Latin laudō, laudāre, from laus (“praise, glory, fame, renown”), from echoic Proto-Indo-European root *leh₁wdʰ- (“song, sound”). Cognate with Old English lēoþ (“song, poem”), German Lied (“song”). Doublet of leed.

parole.significato: Worthy of being lauded.
parole.testo: From Middle English laudable, from Old French laudable or directly from Latin laudabilis; equivalent to laud + -able.

parole.significato: To throw (a projectile such as a lance, dart or ball); to hurl; to propel with force.
parole.testo: From Middle English launchen (“to throw as a lance”), Old French lanchier, another form (Old Northern French/Norman variant, compare Jèrriais lanchi) of lancier, French lancer, from lance.

parole.significato: A grassy plain or pasture, especially surrounded by woodland; a glade.
parole.testo: From Middle English launde, from Old French launde (“wooded area”) (French lande), of Germanic or Gaulish origin, from Proto-Germanic *landą (“land”) or Proto-Celtic *landā, both from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“land, heath”). Doublet of land.

parole.significato: A washerwoman or washerman.
parole.testo: Contracted from Middle English lavender, from Old French lavandiere, from Late Latin lavandera, from Latin lavō (“to wash”).

parole.significato: A laundering; a washing.
parole.testo: From Middle English lavendrie, from Old French lavanderie, from Latin lavandaria. See launder.

parole.significato: To bathe or wash (someone or something).
parole.testo: The verb is derived from Middle English laven (“to bathe, wash; to bail or draw water, drain, exhaust; to dampen, wet; to pour; of water, etc.: to flow, stream”), and then partly: * from Old French laver (“to be washed; to wash”) (modern French laver (“to wash (oneself)”)), from Latin lavāre, the pr

parole.significato: Any of a group of European plants, genus, Lavandula, of the mint family.
parole.testo: From Middle English lavendre, from Anglo-Norman lavendre (French lavande), from Medieval Latin lavendula, possibly from Latin lividus (“bluish”), but influenced by lavō (“to wash”) due to the use of lavender in washing clothes.

parole.significato: Where one laves, a washroom, particularly a lavatorium, the washing area in a monastery.
parole.testo: From Middle English laver, lavour, from Old French laveoir, laveor, laveour, lavor, lavur, from Latin lavātōrium. Doublet of lavatorium and lavatory.

parole.significato: Expending or bestowing profusely; profuse; prodigal.
parole.testo: From Middle English laves, lavas, lavage (“extravagant, wasteful, prodigal”), from lavas (“excessive abundance”), from Old French lavasse, lavache (“torrent of rain”); possibly later conflated in some senses by Middle English laven (“to pour out”), equivalent to lave + -ish. Compare Scots lawage, la

parole.significato: Ground (generally in front of or around a house) covered with grass kept closely mown.
parole.testo: Early Modern English laune (“turf, grassy area”), alteration of laund (“glade”), from Middle English launde, from Old French lande (“heath, moor”), of Germanic or Gaulish origin, from Proto-Germanic *landą (“land”) or Proto-Celtic *landā, both from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“land, heath”). Akin t

parole.significato: Not belonging to the clergy, but associated with them.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English lay, from Old French lai, from Latin lāicus, from Ancient Greek λαϊκός (laïkós). Doublet of laic.

parole.significato: A ballad or sung poem; a short poem or narrative, usually intended to be sung.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English lay, from Old French lai (“song, lyric, poem”), from Frankish *laih (“play, melody, song”), from Proto-Germanic *laikaz, *laikiz (“jump, play, dance, hymn”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyg- (“to jump, spring, play”). Akin to Old High German leih (“a play, skit, melody,

parole.significato: A law.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English lay, lai, laye, ley, lei, borrowed from Old French lei (“law”). Possibly also from or influenced by the etymologically unrelated Middle English lawe (“law”) (with variants including laige, laiȝh, læȝe), from Old English lagu (“law”). More at law.

parole.significato: Synonym of leper: a person suffering from Hansen's disease; a person suffering any contagious disease requiring similar…
parole.testo: From Middle English lazare, from Old French lazare, from Medieval Latin lazarus (“leper”), an antonomasia from Lazarus, from Koine Greek Λᾱ́ζᾱρος (Lā́zāros), the given name of the Biblical figure found in Luke 16, from Hebrew אֶלְעָזָר (“Eleazar”), a given name shared by various figures in the Hebre

parole.significato: Next to, near (still used in some place names).
parole.testo: borrowed from Old French lez (“side”).

parole.significato: Any agent used to make dough rise or to have a similar effect on baked goods.
parole.testo: From Middle English levayn, borrowed from Old French levain, from Vulgar Latin *levāmen, a noun based on Latin levō (“raise”).

parole.significato: A lecherous person: someone given to excessive sexual activity or debauchery.
parole.testo: From Middle English lechour, from Old French lecheor (“glutton, sensualist, libertine”) , from Old French lecher, lechier, lekier, lescher (“to lick, live in gluttony or sensuality”), from Old Frankish *likkōn (“to lick”), from Proto-Germanic *likkōną (“to lick”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵʰ- (“

parole.significato: Given to excessive sexual activity and debauchery.
parole.testo: From Middle English lecherous, licherous, from Old French *lecherous (attested in Old French lecherousement (“lecherously”)), from Old French lecherie, licherie (“gluttony, sensuality, lewdness, lechery”), from Old French lecher, lechier, lekier, lescher (“to lick, live in gluttony or sensuality”),

parole.significato: Inordinate indulgence in sexual activity.
parole.testo: From Old French and Anglo-Norman lecherie. See lecher.

parole.significato: A stand with a slanted top used to support a Bible from which passages are read during a church service.
parole.testo: 15th century partial re-Latinization of early 14th century Middle English lettorne, lettron, from Old French leitrun, from Medieval Latin lectrinum, from Late Latin lectrum, from lectus (from whence also lecture), form of Latin legō (“to read”).

parole.significato: The act of reading.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French lection, from Latin lēctiōnem, form of lēctiō, from legō (“to read; to gather”). Doublet of lesson.

parole.significato: The sediment that settles during fermentation of beverages, consisting of dead yeast and precipitated parts of the frui…
parole.testo: From Old French lies, from Medieval Latin lias (“lees, dregs”) (descent via winemaking common in monasteries), from Gaulish *ligyā, *legyā (“silt, sediment”) (compare Welsh llai, Old Breton leh (“deposit, silt”)), from Proto-Celtic *legyā (“layer”), from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ- (“to lie (down)”).

parole.significato: Money or property bequeathed to someone in a will.
parole.testo: From Middle English legacie, from Old French legacie and Medieval Latin lēgātia, from Latin lēgātum. Compare legatee. The boardgame sense was coined by game designer Rob Daviau in 2011 with the game Risk Legacy.

parole.significato: A deputy representing the pope, specifically a papal ambassador sent on special ecclesiastical missions.
parole.testo: Inherited from Old English legat(e), from Old French legat, from Latin lēgātus, substantivized from the perfect passive participle of lēgō (“to bequeath, send as envoy”).

parole.significato: The life story of a saint (such stories are often embellished, but any kind is called a legend).
parole.testo: From Middle English legende, from Old French legende, from Medieval Latin legenda (“a legend, story, especially the lives of the saints”), from Latin legenda (“things which ought to be read”), from lego (“to read”).

parole.significato: Sleight of hand; "magic" trickery.
parole.testo: From Middle English legerdemeyn, lechardemane, from Old French léger de main (literally “light of hand”), a phrase that meant “dexterous, skillful at fooling others (especially through sleights of hand)”, which was however treated as a noun when it was borrowed by late Middle English. The Modern Fre

parole.significato: Numerous; vast; very great in number.
parole.testo: Attested (in Middle English, as legioun) around 1200, from Old French legion, from Latin legiō, legionem, from legō (“to gather, collect”); akin to legend, lecture. Doublet of León, which was borrowed from Spanish. Generalized sense of “a large number” is due to an allusive phrase in Mark 5:9, "My n

parole.significato: A yellowish citrus fruit.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English lymon, from Old French lymon (“citrus”), from Arabic لَيْمُون (laymūn) or Classical Persian لِیمُون (līmūn), a variant of Classical Persian لِیمُو (līmū, līmō), from Sanskrit निम्बू (nimbū, “lime”), ultimately from Proto-Malayo-Polynesian *limaw or Munda. Doublet of lim

parole.significato: Any of several plants of the genus Lens, especially Lens culinaris, from southwest Asia, that have edible, lens-shaped…
parole.testo: From Middle English lentile, from Old French lentille from Latin lenticula, diminutive of lēns, from a pre-Indo-European substrate source shared by German Linse, Ancient Greek λάθυρος (láthuros) and Lithuanian lęšis. Doublet of lenticula.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of a lion; lionlike.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English leonin, leonine (“characteristic of a lion, lionlike”), from Old French leonin, and from its etymon Latin leōnīnus (“of or pertaining to a lion”), from leō (“lion”) (from Ancient Greek λέων (léōn, “lion”); further etymology uncertain) + -īnus (suffix meaning ‘of or pertainin

parole.significato: A large wild cat with a spotted coat native to Africa and Asia (Panthera pardus).
parole.testo: From Middle English leopard, leopart, lepard, leperd, from Old French leopard (“leopard”), from Late Latin leopardus (“leopon, lipard”) from late Ancient Greek λεόπαρδος (leópardos, “leopon, lipard”), from λέων (léōn, “lion”) + πάρδος (párdos, “pard, male leopard”), from earlier πάρδαλις (párdalis,

parole.significato: A person who has leprosy, a person suffering from Hansen's disease.
parole.testo: From Middle English lepre, leprosy, from Old French [Term?], from Latin leprae, lepra, from Ancient Greek λέπρα (lépra).

parole.significato: A wound or injury.
parole.testo: From Middle English lesioun (“physical injuring of the body”), from Old French lesion (“hurt, offense, wrong, injury, wound”), from Latin laesiō (“hurt, harm, injury”) (whence -ion (“noun suffix denoting action, result, process, state, condition”)), from laesus (“hurt, injured, wounded, damaged”), p

parole.significato: To instruct to teach.
parole.testo: From Middle English lessoun, from Old French leçon, from Latin lēctiō, lēctiōnem (“a reading”), from legō (“to read; to gather”). Doublet of lection.

parole.significato: To print, inscribe, or paint letters on something.
parole.testo: From Middle English letter, lettre, from Old French letre, from Latin littera (“letter of the alphabet"; in plural, "epistle”). Displaced Old English bōcstæf (literally “book staff”) in sense 1 and ǣrendġewrit (literally “message writing”) in sense 2.

parole.significato: An edible plant, Lactuca sativa and its close relatives, having a head of green or purple leaves.
parole.testo: From Middle English letuse, of uncertain precise origin, probably from the plural form Old French laitues, derived from Latin lactūca (“lettuce”), from lac (“milk”), because of the milky fluid in its stalks. Replaced Old English lēahtric. (money): Likely from the green color of US banknotes.

parole.significato: The same height at all places; parallel to a flat ground.
parole.testo: From Middle English level, from Old French livel, liveau m, later nivel, niveau, from Latin libella f (“a balance, a level”), diminutive of libra f (“a balance, a level”); see libra, librate. Doublet of libella and niveau. The verb is from Middle English levelen, from the noun.

parole.significato: A rigid piece which is capable of turning about one point, or axis (fulcrum), and in which are two or more other points…
parole.testo: From Middle English lever, levore, levour, from Old French leveor, leveur (“a lifter, lever (also Old French and French levier)”), from Latin levātor (“a lifter”), from levō (“to raise”). Doublet of levator.

parole.significato: A young hare less than one year old.
parole.testo: From Middle English leveret(te), from Old French leveret, diminutive of lievre (“hare”), from Latin leporem, of obscure origin.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: A cramp iron inserted into a cavity in order to lift heavy stones; used as a symbol of strength in Freemasonry.
parole.testo: From Middle English lewis, of uncertain origin. Possibly from Old French lous, plural of lou, loup (“the name of a kind of siege engine”, literally “wolf”); or related to clevis.

parole.significato: Bound or obliged in law or equity; responsible; answerable.
parole.testo: From Old French lier (“to bind”), from Latin ligō, ligāre (“to bind, to tie”). Compare typologically Russian обя́занный (objázannyj), обяза́тельный (objazátelʹnyj) (akin to вяза́ть (vjazátʹ)).

parole.significato: Union; alliance.
parole.testo: Compare Old French liage (“a bond”). See liable.

parole.significato: A written or pictorial false statement which unjustly seeks to damage someone's reputation.
parole.testo: From Middle English libel, from Old French libelle, from Latin libellus (“petition”, literally “booklet”). Doublet of libelle.

parole.significato: Generous; permitting liberty; willing to give unsparingly.
parole.testo: The adjective is from Old French liberal, from Latin līberālis (“befitting a freeman”), from līber (“free”); it is attested since the 14th century. The noun is first attested in the 1800s.

parole.significato: The property of being liberal; generosity; charity.
parole.testo: From Middle English liberalite, from Old French liberalité, from Latin līberālitās (“a noble, kind, or friendly disposition; generosity”), equivalent to liberal + -ity.

parole.significato: The condition of being free.
parole.testo: From Middle English liberte, from Old French liberté, from Latin libertas (“freedom”), from liber (“free”); see liberal.

parole.significato: To authorize officially.
parole.testo: From Middle English licencen, licensen, lisensen, licent, from Old French licencer, licencier, licenciier, licenser, from Medieval Latin licentiō (cf. English licentiate).

parole.significato: A plant of species Glycyrrhiza glabra, or sometimes in North America, the related American licorice plant Glycyrrhiza l…
parole.testo: From Middle English lycorys, from Old French licoresse, from Late Latin liquiritia, alteration of Ancient Greek γλυκύρριζα (glukúrrhiza): γλυκύς (glukús, “sweet”) + ῥίζα (rhíza, “root”) (English glucose, English rhizome). Doublet of glycyrrhiza.

parole.significato: An estate in land which is given by a grantor to a party only for the duration of the life of a third party, and for wh…
parole.testo: From life estate + Old French pur ("for"), autre ("another"), vie ("life").

parole.significato: An allegiance.
parole.testo: From Middle English legiaunce, from Old French ligeance, legeance, ligance; equivalent to liege + -ance; compare allegiance.

parole.significato: Being a fixed limit game.
parole.testo: From Middle English limit, from Old French limit, from oblique stem of Latin līmes, līmit- (“a cross-path or balk between fields, hence a boundary, boundary line or wall, any path or road, border, limit”). Displaced native Old English ġemǣre. Doublet of limes.

parole.significato: To restrict; to circumscribe; not to allow to go beyond a certain bound, to set boundaries.
parole.testo: From Middle English limiten, from Old French limiter, from Latin līmitō (“to bound, limit, fix, determine”), from līmes; see noun.

parole.significato: To draw or paint; to delineate.
parole.testo: From Middle English limnen, limyne, lymm, lymn, lymne (“to illuminate (a manuscript)”), a variant of luminen (“to illuminate (a manuscript)”), short form of enluminen (“to shed light on, illuminate; to enlighten; to make bright or clear; to give colour to; to illuminate (a manuscript); to depict, de

parole.significato: Descent in a line from a common progenitor; progeny; descending line of offspring or ascending line of parentage.
parole.testo: From Middle English linage, from Old French linage, from ligne, from Latin linea (“line”); equivalent to line + -age.

parole.significato: Pertaining to lines; consisting of lines.
parole.testo: From Old French lineal, from Latin līneālis, from līnea (“a line”) + -ālis (adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, line + -al. Doublet of linear.

parole.significato: A small passerine bird, the common linnet (Linaria cannabina syn. Carduelis cannabina), in the finch family Fringillida…
parole.testo: From Old French linette, from lin (“flax”), from the bird's fondness for the seeds of flax, the source of linen and Old English līnete, līnetwige (“linnet”) (> dialectal English lintwhite).

parole.significato: Clinging fuzzy fluff that clings to fabric or accumulates in one's pockets or navel etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English lynet, linet, from Old French linette (“grain of flax”), diminutive of lin (“flax”); or, from Medieval Latin linteum, from Latin līnum (“flax”).

parole.significato: A horizontal structural beam spanning an opening, such as between the uprights of a door or a window, and which support…
parole.testo: From Middle English lyntel, from Old French lintel, from Vulgar Latin *līntellus, for *līmitellus, diminutive noun from līmes. Equivalent to limit + -el.

parole.significato: A big cat, Panthera leo, native to Africa, India and formerly much of Europe.
parole.testo: From Middle English lyoun, lion, leon, borrowed from Old French lion, from Latin leō, (accusative: leōnem), from Ancient Greek λέων (léōn), of unclear origin. Doublet of Leo, leu, lev, and Lyon. Displaced Old English lēo, from the same Latin source.

parole.significato: lion cub
parole.testo: From Old French [Term?], diminutive of lion.

parole.significato: A female lion (animal).
parole.testo: From Middle English leonesse, lyonesse, from Old French leonesse, lionesse; equivalent to lion + -ess.

parole.significato: A substance that is flowing, and keeping no shape, such as water; a substance of which the molecules, while not tending…
parole.testo: From Middle English liquide, from Old French liquide, from Latin liquidus (“fluid, liquid, moist”), from liqueō (“to be liquid, be fluid”). Doublet of liquidus. As a term for a consonant, it comes from Latin liquida (cōnsōnāns), a calque of Ancient Greek ὑγρὸν (σύμφωνον) (hugròn (súmphōnon), “liquid

parole.significato: A pendent part of the old clerical tippet.
parole.testo: From Old French liripipion, liripion, Latin liripipium. Said to be corrupted from cleri ephippium (“the clergy's caparison”).

parole.significato: A strip of fabric, especially from the edge of a piece of cloth.
parole.testo: From Middle English lī̆st, lī̆ste (“band, stripe; hem, selvage; border, edge, rim; list, specification; barriers enclosing area for jousting, etc.”), from Old English līste (“hem, edge, strip”), or Old French liste, listre (“border; band; strip of paper; list”), or Medieval Latin lista, all from Pro

parole.significato: A ritual liturgical prayer in which a series of prayers recited by a leader are alternated with responses from the cong…
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French letanie, from Latin litania, from Ancient Greek λιτανεία (litaneía, “prayer”), from λιτή (litḗ, “prayer, entreaty”).

parole.significato: In a literal manner; exactly as stated, word for word.
parole.testo: From Middle English litteraly. See literal and letter. By surface analysis, literal + -ly.

parole.significato: The body of all written works.
parole.testo: From Middle English literature, from Old French littérature, from Latin literatura or litteratura, from littera (“letter”), from Etruscan, from Ancient Greek διφθέρᾱ (diphthérā, “tablet”). Displaced native Old English bōccræft, literally "book + -craft", see Modern English bookcraft.

parole.significato: lead monoxide (PbO) a toxic solid formed from oxidation of lead in air, and used as a pigment.
parole.testo: From Middle English litarge, from Old French litarge, from Latin lithargyrus, from Ancient Greek λιθάργυρος (lithárguros), from λίθος (líthos, “stone”) + αργυρός (argurós, “silver”).

parole.significato: A bottom-feeding freshwater fish in the superfamily or suborder Cobitoidea.
parole.testo: From Middle English loche, from Old French loche, further origin uncertain, possibly from Vulgar Latin *laukka (“loach”), which could be from Gaulish *leuca (“loach, slug”), also attested as the feminine name Leuca, from leux (“bright, light”), a reference to slugs' bright appearance, the fish later

parole.significato: To be firmly fixed in a specified position.
parole.testo: From Middle English logge, from Old French loge (“an arbour, a covered walk-way”). See also Medieval Latin lobia, laubia; also Old High German louba (“a porch, a gallery”) (German Laube (“bower, arbor”)), Old High German loub (“leaf, foliage”), Old English lēaf (“leaf, foliage”). Doublet of loggia a

parole.significato: Logical.
parole.testo: From Middle English logike, from Old French and Latin logicus, from Ancient Greek λογῐκός (logĭkós). Displaced native Old English flitcræftlīċ.

parole.significato: A method of human thought that involves thinking in a linear, step-by-step manner about how a problem can be solved. Lo…
parole.testo: From Middle English logik, from Old French logike, from Latin logica, from Ancient Greek λογική (logikḗ, “logic”), from feminine of λογικός (logikós, “of or pertaining to speech or reason or reasoning, rational, reasonable”), from λόγος (lógos, “speech, reason”). Displaced native Old English flitcræ

parole.significato: A person who studies or teaches logic.
parole.testo: From Middle English logicien, logissian, from Old French logicien. Equivalent to logic + -ian.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: The part of the body (of humans and quadrupeds) at each side of the backbone, between the ribs and hips.
parole.testo: From Middle English loyne, from Old French loigne, from Vulgar Latin *lumbea, from Latin lumbus, of uncertain origin, possibly from Oscan-Umbrian *londwo- or Proto-Germanic *lundwuz, both ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“kidney, waist”). Cognate with Modern English lend (“loin”), Dutch

parole.significato: A member of a Germanic people who invaded Italy in the 6th century.
parole.testo: From Middle English Lombard, Lumbard, borrowed from Old French Lombard, Lombart (“a Lombard”), from Late Latin langobardus, longobardus (“a Lombard”), from Germanic, derived from the Proto-Germanic *langabardaz from elements *langaz + *bardaz; equivalent to long + beard. Some sources derive the seco

parole.significato: Angular distance measured west or east of the prime meridian.
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French longitude, from Latin longitūdō (“length, a measured length”), from longus (“long”).

parole.significato: Praise; fame; reputation.
parole.testo: From Middle English loos, lōs (“reputation, renown, fame, infamy, rumor, news”), from Old French los, from Latin laus (“praise, glory, fame, renown”). Doublet of laud.

parole.significato: A person who makes the bits and other metal parts of a horse's bridle, and other small metal pieces.
parole.testo: From Old French lormier, loremier, from Latin loranum (“bridle”), lorum (“thong, the rein of a bridle”).

parole.significato: A flatterer or deceiver.
parole.testo: From Middle English losengeour, losenger, from Old French losengier, losengeor (“flatterer”), from Old French losengier (“to deceive, flatter”), from Old French losenge (“flattery”), from Frankish *lausungu (“deception, flattery”). Doublet of leasing ("lying, falsehood").

parole.significato: A type of turret on the roof of certain medieval buildings designed to allow ventilation or the admission of light.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English lover, from Old French lovier, lover (“skylight”), from Medieval Latin *lōdārium (attested as lōvārium), extension of lōdium, of unclear origin, but probably of Germanic origin and related to Frankish *laubijā (“shelter”). Compare Old Norse ljóri.

parole.significato: The state of being loyal; fidelity.
parole.testo: From Middle English loialte, borrowed from Old French loialte, loiauté (Modern loyauté) from loial + -té, equivalent to loyal + -ty.

parole.significato: A thin rhombus, having two acute and two obtuse angles.
parole.testo: From Middle English losenge, from Old French losenge (“rhombus”), of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: A clumsy or lazy person.
parole.testo: From Middle English, perhaps from Old French lobeor (“swindler”), from Old French lober to mock, to jeer, or of Scandinavian origin, compare dialectal Swedish lubber. The grasshopper was likely so called after sense 1 (“a clumsy or lazy person”).

parole.significato: The pike, Esox lucius, when fully grown.
parole.testo: From Old French lus, luis, from Latin lūcius.

parole.significato: A device for making braided cord.
parole.testo: From Middle English lucet (“heraldic representation of a pike fish”), from Old French lucet (“small pike”), from Old French lus + -et, from Latin lucius (“pike fish”).

parole.significato: Money, riches, or wealth, especially when seen as having a corrupting effect or causing greed, or obtained in an underh…
parole.testo: From Middle English lūcre, lucor, lucour, lucur (“gain in money, profit; money; wages; illicit gain; advantage, benefit”), from Old French lucre or Latin lucrum (“advantage, profit; love of gain, avarice”), from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂w- (“gain, profit”) + *-tlom (variant of *-trom (suffix forming

parole.significato: The drug LSD.
parole.testo: From Middle English Lucy, from Old French Lucie (notably after the Christian martyr Lucia of Syracuse), from Latin Lucia (feminine of Lucius, a Roman praenomen), from lux (“light”). The name of the Australopithecus skeleton came from the Beatles song “Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds”, which was being

parole.significato: The vertical edge of a sail that is closest to the direction of the wind.
parole.testo: From Old French lof. Collins English Dictionary states that this word is ultimately derived from Middle Dutch loef. Ellert Ekwall's Shakspere's Vocabulary: its etymological elements (1903) related this verb and loof instead to the East Frisian verb lofen, lufen, which would make it cognate to the Fr

parole.significato: One who is an inspiration to others; one who has achieved success in one's chosen field; a leading light.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English lūminārī, lūminārīe (“lamp; source of spiritual light, example of holiness; glory”), borrowed from Old French luminarie (“lamp, lights, lighting; candles; brightness, illumination”), variant of luminaire (“light fixture”) (modern French luminaire), from Medieval Latin lūminā

parole.significato: To illuminate.
parole.testo: From Middle English lūminen, clipping of enlūminen, from Old French enluminer, from Latin illūminō, from lūminō, from lūmen.

parole.significato: An insane person.
parole.testo: From Middle English lunatik, from Old French lunatique, from Late Latin lunaticus (“moonstruck”), derived from Latin luna (“moon”), the connection stemming from the belief that changes of the moon caused intermittent insanity.

parole.significato: A lingerer, lanky person, or dullard.
parole.testo: Old French longis. See lounge.

parole.significato: Any member of the genus Lupinus in the family Fabaceae.
parole.testo: From Middle English lupyne, lupine, from Old French lupin, from Latin lupīnus (“pertaining to the wolf”), because of the wolf-like “fang” within the blossom. It has also been linked to an assumed depletion of nutrients in the soil.

parole.significato: To swallow or eat greedily; to devour; hence, to swallow up.
parole.testo: From Middle English *lurchen (recorded only in Middle English lurcare, lurcard (“glutton”)), from Old French *lurcher, from Latin lurcō (“eat greedily, guzzle”), of uncertain origin. Compare Middle High German slurken (“to slurp”) (whence German schlurken).

parole.significato: A predicament or difficult situation.
parole.testo: From Middle English *lurche (implied in derivative lurching), from Old French lourche (“deceived, embarrassed; also the name of a game”), from Proto-West Germanic *lort (“left; left-handed; crooked; bent; warped; underhanded; deceitful; limping”). Cognate to English lirt.

parole.significato: Chiefly preceded by the.
parole.testo: The noun is derived from fever-lurgy, possibly influenced by or related to lurk (“to hang out or wait”). parole.significato: Thick sticky clay or cement used to close up a hole or gap, especially to make something air-tight.
parole.testo: From Old French lut, ultimately from Latin lutum (“mud”).

parole.significato: Very fine in quality and comfortable.
parole.testo: From Middle English luxurious, from Old French luxurios (modern French luxurieux), from Latin lū̆xuriōsus (“rank, luxuriant, profuse, excessive, immoderate”), from lū̆xuria (“rankness, luxury”), from lū̆xus (“extravagance, luxury”). By surface analysis, luxury + -ous.

parole.significato: Very wealthy and comfortable surroundings; the state of being that they create.
parole.testo: From Middle English luxurie, from Old French luxurie, from Latin luxuria (“rankness, luxury”), from luxus (“extravagance, luxury”).

parole.significato: An ancient stringed musical instrument (a yoke lute chordophone) of Greek origin, consisting of two arms extending from…
parole.testo: From Middle English lire (13th c.), from Old French lire, from Latin lyra, from Ancient Greek λύρᾱ (lúrā, “lyre, a stringed instrument with a sounding-board formed of the shell of a tortoise”). Doublet of lira, lyra, and Lyra.

parole.significato: A heavy fighting club.
parole.testo: From Middle English mace, borrowed from Old French mace, mache, from Vulgar Latin *mattia, *mattea, matia, (compare Italian mazza, Spanish maza), probably from Proto-West Germanic *mattjō (“cutting tool, hoe”).

parole.significato: Certain smaller edible fish, principally true mackerel and Spanish mackerel in family Scombridae, often speckled,
parole.testo: From Middle English mackerell, macrell, macrelle, makarell, makerel, makerell, makerelle, makrel, makrell, makyrelle, from Old French maquerel. Further origin unknown.

parole.significato: A pimp; also, a bawd.
parole.testo: From Middle English makerel, maquerel, from Old French maquerel, from Middle Dutch makelare, makelaer (“broker”) (> makelaar (“broker, peddler”)). See also French maquereau.

parole.significato: A polite form of address for a woman or lady.
parole.testo: From Middle English madame, from Old French madame, from ma (“my”) + dame (“lady”), from post-classical Latin mea domina. Doublet of Madonna.

parole.significato: The application of rituals or actions, especially those based on occult knowledge, to subdue or manipulate natural or s…
parole.testo: From Middle English magik, magyk, from Old French magique (noun and adjective), from Latin magicus (adjective), magica (noun use of feminine form of magicus), from Ancient Greek μαγικός (magikós, “magical”), from μάγος (mágos, “magus”). Ultimately from Old Iranian, probably derived from Proto-Indo-E

parole.significato: grandeur, brilliance, lavishness or splendor
parole.testo: From Middle English magnificence, from Old French magnificence, from Latin magnificentia.

parole.significato: One of several kinds of bird in the family Corvidae, especially Pica pica.
parole.testo: From Mag, a nickname for Margaret that was used to denote a chatterer, + archaic pie (“magpie”), from Middle English pie, pye, from Old French pie, from Latin pīca, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)peyk- (“woodpecker, magpie”). Displaced native Old English agu (“magpie”) and Middle English aguster (“mag

parole.significato: Armour consisting of metal rings linked together.
parole.testo: From Middle English mayle (“mail armor”), borrowed from Old French maille (“loop, stitch”), from Vulgar Latin *macla, from Latin macula (“blemish, mesh”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *smh₁-tleh₂, from *smeh₁- (“smear, rub”). Compare maillot.

parole.significato: To keep up; to preserve; to uphold (a state, condition etc.).
parole.testo: From Middle English mayntenen, from Old French maintenir, from Late Latin manūteneō, manūtenēre (“I support”), from Latin manū (“with/in/by the hand”, ablative of manus) + tenēre (“to hold”).

parole.significato: One who, not being an interested party, maintains a cause depending between others, by furnishing money, etc., to eithe…
parole.testo: Old French mainteneor, French mainteneur.

parole.significato: a term of address for royalty and imperiality
parole.testo: From an alternative capitalization of English majesty, from Middle English maieste, mageste, from Old French majesté, from Latin māiestās, derived from Proto-Indo-European *meǵh₂s (“great”).

parole.significato: The quality of being impressive, great, dignified, powerful, sovereign, or any combination thereof.
parole.testo: From Middle English majeste, mageste, from Old French majesté, from Latin maiestātem, (literally, "the quality of being greater”). Ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *meǵh₂s (“great”) See mega-.

parole.significato: bad, badly
parole.testo: From Old French mal- from Latin male (“badly”), from malus (“bad”).

parole.significato: Any ailment or disease of the body; especially, a lingering or deep-seated disorder.
parole.testo: From Middle English maladie, from Old French maladie (“sickness, illness, disease”), from malade (“ill, sick”), from Latin male habitus (“ill-kept, not in good condition”), 1st century AD. See also malice and habit.

parole.significato: One of the male (masculine) sex or gender.
parole.testo: From Middle English male, borrowed from Old French malle, masle (Modern French mâle), from Latin masculus (“masculine, a male”), diminutive of mās (“male, masculine”). Doublet of macho. Displaced native Old English wǣpned (“male”, literally “weaponed”).

parole.significato: Having or displaying ill will; wishing harm on others.
parole.testo: From Middle English *malevolent (suggested by Middle English malevolence), from Old French malivolent and Latin malevolentem, from male (“badly, wrongly”) + volens (“willing, wishing”), from velle (“to wish”).

parole.significato: Wrongdoing.
parole.testo: From Old French malfaisance, derived from malfaire, maufaire (“to do evil”), from Latin malefaciō (“to do evil”), from male (“evilly”) + faciō (“to do, make”).

parole.significato: Intention to harm or deprive in an illegal or immoral way. Desire to take pleasure in another's misfortune.
parole.testo: From Middle English malice, borrowed from Old French malice, from Latin malitia (“badness, bad quality, ill-will, spite”), from malus (“bad”).

parole.significato: Intending to do harm; characterized by spite and malice.
parole.testo: From Middle English malicious, from Old French malicios, from Latin malitiōsus, from malitia (“malice”), from malus (“bad”). Displaced native Middle English ivelwilled and ivelwilly (“malicious”), related to Old English yfelwillende (literally “evil-willing”). By surface analysis, malice + -ious.

parole.significato: Evil or malignant in disposition, nature, intent or influence.
parole.testo: From Middle English maligne, from Old French maligne, from Latin malignus, from malus (“bad”) + genus (“sort, kind”). Compare benign.

parole.significato: A curse, a malediction.
parole.testo: From Middle English malisoun, from Old French maleison, from Latin maledictiō, from the past participle stem of maledīcō (“to speak ill of”), from male (“wickedly, badly”) + dīcō (“say, speak”). Doublet of malediction.

parole.significato: Anas platyrhynchos, a common and widespread dabbling duck, natively found throughout the Northern Hemisphere, whose mal…
parole.testo: From Middle English malard, mawlard, from Old French malard, malart, mallart (“male wild duck”), from Old French male, masle (“male”) + -ard, -art. Cognate with Medieval Latin maslardus, mallardus.

parole.significato: A type of hammer with a larger-than-usual head made of wood, rubber or similar non-iron material, used by woodworkers f…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English maylet, borrowed from Old French maillet, from mail + -et.

parole.significato: manacle
parole.testo: From Middle English manicle, from Old French manicle, from Latin manicula, diminutive form of manus (“hand”).

parole.significato: To direct or be in charge of.
parole.testo: From Early Modern English manage, menage, from Middle English *manage, *menage, from Old French manege (“the handling or training of a horse, horsemanship, riding, maneuvers, proceedings”), probably from Old Italian maneggiare (“to handle, manage, touch, treat”), from Vulgar Latin *manizāre (“handle

parole.significato: A person in charge of purchasing and storing food and other provisions in a monastery, college, or court of law.
parole.testo: From Middle English maunciple, from Old French manciple, from Medieval Latin mancipiolum (“lowly servant”), diminutive of Latin mancipium (“slave”).

parole.significato: A commandment or directive.
parole.testo: From Middle English maundement, from Old French mandement. Doublet of mandamento.

parole.significato: A skin disease of nonhuman mammals caused by parasitic mites (Sarcoptes spp., Demodecidae spp.).
parole.testo: From Middle English manjewe, manjeue, from Old French manjue, derived from mangier (“to eat”) (modern French manger (“to eat”)), from Latin manducare.

parole.significato: A trough in a stable or barn for animals to eat from.
parole.testo: From Middle English manger, from Old French mangeoire, menjoere, from mangier (“to eat”) (modern French manger). Cognate with Galician manxadoira, Italian mangiatoia, Occitan manjadoira, French mangeoire.

parole.significato: A feast; a banquet.
parole.testo: From Middle English mangerie, from Old French mangerie (“eating”).

parole.significato: A military engine formerly used for throwing stones and burning objects.
parole.testo: From Old French mangonel, from Latin manganellus, manganum, from Ancient Greek μάγγανον (mánganon).

parole.significato: A landed estate.
parole.testo: From Middle English maner, manour; from Old French manoir, from earlier maneir, from Latin manēre. Doublet of maenor.

parole.significato: A short sleeveless cloak or cape.
parole.testo: From Middle English mauntelet, from Old French mantelet, diminutive of mantel (“mantle”). Doublet of mantelletta.

parole.significato: Synonym of handbook.
parole.testo: From Middle English manuel, from Old French manuel, from Late Latin manuāle (“handbook, manual”).

parole.significato: A visual representation of an area, whether real or imaginary, showing the relative positions of places and other featu…
parole.testo: Shortening or back-formation of Middle English mappemounde, mapemounde (“world map”), from Old French mapamonde, from Medieval Latin mappa mundī, compound of Latin mappa (“napkin, cloth”) and mundus (“world”). See mop for more on the first component. Doublet of mop, nape, and nappe.

parole.significato: A border region, especially one originally set up to defend a boundary.
parole.testo: From Middle English marche (“tract of land along a country's border”), from Old French marche (“boundary, frontier”), from Frankish *marku, from Proto-Germanic *markō, from Proto-Indo-European *mórǵs (“edge, boundary”).

parole.significato: Having the color of marigolds, a bright yellowish-orange hue.
parole.testo: From Middle English marigolde, marygoldye, from Mary (referring to the Virgin Mary) + Middle English golde (“marigold”).

parole.significato: A herb of the mint family, Origanum majorana, having aromatic leaves.
parole.testo: From Old French majorane, from Medieval Latin maiōrana.

parole.significato: A mixed earthy substance, consisting of carbonate of lime, clay, and possibly sand, in very variable proportions, and a…
parole.testo: From Middle English marle, from Old French marle, from Late Latin margila, diminutive of marga (“marl”). Doublet of marla.

parole.significato: A nobleman in England, France, and Germany, of a rank next below that of duke, but above a count. Originally, the marqu…
parole.testo: From Middle English markis, from Old French markis, marchis, from Late Latin marchensis, from Old High German marcha and Frankish *marku, from Proto-Germanic *markō, from Proto-Indo-European *mórǵs (“edge, boundary”). Meaning is “lord of the march”, in sense of march (“border country”).

parole.significato: The state of being married.
parole.testo: From Middle English mariage, from Old French mariage, from marier (“to marry”), from Latin marītō (“marry”, verb, literally “give in marriage”), from marītus (“lover”, “nuptial”), from mas (“male, masculine, of the male sex”). Equivalent to marry + -age. Doublet of maritage. Displaced native Old Eng

parole.significato: A kind of fabric made from two series of threads interlacing each other, thus forming a double cloth, quilted in the lo…
parole.testo: From Old French Marseilles (nominative of Marseille), from Latin Massilia, Marsilia, from Ancient Greek Μασσαλία (Massalía), probably from a pre-Latin language of Italy, perhaps Ancient Ligurian mas (“spring”).

parole.significato: A hammer, especially a war hammer.
parole.testo: From Middle English martel, from Old French martel m (modern French marteau m), from Late Latin martellus m, from Latin martulus m, a variant of marculus m (“small hammer”).

parole.significato: A weapon resembling a hammer, often having one side of the head pointed, used by horsemen in the Middle Ages to break a…
parole.testo: Old French, hammer of iron.

parole.significato: Any carnivorous mammal of the genus Martes.
parole.testo: From Middle English martren, martryn, from Old French martrine (“marten fur”), from Old Dutch *marthrīn (“of marten fur”), from *marthar (“marten”). Displaced related Old English mearþ, from Proto-Germanic *marþuz.

parole.significato: That which causes wonder; a prodigy; a portent.
parole.testo: First attested from 1300, from Middle English merveile, from Old French merveille (“a wonder”), from Vulgar Latin *miribilia, from Latin mīrābilia (“wonderful things”), from neuter plural of mīrābilis (“strange, wonderful”), from mīror (“to wonder at”), from mīrus (“wonderful”). Doublet of mirabilia

parole.significato: Exciting wonder or surprise; astonishing; wonderful.
parole.testo: First attested from 1300 as Middle English merveilous, from Old French merveillus, from merveille (“a wonder”) + -us. Doublet of merveilleux. See also marvel.

parole.significato: Exciting wonder or surprise; astonishing; wonderful.
parole.testo: First attested from 1300 as Middle English merveilous, from Old French merveillus, from merveille (“a wonder”), equivalent to marvel + -ous.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the male gender.
parole.testo: From Middle English masculyne, masculyn, from Old French masculin, from Latin masculīnus, diminutive of masculus (“male, manly”), itself a diminutive of mās (“male”). Displaced native Old English werlīċ (literally “manly”).

parole.significato: The art or occupation of a mason.
parole.testo: From Middle English masonry, masonrie, partly from Old French maçonerie and partly from mason + -ry.

parole.significato: The principal liturgical service of the Church, encompassing both a scripture service (Liturgy of the Word) and a eucha…
parole.testo: From Middle English messe, from Old English mæsse and Old French messe, both from Late Latin missa, from Latin mittō (“to send, dismiss”), compare French messe. parole.significato: The Eucharist, now especially in Roman Catholicism.
parole.testo: From Middle English messe, masse, from Old English mæsse (“the mass, church festival”) and Old French messe, from Vulgar Latin *messa (“Eucharist, dismissal”), from Late Latin missa, noun use of feminine past participle of classical Latin mittere (“to send”), from ite, missa est (“go, (the assembly)

parole.significato: Executed in the manner of a master; showing competence and skill; masterful.
parole.testo: PIE word  *méǵh₂s From Middle English maisterli, from maister (“leader, ruler; high official; official in charge of a place; person in control; employer; owner; schoolmaster, teacher; scholar, sage; holder of a master's degree; religious teacher; master craftsman; expert; magician; social superior;

parole.significato: The position or authority of a master; dominion; command; supremacy; superiority.
parole.testo: From Middle English maistery, maistrie, mastere, mastry, from Old French maistrie, equivalent to master + -y.

parole.significato: An evergreen shrub or small tree, Pistacia lentiscus (mastic tree), native to the Mediterranean.
parole.testo: From Middle English mastik, from Old French mastic, from Latin mastiche, from Ancient Greek μαστίχη (mastíkhē), from μαστιχάω (mastikháō, “to chew”) (note the chewing gum sense). Related to masticate. The broad sense for cements came via extension from predecessor cements made with the tree's resin.

parole.significato: One of an old breed of powerful, deep-chested, and smooth-coated dogs, used chiefly as watchdogs and guard dogs.
parole.testo: From Middle English mastif, mastyf, an aberrant derivation (with influence from Old French mestif) from Old French mastin (modern French mâtin), from Vulgar Latin *mansuetinus (“tamed (animal)”), from Latin mansuetus (“tamed”).

parole.significato: A small wooden stick specially treated with chemicals to produce flame upon contact with another chemical, from the fri…
parole.testo: From Middle English macche, mecche (“wick (of a candle)”), from Old French mesche, meische, from Vulgar Latin micca (compare Catalan metxa, Spanish mecha, Italian miccia), which in turn is probably from Latin myxa (“nozzle, curved part of a lamp”), from Ancient Greek μύξα (múxa, “lamp wick”).

parole.significato: To confuse; to confound.
parole.testo: From Middle English maten (“to overpower”), from Old French mater (“to kill”), from Vulgar Latin *mattō, of unclear origin.

parole.significato: Mathematical.
parole.testo: From Middle English mathematik, from Old French mathematique or directly from Latin mathēmaticus, from Ancient Greek μᾰθημᾰτῐκός (măthēmătĭkós), from μάθημα (máthēma, “learning; mathematics”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”, adjective suffix).

parole.significato: An abstract representational system studying numbers, shapes, structures, quantitative change and relationships between…
parole.testo: First use appears c. 1545. From mathematic (noun) + -ics, from Middle English mathematique, methametik, matematik, matamatik, from Old French mathematique, from Latin mathēmatica (“mathematics”), from Ancient Greek μαθηματικός (mathēmatikós, “on the matter of that which is learned”), from μάθημα (má

parole.significato: Either of two British infantry tanks in use during World War II, the Infantry Tank Mark I or Infantry Tank Mark II.
parole.testo: From Middle English Matilda, from Old French Mathilde, from Old High German Mahthilt, Mehthilt, from Proto-West Germanic *Mahtihild, from Proto-Germanic *Mahtihildiz; compare German Mechthild, Old English Mæþhild (“Matilda”).

parole.significato: Together with lauds, the earliest of the canonical hours; traditionally prayed at sunrise or earlier.
parole.testo: From Middle English matyns, matynes, from Old French matines.

parole.significato: A female leader of a family, a tribe or an ethnic or religious group.
parole.testo: Of Latin origin, via or reinforced by Old French matriarche, from Latin māter (“mother”) + -archa, -arches, from Ancient Greek -άρχης (-árkhēs), from ἀρχός (arkhós, “chief”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ergʰ- (“to begin, rule, command”). By surface analysis, matri- + -arch.

parole.significato: Marriage; the state of being married.
parole.testo: From Old French matremoine, from Latin mātrimōnium (“marriage, wedlock”), from mātri(s) (“mother”) + -mōnium (“obligation”). By surface analysis, matri- + -mony. Compare patrimony.

parole.significato: A mature or elderly woman, especially one of a higher social rank.
parole.testo: From Middle English matrone, from Old French matrone, from Latin mātrōna (“married woman”), from māter (“mother”). Doublet of matrona.

parole.significato: A pad on which a person can recline and sleep, usually having an inner section of coiled springs covered with foam or o…
parole.testo: From Middle English materas, from Old French matras, from Arabic مَطْرَح (maṭraḥ, “place where something is thrown”), from طَرَحَ (ṭaraḥa, “to throw”). Compare divan, from Persian via Turkish (both of Middle Eastern origin, due to the local custom of lying on padding on floor being foreign to Europe

parole.significato: The state of being mature, ready or ripe; the prime state of productibility and self expression.
parole.testo: From Middle English maturitee, maturyte, from Old French maturité, from Latin mātūritātem. By surface analysis, mature + -ity.

parole.significato: The Magdalene; Mary Magdalene.
parole.testo: From Middle English Maudelen, a dialectal form of Mary Magdalene (typically depicted weeping), from Old French Madelaine (whence Madeleine), from Late Latin Magdalena (see Magdalena, Magdalene, and Maudlin).

parole.significato: A long stylised sleeve.
parole.testo: From Middle English maunche, from Old French maunche, one of the variants of manche, from Latin manica. Doublet of manche.

parole.significato: A wicker basket.
parole.testo: From Middle English maunde, maundie, borrowed from Old French mande, borrowed from Middle Dutch mande, from Old Dutch *manda, from Proto-West Germanic *mandu.

parole.significato: A commandment.
parole.testo: From Middle English maundee, maunde, from Old French mandée (“mandated”), from Latin mandatum (“commandment”). Doublet of mandate. The word came to refer to the foot-washing ceremony performed on Thursday before Easter because of the phrase used by Jesus to explain his act of foot-washing, which in

parole.significato: Having the mean as its value; average.
parole.testo: From Middle English meene, borrowed from Old French meien (French moyen), Late Latin mediānus (“that is in the middle, middle”), from Latin medius (“middle”). Cognate with mid. For the musical sense, compare the cognate Italian mezzano. Doublet of median and mizzen.

parole.significato: A red spot of the kind that appears on the skin of someone suffering from measles.
parole.testo: From Middle English mesel, from Old French mesel (“leprous”), from Latin misellus (“wretched", "unfortunate”), diminutive of miser (“wretched, sick”), of unknown ultimate origin.

parole.significato: Able to be measured.
parole.testo: From Old French mesurable, equivalent to measure + -able. Doublet of mensurable.

parole.significato: A prescribed quantity or extent.
parole.testo: From Middle English mesure, from Old French mesure, from Latin mēnsūra (“a measure”), mētior (“to measure”, supine stem in mēns-) + -tūra. Largely displaced native Old English metan ("to measure" whence modern mete) and ġemet (“a measure”). See also -ure.

parole.significato: mechanical; relating to mechanics or the laws of motion in physics
parole.testo: From Middle English mekanyk (“mechanical”), from Old French mecanique, from Latin mechanicus (“of or belonging to machines or mechanics, inventive”), from Ancient Greek μηχανικός (mēkhanikós, “pertaining to machines or contrivance, mechanic, ingenious, inventive”), from μηχανή (mēkhanḗ, “a machine,

parole.significato: A devotional exercise of, or leading to, contemplation.
parole.testo: From Old French meditacion, from Latin meditatio, from meditatus, the past participle of meditārī (“to meditate, to think over, consider”), itself from Proto-Indo-European *med- (“to measure, limit, consider, advise”).

parole.significato: Mespilus germanica, common medlar (now often Crataegus germanica).
parole.testo: From Middle English medler, medeler, from Old French medler, meslier, from medle, mesdle (“medlar fruit”), from Latin mespilum, from Ancient Greek μέσπιλον (méspilon). Related to the rare mesple, via Proto-West Germanic *mespilā. Displaced Old English openærs (“open-arse”) (and similar names, from a

parole.significato: Black bile, formerly thought to be one of the four "cardinal humours" of animal bodies.
parole.testo: From Middle English malencolie, from Old French melancolie, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολία (melankholía, “atrabiliousness”) (from μέλας (mélas), μελαν- (melan-, “black, dark, murky”) + χολή (kholḗ, “bile”)), referring to the humour which ancient Hippocratic and later Galenic medicine associated with

parole.significato: To deal, concern oneself; to interfere or meddle.
parole.testo: From Middle English mellen, medlen, from Old French meller, mesler (“to mix, mingle”). Doublet of meddle.

parole.significato: A sequence of notes that makes up a musical phrase.
parole.testo: From Middle English melodie, melodye, from Old French melodie, from Latin melodia, from Ancient Greek μελῳδίᾱ (melōidíā, “singing, chanting”), from μέλος (mélos, “musical phrase”) + ἀοιδή (aoidḗ, “song”), contracted form ᾠδή (ōidḗ).

parole.significato: Some of the plants of the family Cucurbitaceae grown for food, generally not including the cucumber.
parole.testo: From Middle English meloun, melon, from Old French melon, from Late Latin melonem, from Latin melopeponem, from Ancient Greek μηλοπέπων (mēlopépōn), from μῆλον (mêlon, “apple”) + πέπων (pépōn, “ripe”).

parole.significato: One who belongs to a group.
parole.testo: From Middle English membre, from Old French membre, from Latin membrum (“limb, body part”), from Proto-Italic *memzrom, from Proto-Indo-European *mḗms, *mēms-rom (“flesh”). Akin to Gothic 𐌼𐌹𐌼𐌶 (mimz, “meat, flesh”), Crimean Gothic menus. Coexists with native limb, from Old English lim (“limb, joint,

parole.significato: A perceived threat or danger.
parole.testo: From Middle English manace, from Old French manace, menace, &c., from Late Latin minācia (“threat, menace”), from Latin mināx (“threatening”) + -ia (suffix forming abstract nouns).

parole.significato: To make threats against (someone); to intimidate.
parole.testo: First attested in 1303: from Middle English manacen, from Old French menacer, manecier, manechier and Anglo-Norman manasser, from the assumed Vulgar Latin *mināciāre, from Latin minācia, whence the noun.

parole.significato: the state of being a beggar; mendicancy or beggary
parole.testo: From Old French mendicité, from Latin mendicitas.

parole.significato: A speaking or noticing of anything, usually in a brief or cursory manner.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English mencioun, mention, from Old French mention, from Latin mentiōnem, accusative of mentiō (“a mention, calling to mind”).

parole.significato: trade; commerce
parole.testo: From Middle English marchaundrye, from Old French marcheanderie.

parole.significato: merciful
parole.testo: From Old French [Term?].

parole.significato: A Eurasian blackbird, Turdus merula.
parole.testo: From Middle English merle, from Old French merle (French merle), from Latin merula (“blackbird”) (whence the directly borrowed Middle English merule, and compare the taxonomic name Turdus merula), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂mes- (“black, blackbird”). Compare Breton moualch (“ouzel”), Welsh mwyalch

parole.significato: A small falcon, Falco columbarius, that breeds in northern North America, Europe, and Asia.
parole.testo: From Middle English merlioun, merlion, marlyon, merlyon, merlinge, from Old French emerillon, esmerillon, from Old Frankish *smiril (“falcon, hawk”), from Proto-Germanic *smirilaz (“falcon, merlin”). Cognate with Old High German smirl (“falcon”), Old Norse smyrill (“falcon”).

parole.significato: The fish Merlangius merlangus, endemic to the North Atlantic, Mediterranean Sea, western Baltic Sea and Black Sea.
parole.testo: From Middle English merlynge, from Old French merlenc, from Latin merula.

parole.significato: A lord entitled to rent or feudal obligations from tenants but who himself owes rent or feudal obligations to another.
parole.testo: Distinguishing the nature of the lord as intermediate (Old French mesne, "middle"), particularly as opposed to lords paramount and tenants-in-chief.

parole.significato: A communication, or what is communicated; any concept or information conveyed.
parole.testo: From Middle English message, from Old French message, from Early Medieval Latin missāticum, derived from Latin mittere (“send”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“to exchange”). Partially displaced Old English ærende (whence errand).

parole.significato: One who brings messages.
parole.testo: From Middle English messengere, messingere, messangere, from Old French messanger, a variant of Old French messagier (French messager), equivalent to message + -er. Doublet of messager. Displaced native Old English boda (“messenger, envoy”) and ǣrendraca (“messenger, ambassador”). For the replacemen

parole.significato: Chemical elements or alloys, their ores, and the mines where their ores come from.
parole.testo: From Middle English metal, a borrowing from Old French metal, from Latin metallum (“metal, mine, quarry, mineral”), itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μέταλλον (métallon, “mine, quarry, metal”).

parole.significato: The field of study of metaphysics.
parole.testo: From Middle English methaphesik, methaphisik, methaphisique, metaphesyk, methafisik, metaphesyk, methephysyk, from Old French metafisique, methaphisique and Medieval Latin metaphysica, methephisica; equivalent to meta- + physic.

parole.significato: A philosopher who specializes in the scholarly study of metaphysics.
parole.testo: From Middle English methafisicien, from methafisik on the model of fisicien or perhaps from rare and late Old French methafisicien.

parole.significato: The branch of philosophy which studies fundamental principles intended to describe or explain all that is, and which ar…
parole.testo: 1560s; plural of metaphysic, from Middle English methaphesik, methaphisik, methaphisique, metaphesyk, methafisik, metaphesyk, methephysyk, from Old French metafisique, methaphisique and Medieval Latin metaphysica, methephisica, from Byzantine Greek μεταφυσικά (metaphusiká), from the title of the col

parole.significato: A boundary or other limit; a boundary-marker; mere.
parole.testo: From Middle English mete, from Old French mete (“boundary, boundary marker”), from Latin mēta (“post, goal, marker”). Cognate with the second element in Old English wullmod (“distaff”).

parole.significato: A severe, disabling headache, usually affecting only one side of the head, and often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, p…
parole.testo: First appears c. 1425. A respelling (following French) of the late 14th century Middle English megrim, from the 13th century Old French migraigne, from Vulgar Latin pronunciation of Latin hemicrania (“a pain in one half of the head”), from Ancient Greek ἡμικρανία (hēmikranía), from ἡμι- (hēmi-, “hem

parole.significato: Common yarrow, Achillea millefolium.
parole.testo: From Old French milfoil (modern French mille-feuille), from Latin millefolium, from mīlle + folium. Doublet of mille-feuille.

parole.significato: Characteristic of members of the armed forces.
parole.testo: From Middle English militari, from Old French militaire, from Latin mīlitāris, from mīles (“soldier”) + -āris (whence -ary). Doublet of militaire.

parole.significato: An excavation from which ore or solid minerals are taken, especially one consisting of underground tunnels.
parole.testo: From Middle English [Term?], from Old French mine, from Late Latin mina, from Gaulish (compare to Welsh mwyn, Irish mianach (“ore”)), from Proto-Celtic *meinis (“ore, metal”).

parole.significato: Any naturally occurring solid material that has a (more or less) definite chemical composition and characteristic physi…
parole.testo: From Middle English mineral, borrowed from Old French mineral, (French minéral), from Medieval Latin minerale, from minera (“ore”), probably ultimately derived from Latin mina (“ore, mine”).

parole.significato: A person who is trained to preach, to perform religious ceremonies, and to afford pastoral care at a Protestant church.
parole.testo: From Middle English ministre, from Old French ministre, from Latin minister (“an attendant, servant, assistant, a priest's assistant or other under official”), from minor (“less”) + -ter; see minor. Doublet of Minorite.

parole.significato: The act of ministering; an instance of providing aid, care, or assistance.
parole.testo: From Middle English ministracioun, from Old French ministracïon, from Latin ministrātio; equivalent to minister + -ation.

parole.significato: A government department at the administrative level, normally headed by a minister (or equivalent rank, e.g. secretary…
parole.testo: From Middle English mynisterie, borrowed from Old French menistere, in turn borrowed itself from Latin ministerium; equivalent to minister + -y.

parole.significato: A light gray or white fur used to trim the robes of judges or state executives, also used in medieval times.
parole.testo: From Old French menu vair (“squirrel, squirrel fur”), from menu (“small”) + vair (“a type of fur”).

parole.significato: A unit of time which is one sixtieth of an hour (sixty seconds).
parole.testo: From Middle English mynute, minute, mynet, from Old French minute, from Medieval Latin minūta (“60th of an hour; note”). Doublet of menu and menudo.

parole.significato: An event that appears inexplicable by the laws of nature and so is held to be supernatural in origin.
parole.testo: From Middle English miracle, from Old French miracle, from Latin mīrāculum (“object of wonder”), from mīror (“to wonder at”), from mīrus (“wonderful”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meyh₂- (“to smile, to be astonished”). Doublet of milagro and miraculum. Partially displaced native wonder, from Old En

parole.significato: A smooth surface, usually made of glass with reflective material painted on the underside, that reflects light so as to…
parole.testo: From Middle English mirour, from Old French mireor (“mirror”, literally “looker, watcher”), from mirer (“look at”), from Latin mīror (“wonder at”), from mīrus (“wonderful”), from Proto-Indo-European *smey- (“to laugh, to be glad”). Displaced native Middle English schewere, schawere, from Old English

parole.significato: Synonym of misfortune, bad luck or mishap, an instance of bad luck.
parole.testo: From Middle English misaventure, from Old French mesaventure, from mes- (“mis-”) + aventure (“adventure”). Equivalent to mis- + adventure. Compare disadventure.

parole.significato: Conduct that playfully causes petty annoyance.
parole.testo: From Middle English myschef, meschef, meschief, mischef, from Old French meschief, from meschever (“to bring to grief”), from mes- (“badly”) + chever (“happen; come to a head”), from Vulgar Latin *capare, from Latin caput (“head”).

parole.significato: To do a mischief to; to harm.
parole.testo: From Middle English myschefen, myscheven, from Old French meschever.

parole.significato: To destroy.
parole.testo: From Middle English myscheven, from Old French meschever, from mes- + chever.

parole.significato: The quality of being miscreant; adherence to a false religion; false faith.
parole.testo: From Middle English myscreaunce, miscreaunce, from Old French mescreänce.

parole.significato: Lacking in conscience or moral principles; unscrupulous.
parole.testo: From Middle English myscreaunt, miscreaunt, from Old French mescreant (1080) "mis-believer", present participle of mescreire "to misbelieve" (modern mécroire). Cognate with French mécréant.

parole.significato: Suffering, distress.
parole.testo: From Middle English myssease, from Old French mesaise, from mes- (“mis-”) + aise (“ease”). Equivalent to mis- + ease. Cognate with French mésaise.

parole.significato: Relaxation of monastic rules.
parole.testo: From 1200–1250, from Middle English misericorde (“an act of clemency”) from Old French, from Latin misericordia (“pity”). Doublet of misericordia.

parole.significato: Great unhappiness; extreme pain of body or mind; wretchedness; distress; woe.
parole.testo: From Middle English miserie, from Old French miserie (modern: misère), from Latin miseria, from miser, equivalent to miser + -y. Doublet of misère and mizeria.

parole.significato: A prayer book; a church service (book).
parole.testo: From Old French messel (“book of the Mass”).

parole.significato: Of a woman: to master; to learn or develop to a high degree of proficiency.
parole.testo: From Middle English maistresse, from Old French maistresse (whence French maîtresse), feminine of maistre (“master”). By surface analysis, mist(e)r + -ess.

parole.significato: shot or bits of iron used sometimes in loading cannon
parole.testo: From Old French mitaille (“small coins; hence scrap iron, old iron; then grapeshot”); originally diminutive of mite (“small coin”). See also mitrailleur.

parole.significato: A covering for the head, worn on solemn occasions by church dignitaries, which has been made in many reincarnations, mo…
parole.testo: From Middle English mytre, from Old French mitre, from Ancient Greek μίτρα (mítra, “headband, turban”). Its use in reference to a counterfeit coin derived from the bishop's mitre stamped upon it. Doublet of Mithras, Mithra, Mitra, and Mehr.

parole.significato: The act of mixing.
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French misture, from Latin mixtūra (“a mixing”), from mixtus, perfect passive participle of misceō (“mix”); compare mix.

parole.significato: A deep, wide defensive ditch, normally filled with water, surrounding a fortified habitation.
parole.testo: From Middle English mote, from Old French mote (“mound, embankment”); compared also to Old French motte (“hillock, lump, clod, turf”), from Medieval Latin mota (“a mound, hill”), of Germanic origin, perhaps via Frankish *mot, *motta (“mud, peat, bog, turf”), from Proto-Germanic *mutô, *mudraz, *muþr

parole.significato: Capable of being moved, especially on wheels.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin mōbilis (“easy to be moved, moveable”), from moveō (“move”).
