parole.significato: To mimic, to simulate.
parole.testo: From Middle English mokken, from Old French mocquer, moquier (“to deride, jeer”), from Middle Dutch mocken (“to mumble”) or Middle Low German mucken (“to grumble, talk with the mouth half-opened”), both from Proto-West Germanic *mokkijan, *mukkijan (“to low, bellow; mumble”), from Proto-Germanic *mu

parole.significato: A particular means of accomplishing something.
parole.testo: From Old French mode (masculine), from Latin modus (“measure, due measure, rhythm, melody”). Doublet of modus.

parole.significato: To toil, to work hard.
parole.testo: From Middle English mollen (“to soften by wetting”), borrowed from Old French moillier with the same meaning, from Vulgar Latin *molliō, *molliare, from mollis (“soft”).

parole.significato: That which moistens or makes damp or wet; exuding fluid; liquid in small quantity.
parole.testo: From Middle English moisture, from Old French moistour (“moisture, dampness, wetness”). Compare French moiteur.

parole.significato: A hollow form or matrix for shaping a fluid or plastic substance.
parole.testo: From Middle English molde (“mold, cast”), from Old French modle, mole, from Latin modulus, from Latin modus. Doublet of module, modulus, and model.

parole.significato: To sexually assault or sexually harass.
parole.testo: From Middle English molesten, from Old French molester, from Latin molestō (“to trouble, annoy, molest”), from molestus (“troublesome”), from moles (“a burden, difficulty, labor, trouble”); see mole.

parole.significato: The act of molesting.
parole.testo: From Old French molestacion, from Latin molestatio. By surface analysis, molest + -ation.

parole.significato: The act of mollifying.
parole.testo: From Old French mollificacion, from Latin mollificātiō, form of molliō. By surface analysis, mollify + -ification.

parole.significato: A government in which sovereignty is embodied within a single, today usually hereditary head of state (whether as a fig…
parole.testo: From Old French monarchie, from Late Latin monarchia, from Ancient Greek μοναρχία (monarkhía), from μόνος (mónos, “only”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “power, authority”). By surface analysis, mon- (“one, single”) + -archy (“rule, command”).

parole.significato: A residence for monks or others who have taken religious vows.
parole.testo: From Middle English monasterie, from Old French monastere, from Medieval Latin monastērium (“monastery”), from Ancient Greek μοναστήριον (monastḗrion, “hermitage, monastery”), from μοναστήριος (monastḗrios, “alone, made alone”) + -ιον (-ion, “-ium”, suffix forming place names), from μονάζω (monázō,

parole.significato: A unicorn.
parole.testo: From Old French monoceros, from Latin monocerōs.

parole.significato: A terrifying and dangerous creature, especially one of an imaginary or fictional kind.
parole.testo: From Middle English monstre, from Old French monstre, mostre, moustre, from Latin mōnstrum. Displaced native Old English fīfel and Old English þyrs.

parole.significato: An ornamental, often precious receptacle, either open or with a transparent cover, in which the sacramental bread (cons…
parole.testo: From Middle English mustraunce, from Old French mostrance, monstrance, from post-classical Latin mōnstrantia, from classical Latin mōnstrāns, present participle of mōnstrāre (“to show”).

parole.significato: Hideous or frightful.
parole.testo: From Middle English monstrous, from Old French monstrueuse, monstrüos, from Latin mōnstrōsus. Compare monstruous. By surface analysis, monster + -ous.

parole.significato: Monstrous.
parole.testo: From Middle English monstruous, from Old French monstrueuse, monstrüos, from Latin mōnstruōsus.

parole.significato: An upright piece in any framework, such as a muntin or stile.
parole.testo: From Middle English mountant, from Old French montant.

parole.significato: Ascending toward the chief of the escutcheon.
parole.testo: From Old French montant.

parole.significato: To mark or memorialize with a monument.
parole.testo: From Middle English monument, from Old French monument, from Latin monumentum (“memorial, monument, tomb”), from monēre (“to remind”). Partially displaced Old English bēacn.

parole.significato: To wander around aimlessly, often causing irritation to others.
parole.testo: From Middle English moochen, mouchen (“to pretend poverty”), from Old French muchier, mucier, mucer (“to skulk, hide, conceal”), from Frankish *mukkjan (“to hide, conceal oneself”), from Proto-Germanic *mukjaną, *mūkōną (“to hide, ambush”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)mūg-, *(s)mewgʰ- (“swindler, t

parole.significato: A member of an ancient Amazigh people from Mauretania.
parole.testo: From Middle English More, Moore, from Old French More (modern French Maure), from Latin Maurus (“a Moor, meaning a Mauretanian, an inhabitant of Mauretania”), from Ancient Greek Μαυρούσιος (Mauroúsios, “Mauretanian”). Doublet of Moro.

parole.significato: Of or relating to principles of right and wrong in behaviour, especially conforming to principles of rectitude.
parole.testo: From Middle English moral, from Old French moral, from Latin mōrālis (“relating to manners or morals”) (first used by Cicero, to translate Ancient Greek ἠθικός (ēthikós, “moral”)), from mos (“manner, custom”).

parole.significato: To make moral reflections (on, upon, about or over something); to regard acts and events as involving a moral.
parole.testo: From Old French moraliser, equivalent to moral + -ize.

parole.significato: The blunt head of a jousting-lance.
parole.testo: From Old French morne, morné, etc.

parole.significato: A small fragment or share of something, commonly applied to food.
parole.testo: From Middle English morsel, from Old French morsel, from Medieval Latin morsellum (“a bit, a little piece”), diminutive of Latin morsum (“a bit”), neuter of morsus, perfect passive participle of mordeo (“to bite”). Compare French morceau, whence the English doublet morceau.

parole.significato: Death; especially, the death of game in hunting.
parole.testo: From Middle English mort, from Old French mort (“death”).

parole.significato: Susceptible to death by aging, sickness, injury, or wound; not immortal.
parole.testo: From Middle English mortal, mortel, from Old French mortal, and their source Latin mortālis, from mors (“death”). In this sense, displaced native deadly, from Old English dēadlīċ.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being mortal.
parole.testo: From Old French mortalite, from Latin mortālitās, from mortālis (“relating to death”), from mors (“death”); equivalent to mortal + -ity.

parole.significato: A mixture of lime or cement, sand and water used for bonding building blocks.
parole.testo: From Middle English morter, from Old French mortier, from Latin mortārium. Doublet of mortarium.

parole.significato: A hole that is made to receive a tenon so as to form a joint.
parole.testo: From Middle English morteys, from Old French mortaise, from Arabic مُرْتَزّ (murtazz, “fastened”), from اِرْتَزَّ (irtazza).

parole.significato: Commonwealth standard spelling of mold.
parole.testo: Via Middle English molde, moulde (“mould, cast”) and Old French modle, from Latin modulus.

parole.significato: A person who moulds dough into loaves for baking into bread.
parole.testo: Partly from the following: * From Middle English molder, moldere (“maker of bread, baker”), from molden (“to knead or shape (bread); to make bread, bake; to mix (something) by kneading; to shape, mould; to pulverize (?)”) + -er (suffix forming agent nouns, especially names of people engaged in profe

parole.significato: The angle at which a gun is raised for firing.
parole.testo: From Middle English mounture, from Old French mounteure; equivalent to mount + -ure.

parole.significato: Capable of being moved, lifted, carried, drawn, turned, or conveyed, or in any way made to change place or posture; not…
parole.testo: From Old French movable. By surface analysis, move + -able.

parole.significato: A scornful grimace; a wry face.
parole.testo: From Middle English mowe, from Old French moe (“grimace”), from Frankish *mauwa (“pout, protruding lip”), from Proto-Germanic *mawwō (“muff, sleeve”). Akin to Middle Dutch mouwe (“protruding lip”). Doublet of moue ("pout").

parole.significato: Intercession; intervention.
parole.testo: From Middle English moyen, moene, a variation of mene, meene, borrowed from Old French meien (French moyen), Late Latin mediānus (“that is in the middle, middle”), from Latin medius (“middle”). Doublet of mid and mean.

parole.significato: A machine that mixes clay and sand under a roller for use in preparing a mould for metal casting.
parole.testo: From mull (“to mix (clay and sand) under a roller to prepare a mould”) + -er (suffix forming agent nouns). Mull is possibly derived from mull (“(chiefly Northern England) to grind to powder, crumble, powder, pulverize”), from Middle English mollen, mullen (“to moisten (something); to soften (somethi

parole.significato: A fish of the family Mullidae (order Syngnathiformes).
parole.testo: From Middle English molet, mulett, from Old French mulet (now ‘grey mullet’), from Latin mullus (“red mullet”), from Ancient Greek μύλλος (múllos).

parole.significato: A star with straight edges and usually with five or six points.
parole.testo: From Middle English molet, from Old French molette (“rowel”).

parole.significato: A vertical bar between the panes of glass or casements of a window or the panels of a screen.
parole.testo: Alteration of monial (“mullion”), or metathesis of Middle English moyniel, both ultimately from Old French moinel.

parole.significato: To increase the amount, degree or number of (something).
parole.testo: From Old French multiplier, from Latin multiplicō, from multi (“many”) + plicō (“to fold”). The noun presumably derives from the verb.

parole.significato: A great amount or number, often of people; abundance, myriad, profusion.
parole.testo: From Middle English multitude, multitud, multytude (“(great) amount or number of people or things; multitudinous”), borrowed from Old French multitude (“crowd of people; diversity, wide range”), or directly from its etymon Latin multitūdō (“great amount or number of people or things”), from multus (

parole.significato: A grinding of grain, or the grain that is ground.
parole.testo: From Middle English multūr, from Old French molture (modern French mouture), from Medieval Latin molitura, from the past participle stem of molere ‘grind’. Compare mill.

parole.significato: A person who dons a disguising costume, as for a parade or a festival.
parole.testo: From Middle English mummer, mommer, equivalent to mum + -er, perhaps conflating with Old French momeor (“jester, entertainer”), from mommer (“to wear a mask”), from momon (“mask”). Compare German Mumme (“mask”), 16th Century German mummen (“to disguise oneself”), Middle Dutch mommen, mummen (“to go

parole.significato: Worldly, earthly, profane, vulgar as opposed to heavenly.
parole.testo: From Middle English mondeyne, from Old French mondain, from Late Latin mundānus, from Latin mundus (“world”). Compare Danish mondæn. (ordinary): Compare typologically Russian несусве́тный (nesusvétnyj) (<~ не- (ne-) + (rare) сусве́тный (susvétnyj) < свет (svet)).

parole.significato: One of the separators between panes of glass in a composite window.
parole.testo: From Middle English mountaunt, from Old French montant, present participle of monter (“to put up”).

parole.significato: An officer in charge of the town walls, or their repairs.
parole.testo: From Middle English murager, from Old French muragier (“an officer in charge of town walls, receiving toll for repairs”), from murage (“tax levied for the building or repairing of town walls”), from Latin murus (“a wall”) + -aticum.

parole.significato: Any low, indistinct sound, like that of running water.
parole.testo: From Middle English murmur, murmor, murmour, from Old French murmure (modern French murmure), from Latin murmur (“murmur, humming, muttering, roaring, growling, rushing etc.”).

parole.significato: To become lost in thought, to ponder.
parole.testo: From Middle English musen, from Old French muser.

parole.significato: Of, belonging or relating to music, or to its performance or notation.
parole.testo: From Middle English musical, from Old French [Term?], from Medieval Latin mūsicālis, from Latin mūsica (“music”) + -ālis (suffix forming adjectives); equivalent to music + -al.

parole.significato: A composer, conductor, or performer of music; specifically, a person who sings and/or plays a musical instrument as a h…
parole.testo: From Middle English musician, musicien, from Old French musicien (“musician”), equivalent to musike + -ien. By surface analysis, music + -ician.

parole.significato: A greasy secretion with a powerful odour, produced in a glandular sac of the male musk deer and used in the manufacture…
parole.testo: From Middle English muske, borrowed from Old French musc, from Late Latin muscus, from Ancient Greek μόσχος (móskhos), from Middle Persian [script needed] (mwšk' /⁠muʃk⁠/) whence Persian مشک (mošk). Ultimately from Sanskrit मुष्क (muṣka, “testicle”), the shape of the gland of animals secreting the s

parole.significato: The property of being stale or musty.
parole.testo: From Middle English must, from Old English must and Old French must, most, both from Latin mustum.

parole.significato: Of a dark yellow colour.
parole.testo: From Middle English mustard, from Old French moustarde (French moutarde), from moust (“must”), from Latin mustum. Compare Saterland Frisian Muster (“mustard”), Dutch mosterd (“mustard”), German Low German Musterd (“mustard”), Icelandic mustarður (“mustard”). Displaced Middle English senep, from Old

parole.significato: The quality or state of being mutable.
parole.testo: From Middle English mutabilite, from Old French mutabilite, from Latin mutabilitas; equivalent to mutable + -ity.

parole.significato: Changeable, dynamic, evolutive; inclined to change, evolve, mutate.
parole.testo: From Middle English mutable, from Old French mutable, from Latin mutabilis (“liable to change”). By surface analysis, muta- + -able.

parole.significato: The meat of sheep used as food; especially, that of adults.
parole.testo: From Middle English motoun, moton, from Old French mouton (“sheep”), from Vulgar Latin moltō, from Gaulish *multon-, from Proto-Celtic *moltos (“ram, wether”). Doublet of mouton.

parole.significato: The protruding part of an animal's head which includes the nose, mouth and jaws.
parole.testo: From earlier muzle, musle, mousle, mussel, mozell, from Middle English mosel, from Old French musel, museau, muzeau (modern French museau), from Late Latin mūsus (“snout”), probably expressive of the shape of protruded lips and/or influenced by Latin mūgīre (“to moo, bellow”). Doublet of museau. Dis

parole.significato: An evergreen shrub or small tree of the genus Myrtus, native to southern Europe and north Africa.
parole.testo: From Middle English mirtille, from Old French mirtille, mirtile, from myrte, from Latin myrtillus, from myrtus + -illus, from Ancient Greek μύρτος (múrtos, “myrtle”).

parole.significato: Of, or relating to mystics, mysticism or occult mysteries; mystical.
parole.testo: From Old French mistique, from Latin mysticus, from Ancient Greek μυστικός (mustikós, “secret, mystic”), from μύστης (mústēs, “one who has been initiated”). Doublet of mystique.

parole.significato: The beliefs, ideas, or thoughts of mystics.
parole.testo: From mystic + -ism, from Old French mistique (“mysterious, full of mystery”), from Latin mysticus (“mystical, mystic, of secret rites”), from Ancient Greek μυστικός (mustikós, “secret, mystic”), from μύστης (mústēs, “one who has been initiated, initiate”) from μῡ́ω (mū́ō, “to close one's lips or eye

parole.significato: A small drum, of Arabic origin, and the forebear of the European kettledrum.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French nacaire, nacre (cognate with Italian nacchera, mediaeval Latin nacara), ultimately derived from Arabic نَقَّارَة (naqqāra, “drum”). Doublet of nacre.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: The back part of the neck.
parole.testo: From Middle English nape, naape, of uncertain origin. Possibly from Old French hanap (“goblet”), from Frankish *hnapp, from Proto-Germanic *hnappaz ( > Old English hnæpp, hnæp (“cup, bowl, goblet”)), as there is a hollow at the base of the skull. More at nap.

parole.significato: A tablecloth.
parole.testo: From Middle English nape, from Old French nape, nappe (“a cloth”), from Medieval Latin nappa, napa (“cloth, table-cloth, sheet”), alteration of Latin mappa (“a cloth, napkin, towel”). More at map, apron. Doublet of map, mop, and nappe.

parole.significato: A flowering plant of species Nardostachys jatamansi, in the valerian family, that grows in the Himalayas and is used as…
parole.testo: From Middle English narde, from Old French narde, Latin nardus, from Ancient Greek νάρδος (nárdos), from Phoenician [Term?], Sanskrit नलद (nálada, “Indian narde”). Doublet of nardus.

parole.significato: The rump of beef, especially the lower and back part of the rump.
parole.testo: From Old French nache, Late Latin natica, from Latin natis (“the rump, buttocks”). Compare aitchbone.

parole.significato: A historically constituted, stable community of people, formed based on a common language, territory, economic life, et…
parole.testo: From Middle English nacioun, nacion, from Old French nacion, from Latin nātiōnem, accusative of nātiō (“nation”). Displaced Old English þēod.

parole.significato: A person who is native to a place; a person who was born in a place.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English natif, from Old French natif, from Latin nātīvus, from nātus (“birth”). Doublet of naive and neif. Displaced native Middle English thedisch, equivalent to (puristic) theed + -ish. By surface analysis, Latin nat- + -ive. Compare also inborn.

parole.significato: Existing in nature.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English natural, borrowed from Old French natural, naturel, from Latin nātūrālis, from nātus, the perfect participle of nāscor (“be born”, verb). Displaced native Old English ġecynde. By surface analysis, natur(e) + -al.

parole.significato: The condition of being natural; nature, naturalness
parole.testo: From Middle English naturalitee, from Old French naturalité, from Latin nātūrālitās.

parole.significato: The way things are, the totality of all things in the physical universe and their order, especially the physical world…
parole.testo: From Middle English nature, natur, from Old French nature, from Latin nātūra (“birth, origin, natural constitution or quality”), future participle from perfect passive participle (g)natus (“born”), from deponent verb (g)nasci (“to be born, originate”) + future participle suffix -urus. Displaced nati

parole.significato: Required, essential, whether logically inescapable or needed in order to achieve a desired result or avoid some penalty.
parole.testo: From Middle English necessarye, from Old French necessaire, from Latin necessārius (“unavoidable, inevitable, required”), variant of necesse (“unavoidable, inevitable”), probably from ne or non cessum, from the perfect passive participle of cēdō (“yield; avoid, withdraw”); see cede. Older use as a n

parole.significato: The quality or state of being necessary, unavoidable, or absolutely requisite.
parole.testo: From Middle English necessite, from Old French necessite, from Latin necessitās (“unavoidableness, compulsion, exigency, necessity”), from necesse (“unavoidable, inevitable”); see necessary. Doublet of Necessitas.

parole.significato: Divination involving the dead or death.
parole.testo: Circa 1300, from Middle English nigromancye, from Old French nigromancie, from Medieval Latin nigromantia, from Latin necromantia, from Ancient Greek νεκρομαντεία (nekromanteía), νεκρός (nekrós, “dead”) + μαντεία (manteía, “divination”). Medieval Latin spelling, incorporating niger (“black”), influe

parole.significato: The act of negating something.
parole.testo: From Middle English negacioun, from Old French negacion, from Latin negātiō (“a denial; negative word”). Morphologically negate + -ion.

parole.significato: Not positive or neutral; bad; undesirable; unfavourable.
parole.testo: From Middle English negative, negatif, from Old French negatif, from Latin negātīvus (“that denies, negative”), from negāre (“to deny”); see negate.

parole.significato: The state of being negligent.
parole.testo: From Middle English necligence, negligence, from Old French negligence, from Latin neglegentia.

parole.significato: Careless or inattentive.
parole.testo: From Middle English necligent, negligent, from Old French negligent, from Latin negligēns.

parole.significato: A son of one's sibling, brother-in-law, or sister-in-law; either a son of one's brother (fraternal nephew) or a son of…
parole.testo: From Middle English nevew, neveu (“nephew, grandson”), from Old French neveu, from Latin nepos, nepōtem, from Proto-Italic *nepōts (“nephew, grandson”), whence also French neveu, Italian nipote. Displaced or absorbed the inherited English neve (“nephew, grandson, male cousin”), from Middle English n

parole.significato: Free from extraneous substances; pure; unadulterated; neat.
parole.testo: From Middle English net, nette, from Old French net, from Latin nitidus. Doublet of neat and nitid.

parole.significato: Pleasant, satisfactory, complimentary.
parole.testo: From Middle English nyce, nice, nys, from Old French nice, niche, nisce (“simple, foolish, ignorant”), from Latin nescius (“ignorant, not knowing”); compare nesciō (“to know not, be ignorant of”), from ne (“not”) + sciō (“to know”).

parole.significato: A small detail or distinction.
parole.testo: From Middle English nicetee, from Old French niceté (“simpleness, foolishness”), from nice (“simple, foolish”); equivalent to nice + -e- + -ty.

parole.significato: A daughter of one’s sibling, brother-in-law, or sister-in-law; either the daughter of one's brother ("fraternal niece")…
parole.testo: From Middle English nece (“niece, granddaughter”), from Old French nece (“niece, granddaughter”) (Modern French nièce (“niece”)) from Late Latin neptia, representing Latin neptis (“granddaughter”), from Proto-Indo-European *néptih₂ (“granddaughter, niece”). Doublet of nift.

parole.significato: A serf or bondsman born into servitude.
parole.testo: From Old French [Term?], from Latin nativus (“natural”). Doublet of naif and native.

parole.significato: Necromancy; magic involving death.
parole.testo: From Middle English nigromauncy, from Old French nigromancie, nigremance, from Late Latin nigromantia, a blend of niger (“black”) and necromantīa (“necromancy”). Compare black art.

parole.significato: A mineral form of potassium nitrate (saltpetre) used in making gunpowder.
parole.testo: From Middle English niter, nitere, nitre, nytre, from Old French nitre, from Latin nitrum (“native soda, natron”), from Ancient Greek νίτρον (nítron). Ultimately from Egyptian nṯrj (“natron”). Doublet of natron and trona. Compare also natrium, nitrogen. Compare reconstructed Proto-Germanic *lauþrą (

parole.significato: without a doubt; surely.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English ne doute, a calque of Old French saunz doute, itself borrowed unadapted into Middle English.

parole.significato: A noble or privileged social class, historically accompanied by a hereditary title; aristocracy.
parole.testo: From Old French nobilité, from Latin nobilitas. Equivalent to noble + -ity.

parole.significato: An aristocrat; one of aristocratic blood.
parole.testo: From Middle English noble, from Old French noble, borrowed from Latin nōbilis (“knowable, known, well-known, famous, celebrated, high-born, of noble birth, excellent”), from nōscere, gnōscere (“to know”). False cognate of Arabic نبيل (nabīl). Displaced native Middle English athel, from Old English æ

parole.significato: Giving a name; naming; designating.
parole.testo: From Middle English nominatyf, either via Old French nominatif or directly from Latin nōminātīvus (“pertaining to naming, nominative”).

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of Normandy, France.
parole.testo: From Middle English Norman, from Old English Norman (a variant of Norþman) and Old French Normant. It is certain that the word is derived from the base of the Germanic words for north and the Germanic base of the words for man. However, given the frequent movement of Germanic groups especially into

parole.significato: The most northern of the English kings-of-arms, whose jurisdiction lay north of the Trent. Since 1943, the jurisdiction…
parole.testo: From Old French norht, north, nort (“north”) + roi (“king”), Anglo-Norman roy (“king”).

parole.significato: A lawyer of noncontentious private civil law who drafts, takes, and records legal instruments for private parties, and…
parole.testo: From Middle English notarie, from Old French notarie (French notaire), from Latin notārius.

parole.significato: A symbol or annotation.
parole.testo: From Middle English note, from Old English not, nōt (“note, mark, sign”) and Old French note (“letter, note”), both from Latin nota (“mark, sign, remark, note”).

parole.significato: To give (someone) notice (of some event).
parole.testo: From Middle English notifien, a borrowing from Old French notifier, notefiier.

parole.significato: A nurse.
parole.testo: From Middle English norischen, from Old French nouriss-, stem of one of the conjugated forms of norrir, from Latin nutriō (“to suckle, feed, foster, nourish, cherish, preserve, support”).

parole.significato: Newly made, formed or evolved; having no precedent; of recent origin; new.
parole.testo: From Middle English novel, from Old French novel (“new, fresh, recent, recently made or done, strange, rare”) (modern nouvel, nouveau), from Latin novellus (“new, fresh, young, modern”), diminutive of novus (“new”). Doublet of nouveau.

parole.significato: A novelty; something new.
parole.testo: From Middle English novel, from Old French novelle, from Latin novella, feminine of novellus.

parole.significato: Novelty; new things.
parole.testo: Old French novelerie.

parole.significato: The state of being new or novel; newness.
parole.testo: From Middle English novelte, from Old French novelté (Modern French nouveauté), from the adjective novel, ultimately from Latin novellus. By surface analysis, novel + -ty.

parole.significato: A person involved in providing direct care for the sick:
parole.testo: From Middle English norice, from Old French norrice, from Late Latin nūtrīcia, noun based on Latin nūtrīcius (“that which nourishes”), from nūtrīx (“wet nurse”), from nūtriō (“to suckle”).

parole.significato: The act of nourishing or nursing; tender care
parole.testo: From Middle English norture, noriture, from Old French norriture, norreture, from Late Latin nutritura (“nourishment”), from Latin nutrire (“to nourish”).

parole.significato: an eyas (a fledgling falcon)
parole.testo: From Old French niais (“bird from the nest”), from Latin nidus (“nest”).

parole.significato: Any female nature spirit associated with water, forests, grottos, wind, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English nimphe, from Old English nymphē and Old French nimphe, both from Latin nympha (“nymph, bride”), from Ancient Greek νύμφη (númphē, “bride, young maiden”). Doublet of nympha.

parole.significato: The vocative particle, used for direct address.
parole.testo: From Middle English O, o, from Old English o, from Latin o and Ancient Greek ὦ (ô, interjection). Featured prominently in William Tyndale's 1525 translation of the New Testament.

parole.significato: Willing to comply with the commands, orders, or instructions of those in authority; biddable.
parole.testo: From Middle English obedient, from Old French obedient, from Latin oboediēns, present active participle of oboediō (“obey”).

parole.significato: Demonstration of an obedient attitude, especially by bowing deeply; a deep bow which demonstrates such an attitude.
parole.testo: From Middle English obeisaunce (“obedience, obeisance”), from Old French obeïssance, derived from obeïssant (“obedient”), participle of obeïr (“to obey”), from Latin oboediō, obēdiō; ob- (“to, for”) + audiō (“to hear”). Cognate with obedience.

parole.significato: A thing that has physical existence but is not alive.
parole.testo: From Old French object, from Medieval Latin obiectum (“object”, literally “thrown against”), from obiectus, perfect passive participle of obiciō (“to throw against”), from ob- (“against”) + iaciō (“to throw”), as a calque of Ancient Greek ἀντικείμενον (antikeímenon). Doublet of objectum and objet.

parole.significato: The offering of worship, thanks etc. to a deity.
parole.testo: From Middle English oblacioun, from Old French oblacion, from Latin oblātiō (“offering”), from offerō (“to offer, present”). By surface analysis, oblate + -ion.

parole.significato: The act of binding oneself by a social, legal, or moral tie to someone.
parole.testo: From Middle English obligacioun, from Old French obligacion, from Latin obligatio, obligationem, from obligatum (past participle of obligare), from ob- (“to”) + ligare (“to bind”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵ- (“to bind”).

parole.significato: To constrain someone by force or by social, moral or legal means.
parole.testo: From Middle English obligen, from Old French obligier, obliger, from Latin obligō, obligāre, from ob- + ligō. Doublet of obligate, taken straight from Latin.

parole.significato: Dark, faint or indistinct.
parole.testo: From Middle English obscure, from Old French obscur, from Latin obscūrus (“dark, dusky, indistinct”), from ob- + *scūrus, from Proto-Italic *skoiros, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ḱeh₃-. Doublet of oscuro.

parole.significato: The last office for the dead.
parole.testo: From Middle English obseque, from Old French obseque, osseque, from Latin obsequiī (“complaisant, yielding”), alteration of obsequia (“compliance”) (by confusion, in association with exsequia (“funeral rites”), from exsequī (“follow or accompany to the grave”)).

parole.significato: The practice of complying with a law, custom, command or rule.
parole.testo: From Old French observance, from Latin observantia. Equivalent of observe + -ance.

parole.significato: Something that impedes, stands in the way of, or holds up progress, either physically or figuratively
parole.testo: From Middle English obstacle, from Old French obstacle, from Latin obstāculum.

parole.significato: The part of the horizon where the sun last appears in the evening; that part of the earth towards the sunset; the west.
parole.testo: From Middle English occident, from Old French occident, from Latin occidentem (“western sky, part of the sky in which the sun sets”), from occido (“go down, set”).

parole.significato: To take or use.
parole.testo: From Middle English occupien, occupyen, borrowed from Old French occuper, from Latin occupāre (“to take possession of, seize, occupy, take up, employ”), from ob (“to, on”) + capiō (“to take”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to seize, grab”). Doublet of occupate, now obsolete.

parole.significato: One of the large bodies of water separating the continents.
parole.testo: From Middle English *ocean, occean, occian, occyan, from Old French occean (later reborrowed or reinforced by Middle French ocean), from Latin Ōceanus, originally from Ancient Greek Ὠκεανός (Ōkeanós, “Oceanus”, a water deity). Displaced native Old English gārseċġ. Also commonly referred to as the oc

parole.significato: A clay earth pigment containing silica, aluminum and ferric oxide.
parole.testo: From Old French ocre and its source Latin ōchra, from Ancient Greek ὤχρα (ṓkhra, “pale yellow”), from ὠχρός (ōkhrós, “pale, ocher”) (modern Greek ωχρός (ochrós)).

parole.significato: A type of ale traditionally brewed in October.
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French octobre, from Latin Octōber (“eighth month”), from Latin octō (“eight”), from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw (“twice four”); + Latin -ber, from -bris, an adjectival suffix; October was the eighth month in the Roman calendar.

parole.significato: Arousing or meriting strong dislike, aversion, or intense displeasure.
parole.testo: From Middle English odious, from Old French odieus, from Latin odiōsus, from odium (“hate”).

parole.significato: The act of offending.
parole.testo: From Middle English offence, from Old French offense, from Latin offensa (“a striking against; displeasure; injury”).

parole.significato: Assault; attack, offensive; offense.
parole.testo: From Old French [Term?], from Latin offensio (“an offense”).

parole.significato: To propose or express one's willingness (to do something).
parole.testo: From Middle English offren, offrien. In the religious senses inherited from Old English offrian (“to offer, sacrifice, bring an oblation”); otherwise from Old French ofrir. Both ultimately from Latin offerō (“to present, bestow, bring before”, literally “to bring to”), from Latin ob + ferō (“bring,

parole.significato: To provide (someone) with an office.
parole.testo: From Middle English office, from Old French office, from Latin officium (“personal, official, or moral duty; official position; function; ceremony, esp. last rites”), contracted from opificium (“construction: the act of building or the thing built”), from opifex (“doer of work, craftsman”) + -ium (“

parole.significato: Of or about an office or public trust.
parole.testo: From Middle English official, from Old French official, from Latin officiālis, from Latin officium (“duty, service”), by surface analysis, office + -ial.

parole.significato: A double curve in the shape of an elongated S; an object of that shape.
parole.testo: From Middle English *ogeve, egeve, egeove, from Old French œgive, ogive, augive, from Late Latin augiva, of uncertain origin; compare Late Latin ogis (“a support, prop”), Latin augeō (“to increase, strengthen”), Italian and Spanish auge (“highest point of power or fortune, apogee”). Doublet of ogive

parole.significato: The curve of a cumulative distribution function.
parole.testo: From late Middle English ogif, egeve, egeove, from Old French ogive, œgive, augive. Doublet of ogee.

parole.significato: Expression of surprise.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English o.

parole.significato: Liquid fat.
parole.testo: From Middle English oyle, oile (“olive oil”), borrowed from Old French oile, from Latin oleum (“oil, olive oil”), from Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion, “olive oil”), from ἐλαία (elaía, “olive”). Compare Proto-Slavic *lojь. More at olive. Doublet of oleum. Supplanted Middle English ele (“oil”), from Old

parole.significato: A viscous preparation of oils and/or fats, usually containing medication, used as a treatment or as an emollient.
parole.testo: A later form (as if oint + -ment) of Middle English oinement, borrowed from Old French oignement (“an anointing”), from oigner, oindre, ongier (“to anoint”), from Latin ung(u)ō (“I anoint”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃engʷ- (“to smear, anoint”). Partly displaced native Old English sealf, whence mod

parole.significato: An ancient hunting horn, made of ivory.
parole.testo: From Middle English olifaunt, from Old French oliphaunt, from Latin elephantus. See elephant.

parole.significato: elephant
parole.testo: From Middle English oliphaunt, olifaunt, from Old French olifant, from Latin elephantus; see elephant for more information.

parole.significato: Drunk, pissed.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Oliver, from Old French Olivier, by folk etymology derived from the Latin name Olīvārius, but probably representing an Old High German form of Old Norse Óleifr (“ancestral + relic”) (modern Danish Olaf and Swedish Olof), or Proto-Germanic *ala- (“all”) + *wēraz (“true”)

parole.significato: The act of omitting.
parole.testo: From Middle English omissioun, from Old French omission, from Late Latin omissio, omissionem, from Latin omitto.

parole.significato: Unlimited power; commonly attributed to a deity or deities.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English omnipotens, from Old French omnipotence, from Latin omnipotentia.

parole.significato: Having unlimited power, force or authority.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English omnipotent(e), from Old French omnipotent, from Latin omnipotēns, omnipotentem.

parole.significato: A banded variety of chalcedony, a cryptocrystalline form of quartz.
parole.testo: From Middle English onix (c. 1300), earlier oniche (c. 1250), from Old French oniche or onix, from Latin onyx, from Ancient Greek ὄνυξ (ónux, “onyx”). Doublet of unguis.

parole.significato: The method by which a device performs its function.
parole.testo: From Middle English operacioun, from Old French operacion, from Latin operātiō, from the verb operor (“to work”), from opus, operis (“work”). Equivalent to operate + -ion.

parole.significato: An opinionated person.
parole.testo: Old French opiniastre

parole.significato: Suitable for some particular purpose.
parole.testo: From Old French opportun, from Latin opportunus.

parole.significato: To attempt to stop the progression of; to resist or antagonize by physical means, or by arguments, etc.; to contend aga…
parole.testo: From Middle English opposen, from Old French opposer, from Latin ob (“before, against”) + Medieval Latin pono (“to put”), taking the place of Latin opponere (“to oppose”).

parole.significato: Located directly across from something else, or from each other.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English opposit, borrowed from Old French oposite, from Latin oppositus, perfect passive participle of oppōnō (“to oppose”). Compare oppose.

parole.significato: The action of opposing or of being in conflict.
parole.testo: From Middle English opposicioun, from Old French oposicion (whence French opposition), from Late Latin oppositiō, translating Ancient Greek ἀντίθεσις (antíthesis), from the past participle stem of classical Latin oppōnō (“to set against”). Equivalent to oppose + -ition.

parole.significato: To keep down by unjust force.
parole.testo: From Middle English oppressen, from Old French oppresser, from Medieval Latin oppressare (“to press against, oppress”), frequentative of Latin opprimere, past participle oppressus (“to press against, press together, oppress”), from ob (“against”) + premere, past participle pressus (“to press”); see

parole.significato: The exercise of authority or power in a burdensome, cruel, or unjust manner.
parole.testo: From Middle English oppression, from Old French oppression, from Latin oppressiō (“a pressing down, violence, oppression”), from opprimō; see oppress.

parole.significato: Someone who oppresses another or others.
parole.testo: From Middle English oppressour, from Old French opressor and Latin oppressor; equivalent to oppress + -or.

parole.significato: A shrine dedicated to some prophetic deity.
parole.testo: From Middle English oracle, from Old French oracle m, from Latin ōrāculum n.

parole.significato: A spherical body; a sphere, especially one of the celestial spheres; a sun, planet, or star
parole.testo: From Middle English orbe, from Old French orbe, from Latin orbis (“circle, orb”). Compare orbit.

parole.significato: A blank window or panel.
parole.testo: From Old French orb (“blind”), from Latin orbus (“destitute”).

parole.significato: To prearrange unalterably.
parole.testo: From Middle English ordeynen, from Old French ordiner, from Latin ordinare (“to order”), from ordo (“order”). Doublet of ordinate.

parole.significato: Arrangement, disposition, or sequence.

parole.significato: To supply with an organ or organs; to fit with organs.

parole.significato: Someone who tends to a flock of animals: synonym of shepherd.
parole.testo: From Middle English pastour, from Old French pastor (Modern French pasteur), from Latin pāstor.

parole.significato: A baked food item made from flour and fat pastes such as pie crust; also tarts, bear claws, napoleons, puff pastries, e…
parole.testo: From Middle English pastre, pastri, from pastree (variant of pasterie, from Old French pastaierie and Medieval Latin pasteria, from Late Latin pasta, from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá)) or paste + -ri (modern paste + -ry).

parole.significato: The plate used to hold the host during the Eucharist.
parole.testo: From Middle English patene, from Old French patene, from Latin patina, from Ancient Greek πατάνη (patánē). Doublet of patina, patine, and patena.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to one's father, his genes, his relatives, or his side of a family.
parole.testo: From Old French paternal (“of a father”) (12th c.), from Vulgar Latin paternālis (“paternal”), from Latin paternus (“of or pertaining to a father, paternal”), from pater (“father”).

parole.significato: The quality of being patient.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English pacience, from Old French pacience (modern French patience), from Latin patientia (“suffering; endurance, patience”), from patiens, present active participle of patior (“suffer, experience, wait”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₁- (“to hurt”). Displaced Old En

parole.significato: One who protects or supports; a defender or advocate.
parole.testo: From Middle English patroun, patrone, from Old French patron, from Latin patrōnus, derived from pater (“father”). Doublet of padrone, Patronus, patroon, and pattern.

parole.significato: The act of providing approval and support; backing; championship.
parole.testo: From Middle English patronage, from Old French patronage (modern French patronage). Equivalent to patron + -age. Piecewise doublet of patternage.

parole.significato: Any of various types of footwear with thick soles, often used to elevate the foot, especially wooden clogs.
parole.testo: From Middle English patyn, patin, pateyn, from Old French patin, from patte (“paw, hoof”), from Latin patta, of imitative origin.

parole.significato: Model, example.
parole.testo: From earlier patten, paterne, from Middle English patron (“patron; example”), from Old French patron, from Medieval Latin patrōnus (“patron”). Doublet of padrone, patron, Patronus, and patroon.

parole.significato: A piece of armour which covers the abdomen or lower body.
parole.testo: From Middle English paunce, from Old French pance, Middle French pans. Doublet of paunch.

parole.significato: To cover something with paving slabs.
parole.testo: From Old French paver (“to pave, to cover”), from Vulgar Latin *pavāre (“to beat down, to smash”), from Latin pavīre (“to beat, strike, ram, tread down”).

parole.significato: The state of being held as security for a loan, or as a pledge.
parole.testo: From Middle English paun, pawyn, pawnd, from Old French pan, pant (“pledge for a payment”), from a Germanic language, perhaps Frankish *pand (“deposit, security, pledge”), further origin uncertain. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Pound (“deposit, pledge, pawn”), West Frisian pân (“pawn”), Dutch pand

parole.significato: To give money or other compensation to in exchange for goods or services.
parole.testo: From Middle English payen, from Old French paiier (“pay”), from Medieval Latin pācāre (“to settle, satisfy”) from Latin pācāre (“to pacify”). In this sense, displaced native Old English ġield (“pay”) and ġieldan (“to pay”), whence Modern English yield.

parole.significato: To cover (the bottom of a vessel, a seam, a spar, etc.) with tar or pitch, or a waterproof composition of tallow, resin…
parole.testo: From Old French peier, from Latin picāre (“to cover with pitch”).

parole.significato: The act of paying.
parole.testo: From Old French paiement. Equivalent to pay + -ment.

parole.significato: Any tree of species Prunus persica, native to China and now widely cultivated throughout temperate regions, having pink…
parole.testo: From Middle English peche, borrowed from Old French pesche (French pêche), Vulgar Latin *pessica (cf. Medieval Latin pesca) from Late Latin persica, from Classical Latin mālum persicum, from Ancient Greek μᾶλον περσικόν (mâlon persikón, “Persian apple”). Displaced Middle English persogȝe, from Old E

parole.significato: A loud sound, or a succession of loud sounds, as of bells, thunder, cannon, shouts, laughter, of a multitude, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English pele, peil, probably an apheretic variant of Middle English apel, appel, from Old French apel (“an appeal; pealing of bells”). Compare appeal.

parole.significato: To set or adorn with pearls, or with mother-of-pearl.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English perle, from Old French perle of uncertain etymology. Probably via unattested Medieval Latin *pernula, from Latin perna (“haunch; a marine bivalve shaped like a leg of lamb”) but also derived from Medieval Latin perla, from Latin perula (“little bag”). Its typographic us

parole.significato: To remove the skin or outer covering of.
parole.testo: From Middle English pelen, from Old English pilian and Old French peler, pellier; both from Latin pilō, pilāre (“to remove hair from, depilate”), from pilus (“hair”). Doublet of pill.

parole.significato: A shovel or similar instrument, now especially a pole with a flat disc at the end used for removing pizza or loaves of…
parole.testo: From Middle English pele, from Old French pele (modern French pelle), from Latin pāla, from the base of plangō (“fix, plant”). Doublet of pala.

parole.significato: To plunder; to pillage, rob.
parole.testo: From Old French piller (“pillage”).

parole.significato: Peers as a group; the titled nobility or aristocracy.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English perage, from Old French parage. By surface analysis, peer + -age. Doublet of parage.

parole.significato: Constantly complaining, especially in a childish way due to insignificant matters; fretful, whiny.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English pievish, peuysche, pevish, pevysh (“capricious, wilful; perverse, wayward”); further etymology uncertain, possibly from one of the following: * From an unattested Old French word, from Latin perversus (“corrupted, perverted, subverted; overthrown”),

parole.significato: Pain or punishment.
parole.testo: From Old French peine, from Latin poena, from Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ, “penalty, fine, bloodmoney”). Doublet of pain.

parole.significato: A pilgrim.
parole.testo: From Middle English pelerin, from Old French pelerin, from Latin peregrīnus (“foreigner, traveler”). Doublet of pilgrim.

parole.significato: A small, compressed, hard chunk of matter.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English pelote, pelet, from Old French pelote (“small ball”), from Vulgar Latin *pilotta, diminutive of Latin pila (“ball”). Doublet of pelota.

parole.significato: Pelts or skins, collectively; skins with the fur on them; furs.
parole.testo: From Old French peleterie, the trade of a skinner or peltmonger (peletier). Equivalent to pelt + -ry.

parole.significato: Of or relating to punishment.
parole.testo: From Old French peinal, from Medieval Latin penalis, from Latin poenalis, from poena (“punishment”), from Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ, “punishment”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷoynéh₂.

parole.significato: Capable of being penetrated, entered, or pierced.
parole.testo: From Middle English penetrable, penytrable, from Old French penetrable, from Medieval Latin penetrābilis.

parole.significato: The act of penetrating something.
parole.testo: From Middle English penetracioun, from Old French penetracïon, and its source, Latin penetrātiō, from the participle stem of penetrō (“pierce”, verb). Morphologically penetrate + -ion.

parole.significato: painstaking; assiduous
parole.testo: From Middle English penyble, from Old French peinible. Compare painable.

parole.significato: The condition of being penitent; a feeling of regret or remorse for doing wrong or sinning.
parole.testo: First attested circa 13th century, from Middle English penitence, from Old French penitence, from Latin paenitentia (“repentance, penitence”), from paenitēns (“penitent”), present active participle of paeniteō (“regret, repent”). Equivalent to penitent + -ence. Doublet of penance.

parole.significato: Feeling pain or sorrow on account of one's sins or offenses; feeling sincere guilt.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin paenitēns, poenitēns (“penitent”), present participle of paeniteō, poeniteō (“to cause to repent; to regret, repent”). Doublet of penitente.

parole.significato: A flag normally used by naval vessels to represent a special condition.
parole.testo: From Middle English penon, penoun, pynoun, Old French penon, French pennon, from Latin penna (“feather”). See pen (“a feather”), and compare pennon, pinion.

parole.significato: A small pennon (a thin flag or streamer).
parole.testo: From Middle English penoncel, from Old French penuncel, diminutive of penon (“pennon”). See pennon, pennant. By surface analysis, pen + French -on (“diminutive”) + Old French -cel (“diminutive”).

parole.significato: Engaged in, involving, or reflecting deep or serious thought.
parole.testo: From Middle English pensif, pensyfe, pencyve, from Old French pensif (“thoughtful”), from penser (“to think”) (from Latin pēnsō) + -if (English -ive).

parole.significato: Denoting the sense "by" or "per", as in perchance or perhaps.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English per-.

parole.significato: Perchance or maybe; perhaps; supposing.
parole.testo: From Middle English peraventure, peradventure, from Old French par aventure. Spelling modified as though from Latin. Equivalent to per- + adventure.

parole.significato: To become aware of, through the physical senses, to see; to understand.
parole.testo: From Middle English perceyven, borrowed from Old French percevoir, perceveir, from Latin percipiō, past participle perceptus (“take hold of, obtain, receive, observe”), from per (“by, through”) + capiō (“to take”); see capable. Compare conceive, deceive, receive.

parole.significato: Any of the three species of spiny-finned freshwater fish in the genus Perca.
parole.testo: From Middle English perche, from Old French perche, from Latin perca, from Ancient Greek πέρκη (pérkē, “perch”), cognate with περκνός (perknós, “dark-spotted”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *perḱ-, whence also Old English forn (“trout”), German Forelle (“trout”).

parole.significato: A rod, staff, tree branch, ledge, etc., used as a roost by a bird.
parole.testo: From Middle English perche, from Old French perche, from Latin pertica (“staff, long pole, measuring rod”).

parole.significato: Perhaps.
parole.testo: From Middle English parchaunce, from Old French par cheance (“by chance”).

parole.significato: Eternal damnation.
parole.testo: From Middle English perdicioun, from Old French perdiciun, from Late Latin perditio, from Latin perdo (“to destroy, to lose”).

parole.significato: The state of being perdurable.
parole.testo: From Middle English perdurabilite, perdurablete, perdurablyte, perduralite, from Old French pardurablete; equivalent to perdure + -ability.

parole.significato: Very durable; long-lasting.
parole.testo: From Middle English perdurable, from Old French pardurable, from Medieval Latin perdūrābilis, from Latin perdurāre (“to endure”), from per- (“throughout”) + durare (“to last”).

parole.significato: Fully equal.
parole.testo: From Middle English peregal, from Old French par egal (“in the same way”).

parole.significato: Wandering, travelling, migratory.
parole.testo: From Middle English peregrin, borrowed from Old French peregrin, from Latin peregrīnus (“foreign”). Doublet of pilgrim.

parole.significato: Fitting its definition precisely.
parole.testo: From Middle English perfit, from Old French parfit (modern: parfait), from Latin perfectus, perfect passive participle of perficere (“to finish”), from per- (“through, thorough”) + facere (“to do, to make”). The spelling was modified in the 15th century to conform to its Latin etymon. Doublet of par

parole.significato: The quality or state of being perfect or complete, so that nothing substandard remains; the highest attainable state or…
parole.testo: From Middle English perfeccioun, from Old French perfection, from Latin perfectiō. By surface analysis, perfect + -ion. Displaced native Old English fulfremednes.

parole.significato: A situation of serious and immediate danger.
parole.testo: From Middle English peril, from Old French peril, from Latin perīculum. Doublet of periculum.

parole.significato: To decay and disappear; to waste away to nothing.
parole.testo: From Middle English perishen, borrowed from Old French perir (via the stem periss- used in various conjugations), from Latin perīre (“pass away, perish”), from per (“through”) + īre (“pass, go”).

parole.significato: To knowingly and willfully make a false statement of witness while in court.
parole.testo: From Old French parjurer, from Latin periūrō.

parole.significato: permitted.
parole.testo: From Middle English permyssyble, from Old French permissible, from Medieval Latin permissibilis.

parole.significato: One of the ways something exists, or the ways a set of objects can be ordered.
parole.testo: From Middle English permutacioun, permutacyoun, from Old French permutacïon, promutatïon and Medieval Latin permūtātiōnem, accusative of permūtātiō. Morphologically permute + -ation.

parole.significato: To change the order of.
parole.testo: From Middle English permuten, from Old French permuter, from Latin permūtāre.

parole.significato: Causing much harm in a subtle way.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French pernicios, from Latin perniciōsus (“destructive”), from perniciēs (“destruction”), from per (“through”) + nex (“slaughter, death”).

parole.significato: Lasting forever, or for an indefinitely long time.
parole.testo: From Middle English perpetuel, from Old French perpetuel, from Latin perpetuālis (“universal”), from perpetuus, from petō.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being perpetual; endless duration; uninterrupted existence.
parole.testo: From Middle English perpetuitee, perpetuite, perpetuyte, from Old French perpetüité, ultimately from Latin perpetuitās.

parole.significato: To cause to feel baffled; to puzzle.
parole.testo: From Old French, from Latin perplexus (“entangled, confused”), from per (“through”) + plexus, perfect passive participle of plectō (“plait, weave, braid”).

parole.significato: A short mortar used for throwing stone shot.
parole.testo: Old French perriere, perrier, French perrière, pierrier. Compare pederero.

parole.significato: A fermented alcoholic beverage made from pears, similar to hard apple cider.
parole.testo: From Middle English perre; from Old French peré; from Vulgar Latin *piratum; from Latin pirum.

parole.significato: A very dark (almost black) purple or blue-gray colour.
parole.testo: From Middle English pers, from Old French, from Medieval Latin persus, back-formed from Persicus (“Persian”), from Ancient Greek Περσικός (Persikós). Compare peach.

parole.significato: The act of persecuting, especially a specific group of people; an instance of persecution.
parole.testo: Equivalent to persecute + -ion. From Middle English persecucioun, from Old French persecucion, from Ecclesiastical Latin persecūtio (“persecution; chase, pursuit”), from Latin persequor (“follow up, pursue”), from per- (“through”) + sequor (“follow”). Displaced native Old English ēhtnes.

parole.significato: A person or thing that persecutes or harasses.
parole.testo: From Middle English persecutour, from Old French persecutor and Latin persecūtor. Displaced native Old English ēhtere.

parole.significato: Continuing in a course of action without regard to discouragement, opposition or previous failure.
parole.testo: From Middle English perseveraunce, from Old French perseverance, from Latin persevērantia.

parole.significato: To persist steadfastly in pursuit of an undertaking, task, journey, or goal, even if hindered by distraction, difficult…
parole.testo: From Middle English perseveren, from Old French perseverer, from Latin persevērāre (“to continue steadfastly, persist, persevere”), from perseverus (“very strict or earnest”), from per (“through, by the means of”) + severus (“strict, earnest”). Doublet of perseverate.

parole.significato: A view, vista or outlook.
parole.testo: From Middle English perspective, perspectif, attested since 1381, from Old French or Middle French, from the first word of the Medieval Latin perspectiva ars (“science of optics”), the feminine of Latin perspectivus (“of sight, optical”), from perspectus, the past participle of perspicere (“to inspe

parole.significato: To belong to or be connected as a part, adjunct, attribute, or accessory.
parole.testo: From Middle English pertenen, from Old French partenir, pertenir (modern French appartenir), in turn from Latin pertineō, pertinēre.

parole.significato: Holding tenaciously to an opinion or purpose.
parole.testo: From pertinace + -ious, from Old French pertinace, from Latin pertinax, from per- (“very”) + tenax (“tenacious”).

parole.significato: A right that attaches to land, in Scots law.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English pertinent, borrowed from Old French pertinent and Latin pertinēns, pertinentem.

parole.significato: Turned aside while against something, splitting off from a thing.
parole.testo: From Middle English perverse, pervers, from Old French pervers, from Latin perversum (“thoroughly turned”), past participle of pervertere, from per- (“thoroughly”) + vertere (“to turn”).

parole.significato: One who has been perverted; one who has turned to error, or adopted a twisted sense of values or morals.
parole.testo: From Old French pervertir, itself from the Latin pervertō.

parole.significato: A medical device similar to the outer ring of a contraceptive diaphragm, most commonly used to support a displaced uter…
parole.testo: From Middle English pessarie, from Old French pessaire, from Latin pessarium.

parole.significato: Any epidemic disease that is highly contagious, infectious, virulent and devastating.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin pestilentia (“plague”), from pestilens (“infected, unwholesome, noxious”); equivalent to pestilent + -ence.

parole.significato: A club-shaped, round-headed stick used in a mortar to pound, crush, rub or grind things.
parole.testo: From Middle English pestel, pestell, from Old French pestel, from Latin pistillum, from pīnsō (“pound, beat”). Doublet of pistil and pistillum.

parole.significato: Petite: small, little.
parole.testo: From Middle English petit, from Old French petit, from Late Latin *pitittus, diminutive of Latin *pit-, possibly from Proto-Celtic *pett- (“part, bit, piece”) (see Latin pettia), or of imitative origin. Compare also Latin pitinnus (“small”), pitulus, Italian pezza. Doublet of petty.

parole.significato: A formal written request made by an individual or a group of people to a sovereign or political authority, often contai…
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French peticiun, from stem of Latin petitio, petitionem (“a request, solicitation”), from petere (“to require, seek, go forward”).

parole.significato: One of the long benches in a church, seating several persons, usually fixed to the floor and facing the chancel.
parole.testo: From Middle English pewe, from Old French puiee, puïe (“balustrade, balcony”), from Latin podia, plural of podium (“parapet, podium”), from Ancient Greek πόδιον (pódion, “little foot”), from πούς (poús, “foot”). Doublet of podia.

parole.significato: An alloy of approximately 93–98% tin and 1–2% copper, and the balance of antimony.
parole.testo: From Middle English peutre, from Old French peautre, from Vulgar Latin *peltrum (“pewter”), which is of uncertain origin. Possibly related to spelter.

parole.significato: Something seen but having no physical reality; a phantom or apparition.
parole.testo: A learned variant of phantom; from Middle English fantosme, from Old French fantosme, fantasme, from Latin phantasma, from Ancient Greek φάντασμα (phántasma). Doublet of phantom.

parole.significato: Illusive.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English fantome, fanteme, from Old French fantosme, fantasme, from Latin phantasma (“an apparition, specter; (in Late Latin also) appearance, image”), from Ancient Greek φάντασμα (phántasma, “phantasm, an appearance, image, apparition, specter”), from φαντάζω (phantázō, “to mak

parole.significato: A bird of family Phasianidae, often hunted for food.
parole.testo: From Middle English fesaunt, fesant, from Old French fesan, from Latin phāsiānus, from Ancient Greek φᾱσιανός (phāsianós), meaning “[bird] of the river Φᾶσις (Phâsis)”, from where, it was supposed, the bird spread to the west. Replaced native Old English wōrhana, a variant of mōrhana. More at moorhe

parole.significato: A bearing representing the head of a dart or javelin, with long barbs which are engrailed on the inner edge.
parole.testo: Probably Old French.

parole.significato: A kind of transparent reliquary with an ornamental top, designed to exhibit bones.
parole.testo: From Old French filatiere, philatiere. See phylactery.

parole.significato: Synonym of philosophical.
parole.testo: From Middle English philosophik, phylosophyk, from Old French filosofique and Latin philosophicus; equivalent to philosophy + -ic.

parole.significato: An academic discipline that seeks truth through reasoning rather than empiricism, often attempting to provide explanati…
parole.testo: From Middle English philosophie, Old French philosophie, and their source, Latin philosophia, from Ancient Greek φιλοσοφία (philosophía), from φίλος (phílos, “loving”) + σοφία (sophía, “wisdom”). By surface analysis, philo- + -sophy. Displaced Old English ūþwitegung.

parole.significato: The opening of a vein, either to withdraw blood or for letting blood; venesection.
parole.testo: From Old French flebothomie (French phlébotomie), from Late Latin phlebotomia, from Ancient Greek φλεβοτόμος (phlebotómos, “that opens a vein”), from φλέψ (phléps, “vein”). By surface analysis, phlebo- + -tomy.

parole.significato: One of the four humors making up the body in ancient and mediaeval medicine; said to be cold and moist, and often ident…
parole.testo: From Middle English flewme, fleume, fleme, from Old French fleume, Middle French flemme (French flegme), and their source, Latin phlegma, from Ancient Greek φλέγμα (phlégma, “flame; inflammation; clammy humor in the body”), from φλέγειν (phlégein, “to burn”). Possible burning sensation when coughing

parole.significato: Not easily excited to action or passion; calm; sluggish.
parole.testo: From Middle English fleumatik, flewmatik, flematik, fleumatyke, flewmatyk, from Old French fleumatique, from Latin phlegmaticus, from Ancient Greek φλεγματικός (phlegmatikós), from φλέγμα (phlégma), referring to the humour which ancient Hippocratic and later Galenic medicine associated with mildness

parole.significato: A mythological bird, said to be the only one of its kind, which lives for 500 years and then dies by burning to ashes o…
parole.testo: From Old English and Old French fenix, from Medieval Latin phenix, from Latin phoenīx, from Ancient Greek φοῖνιξ (phoînix), from Egyptian b-n:nw*w-G31 (bnw, “grey heron”). Doublet of Bennu. The grey heron was venerated at Heliopolis and associated in Egypt with the cyclical renewal of life because t

parole.significato: A medicine or drug, especially a cathartic or purgative.
parole.testo: From Middle English fysike (noun) and phisiken, fisike (verb; from the noun), from Old French fisike (“natural science, art of healing”), from Latin physica (“study of nature”), from Ancient Greek φυσική (phusikḗ), feminine singular of φῠσῐκός (phŭsĭkós, “natural; physical”), see above.

parole.significato: A practitioner of physic, i.e. a specialist in internal medicine, especially as opposed to a surgeon; a practitioner wh…
parole.testo: From Middle English fisicien, from Old French fisicïen (“physician”) (modern French physicien (“physicist”)), from fisique (“art of healing”), from Latin physica (“natural science”), from Ancient Greek φυσική ἐπιστήμη (phusikḗ epistḗmē, “knowledge of nature”), from φυσικός (phusikós, “pertaining to

parole.significato: The branch of science concerned with the study of the properties and interactions of space, time, matter and energy.
parole.testo: 1580s; from physic (see also -ics), from Middle English phisik, from Old French fisike (“natural science, art of healing”), from Latin physica (“study of nature”), from Ancient Greek φυσική (phusikḗ), feminine singular of φυσικός (phusikós, “natural; physical”), from Ancient Greek φύσις (phúsis, “or

parole.significato: A poitrel, armor protecting a horse's chest.
parole.testo: From Middle English picer, piciere, from Old French piciere; compare modern French pissière.

parole.significato: A type of pastry that consists of an outer crust and a filling. (Savory pies are more popular in the UK and sweet pies…
parole.testo: From Middle English pye, pie, pey (“baked dish, filled pastry”), possibly attested earlier (c. 1199) in the surname Piehus (“pie-house?”). Further origin uncertain. Relation to Middle English pie, pye (“magpie”) has been suggested due to correspondences between other similar foods and the names of b

parole.significato: Magpie.
parole.testo: From Middle English pye, from Old French pie, from Latin pīca, feminine of pīcus (“woodpecker”). Doublet of pica and speight.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: A part of a larger whole, usually in such a form that it is able to be separated from other parts.
parole.testo: From Middle English pece, peece, peice, from Old French piece, from Late Latin pecia, petia (“broken piece, fragment; parcel of land”), of uncertain origin. Possibly ultimately from Gaulish *pettyā, from Proto-Celtic *kʷezdis (“piece, portion, quota”). Compare Welsh peth (“thing, stuff, junk”), Bret

parole.significato: Having two or more colors, especially black and white.
parole.testo: From archaic pie (“magpie”), from Old French pie, from Latin pica. Compare typologically Polish srokaty < sroka.

parole.significato: To puncture; to break through.
parole.testo: From Middle English perce, from conjugated forms of Old French percier such as (jeo) pierce (“I pierce”), probably from Vulgar Latin *pertūsiō, from Latin pertūsus, past participle of pertundō (“thrust or bore through”), from per- (“through”) + tundō (“beat, pound”). Displaced native Old English þȳr

parole.significato: One of several birds of the family Columbidae within the order Columbiformes.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English pygeoun, borrowed from Old French pyjon, inherited from Late Latin pīpiōnem (“chirping bird”), derived from Latin pīpiāre (“to chirp”), of imitative origin. Partly displaced native English dove.

parole.significato: A mass of things heaped together; a heap.
parole.testo: From Middle English pyle, from Old French pile, from Latin pīla (“pillar, pier”).

parole.significato: To steal in small quantities, or articles of small value; to practise petty theft.
parole.testo: From earlier pilfre, from Middle English pilfre (“booty”), from Old French pelfre (“plunder, booty, spoils”), of unknown origin. Compare pelf.

parole.significato: One who travels to visit a site of religious significance.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English pilegrim, from Old English pilegrī̆m, from Old French pelegrin, from Latin peregrīnus (“foreigner”). Doublet of peregrine. The change of /r…r/ to /l…r/ is an effect of dissimilation in early Romance; compare Italian pellegrino.

parole.significato: To loot or plunder by force, especially in time of war.
parole.testo: From Old French pillage, from piller (“plunder”), from an unattested meaning of Late Latin piliō, probably a figurative use of Latin pilō (“to remove (hair)”), from pilus (“hair”).

parole.significato: A large post, often used as supporting architecture.
parole.testo: From Middle English piler, from Old French pilier, from Medieval Latin or Vulgar Latin *pilāre (“a pillar”), from Latin pila (“a pillar, pier, mole”).

parole.significato: Any object that resembles one half of a pair of pincers.
parole.testo: From Middle English pynsor, from Old French pinceure, pinchure, from pincier (“to pinch”).

parole.significato: A gripping tool, pivoted like a pair of scissors, but with blunt jaws.
parole.testo: From Middle English pynsours, from Old French pinceure, pinchure, from pincier (“to pinch”).

parole.significato: A wing.
parole.testo: From Middle English pynyon, from Old French pignon, from Latin penna (“feather”).

parole.significato: The highest point.
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French pinacle, pinnacle, from Late Latin pinnāculum (“a peak, pinnacle”), from Latin pinna (“a pinnacle”); see pin. Doublet of panache.

parole.significato: A unit of volume, equivalent to:
parole.testo: From Middle English pinte, from Old French pinte, assumed from Vulgar Latin *pincta (“a mark used to indicate a level of quantity against a larger measure”), from Latin picta (“painted”), from Latin pingō (“paint”, verb). Doublet of pinto and Pinto.

parole.significato: A pippin, seed of any kind.
parole.testo: Apparently representing a shortened form of pippin, from Middle English pipin, from Old French pepin (“a seed”) (French pépin, q.v.).

parole.significato: A seed.
parole.testo: From Middle English pipin, from Old French pepin (“a seed”) (French pépin). See pip.

parole.significato: A criminal who plunders at sea; commonly attacking merchant vessels, though often pillaging port towns.
parole.testo: From Middle English pirate, pirat, pyrat, from Old French pirate, from Latin pīrāta (“pirate”), from Ancient Greek πειρατής (peiratḗs), from πεῖρα (peîra, “trial, attempt, plot”). Displaced native Old English wīċing, which was the word for both "pirate" and "viking".

parole.significato: A collar or gorget of mail (or, rarely, plate), protecting the neck and upper chest; a standard.
parole.testo: From Middle English pisan, from an Old French word variously spelled pizaine, pizane, pesine, etc, found also in phrases like colarete(s) pizaine, gorgerete(s) pizaine. Probably from Old French piz (“chest”), from Latin pectus, extended like in poitrine, although it has also been suggested that it c

parole.significato: Urine.
parole.testo: From Middle English pisse (noun) and pissen (verb), from Old French pissier, possibly from Vulgar Latin *pīssiāre, probably of imitative origin. Compare Old Norse pissa (“to urinate, piss”). Displaced Old English miċġe (“urine”) and mīgan (“to urinate”).

parole.significato: Provoking pity, compassion, or sympathy.
parole.testo: From Middle English pitous, from Old French piteus, pitus.

parole.significato: A small allowance of food and drink; a scanty meal.
parole.testo: From Middle English pitaunce, from Old French pitance, pitence, from Medieval Latin *pietāntia, from Latin pietās (“piety”).

parole.significato: A thing on which something turns; specifically a metal pointed pin or short shaft in machinery, such as the end of an a…
parole.testo: From Middle English pevet, *pivot, from Old French pivot (“hinge pin, pivot”) (12th c.), possibly from Latin pūgiō.

parole.significato: An area; somewhere within an area.
parole.testo: From Middle English place, conflation of Old English plæċe (“place, an open space, street”) and Old French place (“place, an open space”), both from Latin platēa (“plaza, wide street”), from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa), shortening of πλατεῖα ὁδός (plateîa hodós, “broad way”), from Proto-Indo-Eur

parole.significato: The bubonic plague, the pestilent disease caused by the virulent bacterium Yersinia pestis.
parole.testo: From Middle English plage, borrowed from Old French plage, from Latin plāga (“blow, wound”), from plangō (“to strike”). Cognate with Middle Dutch plāghe (> Dutch plaag), plāghen (> Dutch plagen); Middle Low German plāge; Middle High German plāge, pflāge (> German Plage); plāgen (> German plagen); Sw

parole.significato: Several similar marine flatfish of the righteye flounder family Pleuronectidae:
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English playce, plays, from Old French plaiz, from Late Latin platessa, from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “broad”). See platy-, plat and flat.

parole.significato: To level; to raze; to make plain or even on the surface.
parole.testo: From Old French plain, from Latin plānum (“level ground, a plain”), neuter substantive from plānus (“level, even, flat”). Doublet of llano, piano, and plane.

parole.significato: Full, complete in number or extent.
parole.testo: From Middle English pleyn, borrowed from Old French plein, from Latin plēnus (“full, filled, complete”). Ultimately from Proto-Italic *plēnos, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”). Doublet of plene, plenary, and full.

parole.significato: Sounding sorrowful, mournful or melancholic.
parole.testo: From Middle English pleintif, plentyff, from Old French pleintif (“aggrieved, lamenting”) (whence modern French plaintif), from plainte (“lament, complaint”); see plaint. Doublet of plaintiff.

parole.significato: A deciduous tree of the genus Platanus.
parole.testo: From Middle English plane, borrowed from Old French plane, from Latin platanus, from Ancient Greek πλάτανος (plátanos), from πλατύς (platús, “wide, broad”).

parole.significato: Each of the seven major bodies which move relative to the fixed stars in the night sky—the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Su…
parole.testo: From Middle English planete, from Old French planete, from Latin planeta, planetes, from Ancient Greek πλανήτης (planḗtēs, “wanderer”) (itself an ellipsis of ἀστέρες πλανῆται (astéres planêtai, “wandering stars”)), from Ancient Greek πλανάω (planáō, “wander about, stray”), of unknown origin. Cognate

parole.significato: A long, broad and thick piece of timber, as opposed to a board which is less thick.
parole.testo: From Middle English plank, planke, borrowed from Old French planke, Old Northern French planque (compare French planche, from Old French planche), from Vulgar Latin planca, from palanca, from Latin phalanga. The Latin term derives from the Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx), so it is thus a doublet of p

parole.significato: A member of the dynasty which held the English throne from 1154 to 1485.
parole.testo: Originally a sobriquet of Geoffrey of Anjou (1113-1151), founder of the line, who was said to have worn a yellow broom blossom in his hat, Old French plante genest (French plante genêt), from Latin planta genista (“sprig of broom”), whence Medieval Latin Plantagenistae; subsequently adopted as a sur

parole.significato: A slightly curved but almost flat dish from which food is served or eaten.
parole.testo: From Middle English plate, from Old French plate, from Medieval Latin plata, from Vulgar Latin *plat(t)us, from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “broad, flat, wide”). Compare Spanish plato. (foot): Cockney rhyming slang, from "plates of meat" for "feet".

parole.significato: To cover the surface material of an object with a thin coat of another material, usually a metal.
parole.testo: From Middle English platen, from Old English platian and Old French plater, both ultimately from Latin plata (see above).

parole.significato: mess with, cause trouble for
parole.testo: From Middle English Hob (a diminutive of Robin, from Old French [Term?], a diminutive of Robert) in its connection with Robin Goodfellow and (subsequently) the devil. Compare hobgoblin.

parole.significato: An appeal, petition, urgent prayer or entreaty.
parole.testo: From Middle English ple, from Old French plait, plaid, from Medieval Latin placitum (“a decree, sentence, suit, plea, etc., Latin an opinion, determination, prescription, order; literally, that which is pleasing, pleasure”), neuter of placitus, past participle of placere (“to please”). Cognate with

parole.significato: To present (an argument or a plea), especially in a legal case.
parole.testo: From Middle English pleden, plaiden, from Old French plaider (“to plead, offer a plea”), from plait, from Medieval Latin placitum (“a decree, sentence, suit, plea, etc.", in Classical Latin, "an opinion, determination, prescription, order; literally, that which is pleasing, pleasure”), neuter of pla

parole.significato: That may be pleaded
parole.testo: From Middle English pledable, from Old French; equivalent to plead + -able.

parole.significato: That may be pleased.
parole.testo: From Middle English pleysable, from Old French plaisable; equivalent to please + -able.

parole.significato: A pleasure ground laid out with shady walks, trees and shrubs, statuary, and ornamental water; a secluded part of a gar…
parole.testo: From Middle English plaisaunce, plesaunce, from Old French plaisance. By surface analysis, please + -ance.

parole.significato: Giving pleasure; pleasing in manner.
parole.testo: From Middle English plesaunte, from Old French plaisant. By surface analysis, please + -ant. Related to Dutch plezant (“full of fun or pleasure”). Partly displaced Old English wynsum, which became Modern English winsome.

parole.significato: To make happy or satisfy; to give pleasure to.
parole.testo: From Middle English plesen, plaisen, borrowed from Old French plaise, conjugated form of plaisir or plaire, from Latin placeō (“to please, to seem good”), from the Proto-Indo-European *pleHk- (“pleasingness, permission”). In this sense, displaced native Old English līcian, whence Modern English like

parole.significato: A state of being pleased or contented; gratification.
parole.testo: From Early Modern English pleasur, plesur, alteration (with ending accommodated to -ure) of Middle English plaisir (“pleasure”), from Old French plesir, plaisir (“to please”), infinitive used as a noun, conjugated form of plaisir or plaire, from Latin placeō (“to please, to seem good”), from the Pro

parole.significato: A fold in the fabric of a garment, usually a skirt, as a part of the design of the garment, with the purpose of adding…
parole.testo: From Middle English, from a variant of plait, from Old French pleit. Doublet of plait.

parole.significato: In plenty; abundant.
parole.testo: From Middle English plentewos, plentevous, et al., circa 1300, from Old French plentiveus (“fertile, rich”) (early 13th century), from plentif (“abundant”), from plenté (“abundance”) (Modern French pleinté, English plenty), from Latin plenitatem, accusative of plenitas (“fullness”), from plenus (“co

parole.significato: Inflammation of lung pleura.
parole.testo: From Middle English pleuresi, pleresye, that borrowed from Old French pleuresie (French pleurésie), from Late Latin pleurisis, alteration of Latin pleuritis. By surface analysis, pleur- + -isy.

parole.significato: A warrant or assurance.
parole.testo: From Old French plevine. See replevin.

parole.significato: Capable of plying or bending; readily yielding to force or pressure without breaking.
parole.testo: From Middle English pliaunt, from Old French ploiant, present participle of ploiier (“to fold”).

parole.significato: A little mass of lead, or the like, attached to a line, and used by builders, etc., to indicate a vertical direction.
parole.testo: From Middle English plumbe, plumme, from Old French *plombe, from Latin plumba, plural of plumbum.

parole.significato: One who works in or with lead.
parole.testo: From Middle English plumber, from Old French plummier (French plombier); from Latin plumbārius, from plumbum (“lead or lead shot”). The verb sense “to botch” is perhaps from the negative stereotype of the occupation.
