parole.significato: A line or series of mountains, buildings, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English rengen, from Old French rengier (“to range, to rank, to order”), from the noun renc, reng, ranc, rang (“a rank, row”), from Frankish *hring, from Proto-Germanic *hringaz (“ring, circle, curve”). Doublet of ring.

parole.significato: A row of people or things organized in a grid pattern, often soldiers.
parole.testo: From Middle English rank (“line, row”), from Old French ranc, rang, reng (“line, row, rank”) (Modern French rang), from Frankish *hring (“ring”), from Proto-Germanic *hringaz (“something bent or curved”). Displaced native Old English hād (“rank, status”). Akin to Old High German (h)ring, Old Frisian

parole.significato: To cause irritation, bitterness or acrimony.
parole.testo: From Middle English ranklen, ranclen, from Old French rancler, räoncler, draoncler (“to ulcerate, to form a boil”), from Old French draoncle (“a boil”), from Latin dracunculus (“little serpent”), diminutive of Latin dracō (“serpent, dragon”).

parole.significato: Money paid for the freeing of a hostage.
parole.testo: From the Middle English raunsoun, from the Old French raençon, from stem of Latin redēmptiō. Entered English ca. the 13th century. Doublet of redemption.

parole.significato: The stalks and husks of grapes from which the must has been expressed in winemaking.
parole.testo: From Middle English rape, from rape (“grape stalk, rasper”), from Old French raper, rasper (“to rasp, scratch”), from Old Frankish *raspōn (“to scratch”), related to Old High German raspōn (“to scrape”), Old English ġehrespan (“to strip, spoil”).

parole.significato: The seizure of someone's property by force; pillage; plunder.
parole.testo: From Middle English rapyne, from Old French rapine, from Latin rapīna, from rapiō. Doublet of ravine.

parole.significato: Very uncommon; scarce.
parole.testo: From Middle English rare, from Old French rare, rere (“rare, uncommon”), from Latin rārus (“loose, spaced apart, thin, infrequent”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reh₁- (“friable, thin”). Displaced native English geason (“rare, scarce”) (from Middle English gesen, from Old English gǣsne); and largely

parole.significato: To make rare, thin, porous, or less dense.
parole.testo: From Middle English rarefien, from Old French rarefier (French raréfier), from Latin rarefacere (“make rare”). By surface analysis, rare + -fy.

parole.significato: A dishonest person; a rogue, a scoundrel, a trickster.
parole.testo: Recorded since c.1330, as Middle English rascaile (“people of the lowest class, rabble of an army”), derived from 12th century Old French rascaille (“outcast, rabble”) (modern French racaille), perhaps from rasque (“mud, filth, scab, dregs”), from Vulgar Latin *rasicō (“to scrape”). The singular for

parole.significato: An area of inflamed and irritated skin characterized by reddened spots that may be filled with fluid or pus. Also, prec…
parole.testo: Probably from Old French rasche, rache (“skin eruption, rash; (specifically) scabies, scurf”) (obsolete), from racher (“to scrape; to scratch”) (although this is only directly attested later than the noun), from Vulgar Latin *rāsicāre (“to scrape”), from Latin rāsus (“scraped, scratched; shaved”), t

parole.significato: Chiefly followed by away, down, off, out, etc.: to pluck, pull, or rip (something) violently.
parole.testo: PIE word  *wréh₂ds Probably an aphetic form of arace (“to tear up by the roots; to draw away”) (obsolete), from Middle English aracen (“to remove (something) by force, pluck or pull out, tear out; to grab; to lacerate; to flay or skin (an animal); to erase, obliterate”) [and other forms], from Old F

parole.significato: A coarse file or filelike tool, on which the cutting prominences are distinct points raised by the oblique stroke of a…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English raspen (“to scratch, scrape”), borrowed from Old French rasper (“to grate, scratch”), from Vulgar Latin *raspāre (“to scrape; to scratch”), borrowed from Frankish *hraspōn (“to rasp or grate”), from Proto-Germanic *hraspōną (same meaning, plus “to steal”), from *hrespan

parole.significato: The worth of something; value.
parole.testo: From Middle English rate, from Old French rate, from Medieval Latin rata, from Latin prō ratā parte (“according to a fixed part”), from ratus (“fixed”), from rērī (“think, deem, judge, estimate", originally "reckon, calculate”).

parole.significato: To give formal consent to; make officially valid, to sign off on.
parole.testo: From Middle English ratifien, from Old French ratifier, from Medieval Latin ratifico, from Latin ratus (“reckoned”).

parole.significato: Capable of reasoning.
parole.testo: From Old French rationel, rational, from Latin rationalis (“of or belonging to reason, rational, reasonable; having a ratio”), from ratio (“reason; calculation”).

parole.significato: The breastplate worn by Israelite high priests.
parole.testo: From Old French rational, from Medieval Latin rationale (“a pontifical stole, a pallium, an ornament worn over the chasuble”), neuter of Latin rationalis (“rational”), for which see the first etymology. Translation of λογεῖον (logeîon) or perhaps λόγιον (lógion, “oracle”) in the Septuagint version o

parole.significato: An enthusiastic review (such as of a play).
parole.testo: From Middle English raven (“to rave; talk like a madman”), from Old French raver, variant of resver, of uncertain origin. Compare rave below, and rove.

parole.significato: Very hungry.
parole.testo: From Middle English ravenous, ravynous, from Old French ravineus. By surface analysis, ravin + -ous. As seen at raven and ravin, the word comes from a root referring to predation, not from the root referring to ravens (corvid birds); but folk etymology notes that the latter hypothesis seems plausibl

parole.significato: A beam of light or radiation.
parole.testo: Via Middle English, borrowed from Old French rai, from Latin radius (“staff, stake, spoke”). Doublet of radius.

parole.significato: Any of the superorder Batoidea of marine fish with flat bodies, large wing-like fins, and whip-like tails.
parole.testo: From Middle English raye, rayȝe, from Old French raie, from Latin raia, of uncertain origin. Compare Middle English reyhhe, reihe, reȝge (“ray, skate”), from Old English reohhe (“ray”).

parole.significato: A keen-edged knife of peculiar shape, used in shaving the hair from the face or other parts of the body.
parole.testo: From Middle English rasour, from Old French rasour, from raser (“to scrape, to shave”). More at rat. By surface analysis, raze + -or. Displaced the native Old English sċierseax (literally “shaving knife”).

parole.significato: again, anew
parole.testo: From Middle English re-, from Old French re-, from Latin re-, red- (“back; anew; again; against”), see there for more. Displaced native English ed-, eft-, a-, with-/wither-, gain-/again-.

parole.significato: An action or statement in response to a stimulus or other event.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English reaccion, from Old French reaction, from Latin reāctiō, from the verb reagō, from re- (“again”) + agō (“to act”); more at re-, action; equivalent to react + -ion.

parole.significato: True, genuine, not merely nominal or apparent.
parole.testo: From Middle English real, from Old French reel, from Late Latin reālis (“actual”), from Latin rēs (“matter, thing”), from Proto-Indo-European *reh₁ís (“wealth, goods”). Doublet of realis. In modern times, likely strengthened by or conflated with the use of the prefix re-, analyzable as re- + -al.

parole.significato: A bundle, package, or quantity of paper, nowadays usually containing 500 sheets.
parole.testo: From Middle English reme, from Old French raime, rayme (“ream”) (French rame), from Catalan raima (“ream”), from Arabic رِزْمَة (rizma, “bundle”).

parole.significato: Having the faculty of reason; rational, reasoning.
parole.testo: From Middle English resonable, from Old French resnable, from Classical Latin ratiōnābilis, from ratiō. By surface analysis, reason + -able. Doublet of rationable.

parole.significato: To assure anew; to restore confidence to; to free from fear or self-doubt.
parole.testo: From Old French rasseürer (French rassurer), from re- + asseürer; as if re- + assure.

parole.significato: A deduction from an amount that is paid; an abatement.
parole.testo: From Old French rabatre < batre. See also abate.

parole.significato: A person who resists an established authority, often violently.
parole.testo: From Middle English rebel, rebell, from Old French rebelle, from Latin rebellis (“waging war again; insurgent”), from rebellō (“to wage war again, fight back”), from re- (“again, back”) + bellō (“to wage war”).

parole.significato: To resist or become defiant toward an authority.
parole.testo: From Middle English rebellen, from Old French rebeller, from Latin rebellō (“to wage war again, fight back”), from re- (“again, back”) + bellō (“to wage war”). Doublet of revel.

parole.significato: Armed resistance to an established government or ruler.
parole.testo: From Middle English rebellioun, rebellion, from Old French rebellion, from Latin rebelliō. Equivalent for rebel + -ion.

parole.significato: The recoil of an object bouncing off another.
parole.testo: From Old French rebondir.

parole.significato: To drive back or beat back; to repulse.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English rebutten, rebouten, from Old French reboter, rebuter, rebouter, etc., from re- + boter, buter, bouter (“to butt”). Entered English around 1302-1307.

parole.significato: To be given, sent, or paid something.
parole.testo: From Middle English receyven, from Old French receivre, from Latin recipere (“take back, accept, etc.”), from re- (“back”) + capiō (“to take”); see capacious. Compare conceive, deceive, perceive. Displaced native Middle English terms in -fon/-fangen (e.g. afon, anfon, afangen, underfangen, etc. "to

parole.significato: A protein on a cell wall that binds with specific molecules so that they can be absorbed into the cell in order to cont…
parole.testo: From Middle English receptour, from Old French receptour or Latin receptōrius, from recipiō (“receive”), from re- (“back”) + capiō (“to hold”).

parole.significato: To charge an electric battery after its power has been consumed.
parole.testo: From Old French rechargier, from Old French re- + Old French chargier.

parole.significato: To repeat aloud (some passage, poem or other text previously memorized, or in front of one's eyes), often before an aud…
parole.testo: From Middle English reciten, from Old French reciter, from Latin recitō.

parole.significato: Sequestered; secluded, isolated.
parole.testo: From Old French reclus, past participle of reclure, from Latin reclūdere (“to disclose, to open”), from re- + claudō (“close”).

parole.significato: A form of bail; a promise made by the accused to the court that they will attend all required judicial proceedings and…
parole.testo: From Middle English reconisaunce, from Old French reconissance. Doublet of reconnaissance.

parole.significato: A starting or falling back; a rebound; a shrinking.
parole.testo: From Old French reculer. Further from Latin re- + cūlus.

parole.significato: To bestow commendation on; to represent favorably; to suggest, endorse or encourage as an appropriate choice.
parole.testo: From Middle English recommenden, from Old French recommender (compare French recommander), from Latin re- + commendāre (“to commend, commit; to recommend”), from con- + mandāre (“commit, intrust, enjoin”), from manus (“hand, handwriting, power”) + dare (“to give; to offer or render”). Compare typolo

parole.significato: An equivalent returned for anything given, done, or suffered; compensation; reward; amends; requital.
parole.testo: From Middle English recompense, borrowed from Old French recompense or Medieval Latin recompensa.

parole.significato: To reward or repay (someone) for something done, given etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English recompensen, borrowed from Old French recompenser, from Late Latin recompensare, from Latin re- (“again”) + compensare (“to balance out”).

parole.significato: Enough to break previous records and set a new one; world-class; historic.
parole.testo: From Middle English recorde, borrowed from Old French record, from recorder. See record.

parole.significato: To make a record of information.
parole.testo: From Middle English recorden (“to repeat, to report”), borrowed from Old French recorder (“to get by heart”), from Latin recordārī (“remember, call to mind”), from re- (“back, again”) + cor (“heart; mind”).

parole.significato: The act of giving legal status to a document by making it an official public record.
parole.testo: From Old French recordacion (“record, memory”), from Latin recordatio.

parole.significato: The act of seeking assistance or advice.
parole.testo: From Middle English recours (noun) and recoursen (verb), from Old French recours, from Latin recursus, past participle of recurrō.

parole.significato: recovery
parole.testo: From Middle English recoveraunce, from Old French recovrance; equivalent to recover + -ance.

parole.significato: The act or process of regaining or repossession of something lost.
parole.testo: From recover + -y, from Middle English recoveree, from Old French recovree, from recovrer (“recover”).

parole.significato: The action or process of rectifying.
parole.testo: From Middle English rectificacioun, from Old French rectificacion, from Late Latin rectificatio.

parole.significato: In the Anglican Church, a cleric in charge of a parish and who owns the tithes of it.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English rectour, rector, from Old French rector, rectour and Latin rēctor.

parole.significato: To reject or repudiate (an authority, a person, a court judgment, etc.).
parole.testo: From Late Middle English recusen, from Old French recuser (modern French récuser (“to challenge; to impugn; (formal) to make an objection; (law) to recuse”), and from its etymon Latin recūsāre, the present active infinitive of recūsō (“to decline, refuse, reject; (law) to object to, protest”), from

parole.significato: To censor, to black out or remove parts of a document while leaving the remainder.
parole.testo: From Old French redacter, from Latin redactus, perfect passive participle of redigō (“drive, lead, collect, reduce”), from re- (“back”) + agō (“put in motion, drive”). Piecewise doublet of react.

parole.significato: To recover ownership of something by buying it back.
parole.testo: From Middle English redemen, modified from Old French redimer, from Latin redimō (“release; obviate; atone for”), itself from red- (“back; again”) + emō (“buy; gain, take, procure”).

parole.significato: The act of redeeming or something redeemed.
parole.testo: From Middle English redempcioun, from Old French redemption, from Latin redemptio. Doublet of ransom. Displaced native Old English ālīesung, ālīesnes.

parole.significato: One who redeems (especially used of Jesus).
parole.testo: From Middle English redemptor, redemptoure, from Old French redemptor, from Latin redēmptor.

parole.significato: Shaped like the teeth of a saw; serrated.
parole.testo: From Old French redent. See redan.

parole.significato: Fragrant or aromatic; having a sweet scent.
parole.testo: From Middle English redolent (first attested in 1400), from Old French redolent, from Latin redolentem, present participle of redoleō (“to emit a scent”), from red- + oleō (“to smell”).

parole.significato: To dread.
parole.testo: From Old French redouter, from Latin dubitāre (“doubt”) prefixed with re-. The b was later added back in this word, and the related doubt and redoubtable, to reflect their Latin source.

parole.significato: To bring down the size, quantity, quality, value or intensity of something; to diminish, to lower.
parole.testo: From Middle English reducen, from Old French reduire, from Latin redūcō (“reduce”); from re- (“back”) + dūcō (“lead”). See duke, and compare with redoubt.

parole.significato: The act, process, or result of reducing.
parole.testo: From Middle English reduccion, a borrowing from Old French reducion, from Latin reductiō, reductiōnem. Equivalent to reduce + -tion.

parole.significato: To direct the attention of (someone toward something).
parole.testo: From Middle English referren, from Old French referer, from Latin referre. The noun (used in journalism) is from the verb. Doublet of relate. See also infer, collate and confer, delate and defer, as well as prelate and prefer among others.

parole.significato: An umpire or judge; an official who makes sure the rules are followed during a game.
parole.testo: From Middle English [Term?], from past participle of Old French referer (“to relate, to refer”), from Latin referre (“to carry back, to report, to notify”); as if refer + -ee, that is, the person to whom something is referred for consideration.

parole.significato: To bend back (light, etc.) from a surface.
parole.testo: From Old French reflecter (“to bend back, turn back”), from Latin reflectō (“to reflect”), from re- (“again”) + flectō (“to bend, to curve”). Compare English reflex.

parole.significato: The change of something that is defective, broken, inefficient or otherwise negative, in order to correct or improve it
parole.testo: From Middle English reformen, from Old French reformer, from Latin reformo, reformare. As a noun since 1660s, from French réforme.

parole.significato: To renew or revitalize.
parole.testo: From Middle English refreshen, refreschen, refrisschen, from Old French refrescher (“to refresh”) (modern French rafraîchir), equivalent to re- + fresh.

parole.significato: A state of safety, protection or shelter.
parole.testo: From Middle English refuge, from Old French refuge, from Latin refugium, from re- + fugiō (“flee”). Doublet of refugium.

parole.significato: To return (money) to (someone); to reimburse.
parole.testo: From Middle English refunden, refounden, from Old French refondre, refonder, refunder (“to restore; pay back”), from Latin refundere; prefix re- (“re-”) + fundere (“to pour”): compare French refondre, refonder. See fuse (“to melt”), and compare refound (“to cast again”), and refuse.

parole.significato: To decline (a request or demand).
parole.testo: From Middle English refusen, from Old French refuser, from Vulgar Latin *refūsāre, a blend of Classical Latin refūtāre (whence also refute) and recūsāre (whence also recuse).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or suitable for royalty.
parole.testo: From Middle English regal, from Old French regal (“regal, royal”), from Latin rēgālis (“royal, kingly”), from rex (“king”); also regere (“to rule”). Doublet of royal (“belonging to a monarch”), real (“unit of currency”), ariary, and riyal. Cognate with Spanish real, Italian reale, Catalan reial.

parole.significato: Royalty; sovereignty; sovereign jurisdiction.
parole.testo: From Middle English regalite, from Old French, from Late Latin rēgālitās, from Latin rēgālis (“regal, royal”), equivalent to regal + -ity. Doublet of royalty.

parole.significato: To look at; to observe.
parole.testo: From Middle English regarden, from Old French regarder, reguarder. First attested in late Middle English, circa the early 15th century.

parole.significato: To feel sorry about (a thing that has or has not happened), afterthink: to wish that a thing had not happened, that som…
parole.testo: From Middle English regretten, regreten, from Old French regreter, regrater (“to lament”), from re- (intensive prefix) + *greter, *grater (“to weep”), from Frankish *grātan (“to weep, mourn, lament”), from Proto-Germanic *grētaną (“to weep”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰreh₁d- (“to sound”); and Fran

parole.significato: The kidneys.
parole.testo: From Old French reins, see also rein in French.

parole.significato: To be very happy, be delighted, exult; to feel joy.
parole.testo: From Middle English rejoicen, rejoisen, from Old French resjoir. Doublet of rejoy. Compare French réjouir; Spanish regocijar; Portuguese regozijar; Italian gioire

parole.significato: To rejoice
parole.testo: From Middle English rejoyen, rejoien, from Old French resjoir, equivalent to re- + joy.

parole.significato: To make something loose.
parole.testo: From Middle English relaxen, from Old French relaxer, from Latin relaxāre (“relax, loosen, open”), from re- (“back”) + laxāre (“loosen”), from laxus (“loose, free”). By surface analysis, re- + lax (“open, free, loose”).

parole.significato: The event of setting (someone or something) free (e.g. hostages, slaves, prisoners, caged animals, hooked or stuck mech…
parole.testo: From Middle English relesen, relessen, from Old French relaisser (variant of relascher).

parole.significato: That which remains; that which is left after loss or decay; a remaining portion.
parole.testo: From Middle English relik et al., from Old French relique, from Latin reliquiae (“remains, relics”), from relinquō (“to leave behind, abandon, relinquish”), from re- + linquō (“to leave, quit, forsake, depart from”). Doublet of relict, derelict, and relinquish.

parole.significato: To ease (a person, person's thoughts etc.) from mental distress; to stop (someone) feeling anxious or worried, to allev…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English releven, from Old French relever, specifically from the conjugated forms such as (jeo) relieve (“I lift up”), and its source, Latin relevo (“to lift up, lighten, relieve, alleviate”), combined form of re- (“back”) + levo (“to lift”). Doublet of relevate. Compare levant, levi

parole.significato: Belief in a spiritual or metaphysical reality (often including at least one deity), accompanied by practices or rituals…
parole.testo: From Middle English religioun, from Old French religion, from Latin religiō (“scrupulousness, pious misgivings, superstition, conscientiousness, sanctity, an object of veneration, cult-observance, reverence”). Most likely from the Proto-Indo-European *h₂leg- with the meanings preserved in Latin dīli

parole.significato: To trust; to have confidence in.
parole.testo: From Middle English relien, from Old French relier (“fasten, attach, rally, oblige”), from Latin religo (“fasten, bind fast”), from re- + ligo.

parole.significato: That which is left; relic; remainder.
parole.testo: From Middle English remainen, from Old French remain-, stressed stem of remanoir, from Latin remaneō, maneō, from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to stay”). Displaced native Middle English beliven, bliven (“to remain”) (from Old English belīfan (“to remain, stay”)) due to confluence with related Middle

parole.significato: Capable of being remedied.
parole.testo: From Middle English remediable, from Old French remedïable and Latin remediābilis. By surface analysis, remediate + -able, or perhaps remedy + ‑able.

parole.significato: Something that corrects or counteracts.
parole.testo: From Middle English remedie, from Old French *remedie, remede, from Latin remedium (“a remedy, cure”), from re- (“again”) + mederi (“to heal”). Doublet of remeid.

parole.significato: To recall from one's memory; to have an image in one's memory.
parole.testo: From Middle English remembren, from Old French remembrer (“to remember”), from Late Latin rememorari (“to remember again”), from re- + memor (“mindful”), from Proto-Indo-European *mer-, *(s)mer- (“to think about, be mindful, remember”). Cognate with Old English mimorian, mymerian (“to remember, comm

parole.significato: The act of remembering; a holding in mind, or bringing to mind; recollection.
parole.testo: From Middle English remembraunce, from Old French remembrance, from remembrer (“to remember”), from Late Latin rememorārī (“to call to mind, to remember”). Equivalent to remember + -ance.

parole.significato: To remove.
parole.testo: From Middle English remewen, from Old French remuer, from Medieval Latin remutare, from Latin re- + mutare.

parole.significato: A feeling of regret or sadness for doing wrong or sinning.
parole.testo: First attested circa 14th century as Middle English remors, from Old French remors, from Medieval Latin remorsus, from Latin remordeō (“to torment, vex”, literally “to bite back”), from re- + mordeō (“to bite”). More at remord.

parole.significato: At a distance; disconnected.
parole.testo: From Middle English remote, from Old French remot, masculine, remote, feminine, from Latin remotus, past participle of removere (“to remove”), from re- + movere (“to move”).

parole.significato: Backward motion.
parole.testo: From Old French or directly from Latin remōtiō.

parole.significato: Reasonable.
parole.testo: From Old French resnable. Doublet of reasonable.

parole.significato: To renounce (one’s faith or god), to apostasize from.
parole.testo: From Middle English reneye, from Old French reneier, French renier, renier, from Latin re- (“re-”) + negare (“to deny”). See renegade. Doublet of renege and related to deny.

parole.significato: To cause to become.
parole.testo: From Middle English renderen, rendren, from Old French rendre (“render, give back”), from Late Latin rendere, from Latin reddere (“make, give back”).

parole.significato: An act of renouncing.
parole.testo: From Old French renoncier (French renoncer), from Latin renūntiō. Doublet of renunciate.

parole.significato: The act of renouncing.
parole.testo: From Old French renoncement. By surface analysis, renounce + -ment.

parole.significato: Fame; celebrity; wide recognition.
parole.testo: From Old French renoun (compare with Modern French renom), equivalent to re- + noun.

parole.significato: A payment made by a tenant at intervals in order to lease a property.
parole.testo: From Middle English rent, rente, from Old French rente, from Early Medieval Latin rendita, from Late Latin rendere, from Latin reddere.

parole.significato: Backwards, contourné, facing the opposite direction (sinister/dexter) than usual.
parole.testo: From Old French renverser. Equivalent to re- + inverse.

parole.significato: The act of repairing or resorting to a place.
parole.testo: From Middle English repairen (“to return”), from Old French repairier, from Late Latin repatriare (“to return to one's country”), from re- + patria (“homeland”). Cognate to repatriate.

parole.significato: Synonym of pay back in all senses.
parole.testo: From Old French repaier (“to pay back”), from re- + paiier (“to pay”), from Latin pācāre (“to settle, to make peaceful”), from pāx (“peace”) + -ō (forming verbs). Equivalent to re- + pay. Cognate with repacify and French repayer (“to pay again”).

parole.significato: To do or say again (and again).
parole.testo: From Middle English repeten, from Old French repeter, from Latin repetō, from the prefix re- (“again”) + petō (“to attack, beseech”).

parole.significato: To turn (someone) away from a privilege, right, job, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English repellen, a borrowing from Old French *repeller, from Latin repellere (“to drive back”), from re- (“back”) + pellere (“to drive”). Doublet of repeal.

parole.significato: To feel pain, sorrow, or regret for what one has done or omitted to do; the cause for repenting may be indicated with "…
parole.testo: From Middle English repenten, from Old French repentir, from Vulgar Latin *repaenitīre, from Late Latin paenitīre, from Classical Latin paenitēre. Compare Modern French repentir.

parole.significato: The action of repenting, an instance of it, atonement.
parole.testo: First attested circa 14th century, from Middle English repentance, repentaunce, from Old French repentance. More at repent. By surface analysis, repent + -ance.

parole.significato: Feeling or showing sorrow for wrongdoing.
parole.testo: From Middle English repentant, from Old French repentant, present participle of repentir. By surface analysis, repent + -ant.

parole.significato: To refill; to renew; to supply again or to add a fresh quantity to.
parole.testo: From Middle English replenisshen, borrowed from Old French repleniss-, stem of some of the conjugated forms of replenir, from re- + plenir, from plein, from Latin plenus.

parole.significato: Abounding, amply provided.
parole.testo: From Middle English replete (adjective) and repleten (verb), from Old French replet, from Latin repletus.

parole.significato: The condition of being replete; fullness.
parole.testo: From Middle English replecioun, from Old French repletion, from Latin replētiō, replētiōnem.

parole.significato: To return goods to their rightful owner by replevin; to recover goods.
parole.testo: Old French replevir (“recover”), from re- + plevir (probably from a Germanic source which also gave pledge).

parole.significato: To give a written or spoken response, especially to a question, request, accusation or criticism; to answer.
parole.testo: From Middle English replyen, replien, borrowed from Old French replier (“to reply”), from the Latin replicō, replicāre (“to fold back”) (in Late or Medieval Latin "to reply, repeat"), from re + plicō (“to fold”); the noun derives from the verb by nominalisation. Doublet of replicate and replica.

parole.significato: Someone or something that reports.
parole.testo: From Middle English reportour, from Old French reporteur; equivalent to report + -er.

parole.significato: To present again or anew; to present by means of something standing in the place of; to exhibit the counterpart or imag…
parole.testo: From Old French représenter, from Latin repraesentō. Displaced native Old English spelian (“to represent”).

parole.significato: That which represents something else.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English representacioun, from Old French representacion, from Latin repraesentātiō. By surface analysis, represent + -ation.

parole.significato: A recurrence or resumption of an action.
parole.testo: From Middle English reprise (noun) and reprisen (verb), from Old French reprise, from reprendre. In some senses borrowed anew from Modern French reprise.

parole.significato: A mild rebuke, or an implied criticism.
parole.testo: From Middle English reprochen, from Old French reprochier (Modern French reprocher).

parole.significato: An act or instance of reproving or of reprobating; a rebuke, a reproach, an admonition.
parole.testo: From Old French reprove, from reprover. See reprove.

parole.significato: A (typically scaly and egg-laying) cold-blooded vertebrate tetrapod animal, of the class Reptilia (excluding birds), su…
parole.testo: From Middle English reptil, from Old French reptile, from Late Latin rēptile, neuter of reptilis (“creeping”), from Latin rēpō (“to creep”), from Proto-Indo-European *rep- (“to creep, slink”) (Pokorny; Watkins, 1969).

parole.significato: Extreme aversion, repulsion.
parole.testo: From Middle English repugnance, repugnaunce, from Old French repugnance, repugnaunce (French répugnance) and its etymon Latin repugnantia. Doublet of repugnancy.

parole.significato: Offensive or repulsive; arousing disgust or aversion.
parole.testo: From Middle English repugnaunt, from Old French repugnant, borrowed from Latin repugnans, present participle of repugnare (“to oppose, to fight against”), from re- (“back, against”) + pugnare (“to fight”); see pugnacious. By surface analysis, re- + Latin pugn + -ant.

parole.significato: The act of repulsing or the state of being repulsed.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English repulse, borrowed from Old French repulse, from Latin repulsa (petītiō), from repellō.

parole.significato: Reputation, especially a good reputation.
parole.testo: From Old French reputer, from Latin reputō (“to count over, reckon, calculate, compute, think over, consider”), from re- (“again”) + putō (“to think”).

parole.significato: To ask for (something).
parole.testo: From Middle English request, from Old French requeste (French requête), from Vulgar Latin *requaesita, from Latin requīsīta, feminine of requīsītus (“requested, demanded”), past participle of requīrō (“require, ask”), composed of re- + quaerō (“to seek, look for”), of uncertain origin, but possibly

parole.significato: To demand, to insist upon (having); to call for authoritatively.
parole.testo: From Old French requerre (whence Modern French requérir), from Latin requīrō (“to require, seek, ask for”, literally “to seek back”), from re- (“back; again”) + quaerō (“to seek”, whence query).

parole.significato: A formal request for something.
parole.testo: From Middle English requisicion, from Old French requisicion, from Medieval Latin requisitio. By surface analysis, requisit(e) + -ion.

parole.significato: To repay (a debt owed); specifically, to recompense or reward someone for (a favour, a service rendered, etc.)
parole.testo: The verb is derived from Middle English requiten (“to repay”), and then partly from both of the following: * From re- (prefix meaning ‘again; back, backward’) + quiten (“to pay, pay for; to repay; to acquit (someone of a charge), exonerate; to prove (oneself) innocent; to answer, reply; to atone for

parole.significato: rescue, deliverance
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English [Term?], from Old French rescousse.

parole.significato: To save from any violence, danger or evil.
parole.testo: From Middle English rescouen, from Old French rescoure, rescurre, rescorre; from Latin prefix re- (“re-”) + excutere (“to shake or drive out”), from ex (“out”) + quatiō (“to shake”). Displaced native Old English nerian.

parole.significato: Having a resemblance (to).
parole.testo: From Old French resemblant, present participle of resembler (Modern French ressembler).

parole.significato: Anger or displeasure stemming from belief that one or one's group has been wronged or betrayed by others; indignation.
parole.testo: From resent + -ment, after Middle French and French ressentiment (in Old French as recentement), from an archaic usage of the verb ressentir via Old French sentir, from Latin sentiō, sentīre (“to feel”). Compare Italian risentimento, Portuguese ressentimento, and Spanish resentimiento. Doublet of re

parole.significato: A restriction.
parole.testo: From Old French reserver, from Latin reservō (“to reserve, retain”).

parole.significato: To dwell permanently or for a considerable time; to have a settled abode for a time; to remain for a long time.
parole.testo: From Middle English residen, from Old French resider, from Latin resideō (“remain behind, reside, dwell”), from re- (“back”) + sedeō (“sit”).

parole.significato: The place where one lives (resides); one's home.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English residence, from Old French residence, from Medieval Latin residentia, from residēns, present participle of resideō, equivalent to reside + -ence. Doublet of residencia.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or remaining as a residue; left over.
parole.testo: Recorded since 1570. From residue, itself borrowed during the Middle English period from Old French residu (Modern French résidu), from Latin residuum (“a remainder”), the neuter inflection of residuus (“remaining, left over”), perfect participle of resideō (“to remain behind”), from re- (“back, aga

parole.significato: That which persists or remains following the removal or elimination of other elements.
parole.testo: From Middle English residue, from Old French residu, from Latin residuum, neuter of residuus (“remaining”), from resideō (“to remain behind”). Doublet of residuum.

parole.significato: The act of resigning.
parole.testo: From Middle English resignacion, resignacioun, from Old French resignation, from Medieval Latin resignātiōnem, accusative of resignātio. Equivalent to resign + -ation.

parole.significato: A viscous water-insoluble hydrocarbon exudate of certain plants, or such a substance as a component of a plant exudate;…
parole.testo: From Middle English resyn, resyne, from Old French résine, from Latin resīna. Doublet of rosin.

parole.significato: The act of resisting, or the capacity to resist.
parole.testo: From earlier resistence, from Middle English resistence, from Old French resistence, from Latin resistentia. Morphologically resist + -ance.

parole.significato: To find a solution to (a problem).
parole.testo: From Middle English resolven, from Old French resolver, a learned borrowing of Latin resolvō (“loosen, thaw, melt, resolve”), equivalent to re- + solve. Piecewise doublet of re-solve.

parole.significato: The quality of being resonant.
parole.testo: From Old French resonance (French résonance), from Latin resonantia (“echo”), from resonō (“to resound”).

parole.significato: A place where people go for recreation, especially one with facilities such as lodgings, entertainment, and a relaxing…
parole.testo: From Middle English resorten, from Old French resortir (“to fall back, return, resort, have recourse, appeal”), back-formation from sortir (“to go out”).

parole.significato: An echoing or reverberating sound; a resounding.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English resoun, reson (“echoing or reverberating sound; clangour, din, noise”), from Old French reson, and from its etymon Latin resonus (“echoing, resounding”), from re- (prefix meaning ‘again’) + sonus (“sound; noise; pitch; speech; (figuratively) character, style, tone; tongue, v

parole.significato: An attitude of consideration or high regard; a feeling of admiration or esteem.
parole.testo: From Middle English respect, from Old French respect, also respit (“respect, regard, consideration”), from Latin respectus (“a looking at, regard, respect”), perfect passive participle of respiciō (“look at, look back upon, respect”), from re- (“back”) + speciō (“to see”), equivalent to re- + -spect

parole.significato: To breathe in and out successively.
parole.testo: From Middle English respiren, borrowed from Old French respirer or Latin respīrō (“to blow back, breathe out”), from re- (“back”) + spīrō (“to breathe, blow”).

parole.significato: To say something in return; to answer; to reply.
parole.testo: From Middle English respounden, from Old French respondre, from Late Latin respondō, from Latin respondeō. Cf. Modern French répondre.

parole.significato: An answer or reply, or something in the nature of an answer or reply.
parole.testo: From Middle English respounse, respons, from Old French respons, respuns, responce, ultimately from the Latin respōnsum, a nominal use of the neuter form of respōnsus, the perfect passive participle of respondeō, from re (“again”) + spondeō (“promise”). Doublet of responsum.

parole.significato: That which remains.
parole.testo: From Middle English reste, from Old French reste, from Old French rester (“to remain”), from Latin restō (“to stay back, stay behind”), from re- + stō (“to stand”). Replaced native Middle English lave (“rest, remainder”) (from Old English lāf (“remnant, remainder”)).

parole.significato: To continue to be, remain, be left in a certain way.
parole.testo: From Middle English resten, from Old French rester, from Latin restō.

parole.significato: To restore (something) to its former condition.
parole.testo: From Old French restituer, from Latin restituō (“replace, restore”).

parole.significato: A process of compensation for losses.
parole.testo: From Old French restitucion, from Latin restitutio. By surface analysis, restitute + -ion.

parole.significato: Impatient under delay, duress, or control.
parole.testo: Modification of earlier restiff, from Middle English restyf, from Old French restif, from rester (“to stay, remain”), from Latin restō. * Shares an etymology with rest ("to remain," obsolete) *Merriam-Webster states that this word was originally used to describe horses that disobeyed commands. Presu

parole.significato: Serving to restore.
parole.testo: From Middle English restoratif, restoratyve, from Old French restoratif, restauratif and Medieval Latin restaurātīvus. Equivalent to restore + -ative.

parole.significato: To reestablish, or bring back into existence.
parole.testo: From Middle English restoren, from Old French restorer, from Latin rēstaurāre. By surface analysis, re- + store.

parole.significato: To control or keep in check.
parole.testo: From Middle English restreinen, from Old French restreindre, from Latin rēstringere (“fasten, tighten”).

parole.significato: Something that restrains, ties, fastens or secures.
parole.testo: From Middle English restreynte, from Old French restreinte; more at restrain.

parole.significato: The act of resuscitating.
parole.testo: From Middle English resuscitacion, from Old French ressuscitacion and Latin resuscitātio. Equivalent to resuscitate + -ion.

parole.significato: The sale of goods directly to the consumer, encompassing the storefronts, mail-order, websites, etc., and the corporate…
parole.testo: From the Old French verb retaillier.

parole.significato: A group of attendants or servants, especially of someone considered important.
parole.testo: From Middle English retenue, from Old French retenue, past participle of retenir (“retain”). Doublet of ritenuto.

parole.significato: The act of pulling back or withdrawing, as from something dangerous, or unpleasant.
parole.testo: From Middle English retret, from Old French retrait or retret, from Latin retractus, from retraho. Doublet of retract, retrait, and ritratto.

parole.significato: The outer side of a window or door frame.
parole.testo: From Middle English revēlen, from Old French reveler, from Latin revēlāre (“to reveal, uncover”), from re- (“back, again”) + vēlāre (“to cover”), from vēlum (“a cloth, covering, curtain, veil, awning, sail”) (whence also English veil, English unveil, English voile, Russian вуаль (vualʹ), Russian зав

parole.significato: An instance of merrymaking; a celebration.
parole.testo: From Middle English revelen, from Old French revel, from reveler (“to be disorderly, to make merry”), from Latin rebello (“to rebel”). Doublet of rebel.

parole.significato: The act of revealing or disclosing.
parole.testo: From Middle English revelacioun, from Old French revelacion, from Latin revēlātiō (“disclosure”), from revēlō (“to disclose”), re (“again”) + vēlō (“to cover”); by surface analysis, revelate + -ion.

parole.significato: Synonym of resell: to sell again.
parole.testo: From Old French revendre, from Latin revēndere, from re- (“re-: again, back”) + vēndere (“to sell”). Equivalent to re- + vend.

parole.significato: To take revenge for (a particular harmful action) or on behalf of (its victim); to avenge.
parole.testo: From Middle English revengen, from Old French revengier, revenger.

parole.significato: A violent oscillation or vibration.
parole.testo: From Old French reverberation, from Medieval Latin reverberatio. Morphologically reverberate + -ion.

parole.significato: Veneration; profound awe and respect, normally in a sacred context.
parole.testo: From Middle English reverence (noun) and reverencen (verb), from Old French reverence and Latin reverentia, from Latin revereor (“to stand in awe, respect, revere”), from re- + vereor, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to cover, heed, notice”).

parole.significato: The act or process of reverting something.
parole.testo: Borrowed into late Middle English from Old French reversion (modern réversion), from Latin reversio, from revertō. By surface analysis, revert + -sion.

parole.significato: One who, or that which, reverts.
parole.testo: From Old French revertir, from Vulgar Latin *revertiō, variant of Latin revertō.

parole.significato: A second or subsequent reading of a text or artifact in an attempt to gain new insights.
parole.testo: From Middle English revewe, reveue, from Old French reveüe, revue (Modern French: revue), feminine form of reveü, past participle of reveoir (French: revoir), from Latin revideō, from re- +videō (“see, observe”) (English: video). Equivalent to re- + view. Compare retrospect. Doublet of revue.

parole.significato: To attack (someone) with abusive language.
parole.testo: From Middle English revilen, from re + Old French aviler (“to make vile or cheap, disprize, disesteem”), from a- (“to”) + vil (“vile, cheap”); see vile.

parole.significato: An act or instance of revoking.
parole.testo: From Middle English revocacioun, revocation, from Old French revocacion, from Latin revocationem (accusative of revocatio); equivalent to revoke + -ation.

parole.significato: A political upheaval in a government or state characterized by great change.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English revolucion, borrowed from Old French revolucion, from Late Latin revolūtiō (“the act of revolving; revolution”), from Latin revolvō (“roll back, revolve”).

parole.significato: To bring back into a particular place or condition; to restore.
parole.testo: From Middle English revolven (“to change direction”), borrowed from Old French revolver (“to reflect upon”), from Latin revolvere (“turn over, roll back, reflect upon”), from re- (“back”) + volvō (“roll”); see voluble, volve.

parole.significato: Something of value given in return for an act.
parole.testo: From Middle English reward, rewarde, from Old French reward (“reward”) (compare Old French regard, whence modern French regard, and also English regard through Middle French), from rewarder (“to reward”) (compare Old French reguarder), from re- + warder (“to guard, keep”) (compare Old French guarder

parole.significato: A rhetorician.
parole.testo: From Middle English rethor, from Old French retor and Latin rhētor, rētor, rēthor (“teacher of rhetoric, rhetorician”), from Ancient Greek ῥήτωρ (rhḗtōr).

parole.significato: The art of using language, especially public speaking, as a means to persuade.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English rhetorik, rhetoric, borrowed from Old French rhetorique, borrowed from Latin rhētorica, borrowed from Ancient Greek ῥητορικὴ (rhētorikḕ), ellipsis of ῥητορῐκή τέχνη (rhētorĭkḗ tékhnē).

parole.significato: Synonym of rhetorical.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English rhetorik, borrowed from Old French rhetorique, borrowed from Latin rhētoricus, borrowed from Ancient Greek ῥητορικός (rhētorikós), from ῥήτωρ (rhḗtōr, “public speaker”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós). By surface analysis, rhetor + -ic.

parole.significato: An expert or student of rhetoric.
parole.testo: From Middle English rethoricien, from Old French retoricien; equivalent to rhetoric + -ian.

parole.significato: Coarsely, vulgarly, or lewdly amusing; referring to sexual matters in a rude or irreverent way.
parole.testo: From Middle English ribald, from Old French ribaud, ribauld (“rogue, scoundrel”) ( > English ribaud), from Old French riber (“to be licentious”), from Frankish *rīban (“to copulate, be in heat”, literally “to rub”), from Proto-Germanic *wrībaną (“to turn, twist, writhe”), from Proto-Indo-European *w

parole.significato: Joking or humorous language or behaviour used in a vulgar or lewd fashion.
parole.testo: From Middle English ribaldrie, from Old French ribaulderie, ribauderie, equivalent to ribald + -ry.

parole.significato: To decorate with ribbon.
parole.testo: From Middle English riban, ryban, ryband, from Old French riban, ruban ( > modern French ruban), of uncertain origin. Likely from a Germanic compound whose second element is cognate with English band. Compare Middle Dutch ringhband (“necklace”, literally “ring-band”).

parole.significato: Money, goods, wealth, treasure.
parole.testo: From Middle English riches, plural of riche (“power, wealth”), from Old English rīċe (“power, authority, dominion”). parole.significato: wealth or riches
parole.testo: From Middle English richesse, from Old French richese, richece.

parole.significato: A curtain; bedcurtain.
parole.testo: From Middle English riddel, ridel, redel, rudel, from Old French ridel ("a plaited stuff; curtain"; > Medieval Latin ridellus), from rider (“to wrinkle”), from Old High German rīdan (“to turn; wrap; twist; wrinkle”). More at writhe. Doublet of rideau.

parole.significato: The rabble; crowds; people of a low, disreputable or undesirable class or position.
parole.testo: From Old French rif et raf (“one and all”), of Germanic origin. The first word is from rifler (“to scrape off”) and the last is from raffler, related to rafler (“to plunder”).

parole.significato: A firearm fired from the shoulder; improved range and accuracy is provided by a long, rifled barrel.
parole.testo: Originally short for “rifled gun”, referring to the spiral grooves inside the barrel. parole.significato: One who riots; part of the unruly violent crowd causing a riot.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English riotour, from Old French rioteor; equivalent to riot + -er.

parole.significato: A religious custom.
parole.testo: Via Middle English and Old French, from Latin ritus.

parole.significato: Certain members of the fish family Cyprinidae, including:
parole.testo: From Middle English roche, from Old French roche, from Middle Low German roche, ruche (“ray (fish)”), from Old Saxon *rūh, possibly from Proto-Germanic *rūhaz (“rough”). Cognate with Old English ruhha ("a ray"; > Middle English rouhe, rohȝe), German Rochen (“ray (fish)”).

Cognate with Saterland Frisian rosterje (“to roast”),

parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English robbour, robbere, either directly taken from or from a calque of Old French robeor. Equivalent to rob + -er. parole.testo: From Middle English robe, roobe, from Old French robe, robbe, reube (“booty, spoils of war, robe, garment”), from Frankish *rouba, *rauba (“booty, spoils, stolen clothes”, literally “things taken”), from Proto-Germanic *raubō, *raubaz, *raubą (“booty, that which is stripped or carried away”), from P

parole.significato: radiotelephony clear-code word for the letter R.
parole.testo: From Old French Rogier, from the Frankish equivalent of Old English Hrōþgār (see Hroðgar), from Proto-Germanic *Hrōþigaizaz (“fame-spear”). Compare also Rutger.

parole.significato: To engage in noisy, drunken, or riotous behaviour.
parole.testo: From Old French rustre, from Latin rusticus. Doublet of rustic.

parole.significato: That which is rolled up.
parole.testo: From Middle English rolle, from Old French rolle, role, roule, from Medieval Latin rotulus (“a roll, list, catalogue, schedule, record, a paper or parchment rolled up”); as such, it is a doublet of role and rotulus.

parole.significato: Of or from Rome.
parole.testo: From Old French Romain, from Latin Rōmānus. By surface analysis, Rom(e) + -an. Doublet of Romano. Displaced native Romish. * In reference to the Byzantine Empire, via the Byzantine Greek endonym Ῥωμαῖος (Rhōmaîos).

parole.significato: The group of languages and cultures which are derived from Vulgar Latin.
parole.testo: From Old French romanz (“vernacular language (of France)”), from Late Latin rōmānicē, from Latin rōmānicus < rōmānus + -icus. Extended in the 17th century to all languages derived from Latin.

parole.significato: One who romances another; one who attempt to win another's affections via romance.
parole.testo: From Old French romanceour. By surface analysis, romance + -er.

parole.significato: A romantic story told in verse; a romance.
parole.testo: From Old French romaunt (modern roman), variant of romanz.

parole.significato: A metric form of verse using two rhymes, usually fourteen 8- to 10-syllable lines in three stanzas, with the first line…

parole.significato: A piece shaped like a castle tower, that can be moved only up, down, left or right (but not diagonally) or in castling.

parole.significato: Synonym of rosebush.
parole.testo: From Old French rosier. Doublet of rosary.

parole.significato: A solid form of resin, obtained from liquid resin by vaporizing its volatile components.

parole.significato: A kind of guitar, the notes of which were produced by a small wheel or wheel-like arrangement; an instrument similar to…

parole.significato: Anything having a round form; a round figure; a circle.
parole.testo: From Middle English roundel, rundel, rondel, from Old French rondel (“something round and flat”), a diminutive of rond (“round”). More at round.

parole.significato: A course or way which is traveled or passed.
parole.testo: From Middle English route, from Old French route, from Latin rupta [via] (literally “a path made by force”). Compare Modern French route. See routine. Further via Latin ruptus related with bankrupt. Unrelated to road.

parole.significato: A small spiked wheel on the end of a spur of certain types.
parole.testo: From Middle English rowel, rowell, rowelle, from Old French roel, roiele (compare modern French rouelle), from Late Latin rotella, diminutive of Latin rota (“wheel”). Doublet of rotella.

parole.significato: A king.
parole.testo: From Middle English roy, roye, borrowed from Old French roi (“king”). Doublet of rajah, Rex, rex, and rich.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a monarch or his (or her) family.
parole.testo: From Middle English royal, from Old French roial (Modern French royal), from Latin rēgālis, from rēx (“king”). Doublet of regal (“befitting a king”), real (“unit of currency”), ariary, and riyal. Cognate with Spanish real, Italian reale, Catalan reial. Displaced native Old English cynelīċ.

parole.significato: The rank, status, power or authority of a monarch.
parole.testo: From Middle English royaltee, roialtee, royalte, from Old French roialté, roiauté, realté (compare earlier Old French realted (“realm, kingdom”)), from Vulgar Latin *rēgālitās, from Latin rēgālis, equivalent to royal + -ty. Doublet of regality.

parole.significato: A heading in a book highlighted in red.
parole.testo: From Middle English rubriche, rubrike, from Old French rubrique, from Latin rūbrīca (“red ochre”), the substance used to make red letters, from ruber (“red”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ-.

parole.significato: A clear, deep, red variety of corundum, valued as a precious stone.
parole.testo: From Middle English ruby, rube, from Old French rubi, from Medieval Latin rubīnus. Doublet of rubi and rubine. Etymology 1 sense 7 (“pronunciation guide”) is from the British 5½-point type size (etymology 1 sense 6), used for annotations in printed documents.

parole.significato: Lacking in refinement or civility; bad-mannered; discourteous.
parole.testo: From Middle English rude, from Old French rude, ruide, from Latin rudis (“rough, raw, rude, wild, untilled”).

parole.significato: A fundamental principle or skill, especially in a field of learning.
parole.testo: From Old French rudiment, from Latin rudimentum (“a first attempt, a beginning”), plural rudimenta (“the elements”), from rudis (“rude”); see rude. By surface analysis, rude + -i- + -ment.

parole.significato: Rudeness; ignorance.
parole.testo: From rude + -ity, from Middle English ruditee, ruditē, from Old French rudete, from Latin ruditas (“ignorance”), from rudis (“rude, illiterate”). First use appears c. 1450.

parole.significato: A piece of ivory, generally from a marine mammal.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Middle English rewell bon, ruel bon (“walrus ivory”), from Old French roal, rohal (“walrus ivory”), ultimately from Old Norse hrosshvalr (“walrus”).

parole.significato: To cause the fiscal ruin of; to bankrupt or drive out of business.
parole.testo: From Middle English ruyne, ruine, from Old French ruine, from Latin ruīna (“overthrow, ruin”), from ruō (“to fall down, tumble, sink in ruin, rush”).

parole.significato: Causing ruin; destructive, calamitous.
parole.testo: From Middle English ruynous, from Old French ruinos, ruineus, from Latin ruīnōsus. By surface analysis, ruin + -ous.

parole.significato: A regulation, law, guideline.
parole.testo: From Middle English reule, rewle, rule, borrowed from Old French riule, reule, from Latin regula (“straight stick, bar, ruler, pattern”), from regō (“to keep straight, direct, govern, rule”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃réǵeti (“to straighten; right”), from the root *h₃reǵ-; see regent. D

parole.significato: To regulate, be in charge of, make decisions for, reign over.
parole.testo: From Middle English reulen, rulen, borrowed from Old French riuler, from Latin regulāre (“to regulate, rule”), from regula (“a rule”); see regular and regulate.

parole.significato: Neat and orderly.
parole.testo: Back-formation from unruly, or perhaps a continuation of Middle English rewly, ruly, reuli (“subject to a religious rule, regular”), equivalent to rule + -ly, rule + -y; or perhaps from Old French rulé, reulé, rieulé (“ruled”), past participle of rieuler (“to rule”). More at rule.

parole.significato: To arrange (cargo, goods, etc.) in the hold of a ship; to move or rearrange such goods.
parole.testo: From Middle English ronage, from Old French arrumage (compare French arrimage), from arrumer (“to arrange the cargo in the hold”) (compare French arrimer and Spanish arrumar).

parole.significato: A statement or claim of questionable accuracy, from no known reliable source, usually spread by word of mouth.
parole.testo: From Middle English rumour, from Old French rumeur, from Latin rūmor (“common talk”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rewH- (“to shout, to roar”).

parole.significato: UK, Canada, New Zealand, Australia, and Ireland spelling of rumor.
parole.testo: From Middle English rumour, from Old French rumour, rumor, from Latin rūmor (“common talk”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *rewH- (“to shout, roar”).

parole.significato: A wine measure, equivalent to 18 gallons.
parole.testo: From Middle English roundelet, from Old French rondelet (“roundlet”). More at roundlet.

parole.significato: Relating to the countryside or to agriculture.
parole.testo: From Old French rural, from Latin rūrālis (“rural”), from rūs (“countryside”) + -ālis.

parole.significato: A turning or doubling back, especially of animals to get out of the way of hunting dogs.
parole.testo: From Middle English rūse (“evasive movements of a pursued animal; circuitous course taken by a hunter to pursue a game animal”), from Old French rëuse, ruse (“evasive movements of a pursued animal; trickery”) (modern French ruse (“trick, ruse; cunning, guile”)), from ruser (“to use cunning, to be cr

parole.significato: A twilled woolen material.
parole.testo: From Old French roussel, from Latin russulus, diminutive of russus (“red”).

parole.significato: Sexual desire in any of many mammals, often specific to mating season; the state or season in which this is experienced.
parole.testo: From Middle English rutte (noun) and rutten (verb), from Old French rut (“noise, roar, bellowing”), from Latin rugītus, from rugīre (“to roar”).

parole.significato: Friday, observed in Islam as a day of rest and worship.
parole.testo: From Middle English sabat, sabbat, sabath, from Old English sabat and Old French sabbat, both from Latin sabbatum, from Ancient Greek σάββατον (sábbaton, “Sabbath”), from Hebrew שַׁבָּת (shabát, “Sabbath”), with the spelling ending in -th, probably influenced by the traditional transliteration of th

parole.significato: A small carnivorous mammal of the Old World that resembles a weasel, Martes zibellina, from cold regions in Eurasia and…
parole.testo: Attested since 1275, from Middle English sable, from Old French sable and martre sable (“sable marten”), in reference to the animal or its fur; from Medieval Latin sabelum, from Middle Low German sabel (compare Middle Dutch sabel, Middle High German zobel, whence German Zobel); ultimately from a Sla

parole.significato: Of or relating to priests or a high religious order; priestly.
parole.testo: From Middle English sacerdotale, from Old French sacerdotal, from Latin sacerdōtālis (“priestly”).

parole.significato: A sacred act and the attendant ceremony, considered (theology) an outward sign of divine grace, instituted by Jesus Chr…
parole.testo: From Middle English sacrament, from Old French sacrement, from Ecclesiastical Latin sacrāmentum (“sacrament”), from Latin sacrō (“hallow, consecrate”), from sacer (“sacred, holy”), originally sum deposited by parties to a suit.

parole.significato: Used in, or relating to, a sacrament.
parole.testo: From Old French sacramental, from Ecclesiastical Latin sacrāmentālis.

parole.significato: To consecrate.
parole.testo: From Middle English sacren, sakeren (“to make holy, hallow”), from Old French sacrer (“to hallow, consecrate, anoint, dedicate”), from Latin sacrō (“to make sacred, consecrate”), from sacer (“sacred, holy”), from Proto-Indo-European *sh₂krós (“sacred”), from *seh₂k- (“to sanctify, to make a treaty”)

parole.significato: Desecration, profanation, misuse or violation of something regarded as sacred.
parole.testo: Circa 1300, original sense “stealing something sacred”. From Middle English sacrilege, from Old French sacrilege, from Latin sacrilegium, from sacrilegus (“sacrilegious”). Sense of “profanation” from late 14th century.

parole.significato: Not in danger; out of harm's reach.
parole.testo: From Middle English sauf, safe, saf, saaf, from Old French sauf, saulf, salf (“safe”), from Latin salvus (“whole, safe”), from Proto-Italic *salawos, from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂- (“whole, every”). Displaced Old English sicor (“secure, sure”).

parole.significato: The security given by authority of a government to a stranger for his quietly coming into and passing out of the territ…
parole.testo: Attested as early as the 14th century in Robert of Gloucerster's chronicles written in Middle English; ultimately a calque of Old French sauf-conduit.

parole.significato: A document that grants safe passage through enemy territory in times of war.
parole.testo: Attested as early as the 14th century in Robert of Gloucerster's chronicles written in Middle English; ultimately a calque of Old French sauf-conduit.

parole.significato: The condition or feeling of being safe; security; certainty.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English savete, from Old French sauveté, from earlier salvetet, from Medieval Latin salvitās, salvitātem, from Latin salvus.

parole.significato: A plant of species Crocus sativus, a crocus.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English saffron, borrowed from Old French safran, borrowed from Medieval Latin safranum, borrowed from Arabic زَعْفَرَان (zaʕfarān), from Aramaic צפר.

parole.significato: Wise.
parole.testo: From Middle English sage, from Old French sage (11th century), from Vulgar Latin *sapium, from Latin sapere (“to taste, to discern, to be wise”). The noun meaning "man of profound wisdom" is recorded from circa 1300. Originally applied to the Seven Sages of Greece.

parole.significato: A food consisting principally of raw vegetables (especially greens, e.g. lettuce), other savoury ingredients (typically…
parole.testo: PIE word  *sḗh₂l Etymology tree Italian salatader. Old French saladebor. Middle English salade English salad From Middle English salade, from Old French salade, borrowed from Northern Italian salada, salata (compare insalata), from Vulgar Latin *salāta, from *salāre, from Latin saliō, from sal (“sal

parole.significato: salt cellar
parole.testo: From Middle English salar, saler, salere, saller, salure, seler, from Old French saler, salere, salier and Medieval Latin salare, from Latin sāl (“salt”).

parole.significato: An ordinary (geometric design) in the shape of an X. It usually occupies the entire field in which it is placed.
parole.testo: From Middle English sawtoure, from Old French sautoir (“stile, saltire”) (compare French sautoir (“saltire”)), from sauter (“to jump, to leap”) + -oir (subject forming nouns denoting physical objects from verbs), from Latin saltāre (“to dance, to jump”) + -orium, -oria.

parole.significato: Potassium nitrate.
parole.testo: From Middle English saltpetre, alteration of Old French salpetre, from Medieval Latin sāl petrae (“salt of the rock”), named so being found as an incrustation. Alteration of the first element is from folk-etymological association with salt (which is, nevertheless, cognate to Latin sāl).

parole.significato: The quality of being salubrious or invigorating.
parole.testo: From salubr(ious) + -ity, from Middle English salubritē, from Old French salubrité, from Latin salūbritātem, accusative of salūbritās.

parole.significato: To greet; to salute.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English saluen, borrowed from Old French saluer, from saluder, from Latin salūtāre, from salūs + -āris.

parole.significato: A greeting, salute, or address; a hello.
parole.testo: From Middle English salutacioun, from Old French salutacion, from Latin salutatio (“a greeting, a wishing health to”), from saluto (“wish one’s health, greet”), from salus (“well-being”). Compare the Latin greeting salve (literally “be well”).

parole.significato: The rescue of a ship, its crew and passengers or its cargo from a hazardous situation.
parole.testo: From Old French salver (see also save, from a variant form), from Late Latin salvare (“to make safe, secure, save”), from Latin salvus (“safe”) with the English suffix -age.

parole.significato: The process of being saved, the state of having been saved (from hell).
parole.testo: From Middle English savacioun, from Old French savaciun, salvaciun, from Latin salvātiō. Displaced native Old English hǣlu.

parole.significato: A material of rich silk, sometimes with gold threads, especially prized during the Middle Ages.
parole.testo: From Middle English samite, from Old French samit, from Medieval Latin samitum, examitum, from Byzantine Greek ἑξάμιτον (hexámiton), from ἕξ (héx, “six”) + μίτος (mítos, “thread”).

parole.significato: A part or snippet of something taken or presented for inspection, or shown as evidence of the quality of the whole; a s…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English saumple, sample, from Old French essample (“example”), from Latin exemplum. Doublet of example and exemplum.

parole.significato: A piece of needlework embroidered with a variety of designs.
parole.testo: From Old French essamplaire, from Latin exemplāris. Doublet of exemplar.

parole.significato: The (usually gradual or uncompleted) process by which a Christian believer is made holy through the action of the Holy…
parole.testo: From Old French sanctificacion, from ecclesiastical Latin sanctificātionem, from sanctificāre (“to sanctify”).

parole.significato: Holiness of life or disposition; saintliness
parole.testo: From Middle English sanctity, from Old French sanctete, from Latin sānctitās.

parole.significato: A place of safety, refuge, or protection.
parole.testo: From Middle English seyntuarie, from Old French saintuaire, from Late Latin sanctuarium (“a sacred place, a shrine, a private cabinet, in Medieval Latin also temple, church, churchyard, cemetery, right of asylum”), from Latin sanctus (“holy, sacred”); see saint.

parole.significato: A type of open shoe made up of straps or bands holding a sole to the foot
parole.testo: From Middle English sandal (“sandal”), from Old French sandale, from Latin sandalium, from Ancient Greek σανδάλιον (sandálion), diminutive of σάνδαλον (sándalon, “sandal”), of unknown origin. Often mistakenly parsed as related to sand.

parole.significato: sandalwood, especially the red sandalwood
parole.testo: From Middle English saundres (“sandalwood”), from Old French sandre, from Medieval Latin sandalum, from Byzantine Greek σάνδανον (sándanon), σάνταλον (sántalon), from Arabic صَنْدَل (ṣandal), from Middle Persian [script needed] (cndl /⁠čandal⁠/, “sandalwood”), from Sanskrit चन्दन (candana, “sandalwo

parole.significato: Having the colour of blood; blood red.
parole.testo: From Middle English sanguine, from Old French sanguin, ultimately from Latin sanguineus (“of blood”), from sanguis (“blood”) (of uncertain origin, but probably from Proto-Indo-European *h₁sh₂-én-, from *h₁ésh₂r̥ (“blood”), with an obscure suffix such as *-ǵʰ- (related to body parts)) + -inus + -eus.

parole.significato: Containing or tinged with blood.
parole.testo: From Middle English sanguinolent, from Old French sanguinolent, from Latin sanguinolentus (“of blood”).

parole.significato: Without; lacking; especially with regard to something expected or with precedent.
parole.testo: From Middle English saunz, sans, borrowed from Old French sans, senz, sens, from Latin sine (“without”) conflated with absēns (“absent, remote”). Compare French sans, Italian senza, Portuguese sem, and Spanish sin.

parole.significato: The property of being sapient, the property of possessing or being able to possess wisdom.
parole.testo: From Middle English sapience, from Old French sapience, from Latin sapientia.

parole.significato: Possessing or conferring wisdom, especially religious wisdom.
parole.testo: From Middle English sapyencyall, from Old French or Late Latin/Ecclesiastical Latin sapientiālis, from Latin sapientia (“wisdom”) + -ālis (“-al”).

parole.significato: A clear deep blue variety of corundum, valued as a precious stone.
parole.testo: From Middle English saphir, from Old French saphir, from Latin sapphir, sappir, sapphīrus, from Ancient Greek σάπφειρος (sáppheiros, “precious stone, gem”), from a Semitic language such as Hebrew סַפִּיר (sappī́r, “lapis lazuli”), originally from Assyrian Akkadian šipirtu (“lapis lazuli”).

parole.significato: One of the outer pinions or feathers of the wing of a bird, especially a hawk.
parole.testo: From Old French cercel, French cerceau, Latin circellus, diminutive of circulus. See circle.

parole.significato: Sarcelly, having curled ends (compare moline).
parole.testo: From Old French cercel, from Latin circellus, diminutive of circulus (“circle”).

parole.significato: A variety of carnelian, of a rich reddish yellow or brownish red color.
parole.testo: From Middle English sarde, borrowed from Old French sarde, from Latin sarda, sardius. Doublet of sardius.

parole.significato: sard (a variety of carnelian)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English sardoyne, sardone, from Old French sardoine, sardone (whence Modern French sardoine) or Anglo-Norman sardonie, ultimately from Latin sardonyx. Doublet of sardonyx.

parole.significato: An assart, or clearing; land cleared for agriculture.
parole.testo: From Middle English sart, from Old French sart, from Medieval Latin sarrītum (“to hoe”).

parole.significato: A bag or case with one or two shoulder straps, especially used to carry books etc.
parole.testo: First recorded circa 1340 as Middle English sachel, from Old French sachel, from Late Latin saccellum (“money bag, purse”), a diminutive of Latin sacculus, itself a diminutive of saccus (“bag”). See sack.

parole.significato: A fulfilment of a need or desire.
parole.testo: From Middle English satisfaccioun, from Old French satisfaccion and Latin satisfactiō, satisfactiōnis.

parole.significato: To be enough (for)
parole.testo: From Middle English satisfyen, satisfien, from Old French satisfiier, satisfier (also Old French satisfaire), from Latin satisfacere, from satis (“enough, sufficient”) + faciō (“to make; to do”).

parole.significato: Of a person: having a tendency to be cold and gloomy.
parole.testo: From Middle English saturnine, satournine, satournyne, saturnin, saturnyn, saturnyne (“pertaining to or under the influence of the planet Saturn; line on the palm of the hand associated with Saturn”), from Old French saturnine, saturnin (modern French saturnin (“of, pertaining to, resembling or cont

parole.significato: A creature with a human head and the limbs of different animals.
parole.testo: From Old French satirel (“little satyr”); see satyr for more.

parole.significato: A liquid (often thickened) condiment or accompaniment to food.
parole.testo: PIE word  *sḗh₂l From Middle English sauce, from Old French sause, from Vulgar Latin *salsa, noun use of the feminine of Latin salsus (“salted”), past participle of saliō (“to salt”), from sal. Doublet of salsa. For the meaning development compare Ancient Greek ἥδυσμα (hḗdusma) ultimately from Proto

parole.significato: A small shallow dish to hold a cup and catch drips.
parole.testo: From Middle English saucer, from Old French saussier (and feminine saussiere; hence modern French saucier m, saucière f).

parole.significato: The part of a noble estate dedicated to making sauces.
parole.testo: From Middle English saucerie, from Old French sausserie.

parole.significato: Wild; not cultivated or tamed.
parole.testo: From Middle English savage, from Old French sauvage, salvage (“wild, untamed”), from Late Latin salvāticus, alteration of Latin silvāticus (“wild”, literally “of the woods”), from silva (“forest; grove”). Doublet of sylvatic.

parole.significato: To prevent harm or difficulty.
parole.testo: From Middle English saven, sauven, a borrowing from Old French sauver, from Late Latin salvāre (“to save”). Displaced native Old English nerian.

parole.significato: The act of saving; salvation.
parole.testo: From Middle English savement, from Old French sauvement. Equivalent to save + -ment.

parole.significato: The evergreen shrub Juniperus sabina, endemic to Europe, which yields a medicinal oil.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English savyne, from Old French savine, from Latin sabīna. Compare Old English safine.

parole.significato: A person who saves someone, rescues another from harm.
parole.testo: First attested in 1300 as Middle English saveour, from Old French sauveour, from Late Latin salvātor, from salvō. Doublet of salvator. Displaced native Old English hǣlend.

parole.significato: Tasty, attractive to the palate.
parole.testo: From the Middle English savory, savourie, from Old French savouré, from Old French savourer, from Late Latin sapōrāre, from Latin sapor (“taste, flavour”), from sapiō, sapere (“taste of, have a flavour of”).

parole.significato: Any plant in the genus Saxifraga.
parole.testo: From Old French saxifrage, from Late Latin saxifraga, from Latin saxifragus (“stone-breaking”). Doublet of sassafras.

parole.significato: A member of an ancient West Germanic tribe that lived at the eastern North Sea coast and south of it.
parole.testo: Partially from Middle English Saxe, Sax; from Old English *Seaxa (attested in plural Seaxan), and Saxoun, from Old French *Saxoun, Saxon (“Saxon”), from Late Latin Saxōnem, accusative of Saxō (“a Saxon”), both from Proto-West Germanic *sahs, from Proto-Germanic *sahsą (“rock, knife”), from Proto-Ind

parole.significato: A medieval peasant's sleeveless jacket.
parole.testo: From Old French saye (“serge”).

parole.significato: To roughly dress stone.
parole.testo: From Middle English scaplen, from Old French escapler (“to dress timber”), from es- (“off”) (from Latin ex-) + capler (“to cut”) (from Vulgar Latin *capulre, *cappulre).

parole.significato: Synonym of escaline, (particularly) the form circulated by Stephen de Fulbourn in Ireland as a debased form of the ster…
parole.testo: From Old French escalin, from Middle Dutch schelling (“shilling”). Doublet of shilling.

parole.significato: Part of an overlapping arrangement of many small, flat and hard pieces of keratin covering the skin of an animal, parti…
parole.testo: From Middle English scale, from Old French escale, from Frankish and/or Old High German skala, from Proto-Germanic *skalō. Cognate with Old English sċealu (“shell, husk”), whence the modern doublet shale. Further cognate with Dutch schaal, German Schale, French écale.

parole.significato: Any of various marine bivalve molluscs of the superfamily Pectinoidea.
parole.testo: From Old French escalope (“shell”). Doublet of escalope. Related to scale and shell.

parole.significato: Any member of the species Convolvulus scammonia, a twining perennial bindweed native to the eastern part of the Mediter…
parole.testo: From Middle English scamōnīe, from Old French scamonie, from Latin scammōnia, from Ancient Greek σκαμμώνιον (skammṓnion).

parole.significato: Of a thing: causing or having the nature of a scandal; regarded as so immoral or wrong as to be extremely disgraceful;…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English scandalouse (“disgraceful, shameful”), borrowed from Old French scandaleux (“scandalous”) (modern French scandaleux), from Medieval Latin scandalōsus, from Ecclesiastical Latin scandalum (“scandal”) + Latin -ōsus (suffix meaning ‘full of; prone to’ forming adjectives). Scand

parole.significato: To scant; to be niggardly with; to divide into small pieces; to cut short or down.
parole.testo: Old French escanteler, eschanteler.

parole.significato: A small pattern or quantity.
parole.testo: From Old French eschantelet (“corner”).

parole.significato: The set size or dimension of a piece of timber, stone etc., or materials used to build ships or aircraft.
parole.testo: Alteration of scantillon + -ling, from Old French escantillon (“sample pattern”) (Modern French échantillon). Later senses also influenced by similarity with scant.

parole.significato: A permanent mark on the skin, sometimes caused by the healing of a wound.
parole.testo: From Middle English scar, scarre, a conflation of Old French escare (“scab”) (from Late Latin eschara, from Ancient Greek ἐσχάρα (eskhára, “scab left from a burn”), and thus a doublet of eschar) and Middle English skar (“incision, cut, fissure”) (from Old Norse skarð (“notch, chink, gap”), from Prot

parole.significato: The act of scarifying: raking the ground harshly to remove weeds, etc.
parole.testo: From Old French scarificacion, from Late Latin scarificatio. See scarify for more.

parole.significato: A brilliant red colour sometimes tinged with orange.
parole.testo: From Middle English scarlet, scarlat, borrowed from Old French escarlate (“a type of cloth”), from Medieval Latin scarlātum (“scarlet cloth”), of uncertain origin. parole.significato: A distinctive smell.
parole.testo: From Middle English sent (noun) and senten (verb), from Old French sentir (“to feel, perceive, smell, sense”), from Latin sentiō, sentīre (“to feel, sense”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sent- (“to feel”), and thus related to Saterland Frisian Sin (“sense”), West Frisian sin (“sense”), Dutch

parole.significato: An ornamental staff held by a ruling monarch as a symbol of power.
parole.testo: From Middle English septre, sceptre, from Old French sceptre, from Latin scēptrum, from Ancient Greek σκῆπτρον (skêptron, “staff, stick, baton”), from σκήπτω (skḗptō, “to prop, to support, to lean upon a staff”).

parole.significato: A split or separation within a group or organization, typically caused by discord.
parole.testo: From Middle English scisme, from Old French cisme or scisme, from Ancient Greek σχίσμα (skhísma, “division”), from σχίζω (skhízō, “I split”). Doublet of schisma. Compare chasm.
