parole.significato: scholarship
parole.testo: Old French scholarité, or Latin scholaritias.

parole.significato: A particular discipline or branch of knowledge that is natural, measurable or consisting of systematic principles rathe…
parole.testo: From Middle English science, scyence, borrowed from Old French science, escience, from Latin scientia (“knowledge”), from sciēns, the present participle stem of scire (“to know”).

parole.significato: A descendant, especially a first-generation descendant of a distinguished family.
parole.testo: From Middle English sion, sioun, syon, scion, cion, from Old French cion, ciun, cyon, sion, from Frankish *kīþō, *kīþ, from Proto-Germanic *kīþô, *kīþą, *kīþaz (“sprout”), from Proto-Indo-European *geye- (“to split open, sprout”), same source as Old English ċīþ (“a young shoot; sprout; germ; sprig”)

parole.significato: The act of division, separation, cutting, cleaving, or severing; cleavage.
parole.testo: Via Middle English and Old French, from Late Latin scissio, scissionem, from Latin scindere.

parole.significato: To cut using, or as if using, scissors.
parole.testo: From Middle English cysour, cysoure, cysowre, altered from sisours (“scissors”), from Old French cisoires, cisours, cisur, from Latin caedere (“to cut”); current spelling influenced by Latin scindere, scissus (“to split”).

parole.significato: A tool used for cutting thin material, consisting of two crossing blades attached at a pivot point in such a way that t…
parole.testo: From Middle English sisours (attested since 1350–1400), from Old French cisoirs, from Late Latin cīsōria, plural of cīsōrium (“cutting tool”); from Latin word root -cīsus (compare excise) or caesus, past participle of caedō (“to cut”). Partially displaced native Old English sċēara (“scissors, shears

parole.significato: A fixture for a light, which holds it and provides a screen against wind or against a naked flame or lightbulb.
parole.testo: From Middle English sconce, sconse (“candlestick or lantern (with screen)”), from Old French esconse (“lantern”), from Latin absconsus (“hidden”), perfect passive participle of abscondō (“hide”). Cognate with abscond.

parole.significato: A person sent out to gather and bring back information; especially, one employed in war to gain information about the e…
parole.testo: From Middle English scout, scoult, from Old French escoute (“action of listening”), verbal noun from escouter (“to listen, heed”), from Latin auscultō (“to listen”). The verb comes from the noun.

parole.significato: To scrape or scratch.
parole.testo: From Middle French and Old French schrabben (“to scrape, scratch”), from Frankish *skaban, from Proto-Germanic *skabaną, from Proto-Indo-European *skabʰ- (“to scratch”); compare Old High German skaban, Irish scríobann and sgrìoban.

parole.significato: A device that has a helical function.
parole.testo: From Middle English screw, scrue (“screw”); apparently, despite the difference in meaning, from Old French escroue (“nut, cylindrical socket, screwhole”), from Latin scrōfa (“female pig”) through comparison with the corkscrew shape of a pig's penis. There is also the Old French escruve (“screw”), fr

parole.significato: Someone who writes; a draughtsperson; a writer for another; especially, an official or public writer; an amanuensis, se…
parole.testo: From Middle English scribe, from Old French scribe (“scribe”), from Late Latin usage of scrība (“secretary”) (used in the Vulgate Bible translation to render Ancient Greek γραμματεύς (grammateús, “scribe, secretary”), which had been used in its turn to render the Hebrew סופר (“writer, scholar”)) fro

parole.significato: To create (a small ornamental handicraft also called a scrimshaw) by carving or engraving on bone (originally whalebone…
parole.testo: The origin of the verb is unknown, but it has possibly been influenced by the surname Scrimshaw. parole.significato: A chest or other box for storing valuables.
parole.testo: From Old French escrin (French écrin), from Latin scrīnium. Doublet of shrine.

parole.significato: A small medieval bag used to carry food, money, utensils etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English scrippe, an aphetism of Old French escrepe (“purse, alms-bag”), a variant of escharpe, from Old Norse skreppa. Cognate with Danish skreppe (“scrip”), Norwegian skreppa (“bag”). Doublet of scarf.

parole.significato: To make or write a script.
parole.testo: From Middle English scrit, borrowed from Old French escrit, from Latin scriptum (something written), from scrībō (“write”).

parole.significato: A roll of paper or parchment; a writing formed into a roll.
parole.testo: From Middle English scrowle, scrolle, from earlier scrowe, scrouwe (influenced by Middle English rolle), from Old French escroe, escrowe, escrouwe (“scroll, strip of parchment”), from Frankish *skrōda (“a shred”), from Proto-Germanic *skraudō, from *skrew- (“to cut; cutting tool”), extension of *(s)

parole.significato: scroll
parole.testo: From Middle English scrowe, from Old French escroe (“register, note; bit of parchment; piece”), from Frankish *skrōda (“piece”), from Proto-Germanic *skraudō, derivative of Proto-Germanic *skraudaną (“to shred”).

parole.significato: Hesitation to act from the difficulty of determining what is right or expedient; doubt, hesitation or unwillingness due…
parole.testo: From Old French scrupule, from Latin scrūpulus (“(literally) a small sharp or pointed stone; uneasiness of mind, anxiety, doubt, trouble; scruple”) and scrūpulum (“one twenty-fourth of an ounce”), diminutives of scrūpus (“a rough or sharp stone; anxiety, uneasiness”); perhaps akin to Ancient Greek σ

parole.significato: To magically or supernaturally look into or (as an entertainer) predict (the future), using crystal balls or other obje…
parole.testo: From Middle English scrien, scryen, a shortened form of Middle English ascrien, from Old French escrier (“to cry out”). Influenced by Middle English descrien (“to descry”).

parole.significato: A three-dimensional work of art created by shaping malleable objects and letting them harden or by chipping away pieces…
parole.testo: From Middle English sculpture, from Old French sculpture, from Latin sculptūra (“sculpture”), from sculpō (“to cut out, to carve in stone”).

parole.significato: Dung; excrement.
parole.testo: Perhaps Old French escumbrier (“to disencumber”).

parole.significato: A hare; (hunting, also figuratively) a hare as the game in a hunt.
parole.testo: From Middle English scut (“hare”); further etymology uncertain, possibly related to Middle English scut, scute (“short”), possibly from Old French escorter, escurter, or Latin excurtāre, scurtāre, from curtō (“to cut short, shorten”), from curtus (“short; shortened”) (from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ke

parole.significato: Grease; tallow; lard.
parole.testo: From Middle English seym (“grease”), from Old French saim (“fat”). Compare French saindoux (“lard”).

parole.significato: Part of a gun that retards the hammer until the trigger is pulled.
parole.testo: Possibly from Old French serre (“claw, talon, grasp”)

parole.significato: One who searches.
parole.testo: From Middle English serchour, sercher, from Old French cercheor; equivalent to search + -er.

parole.significato: Each of the divisions of a year based on the prevailing weather: spring, summer, autumn (fall) and winter; or the rainy…
parole.testo: From Middle English sesoun, seson (“time of the year”), from Old French seson, saison (“time of sowing, seeding”), from Latin satiō (“act of sowing, planting”) from satum, past participle of serō (“to sow, plant”) from Proto-Indo-European *seh₁- (“to sow, plant”). Akin to Old English sāwan (“to sow”

parole.significato: Number-two; following after the first one with nothing between them. The ordinal number corresponding to the cardinal n…
parole.testo: From Middle English secunde, second, secound, secund, borrowed from Old French second, seond, from Latin secundus (“following, next in order”), from root of sequor (“to follow”), from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to follow”). Doublet of secund and secundo. Displaced native twoth and partially displa

parole.significato: A unit of time historically and commonly defined as a sixtieth of a minute which the International System of Units more…
parole.testo: From Middle English secunde, seconde, borrowed from Old French seconde, from Medieval Latin secunda, short for secunda pars minuta (“second diminished part (of the hour)”).

parole.significato: Concealment; the condition of being secret or hidden.
parole.testo: An alteration (on the model of primacy, etc.) of Late Middle English secretee, from Old French secré.

parole.significato: Being or kept hidden.
parole.testo: From Middle English secrette, from Old French secret, from Latin sēcrētus (“separated, hidden”), from ptp of sēcernō (“separate, to set aside, sunder out”), from cernō, from Proto-Indo-European *krey-. Displaced Old English dēagol (“secret”).

parole.significato: To cut, divide or separate into pieces.
parole.testo: From Middle English seccioun, from Old French section, from Latin sectiō (“cutting, cutting off, excision, amputation of diseased parts of the body, etc.”), from sectus, past participle of secāre (“to cut”). More at saw.

parole.significato: Not specifically religious; lay or civil, as opposed to clerical.
parole.testo: From Middle English seculer, from Old French seculer, from Latin saeculāris (“of the age”), from saeculum.

parole.significato: Organized incitement of rebellion or civil disorder against authority or the state, usually by speech or writing.
parole.testo: From Old French sedicion, from Latin sēditiō (“sedition, discord”), from sēd- (“apart”) (an alternative form of sē-) + itiō (“going”).

parole.significato: A diocese or archdiocese: a region of a church, generally headed by a bishop or an archbishop.
parole.testo: From Middle English se, see, from Old French see, sié (“seat, throne; town, capital; episcopal see”), from Latin sēdēs (“seat”), referring to the bishop's throne or chair (compare seat of power) in the cathedral; related to the Latin verb sedēre (“to sit”). Doublet of sedes.

parole.significato: To sew together the eyelids of a young hawk.
parole.testo: From Middle English silen, from Old French siller, ciller (“to sew up the eyelids of, hoodwink, wink”), from cil (“eyelid”), from Latin cilium (“eyelid, eyelash”).

parole.significato: A feudal lord; a nobleman who held his lands by feudal grant; any lord (holder) of a manor.
parole.testo: From Middle English senyour, from Old French seignor, seignior, from Latin senior, seniōrem. Doublet of seigneur, senhor, senior, señor, senyor, signore, sir, and sire.

parole.significato: The estate of a feudal lord.
parole.testo: From Middle English seignurie, from Old French seignurie, from seignor + -ie.

parole.significato: In the Middle Ages, relating to or befitting of a nobleman.
parole.testo: Old French *seignorial, from seignor (“master, lord”) + -ial (adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: To vest ownership of an estate in land (to someone).
parole.testo: From Middle English seisen, from Old French seisir (“to put in possession of", "to take possession of”), from Early Medieval Latin sacīre, from Frankish *sakjan (“to sue, bring a legal charge against”), from Proto-Germanic *sakōną (“to charge, seek legal action against”), from Proto-Indo-European *s

parole.significato: An entitlement to a freehold estate with a right to immediate possession.
parole.testo: From Middle English seisin, seysen, from Old French seisin, from the verb seisir, from Early Medieval Latin sacīre, from the same Proto-Indo-European root as Gothic 𐍃𐌰𐍄𐌾𐌰𐌽 (satjan) and Old English settan. More at seize, seise.

parole.significato: A mediaeval open strip of land or small field used for growing crops.
parole.testo: Old French seillon (“a measure of land”), French sillon (“a ridge, furrow”), Latin selio (“a measure of land”).

parole.significato: To imitate; to make a representation or likeness.
parole.testo: From Middle English semblen, from Old French sembler (“to resemble”).

parole.significato: Like; resembling.
parole.testo: From Middle English semble, from Old French semble.

parole.significato: Of or relating to seed or semen.
parole.testo: From Middle English seminal, semynal, from Old French seminal, seminale, from Latin sēminālis, ultimately from oblique stem of Latin sēmen, sēminis (“seed”) + -al.

parole.significato: Everlasting, eternal.
parole.testo: From Old French sempiternel, from Medieval Latin sempiternālis, from Latin sempiternus, a contraction of semperæternus, from semper (“always”) + æternus (“eternal”).

parole.significato: In some bicameral legislative systems, the upper house or chamber.
parole.testo: From Middle English senat, from Old French senat, from Latin senātus (“council of elders; a senate”), from senex (“old”).

parole.significato: A light silk cloth.
parole.testo: From Old French cendal.

parole.significato: Senna.
parole.testo: From Old French sene.

parole.significato: A steward, particularly (historical) one in charge of a medieval nobleman's estate.
parole.testo: From Middle English seneschal (recorded in English since 1393), from Old French seneschal, from Medieval Latin siniscalcus, from Frankish *siniskalk, from Proto-Germanic *siniskalkaz, from Proto-Germanic *siniz (“senior”) + *skalkaz (“servant”); latter term as in marshal. As an officer of the French

parole.significato: A physical feeling or perception from something that comes into contact with the body; something sensed.
parole.testo: From Old French, from Medieval Latin sensatio, from Latin sensus.

parole.significato: Any of the manners by which living beings perceive the physical world: for humans sight, smell, hearing, touch, taste.
parole.testo: From Middle English sense, from Old French sens, sen, san (“sense, perception, direction”); partly from Latin sēnsus (“sensation, feeling, meaning”), from sentiō (“feel, perceive”); partly of Germanic origin (whence also Occitan sen, Italian senno), from Vulgar Latin *sennus (“sense, reason, way”),

parole.significato: A general thought, feeling, or sense.
parole.testo: From Old French sentement, from Latin sentimentum.

parole.significato: A guard, particularly on duty at the entrance to a military base.
parole.testo: From earlier sentrie, sentery, of uncertain origin. Perhaps an alteration of sentinel or sanctuary; or perhaps from Old French senteret (“a path”), diminutive of sentier, from Medieval Latin semitarius (“a path”).

parole.significato: The mustard plant or its seed.
parole.testo: From Middle English senvey, senevey, from Old French senevé, senevei, from Vulgar Latin *sināpātium, from Latin sināpi (→ Old French senef), from Ancient Greek σίνᾱπι (sínāpi).

parole.significato: The act of disuniting two or more things, or the condition of being separated.
parole.testo: Attested in the 15th Century C.E.; from Middle English separacioun, from Old French separacion, from Latin separatio, separationem. Morphologically separate + -ion.

parole.significato: A burial chamber.
parole.testo: From Middle English sepulchre, sepulcre, sepulker, from late Old English sepulcer, Old French sepulchre, sepulcre, and their etymon Latin sepulchrum, sepulcrum (“grave, burial place”).

parole.significato: To inter in a sepulture.
parole.testo: From Middle English sepulture, sepultur, from Old French sepulture, from Latin sepultura.

parole.significato: A set of things next to each other in a set order; a series.
parole.testo: From Middle English sequence, from Old French sequence (“a sequence of cards, answering verses”), from Late Latin sequentia (“a following”), from Latin sequēns (“following”), from sequī (“to follow”); see sequent.

parole.significato: To separate from all external influence; to seclude; to withdraw.
parole.testo: From Middle English sequestren (verb) and sequestre (noun), from Old French sequestrer, from Late Latin sequestrō (“separate, give up for safekeeping”), from Latin sequester (“mediator, depositary”), probably originally meaning "follower", from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“follow”).

parole.significato: A claw, a talon.
parole.testo: From Old French serre (modern French serre (“talon”)), from serrer (“to grip tightly; to shut”) (modern French serrer (“to squeeze; to tighten”)), from Vulgar Latin serrāre (“to close, shut”), from Late Latin serāre, present active infinitive of serō (“to fasten with a bolt; to bar, bolt”), from ser

parole.significato: The state of being serene; calmness; peacefulness.
parole.testo: From Middle English serenyte, from Old French serenité, from Latin serēnitās, equivalent to serene + -ity.

parole.significato: A partially free peasant of a low hereditary class, attached like a slave to the land owned by a feudal lord and requir…
parole.testo: From Middle English serf, from Old French serf, from Latin servus (“slave, serf, servant”).

parole.significato: A type of worsted cloth.
parole.testo: From Middle English sarge, from Old French sarge, serge, from Vulgar Latin *sarica, from Latin sērica (“silken, silk things”), from Ancient Greek σηρικός (sērikós, “silken”), from σήρ (sḗr, “silkworm”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”), possibly from Old Chinese 絲 (*sə, “silk”). Doublet of silk and seric.

parole.significato: A large wax candle used in some church ceremonies.
parole.testo: From Middle English cerge, from Old French ci(e)rge, cerge & chierge.

parole.significato: A UK army rank with NATO code OR-6, senior to corporal and junior to warrant officer ranks.
parole.testo: From Middle English sergeant, sergeaunt, serjent, serjaunt, serjawnt, sergant, from Old French sergeant, sergent, serjant, sergient, sergant (“sergeant, servant”), from Medieval Latin servientem, accusative of serviēns (“a servant, vassal, soldier, apparitor”), from Latin serviēns (“serving”), prese

parole.significato: Without humor or expression of happiness; grave in manner or disposition.
parole.testo: From Middle English seryows, from Old French serieux, from Medieval Latin sēriōsus, an extension of Latin sērius (“grave, earnest, serious”), possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“heavy”). (If this root is correct, cognate with German schwer (“heavy, difficult, severe”), Old English

parole.significato: In a serious or literal manner.
parole.testo: From Middle English seriously, sereously, ceryously, seryowslech (“earnestly”), equivalent to serious + -ly.

parole.significato: A land tenure in which a tenant provided his liege with some kind of personal service, as opposed to nonpersonal servic…
parole.testo: From Middle English sergeauntie, serjaunte, from Old French serjantie, sergantie and Medieval Latin serjantia, sergantia. Compare sergeancy.

parole.significato: To discourse to or of, as in a sermon.
parole.testo: From Middle English sermonen, from Old French sermoner, from sermon (see above).

parole.significato: A plant of the genus Laserpitium.
parole.testo: From Middle English sermontayne, from Old French sermontain. The modern English form has been remodelled after mountain.

parole.significato: To wind or meander
parole.testo: From Middle English serpent, from Old French serpent (“snake, serpent”), from Latin serpēns (“snake”), present active participle of serpere (“to creep, crawl”), from Proto-Italic *serpō, from Proto-Indo-European *serp-. In this sense, displaced native Old English nǣdre (“snake, serpent”), whence Mod

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of snakes.
parole.testo: From Middle English serpentine, from Old French serpentin, from Latin serpentīnus, from serpēns (“serpent”), equivalent to serpent + -ine.

parole.significato: Servitude, bondage.
parole.testo: From Middle English servage, from Old French servage; equivalent to serve + -age.

parole.significato: One who is hired to perform regular household or other duties, and receives compensation. As opposed to a slave.
parole.testo: From Middle English servaunt, from Old French servant, from the present participle of the verb servir. Doublet of sergeant and servient. Morphologically serve + -ant. Displaced native Old English þeġn.

parole.significato: An act of being of assistance to someone.
parole.testo: From Middle English servise, from Old English serfis, from Old French servise (French service), from the verb servir, from Latin servitium (compare Portuguese serviço, Italian servizio, Norman sèrvice, Spanish servicio), from servus (“servant; serf; slave”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ser-

parole.significato: Easy to service.
parole.testo: From Middle English servisable, from Old French servisable, from servise. By surface analysis, service + -able.

parole.significato: Excessively eager to please; obsequious.
parole.testo: From Middle English servyle, from Old French servil, servile, from Latin servīlis, from servus (“slave”). By surface analysis, serve + -ile.

parole.significato: To hold or participate in a jam session with other musicians.
parole.testo: From Middle English session, from Old French session, from Latin sessiō (“a sitting”), from sedeō (“sit”).

parole.significato: A young plant fit for setting out; a slip; shoot.
parole.testo: From Middle English set, sete, sette (“that which is set, the act of setting, seat”), from Old English set (“setting, seat, a place where people remain, habitation, camp, entrenchment, a place where animals are kept, stall, fold”) and Old English seten (“a set, shoot, slip, branch; a nursery, planta

parole.significato: The plant valerian.
parole.testo: From Old French citoual.

parole.significato: To cut free.
parole.testo: From Middle English severen, from Old French sevrer, from Latin separāre (“to separate”), from se- (“apart”) + parāre (“provide, arrange”). Doublet of separate, from the past participle of that Latin verb.

parole.significato: A category into which sexually-reproducing organisms are divided on the basis of their reproductive roles in their spec…
parole.testo: From Middle English sexe (“sex [distinction between male and female] and gender”), from Old French sexe (“genitals; gender”), from Latin sexus (“gender; gender traits; males or females; genitals”), from Proto-Italic *seksus, from Proto-Indo-European *séksus, from *sek- (“to cut, cut off, sever”), th

parole.significato: A church official who looks after a church building and its graveyard and may act as a gravedigger and bell ringer.
parole.testo: From Old French segrestien, from Medieval Latin sacristanus, based on Latin sacer (“sacred”). Doublet of sacristan.

parole.significato: A sacristy; vestry; a room for holy objects.
parole.testo: From Middle English sextriȝe, cextrye, sextrye, sextry, probably a reduced form of Old French secresterie or Anglo-Latin secrestāria, a variant of Medieval Latin sacristāria.

parole.significato: A mediaeval double-reed wind instrument with a conical wooden body.
parole.testo: From Middle English shalmuse, from Old French chalemel (modern French chalumeau), from Late Latin calamellus, from Latin calamus (“reed”), from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos). Doublet of caramel, chalumeau, and qalam, as well as related to calame, calamus, culm, and haulm.

parole.significato: Military action.
parole.testo: From Middle English sege, from Old French sege, siege, seige (modern French siège), from Vulgar Latin *sēdicum, from Latin sēdicŭlum, sēdēcula (“small seat”), from Latin sēdēs (“seat”). The military sense of the term is derived from the notion of an army "sitting down" in front of its target.

parole.significato: A visible fact that shows that something exists or may happen.
parole.testo: From Middle English signe, sygne, syng, seine, sine, syne, from Old English seġn (“sign; mark; token”) and Old French signe, seing (“sign; mark; signature”); both from Latin signum (“a mark; sign; token”); root uncertain. Doublet of signum and signal. Partially displaced native token.

parole.significato: A sequence of states representing an encoded message in a communication channel.
parole.testo: From Old French segnal, seignal or Medieval Latin signāle; noun use of the neuter of Late Latin signālis, from Latin signum; verb use from 1805, as a shortened from signalize (1650s). Doublet of signum and sign.

parole.significato: An object (especially a ring) formerly used to impress a picture into the sealing wax of a document as a proof of its o…
parole.testo: From Old French signet (“small seal”), from Medieval Latin signētum, diminutive of Latin signum (“sign”).

parole.significato: signification, meaning
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English signifiaunce, from Old French senefiance, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin significantia. Doublet of significance.

parole.significato: The act of signifying, or something that is signified; significance.
parole.testo: From Old French significacion, from Latin significātiō.

parole.significato: To create a sign out of something.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English signifien, from Old French signifier, from Latin significare.

parole.significato: The absence of any sound.
parole.testo: From Middle English silence, from Old French silence, from Latin silentium (“silence”), from silēns (“quiet, silent”, present participle of silēre) + -ium. Displaced native Old English swīġe and sālnes.

parole.significato: Similarity or resemblance to something else.
parole.testo: From Old French similitude, from Latin similitūdō. By surface analysis, similar + -itude.

parole.significato: A rich fruit cake, with a decorated marzipan covering, traditionally eaten on Simnel Sunday or Easter.
parole.testo: From Middle English simenel (also simle), from Old French simenel (“fine wheat flour; flat bread cake, Lenten cake”), probably by dissimilation from Vulgar Latin *siminellus, a diminutive of Latin simila (“fine flour”) (see semolina). Compare also Middle Dutch semel, Middle Low German semele.

parole.significato: The buying or selling of spiritual or sacred things, such as ecclesiastical offices, pardons, or consecrated objects.
parole.testo: From Middle English simonie, symonye, from Old French simonie, from Late Latin simonia, named after Simon Magus (Hebrew שִׁמְעוֹן (Šimʻôn, “Simon”)), with reference to Acts 8:18–20.

parole.significato: Uncomplicated; lacking complexity; taken by itself, with nothing added.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English symple, from Old French simple, from Latin simplex (“simple”, literally “onefold”) (as opposed to duplex (“double”, literally “twofold”)), from semel (“the same”) + plicō (“to fold”). See same and fold. Compare single, singular, simultaneous, etc. Partially displaced na

parole.significato: The state or quality of being simple
parole.testo: From Middle English simplicite, from Old French simplicite, from Latin simplicitās, from simplex (“simple”). See simple. By surface analysis, simple + -icity. Partially displaced native English onefoldness.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being sincere.
parole.testo: From Middle English sinceritie, from Old French sincerité and Medieval Latin sincēritās; both from Latin sincēritās, from sincērus + -tās. Equivalent to sincere + -ity.

parole.significato: Not accompanied by anything else; one in number.
parole.testo: From Middle English single, sengle, from Old French sengle, saingle, sangle, from Latin singulus, a diminutive derived from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“one”). Akin to Latin simplex (“simple”). See simple, and compare singular.

parole.significato: Singular.
parole.testo: From Middle English singler, from Old French sangler, seingler, sengler (“single, individual”) and a shortened form of Middle English singuler.

parole.significato: Being only one of a larger population; single, individual.
parole.testo: From Middle English singuler, from Old French, from Latin singulāris (“alone of its kind”), from Latin singulus (“single”).

parole.significato: Inauspicious, ominous, unlucky, illegitimate.
parole.testo: From Middle English sinistre (“unlucky”), from Old French senestre, sinistre (“left”), from Latin sinister (“left hand”).

parole.significato: A shade of red; sinoper.
parole.testo: From Old French sinople, from Latin Sinōpis, from Ancient Greek Σινωπίς (Sinōpís, “of Sinope”), a town that exported a red ocher. The unexpected change to meaning "green" in heraldry occurred in French texts around 1350 for unclear reasons.

parole.significato: A man of a higher rank or position.
parole.testo: From Middle English sir, unstressed form of sire, borrowed from Old French sire (“master, sir, lord”), from Latin senior (“older, elder”), from senex (“old”). Doublet of seigneur, seignior, senhor, senior, señor, senyor, signore, and sire.

parole.significato: A lord, master, or other person in authority, most commonly used vocatively: formerly in speaking to elders and superio…
parole.testo: From Middle English sire, from Old French sire, the nominative singular of seignor; from Latin senior, from senex. Doublet of seigneur, seignior, senhor, senior, señor, senyor, signore, and sir. Cognate with French monsieur.

parole.significato: One of a group of nymphs who lured mariners to their death on the rocks.
parole.testo: From Middle English siren, from Old French sereine and Latin Sīrēn, Sīrēna, from Ancient Greek Σειρήν (Seirḗn). parole.significato: A cut of beef from the lower part of the back, where the last ribs are (called rump in UK English).
parole.testo: From Middle English surloine, from Old French surlonge, from sur la longe (literally “above the loin”).

parole.significato: To adjust the size of; to make a certain size.
parole.testo: Attested since the 14th century, originally meant a “law or regulation that determines the amount to be paid”, from Middle English syse, sise (“regulation, control, limit”), from Old French cise, sise, aphetism of assise (“assize”), from the verb asseoir (“to sit down”), from Latin assidēre, compose

parole.significato: A quantity of thread, yarn, etc., wound on a reel then removed and loosely knotted into an oblong shape; a skein of cot…
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Middle English skaine, skayne (“quantity of string, thread, etc., wound on a reel; the string, thread, etc., so wound”), from Old French escaigne (modern French écagne, écaigne (Picardy)); further etymology uncertain, probably from Proto-Celtic, from Proto-Indo-European *ske

parole.significato: A large and heavy saucepan or frying pan with legs and, usually, a long handle designed for heating food in a fireplace.
parole.testo: From Old French escuëlette, diminutive of escuëlle (“a porringer”), (French écuelle), from Vulgar Latin scutella, diminutive of scutra, scuta (“tray, dish”). Compare scuttle (“basket”).

parole.significato: To pass lightly; to glide along in an even, smooth course; to glide along near the surface.
parole.testo: From Middle English skemen, skymen, variants of scumen, from Old French escumer (“to remove scum”), from escume (“froth, foam”), from Frankish *skūm (“froth, foam”), from Proto-Germanic *skūmaz (“foam”), from Proto-Indo-European *skew- (“to cover, conceal”). See scum.

parole.significato: A brief battle between small groups, usually part of a longer or larger battle or war.
parole.testo: From Middle English skirmish (as a verb), from Old French escarmouche (“skirmish”), from Italian scaramuccia, earlier schermugio. Doublet of escarmouche, Scaramouche, and Scaramucci.

parole.significato: A false or unsupported, malicious statement (spoken, not written), especially one which is injurious to a person's repu…
parole.testo: From Middle English slaundre, sclaundre, from Old French esclandre, from Ecclesiastical Latin scandalum (“stumbling block, temptation”), from Ancient Greek σκάνδαλον (skándalon, “scandal”). Doublet of scandal.

parole.significato: A thin, narrow strip or bar of wood (lath), metal, or plastic.
parole.testo: From Middle English slatte, sklatte, sklat, sclat, from Old French esclat (“piece broken or split off, shiver, splinter”), from Old French esclater (“to split, burst”), from Frankish *slaitijan (“to split, break”), from Proto-Germanic *slītaną (“to rend, split”). Doublet of slate and éclat.

parole.significato: A flake or piece of certain types of stone that tend to cleave into thin layers.
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Middle English sclate, slat, slate (“type of rock; roofing slate; writing slate”), from Old French esclate, a feminine form of esclat (“broken piece, shard”) (modern French éclat), from Old French esclater (“to break, shatter”), from Frankish *slaitijan (“to split, break”),

parole.significato: A person who is held in servitude as the property of another person, and whose labor (and often also whose body and lif…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English sclave, from Old French esclave, from Medieval Latin sclavus (“slave”), from Late Latin Sclavus (“Slav”), traditionally assumed to be because Slavs were often forced into slavery in the Middle Ages. The Latin word is from Byzantine Greek Σκλάβος (Sklábos); see that entr

parole.significato: Thin; slim.
parole.testo: From Middle English slendre, sclendre, from Old French esclendre (“thin, slender”), from Middle Dutch slinder (“thin, lank”), from Proto-Germanic *slindraz (“sliding, slippery”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃sleydʰ- (“to slip”). Cognate with Bavarian Schlenderling (“that which dangles”), German schle

parole.significato: That which is thin and broad.
parole.testo: From Middle English sclise, sklise, from Old French esclice, esclis (“a piece split off”), deverbal of esclicer, esclicier (“to splinter, split up”), from Frankish *slitjan (“to split up”), from Proto-Germanic *slitjaną, from Proto-Germanic *slītaną (“to split, tear apart”), from Proto-Indo-European

parole.significato: To put something (such as a coin) into a slot (narrow aperture).
parole.testo: From Middle English slot, from Old French esclot, likely from Old Norse slóð (“track”). As a gambling machine, via clipping of slot machine. Compare sleuth. The scheduling (calendar) sense is by a metaphor whereby the time span is equated with the segment of a page or part of a device that represent

parole.significato: To fly high with little effort, like a bird.
parole.testo: From Middle English soren, from Old French essorer (“to fly up, soar”), from Vulgar Latin *exaurare (“to rise into the air”), from Latin ex (“out”) + aura (“the air, a breeze”), from Ancient Greek αὔρα (aúra, “breath”). Compare aura, and exhale.

parole.significato: Not drunk; not intoxicated.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English sober, from Old French sobre, from Latin sōbrius, from se- (“without”) + ebrius (“intoxicated”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁egʷʰ- (“drink”). In the sense "not drunk," displaced native undrunken, from Old English undruncen.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being sober.
parole.testo: From Old French sobriete, from Latin sobrietas.

parole.significato: One who practices sodomy; a sodomist.
parole.testo: From Middle English sodomyte, sodomite, from Old French Sodomite and Latin sodomīta, from Ancient Greek σοδομίτης (sodomítēs). Equivalent to Sodom + -ite.

parole.significato: To make dirty.
parole.testo: From Middle English soilen, soulen, suylen (“to sully, make dirty”), partly from Old French soillier, souillier (“to soil, make dirty, wallow in mire”), from Old Frankish *saulijan, *sulwijan (“to make dirty, soil”); partly from Old English solian, sylian (“to soil, make dirty”), from Proto-Germanic

parole.significato: A wet or marshy place in which a boar or other such game seeks refuge when hunted.
parole.testo: From Middle English soyl, from Old French soil, souil (“quagmire, marsh”), from Frankish *sōlja, *saulja (“mire, miry place, wallow”), from Proto-Germanic *saulijō (“mud, puddle, feces”), from Proto-Indo-European *sūl- (“thick liquid”). Cognate with Old English syle, sylu, sylen (“miry place, wallow

parole.significato: To feed, as cattle or horses, in the barn or an enclosure, with fresh grass or green food cut for them, instead of send…
parole.testo: From Old French saoler, saouler (“to satiate”).

parole.significato: Making or becoming dirty; soiling, staining.
parole.testo: From Old French soilleure, from soillier (“to soil”).

parole.significato: A short stay somewhere.
parole.testo: From Middle English sojourne (noun) and sojournen (verb), from Old French sojor, sojorner (modern séjour, séjourner), from (assumed) Vulgar Latin *subdiurnāre, from Latin sub- (“under, a little over”) + Late Latin diurnus (“lasting for a day”), from Latin dies (“day”).

parole.significato: An old coin from France and some other countries worth 12 deniers.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Old French sol (“French coin”) (modern French sou), from Latin solidum, the accusative singular of solidus (“Roman gold coin; (adjective) solid”). Doublet of sold, soldo, solid, solidus, sou, and xu.

parole.significato: Comfort or consolation in a time of loneliness or distress.
parole.testo: From Old French solas, from Latin sōlācium (“consolation”), root from Proto-Indo-European *selh₂- (“mercy, comfort”).

parole.significato: The ruler of a major Muslim state in the Middle Ages, especially the Sultan of Egypt.
parole.testo: From Middle English soudan, from Old French soudan, from Arabic سُلْطَان (sulṭān). Doublet of sultan.

parole.significato: Any of various easily melted alloys, commonly of tin and lead, that are used to mend, coat, or join metal objects, usua…
parole.testo: From Middle English souder, soudere, soudur (noun), from Old French soldure, soudeure (noun), from Old French souder, solder (“to solder”, verb) (> Middle English souden (“to solder”)), from Latin solidāre (“make solid”).

parole.significato: A member of a ground-based army, of any rank, but especially an enlisted member.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English soudeour, from Old French soudier or soudeour (“mercenary”), from Medieval Latin soldarius (“soldier (one having pay)”), from Late Latin solidus, a type of coin. Displaced Old English cempa (whence obsolete kemp). (red herring): An allusion to soldiers' red uniforms; re

parole.significato: Only.
parole.testo: From Middle English sole, soule, from Old French sol, soul (“alone”), from Latin sōlus (“alone, single, solitary, lonely”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swé (reflexive pronoun). parole.significato: The quality of being deeply serious and sober or solemn.
parole.testo: From solemn + -ity, from Middle English solemnity (“observance of formality and ceremony”), frequently in the phrases in solemnity, with solemnity, which from Old French solemnite, from Latin sollemnitās, from sollemnis. (Compare solemn.)

parole.significato: To make solemn, or official, through ceremony or legal act.
parole.testo: From Middle English solempnisen, from Old French solemnisier, from Medieval Latin solemnizare, from Latin solemnis.

parole.significato: To persistently endeavor to obtain an object, or bring about an event.
parole.testo: From Middle English soliciten, solliciten, from Old French soliciter, solliciter, borrowed from Latin sollicitō (“stir, disturb; look after”), from sollicitus (“agitated, anxious, punctilious”, literally “thoroughly moved”), from sollus (“whole, entire”) + perfect passive participle of cieō (“shake,

parole.significato: The state of being solicitous; uneasiness of mind occasioned by fear of evil or desire for good; anxiety.
parole.testo: From Middle English solicitude, from Old French sollicitude, from Latin sollicitūdō (“anxiety”), from sollicitus, solicitus (“anxious, solicitous”). See solicitous.

parole.significato: That can be picked up or held, having a texture, and usually firm. Unlike a liquid, gas or plasma.
parole.testo: From Middle English solide, borrowed from Old French solide, from Latin solidus (“solid”), from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂-i-dʰ-o-s (“entire”), suffixed form of root *solh₂- (“integrate, whole”). Doublet of sol, sold, soldo, solidus, sou, and xu.

parole.significato: Aloneness; the state of being alone, solitary, or by oneself.
parole.testo: From Middle English solitude, from Old French solitude, from Latin sōlitūdō. By surface analysis, sole + -itude.

parole.significato: A solar, or garret room.
parole.testo: From Old French soler, solier, from Latin solarium (“a terrace or flat roof”), from sol (“sun”).

parole.significato: One of the two points in the ecliptic at which the sun is furthest from the celestial equator. This corresponds to one…
parole.testo: From Middle English solstice, from Old French solstice, from Latin sōlstitium.

parole.significato: Able to be dissolved.
parole.testo: From Middle English soluble, from Old French soluble, from Late Latin solūbilis, from Latin solvere (“to loosen”) + -bilis. Piecewise doublet of solvable.

parole.significato: A homogeneous mixture, which may be liquid, gas or solid, formed by dissolving one or more substances.
parole.testo: From Middle English solucioun, from Old French solucion (French solution), from Latin solūtiōnem, accusative singular of solūtiō, from the verb solvō. Compare solve, -tion.

parole.significato: pack animals.
parole.testo: From Old French [Term?]

parole.significato: The school of the sophists in antiquity; their beliefs and method of teaching philosophy and rhetoric.
parole.testo: From Middle English sophim, from Old French soffime, sofime, sofisme, sophisme, from Latin sophisma (“fallacy, sophism”), from Ancient Greek σόφῐσμᾰ (sóphĭsmă), from σοφίζω (sophízō) + -μα (-ma).

parole.significato: Enlightenment or education.
parole.testo: From Middle English sophisticacion, sophisticacioun, sophisticacoun, from Old French sofisticacion, sophisticacion, from Medieval Latin sophisticātiōnis. By surface analysis, sophisticate + -ion.

parole.significato: The actions or arguments of a sophist.
parole.testo: From Middle English safistre, soffistre, sofystry, sophestrie, sophestry, sophestrye, sophistre, sophistri, sophistrie, sophistry, sophistrye, sophystrye, from Old French sofisterie, sophistrie and Medieval Latin sophistria, Anglo-Latin sophestria, from Latin sophista, from Ancient Greek σοφιστής (s

parole.significato: A flock of mallards.
parole.testo: From Middle English sowrde, from Old French sourdre (“to rise”), that is, "to rise in flight, as a flock of birds", from Latin surgō. Related to surge.

parole.significato: A young hawk or falcon in its first year.
parole.testo: From Middle English sor (“sorrel”), from Old French sor (“sorrel; reddish”). Compare French saur (“(archaic) reddish-brown; describing a young bird of prey”).

parole.testo: From Middle English sorel, from Old French sorel, surele (“sorrel”), from Old French sur (“sour”), of Germanic origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *sūraz (“sour”); equivalent to sour + -el (diminutive suffix). parole.significato: A general type.
parole.testo: From Middle English sort, soort, sorte (cognate Dutch soort, German Sorte, Danish sort, Swedish sort), borrowed from Old French sorte (“class, kind”), from Latin sortem, accusative form of sors (“lot, fate, share, rank, category”).

parole.significato: To separate items into different categories according to certain criteria that determine their sorts.
parole.testo: From Middle English sorten, from Old French sortir (“to allot, sort”), from Latin sortīre (“draw lots, divide, choose”), from sors.

parole.significato: Witchcraft, magic, especially as a means of making decisions or predictions.
parole.testo: From Old French sortilège, from Medieval Latin sortilegium (“witchcraft”), from Latin sortilegus (“sorcerer, diviner”), from sors (“fate”) + legere (“choose”).

parole.significato: Of a whale, to dive downwards.
parole.testo: From Middle English sounden, from Old French sonder, from sonde (“sounding line”) of Germanic origin, compare Old English sundgyrd (“a sounding rod”), sundline (“a sounding line”), Old English sund (“water, sea”). More at Etymology 3 above.

parole.significato: Any of various dishes commonly made by combining liquids, such as water or stock, with other ingredients, such as meat…
parole.testo: The noun is from Middle English soupe, sowpe, from Old French soupe, souppe, sope, from Late Latin suppa (“sopped bread”), from Proto-Germanic *supô (compare Middle Dutch sope (“broth”)). Doublet of sop and zuppa. See also sup and supper. The verb is from the noun.

parole.significato: The person, place, or thing from which something (information, goods, etc.) comes or is acquired.
parole.testo: From Middle English sours, from Old French sorse (“rise, beginning, spring, source”), from sors, past participle of sordre, sourdre, from Latin surgō (“to rise”), which is composed of sub- (“up from below”) + regō (“lead, rule”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃réǵeti (“to straighten; right”)

parole.significato: To arise, issue or emerge; to give rise.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English sourden, from Old French sourdre, from Latin surgō, contraction of earlier subrigō. Compare source. Doublet of surge.

parole.significato: Something kept or steeped in brine.
parole.testo: From Middle English souse (“to salt pickle”) also a noun (“liquid for pickling,” “pickled pig parts”), from Old French sous (“preserved in salt”), from Frankish *sultija (“saltwater, brine”), from Proto-Germanic *sultijō (“saltwater, brine”). Cognate with Old Saxon sultia (“saltwater”), Old High Ger

parole.significato: Memory, remembrance.
parole.testo: From Old French souvenance, from the verb sovenir.

parole.significato: remembrance
parole.testo: Old French souvenance.

parole.significato: Exercising power of rule.
parole.testo: From Middle English sovereyn, from Old French soverain (whence also modern French souverain), from Vulgar Latin *superānus (compare Italian sovrano, Spanish soberano) from Latin super (“above”). Spelling influenced by folk-etymology association with reign. Doublet of soprano, from the same Latin roo

parole.significato: Having plenty of space; roomy; capacious.
parole.testo: From Middle English spacious, from Old French spacios, from Latin spatiōsus. By surface analysis, space + -ious.

parole.significato: A person from Spain or of Spanish descent.
parole.testo: From Middle English Spaignarde, from Old French Espaignard, from Espaigne. Equivalent to Spain + -ard.

parole.significato: Any of various small to medium-sized breeds of gun dog having a broad muzzle, long, wavy fur and long ears that hang at…
parole.testo: From Middle English spaynol, from Old French espaigneul (modern French épagneul), from Old Occitan espaignol, from Vulgar Latin *Hispāniolus (“Spanish”), from Hispānia (“Spain”).

parole.significato: A European smelt (Osmerus eperlanus).
parole.testo: From Middle English sperlynge, shortened from Old French esperlinge, a Germanic borrowing, found in German Spiering, Spierling, Middle Low German spirling, Middle Dutch spierling, suffixed from the word now Dutch spier (“spar, pole; muscle”). See also sparrow for a homonymic bird-name.

parole.significato: A canopy for a bed.
parole.testo: From Middle English sperver (“sparrow-hawk, canopy”), from Old French esprevier, from Old Dutch *sparwari (“sparrow-hawk”, literally “sparrow-eagle”).

parole.significato: A sudden, involuntary contraction of a muscle, a group of muscles, or a hollow organ.
parole.testo: From Middle English spasme, from Old French spasme, from Latin spasmus, from Ancient Greek σπασμός (spasmós, “spasm, convulsion”), from σπάω (spáō, “to draw out, pull out”).

parole.significato: A spatula.
parole.testo: From Middle English spatyll, spatyl, spatule, from Old French spatule, espatule, from Late Latin spatula.

parole.significato: The shoulder.
parole.testo: From Middle English spawde, spaude, spalde, from Old French espalde (French épaule), from Latin spatula. Doublet of spatula.

parole.significato: A bony swelling which develops in a horse's leg where the shank and splint bone meet, caused by inflammation of the car…
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Middle English spavein, spaveine (“swelling on horse’s leg causing lameness; disease causing lameness in horses”), from Old French espavain, a variant of esparvain, esprevain, esprevin (modern French éparvin, épervin). The further etymology is unknown; one suggestion is that

parole.significato: Distinguished by a unique, particular, or unusual quality.
parole.testo: From Middle English *special, especial, especiall, from Old French especial (whence also French spécial), from Latin speciālis (from speciēs). In this sense displaced native Old English synderlīċ. Doublet of especial.

parole.significato: That in which one specializes; a chosen expertise or talent; bailiwick.
parole.testo: From Middle English specialte, Old French specialte, especialte, from Latin specialitas.

parole.significato: Explicit or definite.
parole.testo: From Old French specifique, from Late Latin specificus (“specific, particular”), from Latin speciēs (“kind”) + -ific.

parole.significato: To state explicitly, or in detail, or as a condition.
parole.testo: From Middle English specifien, from Old French specifier, especefier, or directly from Medieval Latin specificō, from specificus (“specific”).

parole.significato: The process or act of thinking or meditating on a subject.
parole.testo: From Middle English speculacioun, speculation, from Old French speculation (compare French spéculation), from Late Latin speculātiō, speculātiōnem, from Latin speculor. Morphologically speculate + -ion.

parole.significato: Characterized by speculation; based on guessing, unfounded opinions, or extrapolation.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English speculatyf, borrowed from Old French speculatif or directly from Late Latin speculativus, from Latin speculor.

parole.significato: A cave, cavern or grotto.
parole.testo: From Middle English spelunke, from Old French spelonque and/or Latin spelunca, from Ancient Greek σπῆλυγξ (spêlunx, “cave”), related to σπέος (spéos). Cognates include Middle Dutch spelunke, spelonke, German Spelunke.

parole.significato: A surface in three dimensions consisting of all points equidistant from a center. .
parole.testo: From Middle English spere, from Old French sphere, from Late Latin sphēra, earlier Latin sphaera (“ball, globe, celestial sphere”), from Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “ball, globe”), of unknown origin. parole.significato: One who seasons with spice.
parole.testo: From Middle English spicer, spycer, spycere, from Old French espicier (> French épicier), from Latin speciarius (“dealer in spices”), equivalent to spice + -er.

parole.significato: Spices, in general.
parole.testo: From Middle English spicerie, from Old French espicerie; equivalent to spice + -ery.

parole.significato: To breathe.
parole.testo: From Old French spirer, and its source, Latin spīrō (“to breathe”).

parole.significato: The soul of a person or other creature.
parole.testo: From Middle English spirit, from Old French espirit (“spirit”), from Latin spīritus (“breath; spirit”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)peys- (“to blow, breathe”). Compare inspire, respire, transpire, all ultimately from Latin spīrō (“to breathe, blow, respire”). In this sense, displaced native Middle

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the spirit or the soul.
parole.testo: From Middle English spiritual, spirituel, from Old French spirituel, from Late Latin spīrituālis, from Latin spīritus. By surface analysis, spirit + -ual.

parole.significato: The state or fact of being spiritual; holiness, spirituality.
parole.testo: From Old French espirituaulté.

parole.significato: Density, thickness; the state or quality of being inspissated or thickened.
parole.testo: From Middle English spissitude, from Old French spissitude and Latin spissitūdō, from spissus (“thick”).

parole.testo: From Middle English spit, a shortening of despit (whence despite), from Old French despit, from Latin dēspectum (“looking down on”), from Latin dēspiciō (“to look down, despise”). parole.significato: Shining; glossy; lustrous.
parole.testo: From Middle English splendaunt, from Old French splendiant, present participle of esplendiier, and esplendent, and Latin splendēns, splendentis, present participle of splendēre (“to shine”).

parole.significato: To strip (someone who has been killed or defeated) of arms or armour.
parole.testo: From Middle English spoilen, spuylen, borrowed from Old French espoillier, espollier, espuler, from Latin spoliō, spoliāre (“pillage, ruin, spoil”).

parole.significato: espousal
parole.testo: From Old French espousaige, from espouser. See spouse (transitive verb).

parole.significato: Espousal; marriage; nuptials.
parole.testo: From Middle English spousaille, from Old French esposaille, espousaille, espousalle, Anglo-Norman (e)spusaille, esposalie, sposale, spousaille.

parole.significato: A piece of otter dung.
parole.testo: Old French espraintes, espreintes, French épreintes from espreinte (“a desire to go to stool”); cf. épreinte (“a piece of otter dung”).

parole.significato: An ancient military engine for launching stones and arrows by means of a spring.
parole.testo: From Old French espringale; of Germanic origin, akin to English spring.

parole.significato: To draw a (specifically) pixel art sprite.
parole.testo: From Middle English sprite, spryt, spreyte, from Old French esprit (“spirit”), from Latin spīritus. Doublet of spirit, spiritus, spirytus, spright, and esprit. parole.significato: Foam or froth of liquid, particularly that of seawater.
parole.testo: From Middle English spume, from Old French espume, from Latin spūma.

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Euphorbia, a diverse genus of over 2,000 species.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English spurge, from Old French espurge, from espurgier (“to purge”), from Latin expurgo (“to purge”); the bitter milky sap of these plants was formerly used as a purgative.

parole.significato: Any of several European annual herbs of the genus Spergula.
parole.testo: Dutch or Old French spurrie; compare German Spergel, New Latin spergula.

parole.significato: A person who secretly watches and examines the actions of other individuals or organizations and gathers information on…
parole.testo: From Middle English spien, aphetic variant of earlier espien (“to espy”), from Old French espier (“to spy”), from Frankish *spehōn (“to spy”), from Proto-Germanic *spehōną (“to see, look”), from Proto-Indo-European *speḱ- (“to look”). parole.significato: Shaped like a square (the polygon).

parole.significato: A person or animal's natural height when standing upright.
parole.testo: From Middle English stature, from Old French stature, from Latin statūra.

parole.significato: A written law or ordinance passed by a legislative body.
parole.testo: From Middle English statut, from Old French statut, from Late Latin statutum (“a statute”), neuter singular of Latin statutus, past participle of statuō (“to set up, establish”).

parole.significato: An organ in animals that stores food in the process of digestion.

parole.significato: A plug; a stopper.
parole.testo: From Middle English stopple, stoppel, stoppell, from Old French estopail, estopaille. By surface analysis, stop + -le.

parole.significato: To tell as a story; to relate or narrate about.

parole.significato: Straw.

parole.significato: To provide (something), to make (something) available for use.
parole.testo: From Middle English supplien, borrowed from Old French soupleer, souploier, from Latin suppleo (“to fill up, make full, complete, supply”). The Middle English spelling was modified to conform to Latin etymology.

parole.significato: To help keep from falling.
parole.testo: From Middle English supporten, from Old French supporter, from Latin supportō.

parole.testo: From Middle English supposen, borrowed from Old French supposer, equivalent to prefix sub- (“under”) + poser (“to place”); corresponding in meaning to Latin supponere (“to put under, to substitute, falsify, counterfeit”), suppositum. See pose.

parole.significato: A syncopic variant of super-.

parole.significato: A long unpadded strap to pass over and keep in place a blanket, pack or saddle on an animal.
parole.testo: From Old French surcengle, formed with sur (“over”) and cengle (“girdle”).

parole.significato: A loose sleeveless garment worn over a suit of armor, sometimes colored or embroidered with the wearer's coat of arms.
parole.testo: From Middle English surcote, from Old French surcote, formed with sur (“over”) and cote (“coat, robe, tunic, overgarment”), respelled based on coat.

parole.significato: A making sure; surety.
parole.testo: From Middle English surement, from Old French seürement; equivalent to sure + -ment.

parole.significato: Thought, imagination, or conjecture, which may be based upon feeble or scanty evidence; suspicion; guess.
parole.testo: From Old French surmis, past participle of surmetre, surmettre (“to accuse”), from sur- (“upon”) + metre (“to put”).

parole.significato: To get or be over without touching or resting on; to overcome.
parole.testo: From Middle English surmounten, from Old French surmonter (“to rise above, surmount”), from sur- (“above”) + monter (“to mount”), equivalent to sur- + mount.

parole.significato: Overweening pride; arrogance.
parole.testo: From Old French surcuiderie.

parole.significato: To give up into the power, control, or possession of another.
parole.testo: From Middle English surrendren, from Old French surrendre, from sur- + rendre (“render”). Displaced native Old English on hand gān.

parole.significato: The act of surveying; a general view.
parole.testo: From Middle English surveyen, from Old French sourveoir, surveer (“to oversee”), from sour-, sur- (“over”) + veoir, veeir (“to see”), from Latin videre. See sur- and vision. Related to supervision.

parole.significato: To survey; to make a survey of.

parole.significato: To imagine or suppose (something) to be true, or to exist, without proof.
parole.testo: From Old French suspect, from Latin suspectus, perfect passive participle of suspiciō (“mistrust, suspect”), from sub (“under”), + speciō (“watch, look at”).

parole.significato: To halt something temporarily.
parole.testo: From Old French sospendre, from Latin suspendere.

parole.significato: Arousing suspicion.

parole.significato: To maintain, or keep in existence.
parole.testo: From Middle English susteinen, sustenen, from Old French sustenir (French soutenir), from Latin sustineō, sustinēre (“to uphold”), from sub- (“from below, up”) + teneō (“hold”, verb).

parole.significato: Something that provides support or nourishment.

parole.significato: The act or the result of sustaining; sustainment; sustention.
parole.testo: First attested in 1382: from the Old French sustentacion, from the Latin sustentātio, from sustentō; compare the Italian sostentazione, the Occitan sustentacion, the Portuguese sustentação, and the Spanish sustentación. Doublet of sustentatio.

parole.significato: A relation between states in which a subservient nation has its own government, but is unable to take international act…
parole.testo: From Middle English suserente, from Old French suserenete, equivalent to suzerain + -ty.

parole.significato: Any of several North American plane trees, of the genus Platanus, especially Platanus occidentalis (American sycamore),…
parole.testo: Circa 1350 as Middle English sicamour, from Old French sicamor, from Latin sȳcomorus, from Ancient Greek σῡκόμορος (sūkómoros, literally “fig-mulberry”), from σῦκον (sûkon, “fig”) + μόρον (móron, “mulberry”). Possibly influenced by Hebrew שִׁקְמָה (shikmá, “fig-mulberry”). In the 16th c. applied to

parole.significato: A syllable.
parole.testo: From Old French sillabe (“syllable”).

parole.significato: An argument whose conclusion is supported by two premises, of which one contains the term that is the predicate of the…
parole.testo: From Old French silogisme (“syllogism”), from Latin syllogismus, from Ancient Greek συλλογισμός (sullogismós, “inference, conclusion”). Doublet of syllogismus.

parole.significato: An extended piece of music of sophisticated structure, usually for orchestra.
parole.testo: From Middle English symphonye, from Old French simphonie, from Latin symphonia, from Ancient Greek συμφωνία (sumphōnía). By surface analysis, sym- + -phony. Doublet of sinfonia, symphonia, tsampouna, and zampogna.

parole.significato: A place of worship for Jews.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English synagoge, from Old French synagoge, from Latin synagōga, from Ancient Greek σῠνᾰγωγή (sŭnăgōgḗ, “assembly, gathering”), from συνάγω (sunágō, “to gather together”), from σῠ́ν (sŭ́n, “with, together”) & ᾰ̓́γω (ắgō, “to lead”). By surface analysis, syn- + -agogue.

parole.significato: Any thick liquid that has a high sugar content and which is added to or poured over food as a flavoring.
parole.testo: From Middle English sirup, from Old French sirop, from Medieval Latin siruppus, syrupus, from Arabic شَرَاب (šarāb, “a drink, beverage, wine, coffee, syrup”), from شَرِبَ (šariba, “to drink”). Doublet of sirop. Related to sorbet, sherbet, sharbat. Compare French sirop, Italian siroppo, sciroppo, Spa

parole.significato: A silk banner attached to a bugle or trumpet.
parole.testo: From Old French tabart (“simple sleeveless overtunic; heavy overmantel”), of unknown origin.

parole.significato: Any temporary dwelling; a hut, tent, or booth.
parole.testo: From Middle English tabernacle (14th century), from Old French tabernacle, from Latin tabernāculum (“tent, booth, shed”), the diminutive of taberna (“hut, shed”). By surface analysis, taberna + -cle.

parole.significato: A small drum.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French tabour, from Arabic طُنْبُور (ṭunbūr), ultimately from the Middle Persian ancestor of Classical Persian تنبور (tanbūr). Doublet of tambour and tanbur.

parole.significato: A little drum; a tabret.
parole.testo: From Old French tabouret (“a stool, pincushion, base of a pillar; literally, a little drum or tabor”), diminutive of tabour (“drum”). Compare French tambour.

parole.significato: A small, shallow drum; a tabor.
parole.testo: Old French tabourin, French tambourin. See tabor, and compare tambourine.

parole.significato: A crisp, smooth woven fabric made from silk or synthetic fibers.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English, from Old French taffetas, from Medieval Latin taffata, from Classical Persian تافته (tāfta), from تافتن (tāftan).

parole.significato: A thrust with a lance, which fails of its intended effect.
parole.testo: From Middle English taynt, aphetic form of attaynt, atteynt, from Old French atteinte (“a blow, stroke”). Compare with attaint.

parole.significato: A sharp, hooked claw of a bird of prey or other predatory animal.
parole.testo: From Middle English talon, taloun, from Old French talon (“heel, spur”), from Medieval Latin tālōnem, from Proto-Romance *tālōnis, from Latin tālus (“ankle”).

parole.significato: A tropical tree, Tamarindus indica.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English thamarynde, from Old French tamarinde, from Medieval Latin tamarindus, from Arabic تَمْر هِنْدِيّ (tamr hindiyy, literally “Indian date”).

parole.significato: A light, brown-like colour.
parole.testo: From Middle English tan, from Old French tan (“tanbark”), from Gaulish *tannos (“green oak”) – compare Breton tann (“red oak”), Old Cornish tannen –, from Proto-Celtic *tannos (“green oak”), of uncertain origin, but perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *(s)dʰonu (“fir”). parole.significato: A person whose occupation is to tan hides, or convert them into leather by the use of tan.
parole.testo: From Middle English tannere, from Old English tannere; and Old French tannour, equivalent to tan + -er.

parole.significato: A herbaceous plant with yellow flowers, of the genus Tanacetum, especially Tanacetum vulgare.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English tansy, tansey, syncopic forms of earlier tanesie, tanesei, from Old French tanesie, tanoisie, tanasie, tanaisie, from Medieval Latin tanacetum, atanacetum, attested since the 8th century, of obscure origin, speculated from Ancient Greek ἀθανασία (athanasía, “immortality

parole.significato: A heavy woven cloth, often with decorative pictorial designs, normally hung on walls.
parole.testo: From Middle English tapestrie, from Old French tapisserie (“tapestry”), from Ancient Greek τάπης (tápēs), from an Iranian source.

parole.significato: A tapestry-maker.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English tapiser, tapicer, from Old French tapissier, from tapis (“tapestry”) + -ier (“-er”).

parole.significato: Slowness; tardiness.
parole.testo: From Middle English tardite, tarditee, from Old French tardeté and/or Latin tarditās, equivalent to tard(y) + -ity.

parole.significato: Oxidation or discoloration, especially of a decorative metal exposed to air.
parole.testo: From Middle English ternysshen, from Old French terniss-, stem of ternir (“to make dim, make wan”), borrowed from Old High German *ternen, tarnen, from Proto-West Germanic *darnijan (“to conceal”). Doublet of dern and darn.

parole.significato: A type of small open pie, or piece of pastry, now typically containing jelly (US) / jam (UK) or conserve, or sometimes…
parole.testo: From Middle English tart, tarte, from Old French tarte, tartre (“flat pastry”) (compare Medieval Latin tarta), of unknown origin. Perhaps an alteration of Old French torte, tourte, from Latin turta, perhaps from tŏrta f (“twisted”), in which case it would be cognate to torta.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the people or culture of Tartars.
parole.testo: From Old French Tartaire, from Medieval Latin Tartarus (“Tartar, Mongol”), from Old Turkic 𐱃𐱃𐰺 (t¹t¹r¹), spelling influenced by Latin Tartarus (“Hell (in Greek mythology)”), from Ancient Greek Τάρταρος (Tártaros). Doublet of Tatar and tartare.

parole.significato: A red compound deposited during wine making, mostly potassium hydrogen tartrate; wine stone — a source of cream of tart…
parole.testo: From Old French tartre, from Medieval Latin tartarum, from Byzantine Greek τάρταρον (tártaron), said to be from Arabic دُرْدِيّ (durdiyy), though it is already found in Pelagonius’s Ars veterinaria 46 in the adjective tartarālis, if the reading is correct. Arabic etymon from Persian درد (dord, “dreg

parole.significato: A type of fine woolen or silk fabric, probably imported, mentioned from the 14th to the 16th centuries.
parole.testo: From Middle English tartarin, tartaryn, from Old French/Middle French tartarin (“Tartar, Tartarian”); see Tartar for more.

parole.significato: A small tart (pastry).
parole.testo: From Middle English tartelet, from Old French tartelette; equivalent to tart + -let.

parole.significato: tartar
parole.testo: From Old French tartre, from Medieval Latin tartarum, from Byzantine Greek τάρταρον (tártaron).

parole.significato: A heap, pile.
parole.testo: Partly from Middle English tas (“heap”), from Old French tas (“heap”), from Frankish *tas (“mass, pile”); and partly from Middle English taas (“heap, mow of corn”), from Old English tas (“heap, mow of grain”); both from Proto-Germanic *tasaz, *tassaz (“heap, mow, stack”), from Proto-Indo-European *d

parole.significato: A cup or cupful.
parole.testo: From Middle English *tasse, from Old French tasse (Modern French tasse (“cup, cupful”)). Cognate with Dutch tas (“cup”), German Tasse (“mug”). Doublet of tazza.

parole.significato: Synonym of tasse.
parole.testo: From Middle English tasse, tache, from Old French tasse, tasche (“purse; pouch”), from Frankish *taskā (“pouch”), from Proto-Germanic *taskǭ, cognate with Old High German tasca (“pouch”), German Tasche (“pocket; pouch”).

parole.significato: A piece of armor for the hips and thighs: one of a set of plates (each being of one piece or segmented) hanging from th…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English tasse (“armor plate protecting the hip”), derived from Old French tasse, tasche (“purse; pouch”), derived from Frankish *taskā (“pouch”), derived from Proto-Germanic *taskǭ. parole.significato: A ball-shaped bunch of plaited or otherwise entangled threads from which at one end protrudes a cord on which the ball…
parole.testo: From Middle English tassel, from Old French tassel, from Latin tāxillus (“small cube”), from tālus (“ankle”).

parole.significato: One of the sensations produced by the tongue in response to certain chemicals; the quality of giving this sensation.

parole.significato: Very high or tall.
parole.testo: Compare Old French tant (“so great”), French tant (“so much”), Latin tantus (“of such size, so great, so much”). See ataunt.

parole.significato: A restaurant or bar.
parole.testo: From Middle English taverne, from Old French taverne (“wine shop”), from Latin taberna (“inn”). Doublet of taberna and taverna.

parole.significato: Someone who owns or runs a tavern.
parole.testo: From Old French tavernier.

parole.significato: The projection of a mammary gland from which, on female therian mammals, milk is secreted.
parole.testo: From Middle English tete, from Old French tete (“teat”) (compare French tette), from Frankish *tittā, *tittō, from Proto-Germanic *tittaz (“teat; nipple; breast”), ultimately of expressive origin. Compare Old High German zizza ("teat"; modern German Zitze), whence also Italian zizza (“teat”). It hea

parole.significato: Boring, monotonous, time-consuming, wearisome, livelong.
parole.testo: English tedi(um) + -ous, from Old French tedieus, from Late Latin taediōsus, from Latin taedium (“weariness, tedium”).

parole.significato: The lime tree, or linden.
parole.testo: From Old French teil, til, from Latin tilia.

parole.significato: A road pavement having a surface of small stone rolled hard and smooth, distinguished from macadam road by its firm fou…
parole.testo: From Old French taille fer, meaning "(he who) cuts iron" or "iron-cleaver"; used as a nickname for a man who could cleave clean through the armour of his foe. The second syllable was eventually reanalysed as native English 'ford'. * (road): Named after Thomas Telford, a famous civil engineer.

parole.significato: Reckless boldness; foolish bravery.
parole.testo: From Middle English temerite, temeryte, from Old French temerité, from Latin temeritās (“chance, accident, rashness”), from temere (“by chance, casually, rashly”). By surface analysis, temer(arious) + -ity.

parole.significato: A storm, especially one with severe winds.
parole.testo: From Old French tempeste (French tempête), from Latin tempestas (“storm”), from tempus (“time, weather”). Displaced native Old English hrīþ.

parole.significato: A Knight Templar, one of the Knights Templar.
parole.testo: From Middle English templer, from Old French templier; cf. the Medieval Latin templarius, from Latin templum (“temple”).

parole.significato: A barrister having chambers in the Inner Temple or Middle Temple.
parole.testo: From Middle English templer, from Old French templier; cf. the Medieval Latin templārius, from Latin templum (“temple”).

parole.significato: The slightly flatter region, on either side of the head of a vertebrate, including a human, behind the eye and forehead…
parole.testo: From Middle English temple, from Old French temple, from Vulgar Latin *temp(u)la, from Latin tempora (“the temples”), plural of tempus (“temple, head, face”). See temporal bone.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the material world, as opposed to sacred or clerical.
parole.testo: From Middle English temporal, temporel (“transitory, worldly, material, of secular society”), from Old French temporel or Latin temporālis (“of time (in grammar), temporary, relating to time as opposed to eternity”), from tempus (“time, period, opportunity”) + -ālis.

parole.significato: To provoke someone to do wrong, especially by promising a reward; to entice.
parole.testo: From Middle English tempten, from Old French tempter (French: tenter), from Latin temptare, from tentare (“to handle, touch, try, test, tempt”), frequentative of tendere (“to stretch”). Displaced native English costning (“temptation”).

parole.significato: Capable of being tempted; liable to be tempted.
parole.testo: From Middle English temptable, probably from Old French temptable, variant of tentable; compare Latin tentābilis; equivalent to tempt + -able.

parole.significato: The act of tempting.
parole.testo: From Old French temptacion, from Latin temptatio. Morphologically tempt + -ation.

parole.significato: Someone or something that tempts, especially a man that tempts.
parole.testo: From Middle English tempter, temptere, temptour, temptoure, from Old French tempter, temptere, tenteor, Anglo-Norman tempteour, temptur and Middle English tempten (“to tempt”); equivalent to tempt + -er.

parole.significato: A species of freshwater game fish, Tinca tinca.
parole.testo: From Middle English tenche, from Old French tenche, from Late Latin tinca.

parole.significato: Anything which is offered, proffered, put forth or bid with the expectation of a response, answer, or reply.
parole.testo: From Middle English tendren, from Old French tendre (“stretch out”).

parole.significato: Dark, tenebrous.
parole.testo: From Middle English tenebrose, from Old French tenebros, from Latin tenebrōsus (“dark, gloomy”).

parole.significato: The state or quality of being tenebrose or tenebrous.
parole.testo: From Middle English tenebrosite, from Old French tenebrosité, ultimately from Latin tenebrae (“darkness”). Compare Medieval Latin tenebrōsitas, French ténébrosité. By surface analysis, tenebrose + -ity.

parole.significato: A sport played by two players (or four in doubles), who alternately strike the ball over a net using racquets.
parole.testo: From Middle English tennys, teneys, tenis, from Old French tenez (second-person plural imperative of tenir (“to hold”)).

parole.significato: The property of indicating the point in time at which an action or state of being occurs or exists.
parole.testo: From Middle English tens, from Old French tens (modern French temps), from Latin tempus. Doublet of tempo and tempus.

parole.significato: A pavilion or portable lodge consisting of skins, canvas, or some strong cloth, stretched and sustained by poles, used…
parole.testo: From Middle English tente, borrowed from Old French tente, from Vulgar Latin *tenta (“tent”), from the feminine of Latin tentus, ptp. of tendere (“to stretch, extend”), or contracted from *tendita as an alternate past participle. parole.significato: To attend to; to heed.
parole.testo: From Middle English tent (“attention”), aphetic variation of attent (“attention”), from Old French atente (“attention, intention”), from Latin attenta, feminine of attentus, past participle of attendere (“to attend”). Compare tend, from an aphetic variation of attend

parole.significato: A framework upon which cloth is stretched and dried.
parole.testo: Via Old French, perhaps from Latin tentorium.

parole.significato: The third hour of daylight (about 9 am).
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Old French terce, from Latin tertia (“third; the third hour”).

parole.significato: A male falcon, especially a peregrine falcon or goshawk; a tiercel.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English tercelet, from Old French tercelet; equivalent to tiercel + -et.

parole.significato: A Mediterranean tree (Pistacia terebinthus and, possibly, Pistacia palaestina)
parole.testo: From Middle English therebynte, from Old French terebinthe, from Latin terebinthus, from Ancient Greek τερέβινθος (terébinthos), from Pre-Greek. Related to turpentine and terpene.

parole.significato: That which limits the extent of anything; limit, extremity, bound, boundary, terminus.
parole.testo: From Middle English terme, borrowed from Old French terme, from Latin terminus (“a bound, boundary, limit, end; in Medieval Latin, also a time, period, word, covenant, etc.”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *térmn̥ (“stump, end, boundary”). Doublet of terminus and termon. Old English had termen

parole.significato: Dreadful; causing terror, alarm and fear; awesome
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English terrible, from Old French terrible, from Latin terribilis (“frightful”), from terreō (“to frighten, terrify, alarm; to deter by terror, scare (away)”). parole.significato: A challenge, trial.
parole.testo: From Middle English test, teste, from Old French test, teste (“an earthen vessel, especially a pot in which metals were tried”), from Latin testum (“the lid of an earthen vessel, an earthen vessel, an earthen pot”), from *terstus, past participle of the root *tersa (“dry land”). parole.significato: A witness.
parole.testo: From Middle English teste, from Old French teste, test and Latin testis (“one who attests, a witness”).

parole.significato: A solemn, authentic instrument in writing, by which a person declares his or her will as to disposal of his or her inhe…
parole.testo: From Middle English testament, from Old French testament, from Latin testāmentum (“the publication of a will, a will, testament, in Late Latin one of the divisions of the Bible”), from testor (“to be a witness, testify, attest, make a will”), from testis (“one who attests, a witness”).
